p: Exam Strategy, Master Tables and Revision Plan · Commercial Law
x: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball: general offer, acceptance by performance. Lalman Shukla v Gauri Dutt: knowledge of the offer is needed. Bhagwandas Kedia: instantaneous communication; contract formed where acceptance is received. Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose: a minor’s agreement is void ab initio. Chinnaya v Ramayya: a stranger to consideration may sue. M.C. Chacko v SBT: a beneficiary may enforce in trust-like arrangements. Gherulal Parakh: wagering agreements are void, not illegal. Central Inland Water Transport v Brojo Nath: unconscionable terms are void. Satyabrata Ghose: s.56 is wider than the English frustration doctrine. Energy Watchdog v CERC: force majeure is distinct from s.56. Fateh Chand; Kailash Nath: s.74 reasonable compensation. Hadley v Baxendale: remoteness of damages. State of West Bengal v B.K. Mondal: s.70 quasi-contract. Mafatlal Industries: unjust enrichment in refund claims. Bank of Bihar v Damodar Prasad: the surety’s liability is immediate and co-extensive. Rowland v Divall: breach of the implied condition of title gives a full refund. Cox v Hickman: mutual agency is the test of partnership. Salomon v Salomon: corporate personality. Royal British Bank v Turquand: indoor management. Foss v Harbottle: majority rule and the proper plaintiff. Rangappa v Sri Mohan; Bir Singh v Mukesh Kumar: presumption under s.139. Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod: jurisdiction under s.138 (superseded by the 2015 amendment). Tata Consultancy Services v Cyrus Investments: oppression and the removal of the chairman.

p: Exam Strategy, Master Tables and Revision Plan · Commercial Law
x: Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018: specific performance is no longer discretionary; substituted performance; infrastructure courts. NI (Amendment) Acts 2015 and 2018: jurisdiction (s.142(2)) and interim compensation (ss.143A, 148). Companies (Amendment) Acts 2015, 2017, 2019, 2020: removal of minimum capital; commencement-of-business declaration (s.10A, 2019); charge-registration timelines; unspent CSR; decriminalisation of many offences; and the small-company thresholds. Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023: rationalised penalties and decriminalised minor offences in many Acts (the extent of change varies from Act to Act, so check the schedule). LLP (Amendment) Act, 2021: small LLPs, lower penalties and compounding. New criminal codes and evidence law: from 1 July 2024 , the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 , Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act. References to the IPC in s.15 of the Contract Act are read with the BNS, and s.138 NI Act procedure now follows the BNSS. CSR Rules, 2021: mandatory registration of implementing agencies, the Unspent CSR Account, impact assessment, and the Rs. 50 lakh exemption from forming a CSR Committee.

p: Exam Strategy, Master Tables and Revision Plan · Commercial Law
x: Statement-based: underline absolute words (‘only’, ‘always’, ‘never’, ‘must’). Many wrong statements swap a number (30 and 15 days; 20% and 25%) or a section (s.73 and s.74). Match the following: learn section-to-topic pairs in tables (s.124–147 indemnity and guarantee; s.148–181 bailment; s.172–179 pledge; s.182–238 agency). Assertion–Reason: decide separately whether A and R are true, and whether R explains A. Doctrines (frustration, Turquand, veil lifting) often yield ‘both true but R does not explain A’. Sequence questions: for incorporation, the order is: name approval, then DIN and DSC, then MoA and AoA, then filing under s.7, then the certificate, then the registered office within 30 days, then INC-20A within 180 days. For s.138 the order is: dishonour, then notice (30 days), then 15 days to pay, then complaint (1 month). Negative questions: be ready with the exception lists (s.19 Partnership Act implied-authority exceptions; s.25 exceptions; s.27 goodwill exception; s.30 minors; s.230 agent’s personal liability).

p: Exam Strategy, Master Tables and Revision Plan · Commercial Law
x: Week 1: Contract Act, Topics 1 – 3 (build the vocabulary, then cases). Week 2: Specific contracts and SOGA. Week 3: Partnership, LLP and NI Act. Week 4: Company law (twice, since it carries the heaviest weight). Final week: CSR, the numbers sheet, case list and amendments; then solve previous years’ UGC NET Law papers topic by topic and note recurring sections and numbers. Caution: statutes, thresholds and notifications (especially under the Companies Act, LLP Act and CSR Rules) are amended often. I compiled these notes from memory, without checking the bare Acts, so verify figures such as small-company thresholds, LLP audit limits, AGM and meeting time limits, and every section number against the latest bare Act and MCA notifications before relying on them in the exam.

Concept-based: define or identify a concept (e.g., formal vs substantive rule of law; dual vs cooperative federalism). Match-the-following / assertion-reason: matching scholars with ideas, cases with principles, countries with institutions. Analysis-based: statements marked true or false, "which of the following is correct", chronological ordering of events, and odd-one-out.

t: 1.1 Meaning and Nature of Comparative Law
p: Comparative Law: Relevance, Methodology, Problems and Concerns in Comparison · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Comparative law is the study of the similarities and differences between the legal systems, rules, institutions and doctrines of two or more jurisdictions, with a view to understanding, evaluating, improving or harmonising them. It is both a method (a way of studying law) and, according to some, a science (a body of knowledge with its own subject matter). This "method versus science" debate is itself a recurring theoretical point. Key points on the nature of the discipline: Comparative law is not a branch of law in the sense of containing rules that bind anyone. It does not create rights and duties. It is an intellectual activity whose results are used by legislators, judges, scholars and international bodies. It is different from foreign law . Foreign law is the study of one other country's law. Comparative law necessarily involves comparing at least two systems and drawing out similarities and differences. It is different from private international law (conflict of laws) , which decides which country's law applies to a cross-border dispute. Comparative law decides nothing; it only compares. It is different from public international law , which governs relations between states. Comparative public law (the focus of this unit) compares constitutions, governmental structures, federalism, separation of powers, judicial review, administrative accountability and similar subjects. A major part of it is comparative constitutional law .

p: Comparative Law: Relevance, Methodology, Problems and Concerns in Comparison · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Early seeds: Aristotle collected and compared the constitutions of 158 Greek city-states (the "Politics" draws on it). Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) compared laws in relation to climate, geography and culture and is considered a foundation of the comparative approach. Sir Henry Maine ( Ancient Law , 1861) used a historical-comparative method for studying legal institutions (status to contract). 1869: Société de Législation Comparée founded in Paris. 1900: The First International Congress of Comparative Law, Paris , organised by Édouard Lambert and Raymond Saleilles . Comparative law is said to have become a modern discipline here. Saleilles and Lambert are also associated with the idea of a "common law of mankind" ( droit commun de l'humanité ). Édouard Lambert (France) – ambition of a world common law; headed the Lyon Institute of Comparative Law. Ernst Rabel (Germany) – developed the functional method in comparative private law. Zweigert and Kötz – An Introduction to Comparative Law – the most cited text; developed the functional method and the "legal families" (style) theory; the praesumptio similitudinis (presumption of similarity). René David – classification into legal families (Romano-Germanic, Common Law, Socialist, and others). Gutteridge ( Comparative Law , 1946) – English scholar who described comparative law as a method and used it to argue for law reform. Alan Watson – Legal Transplants (1974) – laws migrate across borders easily. Otto Kahn-Freund – "On Uses and Misuses of Comparative Law" (1974) – the transplant of a rule is difficult if the political and social context differs; coined the idea of "degrees of transferability". Pierre Legrand – argued that legal transplants are impossible in a true sense because law is embedded in culture and meaning; the rule changes meaning when it moves. Rodolfo Sacco – theory of legal formants (statutes, judicial decisions, scholarly writings are separate sources which can conflict within one legal system). Lawrence Friedman – "legal culture" – internal and external legal culture.

p: Comparative Law: Relevance, Methodology, Problems and Concerns in Comparison · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Legislative reform: Legislatures look at foreign models while drafting. The Indian Constituent Assembly borrowed heavily: parliamentary system from the UK; fundamental rights, judicial review and Preamble from the USA; Directive Principles from Ireland; federal scheme with a strong Centre and residuary powers from Canada; Concurrent List from Australia; emergency provisions from Germany (Weimar); amending procedure from South Africa; Rule of Law and law-making procedure from the UK; "procedure established by law" from Japan. Judicial interpretation: Courts cite foreign precedents as persuasive authority. The Indian Supreme Court has regularly referred to American, English, Canadian and South African decisions (e.g., on privacy, dignity, proportionality, sexual orientation). Unification and harmonisation: Organisations such as UNIDROIT, UNCITRAL and the Hague Conference work on harmonising private and commercial law. The EU's attempt to build a common European private law is a famous example. International law: Article 38(1)(c) of the ICJ Statute lists "general principles of law recognised by civilised nations" as a source of international law. Identifying such principles requires comparing national laws. Legal education and academic understanding: Understanding one's own system better through contrast. Constitution making and transitions: South Africa, Eastern Europe and post-colonial states used comparative models while drafting new constitutions. Conflict of laws and international commerce: helps lawyers handle cross-border transactions. Combating parochialism: reveals that a rule thought universal is merely local.

p: Comparative Law: Relevance, Methodology, Problems and Concerns in Comparison · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Macro-comparison: compares whole legal systems, their style, sources, methods, and legal families. Micro-comparison: compares specific institutions or rules (e.g., rules on judicial review in two countries). Horizontal comparison: compares systems of equal standing (e.g., India with the USA). Vertical comparison: compares different levels of the same hierarchy (e.g., national law vs state or provincial law; national vs international law). Descriptive comparative law: records similarities and differences without evaluation. Applied comparative law: uses comparison to solve a problem or reform law. Theoretical/Evaluative comparative law: explores the reasons behind similarities and differences and seeks a general theory.

p: Comparative Law: Relevance, Methodology, Problems and Concerns in Comparison · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: (a) Functional Method (dominant approach) Basic principle: "The legal system of every society faces essentially the same problems, and solves these problems by quite different means though very often with similar results." (Zweigert and Kötz) Law is compared by asking: What problem does this rule solve? Rules that solve the same problem are comparable even if their form differs. The common standard is tertium comparationis (a third, neutral element or common denominator used for comparison, here the function or problem). Linked idea: praesumptio similitudinis – the presumption that different legal systems reach practically similar results for the same factual problem. If the result differs, the comparatist must re-check whether the analysis was correct. Chief proponents: Ernst Rabel, Zweigert and Kötz. Criticisms: assumes universal problems and ignores culture, politics, ideology and meaning; "law in books" may be compared more than "law in action". (b) Analytical Method Breaks down legal concepts and structures into elements (rights, duties, powers, status) for logical comparison. Linked to Bentham and Austin's analytical jurisprudence. (c) Structural Method Compares the structure of institutions and norms (e.g., court hierarchy, legislative design). Often used in comparative constitutional law, such as comparing bicameral structures. (d) Historical Method Studies legal systems as products of history. Associated with Maine and Savigny's historical school. Useful for understanding why India follows common-law traditions despite its diversity. (e) Law-in-Context (Socio-legal) Method Studies law along with social, economic, political and cultural conditions. Associated with Kahn-Freund and Legrand's culturalist approach. Compares "law in action". (f) Critical/Culturalist Method Includes critical legal studies, feminist and post-colonial approaches. It questions the neutrality of comparison and its Western bias. (g) Comparison by Legal Families Romano-Germanic (Civil law): codified; France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Latin America, Switzerland (mixed features). Common law: judge-made law and precedent ( stare decisis ); England, USA, India, Canada (except Quebec), Australia. Socialist law: historically in USSR and Eastern Bloc; now largely declined, remains in some forms (China, Cuba, Vietnam). Religious and traditional law: Islamic law, Hindu law, Jewish law. Customary/Far Eastern law: Japan, China, Korea blends. Mixed systems: South Africa (Roman-Dutch and common law), Scotland, Louisiana, Quebec, Israel, Sri Lanka. Zweigert and Kötz classify by "legal style" using factors: historical development, characteristic mode of thought, distinctive institutions, legal sources and ideology.

p: Comparative Law: Relevance, Methodology, Problems and Concerns in Comparison · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Language: legal terms are untranslatable (e.g., "equity", "trust", "consideration", " Rechtsstaat ", " état de droit "). Mistranslation gives a false match. Context and culture: a rule works because of its society; stripping it of context produces misleading results. Choice of comparable units: comparing a unitary and a federal system or a codified and uncodified constitution requires care to avoid mismatching functions. Ethnocentrism/bias: comparatist sees foreign systems through own categories; Western-centric classification of legal families ignores African and Asian systems. Law in books vs law in action: formal texts can differ from actual practice (e.g., a constitution declares separation of powers but practice differs). Availability and reliability of sources: translations, outdated sources, lack of case law. Legal transplants: transplanted rules may be rejected ( legal irritants – Gunther Teubner) or may be transformed. Teubner argued that transplants act as irritants that trigger new evolution in the host system rather than harmonising it. Superficial comparison: comparing without deep knowledge, or "cherry-picking" foreign decisions to justify a preferred result (a concern in judicial use of foreign law). Time: laws change quickly; the comparative picture becomes outdated. Ideological presumption: assuming that all legal systems must converge ("convergence thesis") can ignore deep differences.

x: Functional method = Zweigert and Kötz, Ernst Rabel; tertium comparationis ; praesumptio similitudinis . 1900 Paris Congress = Lambert and Saleilles. Legal transplants = Alan Watson (supporter); Legrand (sceptic); Kahn-Freund (cautious); Teubner (legal irritants). Legal formants = Rodolfo Sacco . Comparative law is not a source of binding law; it is a method. Trap: Comparative law ≠ private international law ≠ foreign law.

p: Forms of Government: Presidential and Parliamentary; Unitary and Federal · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Forms of government can be classified on two main axes: Relationship between the legislature and the executive: parliamentary, presidential, semi-presidential (hybrid) and directorial/collegial. Distribution of power between the centre and units: unitary, federal, and quasi-federal or confederal. Older classification: Aristotle classified by number of rulers and their purpose (monarchy, aristocracy, polity; and degenerate forms – tyranny, oligarchy, democracy). Modern comparative law uses the functional classification above.

p: Forms of Government: Presidential and Parliamentary; Unitary and Federal · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Meaning: The executive (Cabinet/Council of Ministers) is drawn from the legislature, is collectively responsible to it, and remains in office as long as it enjoys the confidence of the lower house. Key features: Dual executive: a nominal head (Monarch/President) and a real executive (Prime Minister and Cabinet). Fusion of powers: ministers are members of the legislature. Collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers; individual responsibility of each minister. Executive can be removed by a vote of no confidence ; the executive can advise dissolution of the lower house. Prime Minister is leader of the majority party or coalition. Party discipline and the concept of an Opposition (in the UK, "His Majesty's Loyal Opposition" with a shadow cabinet). Flexible and responsive but may produce instability in coalitions. Thinkers: Walter Bagehot , The English Constitution (1867) – distinguished the dignified and efficient parts of the constitution; described the Cabinet as "a hyphen which joins, a buckle which fastens" the legislative to the executive. A.V. Dicey – parliamentary sovereignty and conventions. Ivor Jennings – Cabinet Government , The Law and the Constitution . Examples: United Kingdom (the model – Westminster model), India, Canada, Australia, Japan, Germany (chancellor system), Italy.

p: Forms of Government: Presidential and Parliamentary; Unitary and Federal · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Meaning: The executive power is vested in a President who is both head of state and head of government, elected independently of the legislature for a fixed term, and not responsible to the legislature for his tenure (removal only by impeachment). Key features: Single executive – President. Strict separation of powers and checks and balances. Fixed tenure; the President cannot dissolve the legislature, and the legislature cannot remove him by a no-confidence vote. Cabinet members are not members of the legislature ; they are secretaries/advisors appointed by the President (in the USA, with Senate confirmation). Stable executive but risk of deadlock/divided government (Juan Linz argued that presidential systems are more prone to democratic breakdown). Examples: USA (the model), Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Indonesia, Philippines, Nigeria. U.S. specifics: Article II vests executive power in the President. The President is elected indirectly by the Electoral College . Removal by impeachment (House impeaches; Senate tries; two-thirds majority to convict). The 22nd Amendment limits the President to two terms. Veto power with congressional override by two-thirds.

p: Forms of Government: Presidential and Parliamentary; Unitary and Federal · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Feature Parliamentary Presidential Executive Dual (nominal + real) Single Relationship with legislature Fusion; responsible to legislature Separation; independent Tenure Depends on confidence Fixed Dissolution Possible Not possible Ministers Members of legislature Not members Removal No-confidence vote Impeachment Stability Can be unstable More stable but may deadlock Accountability Collective, continuous (question hour) Limited, periodic Examples UK, India USA, Brazil

p: Forms of Government: Presidential and Parliamentary; Unitary and Federal · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Semi-presidential system: A directly elected President with real powers coexists with a Prime Minister and Cabinet responsible to the legislature. Maurice Duverger coined the term. France under the Fifth Republic (1958) is the standard example. Cohabitation occurs when the President and the Prime Minister come from rival political camps (France: 1986–88, 1993–95, 1997–2002). Switzerland (directorial/collegial executive): The Federal Council of seven members is elected by the Federal Assembly for a fixed four-year term and cannot be dismissed by it. The presidency rotates annually among the seven members (first among equals). It is neither purely parliamentary nor presidential. Parliamentary monarchy vs parliamentary republic: UK (monarchy) and Germany/India (republic).

p: Forms of Government: Presidential and Parliamentary; Unitary and Federal · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Meaning: Sovereignty is concentrated in a central government; sub-units (local bodies, provinces) exist only by the will of the centre and can be created, altered or abolished by it. Features: Single legislature with supreme power; no constitutional division of powers. Single citizenship, and uniform laws and courts. Local bodies exercise delegated powers. Can be flexible, efficient and cost-effective; suitable for small, homogeneous states. Devolution (UK: Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland) does not make the UK federal because Parliament remains sovereign and can legally repeal devolution statutes. The UK is commonly described as a unitary state with devolution . Examples: UK, France (although decentralised since the 1982 reforms), Japan, Italy, China (unitary by constitution), Sri Lanka.

p: Forms of Government: Presidential and Parliamentary; Unitary and Federal · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Meaning: Powers are constitutionally divided between a national government and regional units (states, provinces, cantons), each being supreme within its own sphere. Essential features (K.C. Wheare's Federal Government , 1946): A written constitution (generally rigid) – supremacy of the Constitution. Division of powers between centre and units. An independent judiciary to interpret the Constitution and settle disputes (guardian of federalism). Rigid amendment procedure (units usually participate in amendment). Dual government with each level acting directly on the citizen. Usually a bicameral legislature with the second chamber representing the units (Senate, Council of States, Ständerat). K.C. Wheare's definition: the federal principle is the method of dividing powers so that the general and regional governments are each, within a sphere, co-ordinate and independent. He called the Indian Constitution quasi-federal (federal in form but unitary in spirit). Other characterisations of India: Ivor Jennings – "a federation with a strong centralising tendency". Morris-Jones – "bargaining federalism". Granville Austin – "cooperative federalism". Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai v Union of India (1994) – federalism is part of the basic structure; the Constitution is federal in structure with a unitary bias. Classification: Coming-together federations (independent states unite): USA, Switzerland, Australia – units are strong; residuary powers with units. Holding-together federations (a unitary state decentralises to preserve unity): India, Belgium – centre is stronger; residuary powers with the centre. (This terminology is associated with Alfred Stepan .) Confederation: a loose alliance of sovereign states where units retain sovereignty (e.g., the USA under the Articles of Confederation, 1781–89; Switzerland before 1848; the EU is often described as sui generis, with confederal features).

p: Forms of Government: Presidential and Parliamentary; Unitary and Federal · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Feature Unitary Federal Sovereignty Concentrated in centre Divided (co-ordinate) Constitution May be written or unwritten, flexible Written, supreme, usually rigid Division of powers None (delegation only) Constitutional Judiciary Usually single system Guardian of the federal balance Citizenship Single Single (India) or dual (USA) Examples UK, France, Japan USA, Canada, Switzerland, India (quasi)

p: Forms of Government: Presidential and Parliamentary; Unitary and Federal · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Bagehot → "The English Constitution"; dignified and efficient parts. Dicey → rule of law and parliamentary sovereignty. K.C. Wheare → quasi-federal India. UK is unitary despite devolution; France is unitary but semi-presidential. Switzerland : collegial executive (not parliamentary, not presidential). Presidential system → Linz (dangers); semi-presidential → Duverger . India has single citizenship unlike the USA (dual citizenship – national and state). India's integrated judiciary vs the USA's dual court system (federal and state).

p: Models of Federalism: USA, Canada and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Origins and Structure The Constitution of 1787 (in force 1789) replaced the weak Articles of Confederation . It is the oldest written federal Constitution – the classical dual federalism model, a "coming-together" federation. Enumerated powers of Congress are listed in Article I, Section 8; residuary powers belong to the States (Tenth Amendment: powers not delegated to the United States nor prohibited to the States are reserved to the States or the people). Supremacy Clause (Article VI): the Constitution, federal laws and treaties are the supreme law of the land; state judges are bound. Equal representation of states in the Senate (two each), regardless of population; no state can be deprived of equal Senate suffrage without its consent (Article V). Amendment procedure (Article V): proposal by two-thirds of both Houses (or a convention called by two-thirds of the state legislatures), and ratification by three-fourths of the states. Dual court system: federal courts and state courts operate side by side; the Supreme Court is the final interpreter of the Constitution. Dual citizenship: citizen of the USA and of the State of residence (Fourteenth Amendment). Each State has its own Constitution. Phases of American Federalism (Highly Testable) Dual federalism ("layer-cake" – associated with Edward Corwin): till about the 1930s; strict separation of national and state spheres. Cooperative federalism ("marble-cake" – Morton Grodzins): from the New Deal (1930s); shared functions through grants-in-aid and joint programmes. Creative federalism (Johnson's Great Society, 1960s) and New Federalism (Nixon, Reagan, and the later revival of state powers by the Rehnquist Court). Modern debates on coercive and competitive federalism . Landmark Cases McCulloch v Maryland (1819): Chief Justice John Marshall upheld Congress's power to create a national bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause (implied powers) and held that states cannot tax federal institutions ("the power to tax involves the power to destroy"). Gibbons v Ogden (1824): broad reading of the Commerce Clause ; Congress controls interstate commerce. United States v Lopez (1995): first major limit on the Commerce Clause since the New Deal (Gun-Free School Zones Act struck down). New York v United States (1992) and Printz v United States (1997): Congress cannot command state legislatures or officials to enforce federal programmes (the anti-commandeering doctrine ). NFIB v Sebelius (2012): upheld the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate under the taxing power; limited coercive spending conditions on states regarding Medicaid expansion. Erie Railroad v Tompkins (1938): federal courts apply state substantive law in diversity cases. Summary Strong states, strict federal structure, equal Senate representation, rigid amendment, residuary powers with states, and judicial review as the guardian of federalism.

p: Models of Federalism: USA, Canada and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Origins and Structure Constitution Act, 1867 (formerly the British North America Act, 1867): Confederation of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Canada is a parliamentary federation and a constitutional monarchy; the Governor General represents the Crown. Patriation (1982): the Constitution Act, 1982 (including the Charter of Rights and Freedoms ) ended the need to approach the UK Parliament for amendments. The Patriation Reference (1981) held that the federal government's unilateral patriation was legal but violated a convention requiring substantial provincial consent. Quebec did not sign the 1982 agreement. Distribution of powers: Section 91 gives enumerated powers to the federal Parliament and also the residuary power – "peace, order and good government" (POGG) ; Section 92 lists exclusive provincial powers (property and civil rights, local and private matters, administration of justice, etc.); Section 93 deals with education; Section 95 gives concurrent power over agriculture and immigration. The design intentionally gave the centre more power than in the USA, reacting to the American Civil War (Sir John A. Macdonald's vision of a strong centre). Federal paramountcy: in case of conflict between valid federal and provincial laws, the federal law prevails. Senate: appointed (by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister), regionally distributed, not elected, and so weaker as a representative of the provinces than the US Senate. This is a regular criticism. Amendment procedure (Part V, Constitution Act, 1982): general formula (the 7/50 rule ): resolutions of both Houses of Parliament and the legislatures of at least two-thirds of provinces having at least 50% of the population; special formulas apply, including unanimity for certain matters (the office of the Crown, composition of the Supreme Court, the amending formula itself). Notwithstanding clause (Section 33 of the Charter): allows Parliament or a provincial legislature to override certain Charter rights for five years (renewable). Judiciary: a unified court system under the Supreme Court of Canada, with judges appointed federally. It is not a dual system like the USA. Asymmetrical federalism and Quebec: Quebec has distinct civil law, language and cultural recognition. The Quebec Secession Reference (1998) held that Quebec has no unilateral right to secede under Canadian or international law, but a clear majority on a clear question creates a duty to negotiate. The Court identified four underlying constitutional principles: federalism, democracy, constitutionalism and the rule of law, and protection of minorities. Role of the Privy Council (Memory Points) Early interpretation by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (Lord Watson and Viscount Haldane) favoured provinces and narrowed federal power by a restrictive reading of POGG and trade and commerce. In the Labour Conventions case (1937) , the Privy Council held that the federal government cannot implement treaties in areas of provincial jurisdiction merely by signing them. Appeals to the Privy Council ended in 1949; the Supreme Court of Canada later restored a more centralist balance. Summary A centralised federation with strong provinces in practice; parliamentary; residuary power with the centre; appointed Senate; asymmetry for Quebec; the Charter's notwithstanding clause is distinctive.

p: Models of Federalism: USA, Canada and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Constitutional Structure Article 1: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States ." Dr. B.R. Ambedkar explained in the Constituent Assembly that "Union" was used because the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement between states, and no state has a right to secede. He said the Constitution can be both unitary and federal according to the requirements of time and circumstances. Seventh Schedule: Union List, State List and Concurrent List (Article 246). Residuary powers lie with Parliament (Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List). The Concurrent List is borrowed from Australia; the scheme of division from the Government of India Act, 1935. Doctrines for resolving conflicts: pith and substance, colourable legislation, incidental and ancillary powers, harmonious construction, and repugnancy ( Article 254 : a Union law prevails over a State law on a Concurrent subject, unless the State law has received Presidential assent). Article 3: Parliament can form new states and alter areas, boundaries or names of states by simple law; the State's views are only to be ascertained and are not binding ( Babulal Parate v State of Bombay , 1960). This gives the description "an indestructible Union of destructible States" . Emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360): in a national emergency the federal structure converts into a unitary one; Parliament can legislate on State subjects (Article 250). Article 356 (President's Rule) is constrained by S.R. Bommai v Union of India (1994). Other unitary features: single citizenship, integrated judiciary, All-India Services (Article 312), Governors appointed by the President (Article 155), Parliament's power to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest (Article 249, by a two-thirds Rajya Sabha resolution), a single Election Commission, the CAG, and the financial dependence of States on the Centre. Cooperative and fiscal federalism institutions: Inter-State Council (Article 263) , Finance Commission (Article 280) , GST Council (Article 279A, 101st Amendment, 2016) , Zonal Councils (States Reorganisation Act, 1956) , NITI Aayog (replaced the Planning Commission in 2015), inter-State water disputes (Article 262) , and inter-State trade (Articles 301–307) . Amendment (Article 368): most amendments are by Parliament alone; those affecting federal features (Seventh Schedule, representation of States in Parliament, Article 368 itself, election of the President, provisions on the Supreme Court and High Courts, and so on) need ratification by at least half of the State legislatures. Rajya Sabha is a Council of States with representation roughly proportional to population (not equal, unlike the US Senate). Key Cases and Commissions State of West Bengal v Union of India (1962): the Constitution is not truly federal; States are not sovereign; the Union is dominant (federal in structure but unitary in essence). S.R. Bommai v Union of India (1994): federalism is a basic feature ; Article 356 is subject to judicial review; Parliament must approve the Proclamation within two months. Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973): federal character recognised as part of the basic structure. State of Rajasthan v Union of India (1977): upheld dismissal of State governments by the Centre in specific circumstances (later restricted by Bommai). Government of NCT of Delhi v Union of India (2018 and 2023): Constitution Benches emphasised cooperative federalism; in 2023 the Court held that the elected Delhi government controls "services" other than police, public order and land. Parliament then enacted the Government of NCT of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023 , which was challenged. Mineral Area Development Authority v Steel Authority of India (2024): a nine-judge Bench held that States have the power to tax mineral rights (Entry 50 of the State List), subject to limits Parliament may impose under Entry 54 of the Union List. Considered a pro-State ruling. Sarkaria Commission (1983–88): on Centre–State relations; recommended sparing use of Article 356, a permanent Inter-State Council, and norms for appointing Governors. M.M. Punchhi Commission (2007–10): also advocated sparing use of Article 356 and guidelines for Governors; stressed cooperative federalism. Rajamannar Committee (Tamil Nadu, 1969) and the Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973) sought greater State autonomy. Characterisations of Indian Federalism Quasi-federal – K.C. Wheare. Federation with a centralising tendency – Ivor Jennings. Cooperative federalism – Granville Austin. Bargaining federalism – Morris-Jones. Asymmetrical federalism – special provisions for certain States (Articles 371 to 371J) and the earlier special status of Jammu and Kashmir (Article 370 was abrogated in 2019 and the abrogation upheld in In Re Article 370 , 2023). Federal in structure, unitary in spirit – the standard exam phrase.

p: Models of Federalism: USA, Canada and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Residuary powers with States = USA ; with Centre = Canada and India . Concurrent List borrowed from Australia ; the federal scheme with a strong Centre is borrowed from Canada . p: Rule of Law: Formal and Substantive Versions · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: The rule of law means that government and all persons are subject to law, and that law must meet certain standards of fairness, clarity and non-arbitrariness. The core idea is the opposite of arbitrary power : the state may act only on the authority of law. Ancient roots: Aristotle ("it is better for the law to rule than any single citizen"); Magna Carta (1215); Sir Edward Coke (the King is under God and the law – Prohibitions del Roy , 1607; Dr. Bonham's Case , 1610). Related continental concept: Rechtsstaat (Germany), état de droit (France), the state governed by law, with limits on administration through legality. Rule of law ≠ rule by law: "rule by law" treats law as a mere instrument of rulers, even if oppressive; the rule of law constrains rulers themselves.

p: Rule of Law: Formal and Substantive Versions · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Dicey, Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885), identified three meanings: Supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power – no person is punishable except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary legal manner before the ordinary courts. It excludes wide discretionary powers of the government. Equality before the law – all classes are subject to the ordinary law administered by the ordinary courts; officials are not above the law and have no special privileges. Dicey contrasted this with the French droit administratif (a separate system of administrative courts), which he thought gave officials special protection. The constitution is the result of the ordinary law of the land – rights of individuals arise from judicial decisions in ordinary cases (in England, the predominance of the legal spirit ), not from a written declaration of rights. Leading English cases linked to Dicey's principles: Entick v Carrington (1765) – executive cannot act without legal authority; Wilkes v Wood (1763); Leach v Money ; Liversidge v Anderson (1942) – the majority deferred to executive satisfaction while Lord Atkin's dissent is celebrated for upholding the rule of law; M v Home Office (1994) – ministers are subject to the courts' contempt jurisdiction; Re Factortame . Criticisms of Dicey: He misunderstood droit administratif (it is in fact a system protecting citizens against the administration). Modern government needs delegated legislation, administrative discretion and tribunals , which contradict his first principle. Officials and the Crown had immunities (though reduced by the Crown Proceedings Act, 1947 ). Equality is not absolute; many persons (judges, diplomats, members of Parliament) have special immunities. Ignores social and economic inequality. Ivor Jennings ( The Law and the Constitution ) criticised Dicey's approach as being rooted in 19th century laissez-faire. W.A. Robson and Lord Hewart ( The New Despotism , 1929) debated the growth of administrative power.

t: 4.3 Formal (Thin) Conceptions of the Rule of Law
p: Rule of Law: Formal and Substantive Versions · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Formal theories look at the form, procedure and characteristics of law , not its moral content. A legal system can satisfy the formal rule of law even if the laws are unjust, provided they are general, public, prospective, clear and applied fairly. Lon Fuller – The Morality of Law (1964): eight principles (the "inner morality of law"): Generality – rules, not ad hoc decisions. Promulgation – laws must be publicised. Non-retroactivity – prospective laws. Clarity – laws must be understandable. Non-contradiction – no conflicting rules. Possibility of compliance – no demand for the impossible. Constancy through time – no frequent changes. Congruence between declared rules and official action. Fuller's eight failures are illustrated through the story of King Rex . Fuller argues these are a procedural natural law ("inner morality"), distinct from the "external morality" of law (the content). The Hart–Fuller debate (1958) concerned whether immoral Nazi-era laws are law at all. Joseph Raz – "The Rule of Law and its Virtue" (1977): adopts a formal, positivist approach. Law must be capable of guiding conduct: prospective, open and clear; relatively stable; made under open, stable, clear and general rules; independence of the judiciary; principles of natural justice; courts have review power; courts easily accessible; discretion of crime-preventing agencies should not pervert the law. Raz said that the rule of law is "a virtue of law, not a moral virtue in itself" and compared it to the sharpness of a knife – it makes law efficient, whether for good or ill; it does not guarantee a just law. He believed rule of law should not be conflated with democracy, justice, equality or human rights. F.A. Hayek – The Road to Serfdom (1944) and The Constitution of Liberty (1960): rule of law means that the government in all its actions is bound by rules fixed and announced beforehand, so that one can foresee how the authority will use its coercive powers. Strongly opposed to the planning state and discretionary powers; a formal approach linked to economic liberalism. Other formal approaches: Albert Venn Dicey (largely formal), John Rawls (a rule-of-law account in A Theory of Justice as part of formal justice), Jeremy Waldron (procedural features, such as hearings and reasoned decisions). Advantages of formal conceptions: clarity, neutrality, wide acceptance, and a minimal, objective standard for all legal systems. Criticism: a tyranny could comply (the rule of law in a "thin" sense can coexist with oppressive laws, like apartheid legislation).

t: 4.4 Substantive (Thick) Conceptions of the Rule of Law
p: Rule of Law: Formal and Substantive Versions · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Substantive theories include moral and political values – especially fundamental rights, democracy, equality and dignity – within the rule of law itself. A law that violates fundamental rights fails the rule of law. Ronald Dworkin ( A Matter of Principle , 1985): distinguishes the "rule-book" conception (formal: legal rules published, citizens subject to them) from the "rights" conception (substantive: the rule of law presupposes moral rights of citizens against the state, enforceable in courts). He argued that the rights conception requires judges to interpret law in the light of political morality. T.R.S. Allan ( Law, Liberty and Justice ; Constitutional Justice ): the rule of law is bound up with equality, fairness and dignity; legal reasoning embodies a common-law constitutionalism. Lord Bingham ( The Rule of Law , 2010): offered eight sub-rules: (1) the law must be accessible, intelligible, clear and predictable; (2) legal rights should be resolved by law, not discretion; (3) equality before the law; (4) powers must be exercised lawfully, fairly and for the purpose conferred; (5) protection of fundamental human rights; (6) means for resolving disputes without prohibitive cost; (7) fair trial; (8) compliance with obligations in international law. Declaration of Delhi (1959), International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) – a dynamic and substantive concept: the rule of law should be used to safeguard and advance the civil and political rights of the individual and to establish social, economic, educational and cultural conditions in which the individual's legitimate aspirations and dignity may be realised. It emphasised an independent judiciary and legal profession. This is a classic exam question as it is linked to India and to the Delhi Congress of Jurists, 1959 . Paul Craig ("Formal and Substantive Conceptions of the Rule of Law", 1997) provided the now-standard analytical distinction. Brian Tamanaha ( On the Rule of Law , 2004) proposed a spectrum from thin (rule by law, formal legality) through thicker (democracy and individual rights) to thickest (social welfare and substantive equality). Criticisms of substantive conceptions: they merge the rule of law with a general theory of justice, making it vague and contested; any good political value could be said to be part of it.

t: 4.6 Rule of Law in India, UK and USA
p: Rule of Law: Formal and Substantive Versions · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: India: The Preamble, Article 14 (equality before law and equal protection – the Supreme Court in E.P. Royappa v State of Tamil Nadu (1974) treated arbitrariness as antithetical to equality), Article 21 (due process after Maneka Gandhi v Union of India, 1978 ), Article 32 and 226 (judicial review), and Article 13 incorporate the rule of law in a substantive manner. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975) held the rule of law to be part of the basic structure. ADM Jabalpur v Shivkant Shukla (1976) (habeas corpus case during the Emergency) represented a failure of the rule of law and was expressly overruled by the nine-judge bench in K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017). Rule of law as a reasoned and fair procedure : Maneka Gandhi , Olga Tellis , Vishaka . Indian courts follow a substantive version of the rule of law. UK: Rule of law is an unwritten constitutional principle. Constitutional Reform Act 2005, section 1 says the Act does not adversely affect "the existing constitutional principle of the rule of law". R (Jackson) v Attorney General (2005) – Lord Steyn and Lord Hope's obiter remarks on whether the rule of law is the ultimate controlling factor over parliamentary sovereignty. R (Miller) v Prime Minister (2019) also upheld constitutional principles. USA: The rule of law is embodied in the Due Process Clauses (Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments) , equal protection, judicial review ( Marbury v Madison , 1803), and the principle of a "government of laws and not of men" ( John Adams , Massachusetts Constitution of 1780). American constitutionalism treats the rule of law as having both formal and substantive aspects (substantive due process).

t: Memory Capsule: Rule of Law: Formal and Substantive Versions

x: Dicey = three principles; Fuller = eight principles (inner morality); Raz = formal "virtue of law", sharp knife; Hayek = Road to Serfdom; Dworkin = rights conception vs rule-book conception; Bingham = eight sub-rules; ICJ Delhi 1959 = dynamic, substantive. Rule of law is part of the basic structure of the Indian Constitution (Kesavananda, Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain). ADM Jabalpur = overruled in Puttaswamy . Dicey's second principle is wrongly said to oppose droit administratif . Rule of law ( limits on rulers ) ≠ rule by law ( law as an instrument of rulers ).

p: Separation of Powers: India, UK, USA and France · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: The doctrine of separation of powers holds that the three functions of government – legislative, executive and judicial – should be exercised by separate organs, so that no single body holds all the power, thereby preventing tyranny and protecting liberty. Three aspects (M.J.C. Vile, Constitutionalism and the Separation of Powers , 1967): separation of functions , separation of personnel , and checks and balances . Vile described the doctrine as a "pure doctrine" and noted that no system implements it fully. Evolution of the doctrine: Aristotle: three elements of a constitution – the deliberative, the magisterial (executive) and the judicial. John Locke ( Two Treatises of Government , 1690): legislative, executive and federative (foreign affairs) powers; judiciary was not separately recognised; supremacy of the legislature. Montesquieu ( The Spirit of the Laws , 1748), based on his study of the English constitution: legislative, executive and judicial powers. "When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty." Also, there is no liberty if the judicial power is not separated from the legislative and the executive. Montesquieu misread the English system, which then had a fusion rather than strict separation. William Blackstone ( Commentaries on the Laws of England ): linked separation to liberty. James Madison ( Federalist Papers Nos. 47 and 51): The accumulation of all powers in the same hands "may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny"; he explained that the Constitution has partial agency , not complete separation, with checks and balances ("ambition must be made to counteract ambition"). Ivor Jennings: distinguished the pure doctrine from the functional view and observed that in the UK there is no strict separation. Contemporary views: Bruce Ackerman's critique of the American separation of powers ("The New Separation of Powers", 2000) advocated a parliamentary model with independent "integrity branch" and "distributive branch"; Eoin Carolan and Jeremy Waldron have analysed the doctrine in a modern sense. Related concepts: Checks and balances: the mechanisms by which each branch limits the others (veto, judicial review, impeachment, confirmation). Fusion of powers: typical of parliamentary systems. Delegated legislation and administrative adjudication: common challenges to strict separation. Independence of the judiciary is the most universally accepted core of the doctrine.

p: Separation of Powers: India, UK, USA and France · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: The American model is the closest to the textbook doctrine, but is better described as "separated institutions sharing powers" (Richard Neustadt). Article I vests legislative power in Congress, Article II executive power in the President, and Article III judicial power in the Supreme Court and lower federal courts. Separation of personnel: the Incompatibility Clause (Article I, Section 6) – no person holding an office under the United States may be a member of Congress. Checks and balances (examples): President's veto over legislation (overridden by two-thirds of both Houses); Senate's advice and consent to appointments and treaties; impeachment by the House and trial by the Senate; Congress's control over appropriations; judicial review ( Marbury v Madison , 1803) over both Congress and the President; presidential nomination of federal judges (with Senate confirmation) and life tenure of judges during good behaviour. Landmark cases: Marbury v Madison (1803): judicial review of legislation established. Myers v United States (1926): President's removal power over executive officers. Humphrey's Executor v United States (1935): Congress may limit presidential removal of members of independent regulatory commissions. Panama Refining Co. v Ryan and A.L.A. Schechter Poultry Corp v United States (1935): applied the non-delegation doctrine (invalidating excessive delegation of legislative power). Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v Sawyer (1952): the steel seizure case – President Truman could not seize steel mills without congressional authority; Justice Jackson's three-category concurrence on presidential power (maximum authority when acting with Congress's authorisation; a "zone of twilight" when Congress is silent; lowest ebb when acting against Congress's will). United States v Nixon (1974): executive privilege is not absolute; the President must comply with a judicial subpoena in a criminal trial. Morrison v Olson (1988): upheld the independent counsel statute. INS v Chadha (1983): a one-House legislative veto is unconstitutional (violates bicameralism and presentment). Clinton v City of New York (1998): the Line Item Veto Act was held unconstitutional. Mistretta v United States (1989): upheld the Sentencing Commission and delegation to it (the "intelligible principle" test). Recent developments: Loper Bright Enterprises v Raimondo (2024) overruled the Chevron deference doctrine, shifting interpretive authority from agencies to courts; Trump v United States (2024) addressed presidential immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts.

p: Separation of Powers: India, UK, USA and France · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: The UK has a fusion of powers , not a strict separation. The doctrine operates mainly as a principle of judicial independence and mutual restraint. Executive and legislature: The Prime Minister and ministers must be members of Parliament; the Cabinet is drawn from and responsible to the House of Commons. This is the core of Bagehot's "close union, the nearly complete fusion" of executive and legislature. Judiciary and legislature: historically, the House of Lords was both the upper chamber of the legislature and the highest court (through the Law Lords). Under the Constitutional Reform Act, 2005 , a Supreme Court of the United Kingdom was created and began functioning in October 2009 , separating the final court of appeal from Parliament. Lord Chancellor: formerly head of the judiciary, a Cabinet minister and Speaker of the House of Lords (all three roles). The 2005 Act changed this: the Lord Chief Justice became head of the judiciary of England and Wales; the Lord Chancellor's role was reformed, and a Speaker of the House of Lords was introduced. A Judicial Appointments Commission now handles appointments. Judicial independence: guaranteed by the Act of Settlement, 1701 (security of tenure for judges during good behaviour) and statutory protections; judges can be removed only by an address of both Houses. Parliamentary sovereignty (Dicey) means Parliament can make or unmake any law; courts do not review the validity of Acts of Parliament (though they may issue declarations of incompatibility under the Human Rights Act, 1998, s 4 ). Cases: Duport Steels v Sirs (1980) – Lord Diplock: "Parliament makes laws, judges interpret them"; the constitutional principle of separation of powers is "a cardinal feature of the British constitution". M v Home Office (1994) – courts can hold a minister in contempt. R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex p Fire Brigades Union (1995) – the executive cannot frustrate Parliament's statutory intention using prerogative powers. R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the EU (2017) – the government cannot trigger Article 50 using the royal prerogative without parliamentary authorisation. R (Miller) v The Prime Minister; Cherry v Advocate General (2019) – the advice to prorogue Parliament was unlawful, as it frustrated Parliament's constitutional function. Anisminic v Foreign Compensation Commission (1969) – courts will not accept an ouster clause that stops review of errors of law. Delegated legislation: large in volume; Henry VIII clauses and the Statutory Instruments Act 1946 exist; the Donoughmore Committee (1932) examined the powers of ministers.

p: Separation of Powers: India, UK, USA and France · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: France is the home of Montesquieu, but its model of separation is distinctive: the traditional emphasis is on the separation of the administration from the ordinary judiciary , not on separation between judiciary and the legislature. Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789), Article 16: "A society in which the guarantee of rights is not assured, nor the separation of powers determined, has no constitution at all." Law of 16–24 August 1790: prohibits ordinary judges from interfering with the operations of the administration. The result is a dual court system: ordinary (judicial) courts headed by the Court of Cassation and administrative courts headed by the Conseil d'État , with the Tribunal des conflits deciding jurisdictional disputes. This system is called droit administratif . Historic distrust of judges: because of the pre-Revolutionary parlements ; Édouard Lambert's Le gouvernement des juges (1921) criticised judicial power; judges were long limited to applying law rather than reviewing it. Fifth Republic (1958): a strong executive with a "rationalised parliamentarism". Article 34 lists areas in which Parliament legislates (the domaine de la loi ), and Article 37 gives the residual field to executive regulation ( pouvoir réglementaire autonome ) – a dramatic reversal of parliamentary supremacy. Article 16 gives the President emergency powers; Article 49(3) allows the Government to pass a bill without a vote unless a motion of censure is passed; the executive can legislate by ordinances (Article 38) with parliamentary authorisation; the President can dissolve the National Assembly (Article 12). Constitutional Council (Conseil constitutionnel): reviews the constitutionality of laws; its 1971 Freedom of Association decision gave constitutional force to the Preamble (rights); the 2008 reform introduced QPC (question prioritaire de constitutionnalité) , an ex post review through a priority question raised in litigation. Judicial independence: guaranteed by the President acting with the Conseil supérieur de la magistrature . Features: President and Prime Minister (semi-presidential); ministers are not allowed to simultaneously serve as members of Parliament (Article 23) – a stronger separation of personnel than in the UK.

p: Separation of Powers: India, UK, USA and France · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: The Indian Constitution does not expressly adopt the doctrine, but a functional separation exists with checks and balances, and the Supreme Court treats the doctrine as part of the basic structure. Textual indications: Article 50 (Directive Principle – State to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services); Articles 53 and 73 (executive power); Article 79 (Parliament); Article 121 and 211 (no discussion in Parliament or legislatures on the conduct of judges); Article 122 and 212 (courts cannot inquire into parliamentary proceedings); Article 124 and 217 (independent judges, removal by a special procedure); Article 361 (immunity of the President and Governors). Fusion in a parliamentary system: ministers are members of the legislature (Article 75, 164) – as in the UK. Overlaps and checks: ordinance-making power of the President/Governor (Articles 123, 213); delegated legislation; tribunals; legislative power to validate invalid laws (but not to overrule judicial decisions directly); impeachment of the President (Article 61) and removal of judges (Article 124(4)); judicial review of legislative and executive action (Articles 13, 32, 226); the Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha controlling executive through questions, no-confidence motions and committees. Leading cases: In re Delhi Laws Act (1951): a legislature cannot delegate its essential legislative functions ; permissible delegation is limited to ancillary functions. Ram Jawaya Kapur v State of Punjab (1955): Chief Justice Mukherjea held that the Indian Constitution has not recognised the doctrine of separation of powers in its absolute rigidity, but the functions of the different parts or branches of government have been sufficiently differentiated. Hence, the executive cannot assume the functions of other organs essentially belonging to them (a classic exam citation). Golaknath v State of Punjab (1967): and Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973): the separation of powers is a basic feature. Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975): the Thirty-ninth Amendment (taking the election of the Prime Minister beyond judicial scrutiny) was struck down as violating the separation of powers, as it amounted to the exercise of a judicial function by the legislature. Minerva Mills v Union of India (1980): judicial review and balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs form the basic structure. Special Reference No. 1 of 1964 (Keshav Singh case / U.P. Legislative Assembly case): reconciled legislative privileges and the powers of the High Courts. State of Bihar v Bal Mukund Sah (2000): the Court said that the doctrine is a basic feature, and that a judicial function cannot be assigned to non-judicial authorities. L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India (1997): tribunals' decisions are subject to High Court scrutiny; judicial review is a basic structure. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India (2015): struck down the 99th Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act as violating judicial independence and the basic structure. Raja Ram Pal v Lok Sabha (2007): limited judicial review of the expulsion of members of Parliament in the "cash for query" case. Madras Bar Association cases and the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021: the Court has repeatedly struck down provisions that reduce the independence of tribunals.

t: Memory Capsule: Separation of Powers: India, UK, USA and France
p: Separation of Powers: India, UK, USA and France · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Montesquieu = The Spirit of the Laws (1748); Locke = legislative, executive, federative; Madison = Federalist No. 47 and 51. Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) : India does not have a rigid separation. Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975) and Kesavananda : separation as basic structure. UK : closest to fusion; Constitutional Reform Act, 2005 created the Supreme Court (functioning 2009). Youngstown = Jackson's three categories; Chadha = legislative veto; Marbury = judicial review.

p: Independence of Judiciary, Judicial Activism and Accountability: India, UK and USA · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Judicial independence means that judges can decide cases impartially, free from pressure by the executive, legislature, litigants, media or their own colleagues. It has two dimensions: Institutional independence: the judiciary as a branch is protected from interference (control over budget, administration, appointments). Individual (decisional) independence: each judge is free to decide without fear of removal, reduction of salary or career penalty. Conventional safeguards: mode of appointment , security of tenure , fixed and protected salary , removal only through a special procedure , prohibition on post-retirement practice or employment (in some systems), immunity for judicial acts, power to punish for contempt , and separation from the executive (Article 50 in India). International standards: UN Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary (1985) ; Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct (2002) (independence, impartiality, integrity, propriety, equality, competence and diligence); the Beijing Statement (1995) for the Asia-Pacific region; the Latimer House Principles (Commonwealth). Independence is accompanied by accountability – in an open system, judges must be answerable through reasoned judgments, open courts, appeals, impeachment, codes of conduct, and public scrutiny. The tension between independence and accountability is the theme of this topic.

p: Independence of Judiciary, Judicial Activism and Accountability: India, UK and USA · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Constitutional Safeguards Appointment: Article 124(2) – Supreme Court judges are appointed by the President after consultation with such judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts as deemed necessary; the Chief Justice is always consulted (except for the Chief Justice himself). Article 217 for High Courts (consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor and the Chief Justice of the High Court). Tenure: retirement at 65 (Supreme Court) and 62 (High Court). Article 124(4) and (5): removal only by an order of the President after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by at least two-thirds of the members present and voting , on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity ; procedure regulated by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. Salary: determined by Parliament (Article 125); allowances, pension and rights cannot be varied to the disadvantage of a judge after appointment (financial emergency exception). Salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (non-votable). Conduct of judges cannot be discussed in Parliament except on a motion for removal (Article 121); the Supreme Court has the power to punish for its contempt (Article 129); the Court controls its own staff and procedure (Articles 145 and 146). Post-retirement bar: a retired Supreme Court judge cannot plead or act before any court or authority in India (Article 124(7)); retired High Court judges cannot practise in the court where they held office (Article 220). Article 50 (DPSP): separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services. Articles 32, 226, 227, 136, 142, 143: wide powers, including the power to do complete justice (Article 142). Judicial review and independence of the judiciary are part of the basic structure (Kesavananda; Minerva Mills; L. Chandra Kumar). Appointments: The Judges Cases (Very High Yield) Case Year Holding S.P. Gupta v Union of India (First Judges case) 1981 "Consultation" does not mean "concurrence"; the executive had primacy in appointments. Also recognised wide public interest standing. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India (Second Judges case) 1993 Overruled S.P. Gupta; "consultation" means concurrence; primacy to the Chief Justice of India , acting with the collegium of CJI and two senior-most judges ; independence of the judiciary is a basic structure. This created the collegium system . In re Special Reference No. 1 of 1998 (Third Judges case) 1998 Presidential Reference (Article 143); the collegium for Supreme Court appointments expanded to CJI and four senior-most judges (for High Courts: CJI and two senior-most judges). Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India (Fourth Judges case – NJAC) 2015 99th Constitutional Amendment (2014) and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014 were struck down (4:1; Justice Chelameswar dissenting) as violating the basic structure (independence of the judiciary and separation of powers). The collegium was restored. Other related cases: Union of India v Sankalchand Himatlal Sheth (1977) (transfer of a High Court judge without consent was held to be punitive and unconstitutional – transfer must be in public interest, after consultation with the CJI). Criticism of the collegium: opaque, lacking formal criteria, nepotism ("judges appointing judges"), no secretariat. Defence of the collegium: protects judicial independence from executive influence. The Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) governs the process. Judicial Accountability in India Removal by impeachment: the procedure under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968: a motion signed by 100 Lok Sabha members or 50 Rajya Sabha members; the presiding officer constitutes a three-member committee (a Supreme Court judge, a High Court Chief Justice, and a distinguished jurist). No judge has been successfully removed so far. Justice V. Ramaswami (1991–93): first judge subjected to impeachment proceedings; the motion failed in the Lok Sabha as Congress members abstained. Justice Soumitra Sen (2011): the Rajya Sabha passed the motion; he resigned before the Lok Sabha could vote. Justice P.D. Dinakaran (2011): resigned before the inquiry concluded. In 2018, notice of a motion for removal of CJI Dipak Misra was rejected by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. K. Veeraswami v Union of India (1991): judges of the higher judiciary are "public servants" under the Prevention of Corruption Act, but no criminal case can be registered against a High Court or Supreme Court judge without prior consultation with the Chief Justice of India. C. Ravichandran Iyer v Justice A.M. Bhattacharjee (1995): the Court emphasised that judicial dignity must be maintained and recognised the need for an in-house procedure. In-house procedure (1999): adopted by the Supreme Court for dealing with complaints against judges. Restatement of Values of Judicial Life (1997) – a code of conduct adopted by the Full Court. A 1997 resolution requires judges to declare their assets. Contempt of Courts Act, 1971: protects the administration of justice; criticised as contrary to freedom of expression (cf. In Re Prashant Bhushan (2020) ); Articles 129 and 215 give constitutional status to contempt jurisdiction. Right to Information: Central Public Information Officer, Supreme Court of India v Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019) – the office of the Chief Justice of India is a "public authority" under the RTI Act, though information about collegium deliberations may be withheld under exemptions subject to a public-interest test. Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill, 2010 (lapsed) proposed binding standards and a complaints mechanism. Other accountability tools: reasoned judgments, appeals, review and curative petitions ( Rupa Ashok Hurra v Ashok Hurra, 2002 ), and public scrutiny.

p: Independence of Judiciary, Judicial Activism and Accountability: India, UK and USA · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Meaning: A judicial philosophy in which judges go beyond the traditional role of interpreting law, take an active role in promoting social justice and rights, correct failures of other branches, and sometimes create new law or policy. The term was coined by Arthur Schlesinger Jr. in a 1947 Fortune magazine article on the US Supreme Court. Opposite concept: judicial restraint (deference to the political branches). Related concept: judicial overreach , where the court is accused of violating separation of powers. Indian Judicial Activism: Phases and Tools Early period (1950–70s): a restrictive and positivist approach ( A.K. Gopalan v State of Madras, 1950 ; ADM Jabalpur, 1976 ). Expansion after 1978 (post-Emergency): Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978) (Articles 14, 19 and 21 are interrelated; procedure must be just, fair and reasonable). Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer, P.N. Bhagwati, O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai led this approach. Public Interest Litigation (PIL)/Social Action Litigation: relaxed locus standi ; epistolary jurisdiction (treating letters as petitions); S.P. Gupta (1981) recognised standing for public-spirited persons; Hussainara Khatoon v State of Bihar (1979) – speedy trial and legal aid for undertrials; Bandhua Mukti Morcha v Union of India (1984) – bonded labour; M.C. Mehta v Union of India (environment; absolute liability in the Oleum Gas leak case , 1986); Olga Tellis v Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) – right to livelihood; Sunil Batra v Delhi Administration (1978) – prisoners' rights; Vishaka v State of Rajasthan (1997) – guidelines against sexual harassment at work (leading to the 2013 Act); D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal (1997) – guidelines on arrest and custody; Lalita Kumari v Government of Uttar Pradesh (2013) – mandatory registration of FIR for cognisable offences; Common Cause v Union of India (2018) – passive euthanasia and living wills; Navtej Singh Johar (2018) – decriminalising consensual same-sex acts. Expansion of Article 21: right to life includes dignity, livelihood, health, education ( Unni Krishnan, 1993 ), clean environment, privacy ( Puttaswamy, 2017 ), speedy trial, free legal aid, and many others. Tools: the doctrine of the basic structure; continuing mandamus; appointment of commissions; use of Article 142 to do "complete justice"; judicial legislation through guidelines. Criticisms: judicial overreach (policy-making without expertise or accountability), "judicial populism", encroachment on legislative and executive domain, and inconsistent standards. Supporters argue that activism filled a vacuum left by a weak executive and legislature. Judicial restraint: the Court has also recognised limits – e.g., Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v Chander Hass (2008) (judges must show restraint and not usurp power).

p: Independence of Judiciary, Judicial Activism and Accountability: India, UK and USA · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Independence Act of Settlement, 1701: judges hold office during good behaviour ( quamdiu se bene gesserint ) and can be removed only by an address of both Houses of Parliament. This is the historical foundation of security of tenure. Constitutional Reform Act 2005 (CRA): section 3 imposes a statutory duty on the Lord Chancellor, ministers and others to uphold continued judicial independence, and bars ministers from seeking to influence judicial decisions through special access; section 1 affirms the rule of law; created the UK Supreme Court (functioning October 2009) ; the Lord Chief Justice became head of the judiciary in England and Wales; the Judicial Appointments Commission (2006) recommends candidates on merit; the Lord Chancellor's role is limited; the Judicial Appointments and Conduct Ombudsman handles complaints. Retirement: the mandatory retirement age for judges has been 70, raised to 75 for most judicial offices by recent legislation (the Public Service Pensions and Judicial Offices Act, 2022). Sub judice convention: matters before courts are not discussed in Parliament; judges are not criticised except on a substantive motion. Accountability Removal: a superior court judge can be removed only by the Crown on an address by both Houses (Senior Courts Act, 1981, s 11(3); CRA 2005 for Supreme Court justices). It is virtually never used. Judicial Conduct Investigations Office (JCIO) (since 2013) investigates complaints about personal conduct (not judicial decisions); disciplinary sanctions are imposed by the Lord Chancellor with the Lord Chief Justice. Appeals and reasoned public judgments are the main routes for correcting decisions; open justice and media reporting. Judicial Activism in the UK The UK's tradition of parliamentary sovereignty makes overt activism rare, but the following are considered activist trends: Lord Denning (Master of the Rolls, 1962–82): a creative, justice-oriented judge (promissory estoppel in Central London Property Trust v High Trees , 1947; the Mareva injunction). Lord Reid, "The Judge as Law Maker" (1972): rejected the "fairy tale" that judges merely find, not make, law. Growth of judicial review: Ridge v Baldwin (1964); Anisminic v Foreign Compensation Commission (1969); GCHQ (Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service, 1985) where Lord Diplock classified grounds as illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety. Human Rights Act, 1998: courts interpret legislation compatibly (section 3) and issue declarations of incompatibility (section 4) without invalidating laws. Constitutional principle cases: Factortame (1990) (disapplied an Act of Parliament in conflict with EU law); R (Jackson) v AG (2005) ; R (Miller) 2017 and 2019 ; R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor (2017) (access to justice as a constitutional right). Criticism: concerns of judicial overreach (e.g., Miller) fed the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 (limiting some remedies). The 2016 "Enemies of the People" headline about judges after the first Miller decision illustrated political pressure.

p: Independence of Judiciary, Judicial Activism and Accountability: India, UK and USA · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Independence Article III: judges of the Supreme Court and inferior courts hold office during good behaviour and receive compensation that cannot be diminished during their continuance in office. Appointment: nominated by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate (Article II, Section 2) – highly political. Removal: only by impeachment (House) and conviction (Senate by two-thirds) for "treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors" (Article II, Section 4). Justice Samuel Chase was impeached in 1804 and acquitted in 1805 – a key precedent for judicial independence. No Supreme Court justice has been removed. Size of the Court: fixed by Congress (nine since 1869). Franklin D. Roosevelt's Court-packing plan (1937) failed but is remembered as "the switch in time that saved nine". State judges: in many States, judges are elected or face retention elections (more accountable but potentially less independent). Ethics: the federal judiciary follows the Code of Conduct for United States Judges ; the Supreme Court adopted its first Code of Conduct in November 2023 (with no formal enforcement mechanism). Judicial Review and Judicial Activism Marbury v Madison (1803) established judicial review; Martin v Hunter's Lessee (1816) and Cooper v Aaron (1958) support the Supreme Court's role as the final interpreter of the Constitution. Schlesinger (1947) identified judicial "activists" and "champions of self-restraint" on the Court. Lochner era (1905–1937): Lochner v New York – the Court struck down social and economic legislation using substantive due process ( conservative activism ); ended with West Coast Hotel v Parrish (1937). Warren Court (1953–69), Chief Justice Earl Warren (liberal activism): Brown v Board of Education (1954) ; Mapp v Ohio (1961) (exclusionary rule applied to States); Baker v Carr (1962) (reapportionment is justiciable – "one person, one vote"); Gideon v Wainwright (1963) (right to counsel); Griswold v Connecticut (1965) (privacy); Miranda v Arizona (1966) (warnings). Later developments: Roe v Wade (1973) recognised abortion rights; it was overruled in Dobbs v Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022) . Bush v Gore (2000) and Citizens United v FEC (2010) are also controversial. Judicial restraint: associated with Justices Holmes, Frankfurter and Learned Hand ; originalism/textualism (Antonin Scalia) is presented as restraint though critics see selective activism. Alexander Bickel , The Least Dangerous Branch (1962), articulated the counter-majoritarian difficulty . Self-limiting doctrines: standing, ripeness, mootness, political question doctrine ( Baker v Carr ; Nixon v United States , 1993), and the Ashwander rules of constitutional avoidance (Justice Brandeis).
