p: Systems of Constitutional Review: India, USA, Switzerland and France · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Constitutional review (including judicial review ) is the power of a court or other body to examine whether laws, executive acts or sometimes constitutional amendments conform to the Constitution, and to invalidate or refuse to apply those that do not. It is the mechanism that makes a constitution supreme . Classification of systems: American (decentralised/diffuse) model: every court can examine constitutionality during an ordinary case (concrete, a posteriori ); the highest court has the final say; the court refuses to apply the unconstitutional law. Countries: USA, India (largely), Canada, Australia, Japan. European/Kelsenian (centralised) model: a special constitutional court has exclusive jurisdiction; designed by Hans Kelsen for the Austrian Constitution of 1920 ; decisions have erga omnes effect (annulment). Countries: Germany (Federal Constitutional Court, 1951), Italy, Spain, South Africa. Political/preventive model: a political-legal body reviews laws before promulgation – France (Conseil constitutionnel) is the classic example. Parliamentary supremacy with no review of statutes: traditionally the UK, and partly Switzerland for federal laws. Weak-form/"new Commonwealth model" (Stephen Gardbaum): courts review rights but the legislature has the final word (Canada's notwithstanding clause; UK's Human Rights Act; New Zealand). Other dimensions: Abstract review (without a concrete case, at the request of officials) vs concrete review (arising in a real dispute). A priori (before a law comes into force) vs a posteriori (after). Incidental (raised in a case) vs principal (direct challenge). Strong-form (final judicial word) vs weak-form (legislature can respond). Counter-majoritarian difficulty (Bickel) – the core theoretical objection: unelected judges overturning the will of elected bodies. Defence: protection of rights and constitutional supremacy ( Hamilton, Federalist No. 78 – the judiciary is the "least dangerous" branch, having neither force nor will, but merely judgment).

p: Systems of Constitutional Review: India, USA, Switzerland and France · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Source: not expressly provided in the text; derived from Article III (judicial power), Article VI (supremacy clause) and Marbury v Madison (1803) – Chief Justice John Marshall: it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is; an Act repugnant to the Constitution is void. The Court held that part of Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional because it expanded the Court's original jurisdiction beyond Article III. Diffuse, concrete, a posteriori review: any court can review; the Supreme Court is the final authority; Article III requires "cases or controversies" ; the Court does not give advisory opinions (a tradition from the 1793 Correspondence of the Justices and Hayburn's Case ). Review of state laws and decisions: Fletcher v Peck (1810) (first state law struck down); Martin v Hunter's Lessee (1816) ; Cohens v Virginia (1821) . A federal law was struck down for the first time in Marbury ; the second time in Dred Scott v Sandford (1857). Cooper v Aaron (1958): judicial supremacy asserted. Justiciability doctrines: standing ( Lujan v Defenders of Wildlife, 1992 ), ripeness, mootness, and the political question doctrine ( Luther v Borden , 1849; Baker v Carr , 1962; Nixon v United States , 1993). Levels of scrutiny: rational basis, intermediate scrutiny, strict scrutiny (footnote 4 of United States v Carolene Products, 1938 ). Certiorari: the Court chooses most of its cases (the "rule of four"). Review of constitutional amendments: generally the Court does not substantively strike down amendments ( National Prohibition Cases, 1920 ); there is no "basic structure" doctrine. Strong-form review with the Supreme Court as the ultimate interpreter; constitutional amendment (Article V) or changes in the Court's composition are the main political responses.

p: Systems of Constitutional Review: India, USA, Switzerland and France · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Source: express constitutional provisions – Article 13 (laws inconsistent with or in derogation of fundamental rights are void), Article 32 (right to constitutional remedies – itself a fundamental right; Dr. Ambedkar called it the "heart and soul" of the Constitution), Article 226 (High Courts – wider, extends to "any other purpose"), Article 131 (original jurisdiction in Centre–State disputes), Articles 132–136 (appeals, special leave), Article 143 (advisory jurisdiction – President's reference), Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule (distribution of powers), Article 254 (repugnancy), Article 368 (amendment). Nature: a hybrid – diffuse like the USA but with the Supreme Court at the apex, direct constitutional jurisdiction (Articles 32 and 226) and an advisory jurisdiction (Article 143). It has no separate constitutional court. Judicial review of ordinary legislation: grounds – violation of fundamental rights, lack of legislative competence, violation of other constitutional provisions; presumption of constitutionality ( Charanjit Lal Chowdhury v Union of India , 1951); proportionality and the "arbitrariness" doctrine ( Shayara Bano, 2017 ). Doctrines: pith and substance; colourable legislation; severability ( R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala v Union of India, 1957 ); doctrine of eclipse ( Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v State of Madhya Pradesh, 1955 : a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with fundamental rights is not dead but "eclipsed", and revives if the inconsistency is removed); doctrine of waiver ( Behram Khurshed Pesikaka v State of Bombay, 1955 : fundamental rights cannot be waived); prospective overruling ( Golaknath, 1967 ); territorial nexus ; harmonious construction ; reading down. Review of constitutional amendments (basic structure doctrine): Shankari Prasad v Union of India (1951) and Sajjan Singh v State of Rajasthan (1965): Parliament can amend any part, including fundamental rights; an amendment is not "law" under Article 13(2). I.C. Golaknath v State of Punjab (1967): Parliament cannot amend fundamental rights (an amendment is "law"); prospective overruling used. 24th Amendment (1971): added Article 13(4) and amended Article 368, declaring that Article 13 does not apply to amendments. Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973): a 13-judge bench by 7:6 held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure (an idea associated with the German scholar Dietrich Conrad 's lectures in India). Basic features include supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism, secularism, democracy, free and fair elections and independence of the judiciary. Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975): the 39th Amendment invalidated. Minerva Mills v Union of India (1980): struck down parts of the 42nd Amendment (Article 368(4) and (5)); harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the basic structure; limited amending power is itself a basic feature. Waman Rao v Union of India (1981): Ninth Schedule laws placed before 24 April 1973 are immune; those after can be reviewed. I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu (2007): Ninth Schedule laws enacted after 24 April 1973 are open to challenge if they violate fundamental rights or the basic structure. L. Chandra Kumar (1997): judicial review by the High Courts and Supreme Court is part of the basic structure. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (2015): 99th Amendment struck down. Review of executive action: presidential proclamations (S.R. Bommai, 1994), ordinances ( Krishna Kumar Singh v State of Bihar, 2017 ), and administrative action generally. Nature: strong-form review with the Supreme Court as the final authority; criticised at times as overreach.

p: Systems of Constitutional Review: India, USA, Switzerland and France · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Switzerland is distinctive: judicial review is limited because of its commitment to popular sovereignty and direct democracy. Federal Supreme Court (Bundesgericht), Lausanne: the highest court; the system also includes the Federal Criminal Court (Bellinzona), Federal Administrative Court (St. Gallen) and Federal Patent Court. Cantonal laws: the Federal Supreme Court can review cantonal laws and acts for compatibility with the Federal Constitution, federal law and international law (both abstract review directly within a time limit after promulgation, and concrete/incidental review ). This protects federal supremacy. Federal laws: under Article 190 of the Federal Constitution (1999) , the Federal Supreme Court and other authorities must apply federal acts and international law. So federal statutes cannot be set aside for being unconstitutional – a result of the principle that the people (through referendum) and Parliament are sovereign. However, courts may interpret federal laws in conformity with the Constitution, and in practice give priority to international human rights law (the Schubert practice , 1973, and the PKK case, 1999 , on the primacy of the European Convention on Human Rights). No separate constitutional court and no judicial review of federal acts. Instead, democratic controls operate: federal acts are subject to the optional referendum (50,000 signatures within 100 days); constitutional amendments require a mandatory referendum with a double majority (majority of the people and the majority of cantons – Ständerat/Ständemehr ); a popular initiative (100,000 signatures within 18 months) can propose a partial revision of the Constitution (Article 139); an initiative can be declared invalid only if it violates unity of form or matter, or mandatory provisions of international law ( jus cogens ). Why limited review? The democratic tradition of 1848; trust in the referendum as the guardian; federal laws are seen as the people's will. Proposals to introduce constitutional jurisdiction over federal laws (including in the 1999 revision) were rejected. Federal Council (executive) and Federal Assembly (Parliament) carry out internal checks (e.g., the Federal Office of Justice advises on constitutionality).

p: Systems of Constitutional Review: India, USA, Switzerland and France · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: France historically rejected judicial review of statutes (law as an expression of the general will – Rousseau; distrust of judges after the Revolution; fear of gouvernement des juges ). The Fifth Republic (1958) created a distinctive model. Conseil constitutionnel (Constitutional Council) – Title VII, Articles 56–63 of the 1958 Constitution. Composition: nine members serving non-renewable nine-year terms , one-third renewed every three years. The President of the Republic, the President of the National Assembly and the President of the Senate each appoint three. Former Presidents of the Republic are ex officio members for life (Article 56). Members are often experienced politicians and jurists, not necessarily judges. A priori (preventive) review: before promulgation ; mandatory for organic laws (lois organiques) and the standing orders of Parliament (Article 61(1)); optional for ordinary laws – referred by the President of the Republic, the Prime Minister, the Presidents of the two Houses, or (since the 1974 reform ) 60 deputies or 60 senators (Article 61(2)). Treaties are checked under Article 54 . The Council normally decides within one month. A posteriori review – Question prioritaire de constitutionnalité (QPC): introduced by the Constitutional Law of 23 July 2008 (in force 1 March 2010; Article 61-1 ). A litigant can raise before any court a claim that a statutory provision violates rights and freedoms guaranteed by the Constitution; the Conseil d'État or Cour de cassation filters and refers it. A provision declared unconstitutional is repealed from the date of publication of the decision or a date fixed by the Council ( Article 62 ). Binding effect: Article 62 – an unconstitutional provision cannot be promulgated or implemented; decisions are not subject to appeal and bind all public, administrative and judicial authorities. Decision of 16 July 1971 (Freedom of Association): a landmark – the Council struck down part of a statute for the first time and gave constitutional status to the Preamble of the 1958 Constitution , thus incorporating the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen and the Preamble of the 1946 Constitution , forming the bloc de constitutionnalité . After this, the Council became a protector of rights. Other functions: supervises presidential elections and referendums, adjudicates disputes on parliamentary elections (Articles 58–60), and polices the division between law and regulation (Articles 37 and 41). Limits: the Council does not review laws adopted by referendum (Decision of 6 November 1962 ) and, in principle, constitutional amendments (Decision of 26 March 2003 ); it does not check conventionality (compatibility of statutes with treaties) – this is done by ordinary and administrative courts ( Decision of 15 January 1975 on abortion; Cour de cassation, Jacques Vabre (1975) and Conseil d'État, Nicolo (1989) under Article 55). Administrative courts: the Conseil d'État reviews the legality of administrative acts (decrees and regulations) – the French dual system ( droit administratif ). Features: semi-political composition; mainly preventive and abstract; erga omnes effect; opposition referrals since 1974 greatly enhanced its role.

t: 8.1 Concept: Why and How Constitutions Are Amended
p: Amendment of the Constitution: India, USA and South Africa · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: A constitution must be stable but also adaptable. Amendment is the formal procedure by which the text is changed, and it distinguishes constituent power (the power to make or change the constitution) from ordinary legislative power. Rigid constitution: needs a special procedure for amendment (USA, Switzerland, Australia). Flexible constitution: amended by the ordinary legislative process (UK). Lord Bryce ( Flexible and Rigid Constitutions ) introduced this classification; K.C. Wheare and Dicey also discuss it. Mixed/partly rigid and partly flexible: India (Nehru said that the Constitution should not be so rigid that it cannot adapt; it is neither too rigid nor too flexible). Methods of amendment: by the legislature with a special majority; by the legislature plus ratification by units (federations); by referendum (Switzerland, Australia); by a special convention; by judicial interpretation (informal amendment). Entrenchment: certain provisions are protected by a stricter procedure (e.g., the equal suffrage in the US Senate; sections 1 and 74 of the South African Constitution; basic structure in India).

p: Amendment of the Constitution: India, USA and South Africa · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Article 368 and Categories of Amendment Part XX (Article 368) deals with the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and its procedure. The Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 amended the heading and text to read "Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor". An amendment bill can be introduced only in Parliament (either House), not in a State legislature, and does not need the President's prior recommendation. There is no provision for a joint sitting in the event of a deadlock. The President must give assent (24th Amendment). There are three categories: Amendment by simple majority of Parliament (outside Article 368, like ordinary legislation): admission or establishment of new States, and alteration of boundaries (Articles 2, 3 and 4); abolition or creation of Legislative Councils in States (Article 169); the Second Schedule (salaries of constitutional officers); quorum in Parliament; Fifth and Sixth Schedules (administration of Scheduled and Tribal areas); citizenship (Articles 5–11); official language; Union territories; parliamentary privileges; and some others. Amendment by special majority: a majority of the total membership of each House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting in each House. This covers most provisions, including Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles. Amendment by special majority plus ratification by at least half of the State legislatures (by simple majority in those legislatures): provisions concerning the federal structure , such as the election of the President (Articles 54, 55); the extent of the executive power of the Union and States (Articles 73 and 162); the Supreme Court and High Courts (Chapter IV of Part V and Chapter V of Part VI); the Union Territories' High Courts (Article 241); the distribution of legislative powers between the Union and States (Chapter I of Part XI); the Seventh Schedule ; the representation of States in Parliament ; and Article 368 itself . The Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016 (GST) was ratified by States for this reason. Kihoto Hollohan v Zachillhu (1992): Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule (barring the courts' jurisdiction) was held invalid because the amendment did not obtain ratification by half of the States. Judicial Limitations: Evolution of the Basic Structure Doctrine Case Holding Shankari Prasad (1951) Amendment is not "law" under Article 13(2); Parliament can amend fundamental rights. Sajjan Singh (1965) Same view, with doubts expressed by some judges. Golaknath (1967) 11-judge bench (6:5): Parliament cannot amend fundamental rights; amendment is "law"; doctrine of prospective overruling. 24th and 25th Amendments (1971) Overturned Golaknath legislatively; 24th added Article 13(4) and clarified amendment power; 25th restricted property compensation and Article 31C. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) 13-judge bench (7:6): Parliament can amend any provision, but not destroy the basic structure . Golaknath overruled. Article 31C partly struck down. Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975) 39th Amendment (election of PM beyond judicial review) struck down. 42nd Amendment (1976) "Mini-Constitution": added Articles 368(4) and (5) to exclude judicial review; inserted "Socialist", "Secular" and "Integrity" into the Preamble; added Fundamental Duties; extended the Lok Sabha term. Minerva Mills (1980) Articles 368(4) and (5) struck down; limited amending power is a basic feature; balance between Parts III and IV is basic. Waman Rao (1981) Cut-off date of 24 April 1973 for the Ninth Schedule. I.R. Coelho (2007) Ninth Schedule laws after 24 April 1973 can be tested against the basic structure. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (2015) 99th Amendment (NJAC) struck down. Basic structure features (illustrative): supremacy of the Constitution; republican and democratic form of government; secular character; separation of powers; federal character; unity and integrity of the nation; sovereignty; rule of law; judicial review; independence of the judiciary; free and fair elections; Parts III and IV harmony; welfare state; Article 32, 226 and 227 jurisdictions. Important Amendments (Memory Table) 1st (1951): Ninth Schedule; reasonable restrictions on free speech; Article 15(4). 7th (1956): reorganisation of States (States Reorganisation Act). 24th (1971), 25th (1971), 39th (1975), 42nd (1976). 44th (1978): property right removed from Part III (Article 300A); restored safeguards for emergency; the term "internal disturbance" replaced by "armed rebellion". 52nd (1985): anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule). 91st (2003): limited the size of the Council of Ministers to 15% of the House. 61st (1988): voting age reduced to 18. 73rd and 74th (1992): Panchayats and Municipalities. 86th (2002): Article 21A (education), fundamental duty in Article 51A(k). 101st (2016): Goods and Services Tax; GST Council (Article 279A). 102nd (2018): constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes. 103rd (2019): 10% reservation for economically weaker sections (EWS), upheld in Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India (2022) by a 3:2 majority. 104th (2020): ended reservation for Anglo-Indians in legislatures and extended SC/ST reservation to 2030. 105th (2021): restored States' power to identify socially and educationally backward classes. 106th (2023): Women's Reservation (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) : one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies reserved for women, to take effect after the next census and delimitation.

p: Amendment of the Constitution: India, USA and South Africa · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Article V provides a two-stage procedure: Proposal: (a) by two-thirds of both Houses of Congress , or (b) by a convention called by Congress on the application of two-thirds of the State legislatures (never used). Ratification: (a) by the legislatures of three-fourths of the States , or (b) by conventions in three-fourths of the States , as Congress decides. Only the 21st Amendment (repealing Prohibition) was ratified by state conventions. The President has no formal role ( Hollingsworth v Virginia , 1798); no presidential signature or veto applies. Entrenched clause: no State, without its consent, can be deprived of its equal suffrage in the Senate. (An earlier clause protecting the slave trade expired in 1808.) Number: 27 amendments. The first ten ( Bill of Rights ) were ratified in 1791. Important ones: 13th (1865, abolition of slavery), 14th (1868, citizenship, due process and equal protection), 15th (1870, race and voting), 16th (1913, income tax), 17th (1913, direct election of Senators), 18th (1919, Prohibition) and 21st (1933, repeal), 19th (1920, women's suffrage), 22nd (1951, two-term limit), 25th (1967, presidential disability and succession), 26th (1971, voting age 18), and 27th (ratified 1992, Congressional pay; first proposed in 1789). Judicial role: the Court treats most questions as political. Hawke v Smith (1920): ratification must be by the legislature, not by a popular referendum, when Congress specifies legislatures; Dillon v Gloucester (1921): ratification within a reasonable time; Coleman v Miller (1939): the question of time limits for ratification is political; National Prohibition Cases (1920) : upheld the 18th Amendment. No "basic structure" doctrine exists in the US. Difficulty: very rigid; many proposed amendments fail (e.g., the Equal Rights Amendment did not achieve ratification by three-fourths of the States within the deadline). Informal amendment: through judicial interpretation ( Marbury , Brown ), custom and convention (e.g., the two-term tradition before the 22nd Amendment), and statutes.

p: Amendment of the Constitution: India, USA and South Africa · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 (Act 108 of 1996) is the supreme law (section 2). It was adopted by the Constitutional Assembly in May 1996; the Constitutional Court refused to certify the first text in the First Certification Judgment (September 1996) and certified the amended text in December 1996. It came into force on 4 February 1997. This unusual certification procedure was required by the Interim Constitution (1993) and its 34 Constitutional Principles. Section 74 – Amendment procedure (three tiers): Section 1 (founding provisions: human dignity, equality, non-racialism and non-sexism, supremacy of the Constitution, universal adult suffrage, multi-party democracy) and Section 74(1) itself: at least 75% of the members of the National Assembly and the support of at least six of nine provinces in the National Council of Provinces (NCOP) . Chapter 2 (Bill of Rights): at least two-thirds of the National Assembly and six provinces in the NCOP (as amended; the Bill of Rights is entrenched at this level). Other provisions: at least two-thirds of the National Assembly ; also the NCOP's support of six provinces if the amendment relates to a matter affecting the NCOP, provincial boundaries, powers, functions or institutions, or specifically deals with a provincial matter. Public participation: at least 30 days before a Bill amending the Constitution is introduced, the proposal must be published in the Gazette for public comment and submitted to provincial legislatures (section 74(5)). An amendment bill may only contain amendments and matters connected with them (section 74(8)). Judicial review of amendments: the Constitutional Court reviews the procedural validity of amendments. In United Democratic Movement v President of the Republic of South Africa (2002) (the "floor crossing" amendments), the Court upheld the amendments and discussed (without deciding) whether there are substantive limits on amendment, acknowledging the Indian basic structure doctrine; the Court said that a constitutional amendment that destroys the basic structure might be invalid. Earlier, Premier of KwaZulu-Natal v President of the Republic of South Africa (1995) dealt with procedural issues. Section 74 shows that the Constitution's founding values (section 1) are entrenched. Recent attempt: the Constitution Eighteenth Amendment Bill (to permit land expropriation without compensation by amending section 25) failed in December 2021 for lack of the required two-thirds majority. Features: a tiered, "value-based" entrenchment; open, participatory; the Constitution of South Africa is moderately rigid; the Indian Constitution's amendment procedure was one of the models for the South African approach (the Indian amending procedure, in turn, drew from the South African Constitution of 1909 as the Constituent Assembly borrowed).

p: Ombudsman: Sweden, UK and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Ombudsman is a Swedish word meaning a representative or agent of the citizen. The Ombudsman is an independent official, usually appointed by the legislature, who investigates complaints against administrative action (maladministration) and recommends remedies, without being a court. The institution protects citizens against bureaucratic injustice, arbitrariness, delay and corruption. Essential features: Independence from the executive and being appointed by (and accountable to) the legislature. Impartiality and non-partisan nature. Accessibility to citizens: low-cost, informal, simple procedure. Investigative power: access to files and officials. Recommendatory power: most Ombudsmen cannot overturn decisions or enforce remedies; they rely on persuasion, publicity and reporting to the legislature ("sunlight as a disinfectant"). Jurisdiction over maladministration rather than merits of policy; exclusion of matters before courts and policy decisions. Reports to the legislature: annual and special. Types: classical/parliamentary Ombudsman; executive Ombudsman; hybrid (human rights and administrative); organisational and sectoral Ombudsman (banking, insurance, police, military, children, consumer). Global spread: Sweden (1809); Finland (1919); Denmark (1955); Norway (1962); New Zealand (1962) , the first in the Commonwealth, with Sir Guy Powles as the first Ombudsman; the UK (1967); Tanzania; Canada's provinces from 1967; and many others. The International Ombudsman Institute was founded in 1978.

p: Ombudsman: Sweden, UK and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Origins: The idea traces to King Charles XII (1713), who created the "Highest Ombudsman" ( Högste Ombudsmannen ) while in exile in Bender (Turkey) after the Battle of Poltava, to supervise officials. It was later renamed the Chancellor of Justice (Justitiekanslern) in 1719 (an executive office appointed by the Government that continues today). Modern Parliamentary Ombudsman (JO – Justitieombudsmannen ): created by the Instrument of Government of 1809 (after the deposition of Gustav IV Adolf) as an officer of the Riksdag (Parliament) , independent of the king, to supervise the application of laws by courts and officials. The first JO was Lars August Mannerheim (1809–10). Appointment: elected by the Riksdag. At present there are four Parliamentary Ombudsmen , one of whom is the Chief Parliamentary Ombudsman , for a term of four years (a legal provision in the Instrument of Government, Chapter 13, and the Act with Instruction for the Parliamentary Ombudsmen). Jurisdiction: the Ombudsmen supervise public authorities, courts, civil servants and employees of the State and municipalities , including the military and the police, to ensure that they observe laws and fulfil their obligations; the Ombudsmen do not usually supervise Members of Parliament and the Government ministers (who are subject to the Committee on the Constitution), or the Chancellor of Justice. Powers: to act on complaints or on their own initiative ( suo motu ) ; to carry out inspections of authorities; to have access to files and officials; to issue statements and opinions (criticism, advice); to initiate disciplinary action and prosecute officials for criminal offences in office (rarely used). They cannot overrule decisions; the effect rests on prestige and publicity. Public access to documents ( offentlighetsprincipen ) and the Freedom of the Press Act of 1766 (the world's oldest freedom of information law) give strength to the system. Other Swedish Ombudsmen: the Equality Ombudsman , Consumer Ombudsman, Children's Ombudsman, and the Data Protection Authority have separate mandates (executive ombudsmen). Significance: it is a model for the world; the Scandinavian model is parliamentary , investigative and informal .

p: Ombudsman: Sweden, UK and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Background: The Whyatt Report (1961) , by JUSTICE, recommended an Ombudsman-style institution for the UK. The Parliamentary Commissioner Act, 1967 created the Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration (PCA) ; the first PCA was Sir Edmund Compton (1967–71). It is now combined with the Health Service Commissioner as the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) (the Health Service Commissioner was created in 1973). Appointment: by the Crown (on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, and the House of Commons has a say through select committee scrutiny); security of tenure like a High Court judge (removal by an address of both Houses). Jurisdiction: complaints about maladministration by central government departments and bodies listed in Schedule 2; Schedule 3 excludes certain matters, such as civil and criminal proceedings, personnel and contract matters, foreign affairs, and extradition. The Act does not define "maladministration" ; the famous Crossman catalogue (Richard Crossman, Leader of the House of Commons, 1966) lists "bias, neglect, inattention, delay, incompetence, ineptitude, perversity, turpitude, arbitrariness and so on". MP filter: the traditional rule that a complaint reaches the PCA only through a Member of Parliament (the "MP filter"), designed to preserve MPs' role; critics argue it limits accessibility, and reforms have been proposed. Procedure and powers: investigates in private; powers similar to the High Court in respect of summoning witnesses and the production of documents; injustice caused by maladministration is the test; reports to the MP and the department; can make recommendations but cannot compel ; a special report may be laid before Parliament if the Government does not comply; the Public Administration Select Committee (PASC) scrutinises the work. Landmark examples: the Barlow Clowes affair (1988–89) (compensation to investors after the PCA's report found maladministration by the Department of Trade and Industry); the Debt of Honour (2005) (Second World War Far East prisoners); the Equitable Life report (2008, Equitable Life: A Decade of Regulatory Failure ); and the Channel Tunnel Rail Link matter. Judicial attitude: R v Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration, ex p Balchin (1997) – the courts reviewed the Ombudsman's findings in respect of the Department of Transport; R (Bradley) v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions (2008) – the Government cannot reject the Ombudsman's findings without a rational and cogent reason; R (Equitable Members Action Group) v HM Treasury (2009) – the Government's decision to reject some recommendations was subject to review. Other UK Ombudsmen: Local Government Ombudsman (Local Government Act, 1974), now the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman ; Scottish Public Services Ombudsman (2002) ; Public Services Ombudsman for Wales (2005) ; Northern Ireland Ombudsman ; Financial Ombudsman Service (2000); and other sectoral schemes.

p: Ombudsman: Sweden, UK and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Background The concept entered Indian discourse in the early 1960s. Dr. L.M. Singhvi coined the terms "Lokpal" and "Lokayukta" (1963). The Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC, 1966–70) , chaired first by Morarji Desai and then by K. Hanumanthaiya , recommended in its report on Problems of Redress of Citizens' Grievances (1966) the creation of two special authorities : Lokpal (at the Centre) and Lokayuktas (in the States), for complaints against ministers and administrators. The Lokpal Bill was first introduced in 1968 (Lok Sabha) and lapsed; it was reintroduced in 1971, 1977, 1985, 1989, 1996, 1998, 2001, 2005, 2008 and 2011 without success. The 2011 India Against Corruption movement (Anna Hazare) accelerated its passing. The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 received Presidential assent on 1 January 2014 , and came into force on 16 January 2014. Key Provisions of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 Composition: a Chairperson and up to eight members , of whom 50% must be judicial members ; 50% of members must be from the SC, ST, OBC, minorities and women. Chairperson: a former Chief Justice of India, or a former Supreme Court judge, or an eminent person with impeccable integrity and outstanding ability, with at least 25 years of expertise in anti-corruption policy, public administration, vigilance, finance, law and management. Selection Committee: the Prime Minister (Chairperson); the Speaker of the Lok Sabha; the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha; the Chief Justice of India (or a judge nominated by him); and an eminent jurist nominated by the President on the recommendation of the other four. Term: five years or till the age of 70, whichever is earlier. Jurisdiction: the Prime Minister (with exceptions for allegations relating to international relations, external and internal security, public order, atomic energy and space; and a special procedure requiring a full bench and a two-thirds majority for inquiry; proceedings in camera ), Ministers, Members of Parliament, Group A–D officials and officers of the Central Government, and persons in entities funded or controlled by the Government or receiving foreign contributions above a threshold under the FCRA. The judiciary is not covered. Wings: an Inquiry Wing (preliminary inquiry) and a Prosecution Wing ; the Lokpal can superintend the CBI in cases referred by it; the preliminary inquiry must usually be completed in 90 days; the investigation in six months; special courts are to try cases within a time limit; there is provision for attachment of assets from corruption; a complaint should be made within seven years of the alleged offence. Lokayuktas: the Act requires States to establish Lokayuktas within one year of commencement (Section 63), but allows States to determine the structure and the powers; so the structure varies. First Lokpal: Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose (a retired Supreme Court judge) was appointed the first Chairperson in March 2019 , five years after the Act. The 2016 amendment relaxed the requirement of public servants to declare assets. (Justice A.M. Khanwilkar was later appointed Chairperson in 2024.) State Lokayuktas Maharashtra was the first State to establish the institution ( Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayuktas Act, 1971 , operational from 1972). Orissa passed an Act in 1970, but it lapsed and was not in force at the time. Others: Rajasthan (1973), Bihar (1974), Uttar Pradesh (1975), Madhya Pradesh (1981), Karnataka (1984 – considered strongest), Gujarat (1986), Delhi (1996), Kerala (1999), etc. Variation: in appointment, jurisdiction (whether the Chief Minister is covered), and powers (investigative or advisory). The Karnataka Lokayukta has police powers and is considered effective. Related Institutions in India Central Vigilance Commission (CVC): set up in 1964 on the recommendation of the Santhanam Committee ; statutory since the CVC Act, 2003. CBI (Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946); Central and State Information Commissions (Right to Information Act, 2005); Banking Ombudsman Scheme (1995) (now integrated under the RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 ); Insurance Ombudsman (1998) ; Income Tax Ombudsman ; National and State Human Rights Commissions (Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993).

p: Open Government and Right to Information: USA, UK and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Open government is the doctrine that the business of government should be open to public scrutiny, based on transparency, participation and accountability. Secrecy should be the exception, not the rule. The idea rests on democratic theory: citizens cannot hold government accountable without information. Justice Louis Brandeis (USA): "Sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants" ( Other People's Money , 1914) – the most quoted line on transparency. James Madison: a popular government without popular information is a prologue to a farce or a tragedy. Sweden: the Freedom of the Press Act, 1766 is the world's first law giving public access to official documents ( offentlighetsprincipen ). Pillars of open government: (1) proactive disclosure ; (2) right to request information ; (3) open meetings and participation; (4) open data ; (5) protection of whistleblowers ; (6) independent oversight of disclosure disputes. Open Government Partnership (OGP) , launched in 2011 by eight founding governments (including the USA, UK, Brazil, Indonesia, Mexico, Norway, Philippines and South Africa). India has not joined the OGP. Limits: national security, privacy, commercial secrets, law enforcement, deliberative processes of government and international relations.

p: Open Government and Right to Information: USA, UK and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), 1966 Enacted in 1966 (signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson, effective from 1967), replacing the weak disclosure provision of the Administrative Procedure Act, 1946. Principle: presumption of disclosure ; the burden of justifying refusal rests on the agency. Amendments: 1974 (after Watergate: judicial review of classification, time limits, fee waivers); 1996 (Electronic FOIA) ; OPEN Government Act, 2007 (created the Office of Government Information Services, OGIS , as FOIA mediator/ombudsman); FOIA Improvement Act, 2016 (a "foreseeable harm" standard : an agency may withhold exempt material only if disclosure would harm an interest protected by the exemption, or if disclosure is prohibited by law). Coverage: federal executive agencies (including independent agencies and government corporations). It does not cover Congress, the federal courts, and the President's immediate staff (the White House Office); State governments have their own laws. Procedure: a request to the agency; a decision within 20 working days ; administrative appeal; then judicial review in a federal district court , de novo , where the agency has the burden. Vaughn v Rosen (1973) led to the "Vaughn index" (the agency's itemised justification for withholding documents). Courts can order production and award attorney fees. The Nine Exemptions (Memory List) Classified national defence or foreign policy information. Internal personnel rules and practices of an agency. Information exempted by other statutes. Trade secrets and confidential commercial or financial information. Inter-agency or intra-agency memoranda that would be privileged in litigation ( deliberative process privilege , attorney–client, work product). Personnel and medical files where disclosure would be a "clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy". Law enforcement records (with specified harms). Records on the regulation or supervision of financial institutions. Geological and geophysical information concerning wells. (Also, there are special exclusions for certain law enforcement and national security records.) Related Statutes Privacy Act, 1974 (protects personal records held by federal agencies; individuals can access and correct their records). Government in the Sunshine Act, 1976 (open meetings of multi-member federal agencies). Federal Advisory Committee Act, 1972 (open advisory committees). Presidential Records Act, 1978 (presidential records are public property; released after a period). Whistleblower Protection Act, 1989. Obama Memorandum on Transparency and Open Government (2009) and the Open Government Directive (2009) ; Data.gov. Leading FOIA Cases EPA v Mink (1973): national security exemption and classification; led to the 1974 amendments. NLRB v Robbins Tire (1978): exemption 7 and the law enforcement process. Department of Justice v Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (1989): privacy exemption; compiled "rap sheets" protected as practical obscurity. National Archives and Records Administration v Favish (2004): privacy interests of family members. Milner v Department of the Navy (2011): narrow reading of exemption 2. Constitutional basis: the US Constitution contains no express right to information; the right is statutory (the First Amendment does not guarantee a general right of access to government information). Some cases (e.g., Richmond Newspapers v Virginia , 1980) recognise a right of access to criminal trials.

p: Open Government and Right to Information: USA, UK and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Freedom of Information Act, 2000 (FOIA 2000) Passed in 2000 ; the right of access came fully into force on 1 January 2005. Earlier, the UK relied on a culture of secrecy: the Official Secrets Act 1911 (section 2) , replaced by the Official Secrets Act 1989 ; the non-statutory Code of Practice on Access to Government Information (1994) . The Labour Government's White Paper Your Right to Know (1997) preceded the Act. Scope: covers public authorities listed in Schedule 1 (government departments, local authorities, NHS, police, schools, universities, etc.). The Scottish FOI Act, 2002 applies to Scottish public bodies. Environmental Information Regulations 2004 cover environmental information. Two main duties (section 1): (1) the duty to confirm or deny whether the authority holds the information; (2) the duty to communicate the information. Section 19: every authority must adopt a publication scheme (proactive disclosure). Timing and cost: 20 working days; no fee for requests but an authority can refuse requests that exceed an appropriate cost limit ( £600 for central government and £450 for other authorities ); vexatious or repeated requests can be refused ( section 14 ). Exemptions (Part II): about two dozen, divided into: Absolute exemptions: no public interest test applies – e.g., section 21 (information accessible by other means), section 23 (security bodies), section 32 (court records), section 34 (parliamentary privilege), section 36 (prejudice to effective conduct of public affairs, as regards the House of Commons/Lords), section 37 (communications with the Sovereign, heir and second in line – absolute since the 2010 amendment), section 40 (personal information of the applicant; and personal data of third parties in some cases), section 41 (information provided in confidence), section 44 (statutory prohibitions). Qualified exemptions: subject to the public interest test (public interest in maintaining the exemption must outweigh the public interest in disclosure) – e.g., section 24 (national security), section 26 (defence), section 27 (international relations), section 29 (economy), section 30 (investigations), section 31 (law enforcement), section 35 (formulation of government policy), section 36 (effective conduct of public affairs), section 38 (health and safety), section 42 (legal professional privilege), section 43 (commercial interests). Enforcement: the Information Commissioner (ICO) (independent; also oversees data protection); appeals lie to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) , then the Upper Tribunal and the courts on points of law. Ministerial veto (section 53): a cabinet minister can issue a certificate overriding the Commissioner's decision. R (Evans) v Attorney General (2015, UK Supreme Court): the "black spider memos" of Prince Charles; the Court held that the Attorney General could not override the court's decision merely because he disagreed, and the certificate was unlawful, upholding the rule of law and the finality of judicial decisions. Historic significance: the MPs' expenses scandal (2009) was uncovered through FOI requests; it advanced the transparency agenda. Open government agenda: the UK was a founding member of the OGP; data.gov.uk and the transparency agenda from 2010. Related laws: Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR; Public Records Act 1958 (30-year rule, reduced to 20 years by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 ); Official Secrets Act 1989 .

p: Open Government and Right to Information: USA, UK and India · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Constitutional Foundations No express provision, but the Supreme Court has read the right to know and to receive information into Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech and expression) and Article 21. State of Uttar Pradesh v Raj Narain (1975): the Court rejected the government's claim of privilege under Section 123 of the Evidence Act , saying that the people have a right to know every public act, done in a public way; Justice K.K. Mathew said that in a government of responsibility, secrecy can only be for a few, and publicity is the rule. S.P. Gupta v Union of India (1981): the right to know is implicit in the right to free speech; open government is the new democratic culture; disclosure is the rule, secrecy the exception. Secretary, Ministry of I&B v Cricket Association of Bengal (1995): airwaves are public property; the right to receive information. Dinesh Trivedi v Union of India (1997): in a modern democracy, the citizen must have the right to know about the affairs of government. Association for Democratic Reforms v Union of India (2002) and PUCL v Union of India (2003): voters have the right to know about the antecedents and assets of candidates; ADR v Union of India (2024) struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme , holding that voters' right to information about political funding is protected under Article 19(1)(a). Pre-RTI secrecy framework: the Official Secrets Act, 1923 (Section 5), Indian Evidence Act (Sections 123, 124) , and the Civil Service Conduct Rules. Road to the RTI Act Grassroots movement: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS) in Rajasthan ( Aruna Roy , Nikhil Dey, Shankar Singh) in the 1990s, which demanded public access to muster rolls and expenditure details ( jan sunwai – public hearings). The National Campaign for People's Right to Information (NCPRI) (1996). Press Council of India draft (1996) and the Shourie Committee (1997) drafted bills. State laws: Tamil Nadu (1997), Goa (1997), Rajasthan (2000), Karnataka (2000), Delhi (2001), Maharashtra (2002), and others. Freedom of Information Act, 2002 (passed by Parliament but never brought into force; criticised as weak). Right to Information Act, 2005: passed in June 2005 (assent 15 June 2005); came fully into force on 12 October 2005 (the National Advisory Council under the UPA government helped to strengthen it). Key Provisions of the RTI Act, 2005 Section 2(h): "public authority" (government bodies, and bodies owned, controlled or substantially financed by the government; NGOs substantially financed by the government). Thalappalam Service Cooperative Bank v State of Kerala (2013) discussed "substantially financed". Section 2(j): the "right to information" includes inspection of work, documents and records; taking notes, extracts or certified copies; taking samples; and obtaining information in electronic form. Section 3: all citizens have the right to information (not non-citizens or companies as such). Section 4: proactive disclosure – Section 4(1)(b) requires publication of 17 categories of information (organisation, functions, duties, powers, decision-making procedures, norms, budget, subsidies and so on). Sections 5–7: Public Information Officers (PIOs) and Assistant PIOs; application with a prescribed fee (typically Rs. 10) – BPL applicants are exempt ; decision within 30 days ; 48 hours where the information concerns the life or liberty of a person. Section 8 – Exemptions: 8(1)(a): information prejudicial to sovereignty and integrity of India, security, strategic, scientific or economic interests, relations with foreign States, or incitement to an offence. 8(1)(b): information expressly forbidden to be published by a court or tribunal, or the disclosure of which may constitute contempt of court. 8(1)(c): breach of privilege of Parliament or State Legislature. 8(1)(d): commercial confidence, trade secrets, intellectual property (unless larger public interest). 8(1)(e): information available to a person in a fiduciary relationship (unless larger public interest). 8(1)(f): information received in confidence from a foreign government. 8(1)(g): information that would endanger the life or physical safety of any person or identify a confidential source. 8(1)(h): information that would impede investigation or prosecution of offenders. 8(1)(i): Cabinet papers , including records of deliberations of the Council of Ministers, Secretaries and other officers (after the decision is taken, and the matter is complete or over, the material is open). 8(1)(j): personal information that has no relationship with any public activity or interest, or that would cause an unwarranted invasion of privacy, unless a larger public interest justifies disclosure. The proviso says that information that cannot be denied to Parliament or a State Legislature cannot be denied to a person. ( The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, section 44(3), amends Section 8(1)(j) to exempt personal information more broadly and to omit the existing qualification, a change criticised by transparency advocates; verify its current commencement status.) 8(2): a public interest override – information may be disclosed if the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to protected interests. 8(3): the exemptions do not apply to information relating to events that occurred 20 years before the request (except for 8(1)(a), (c) and (i)). Section 9: rejection for infringement of copyright; Section 10: severability; Section 11: third-party information. Section 22: the RTI Act overrides the Official Secrets Act, 1923 and other inconsistent laws. Section 24 and Second Schedule: intelligence and security organisations (e.g., IB, RAW, CBI is not exempt but CBI is not listed... check); the exemption does not apply to allegations of corruption and human rights violations (for human rights information, the Information Commission's approval is needed, and the response must be within 45 days). Section 23: the jurisdiction of courts is barred (but the constitutional writ jurisdiction under Articles 32, 226 and 136 remains). Appeals and Information Commissions First appeal: to an officer senior to the PIO within the same authority (within 30 days ). Second appeal (Section 19(3)): to the Central Information Commission (CIC) or State Information Commission (SIC) within 90 days . Complaints (Section 18): directly to the Commission for refusal to accept an application and similar matters. Penalty (Section 20): Rs. 250 per day of delay, up to a maximum of Rs. 25,000 , on the PIO; disciplinary action recommended; compensation (Section 19(8)(b)) to the applicant. Composition: CIC – Chief Information Commissioner and up to 10 Information Commissioners ; appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee: Prime Minister (Chair), Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM. For SICs: the Chief Minister, the Leader of Opposition and a Cabinet Minister nominated by the CM; appointed by the Governor. RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019: removed the statutory tenure (five years or until 65) and the status of Election Commissioners/Chief Election Commissioner , with the Central Government now empowered to prescribe the terms, salaries and tenure by rules. It was criticised as weakening the independence of the commissions. Leading RTI cases: CBSE v Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011): examinees' right to inspect evaluated answer-books; also warned against using the RTI Act to disrupt administration or for impractical demands. Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v Central Information Commissioner (2012): personal information such as income tax returns and service records is exempt under section 8(1)(j) unless there is a larger public interest. Reserve Bank of India v Jayantilal N. Mistry (2015): RBI cannot withhold inspection reports and other documents on banks under the "fiduciary" exemption; transparency in financial regulation. Namit Sharma v Union of India (2012/2013): the earlier decision that Information Commissions should have judicial members was clarified in the review (2013). Central Public Information Officer, Supreme Court of India v Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019): the office of the CJI is a public authority under the RTI Act; the collegium's information is subject to exemptions and a balancing test; RTI is not a tool for surveillance of the judiciary. Anjali Bhardwaj v Union of India (2019): the Court directed timely appointments to Information Commissions. Related law: the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 (not fully operationalised).

x: Match the following: scholar ↔ idea (Bagehot, Dicey, Wheare, Fuller, Raz, Dworkin, Montesquieu, Madison, Kelsen, Zweigert and Kötz); case ↔ principle (Marbury, Kesavananda, Bommai, McCulloch, Ram Jawaya Kapur, Youngstown, Maneka Gandhi). Country ↔ feature: residuary power with the States/Centre; judicial review absent for federal statutes (Switzerland); a priori review (France); Ombudsman in Sweden; collegial executive (Switzerland). Assertion–reason: federalism and basic structure; Article 368 and ratification by States; rule of law and ADM Jabalpur. Chronology: FOIA 1966 → Privacy Act 1974 → FOIA UK 2000 → RTI 2005; Marbury 1803 → Kelsen 1920 → French 1958; Kesavananda 1973 → Minerva Mills 1980 → Coelho 2007. Statements true/false: UK has no strict separation of powers; India has single citizenship; the President in the US has no role in amendments; Switzerland's Federal Supreme Court cannot strike down federal acts. Odd-one-out: e.g., in federal states – USA, Canada, India, UK (UK is unitary).
