t: Overview: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage
p: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage · Family Law
x: Core idea: Hindu marriage is traditionally a sacrament (religious, indissoluble, for lives to come) but the Hindu Marriage Act 1955 introduced contract-like features (divorce, registration, consent). Muslim marriage is a civil contract (nikah) with religious sanctity. Christian marriage is a sacrament in church law and a statutory contract in the Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872. The Special Marriage Act 1954 offers a secular civil marriage open to all.

t: Memory Capsule: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage
p: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage · Family Law
x: Under HMA, marriage within the first year of marriage cannot be dissolved by divorce (Section 14), unless exceptional hardship or depravity. Void marriage under Section 11 does not need a decree to be void; Section 12 voidable marriage is valid until annulled. Section 7 HMA: saptapadi completes the marriage only where the customary rites include it. In Sunni law marriage without witnesses is irregular (fasid), not void; in Shia law witnesses are not required. Muta is Shia only; Hasan and Ahsan are Sunni descriptions; talaq-e-biddat is Hanafi-originated. Section 2(vii) DMMA is about the repudiation of marriage by girl before age 18.

t: Analysis Angle: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage
p: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage · Family Law
x: Recent trend: Dolly Rani (2024) on sanctity and ceremonies; State UCCs ban polygamy, halala, triple talaq and mandate registration of marriages; the Supreme Court has repeatedly said that registration is mandatory for evidence but not a condition of validity.

p: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce · Family Law
x: Theory Meaning Where it appears in Indian law Criticism Fault, guilt or offence theory Divorce is a remedy for an innocent spouse against a spouse who has committed a matrimonial offence (adultery, cruelty, desertion) Section 13(1) HMA; Section 27 SMA; Section 10 Divorce Act; Section 32 Parsi Act Needs proof; encourages mud-slinging; bars a petitioner at fault (Section 23(1)(a)) Mutual consent theory Marriage is a contract that parties can end by agreement Section 13B HMA; Section 28 SMA; Section 10A Divorce Act; Section 32B Parsi Act; khula and mubarat in Muslim law Risk of collusion and coerced consent; consent must persist until decree (Sureshta Devi) Irretrievable breakdown theory Divorce should follow if the marriage is dead, regardless of fault Not a statutory ground under HMA; recommended by Law Commission 71st Report (1978), 217th Report (2009); Marriage Laws (Amendment) Bill 2010 lapsed; Supreme Court uses Article 142 (Shilpa Sailesh, 2023) Judicial discretion; risk to women without economic security (hence alimony safeguards) Frustration by specified circumstances (disease and incapacity theory) Marriage frustrated by incurable mental disorder, communicable disease, renunciation of world, presumption of death Section 13(1)(iii), (v), (vi), (vii) HMA Medical proof issues; stigma Divorce by custom Dissolution under recognised customs Section 29(2) HMA saves customary divorce rights; Section 3(a) defines custom; Gujarat UCC 2026 reportedly abolishes extra-judicial and customary divorce in the State (verify) Evidence of custom must be strict

p: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce · Family Law
x: Conditions: either spouse has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other; the petitioner may apply to the district court for restitution; Section 9(2): the burden of proving reasonable excuse is on the person who has withdrawn. Constitutionality: T. Sareetha v T. Venkata Subbaiah (AP High Court, 1983) struck it down as a violation of privacy, dignity and bodily integrity under Article 21; Harvinder Kaur v Harmander Singh Choudhry (Delhi High Court, 1984) upheld it, saying the remedy aims at cohabitation, not sexual intercourse; Saroj Rani v Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (Supreme Court, 1984) upheld Section 9 as a measure to preserve marriage, not violating Articles 14 or 21. Consequence: a decree is enforced by attachment of property (Order XXI Rule 32 CPC), not by compelling cohabitation. No restitution within one year ends in a ground for divorce: Section 13(1A)(ii). Pending challenge: Ojaswa Pathak v Union of India (a writ challenging Section 9) was pending before the Supreme Court at last report (verify).

p: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce · Family Law
x: Available on any of the Section 13(1) grounds and, for a wife, the Section 13(2) grounds. Effects: no obligation to cohabit, but the marital status continues; the decree can be rescinded by the court (Section 10(2)). After one year without resumption of cohabitation, either party may seek divorce under Section 13(1A)(i) (reduced from two years in 1976).

t: 3.4 Divorce grounds: Section 13(1) HMA (available to both spouses)
p: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce · Family Law
x: Clause Ground Key points and cases (i) Adultery: voluntary sexual intercourse with a person other than spouse after the marriage A single act suffices after 1976; Joseph Shine v Union of India (2018) decriminalised adultery (Section 497 IPC struck down) but it remains a civil ground for divorce (ia) Cruelty (physical or mental) Dastane (1975): standard is balance of probabilities, and the conduct must cause reasonable apprehension that cohabitation would be harmful; Shobha Rani v Madhukar Reddi (1988): wilful or unjustifiable conduct, dowry demand is cruelty; V. Bhagat v D. Bhagat (1994); Samar Ghosh v Jaya Ghosh (2007): non-exhaustive list of mental cruelty indicators; K. Srinivas Rao v D.A. Deepa (2013): false and malicious allegations amount to cruelty; Sonal Talpada v Veerbhan Singh (2026 INSC 620, reported): persistent refusal of sexual intercourse without reasonable cause is mental cruelty (verify) (ib) Desertion for a continuous period of at least two years immediately before the petition Bipinchandra Jaisinghbhai Shah v Prabhawati (1957): factum of separation, animus deserendi, absence of consent and of justification (for the deserting party); constructive desertion recognised (Lachman Utamchand Kirpalani v Meena, 1964) (ii) Conversion: has ceased to be a Hindu by conversion to another religion Gives ground to the petitioner spouse; Section 13(1)(vi) is renunciation by entering a religious order (iii) Unsound mind, incurable, or mental disorder continuous or intermittent of such kind and extent that the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with respondent Explanation covers schizophrenia, psychopathic disorder; Ram Narain Gupta v Rameshwari Gupta (1988); Sharda v Dharmpal (2003): court may order medical examination, not violative of Article 21 (iv) Leprosy Deleted by the Personal Laws (Amendment) Act 2019 (verify) (v) Venereal disease in a communicable form No requirement of wilful transmission (vi) Renunciation of the world by entering any religious order (vii) Not heard of as alive for seven years or more by those who would naturally have heard Presumption of death (Section 108 Evidence Act, now Section 111 BSA) Section 13(1A): either party can petition for divorce if there has been (i) no resumption of cohabitation for one year or more after a decree of judicial separation, or (ii) no restitution of conjugal rights for one year or more after a decree. Section 13(2): grounds only for wife: (i) husband had another wife alive at the commencement of the Act (pre-1955 bigamy); (ii) husband guilty of rape, sodomy or bestiality after marriage; (iii) a decree or order of maintenance (Section 18 HAMA or Section 125 CrPC) passed against husband and no cohabitation for one year or more thereafter; (iv) repudiation: marriage solemnised before she was 15 and she repudiated it after 15 and before 18. In 2026 the Supreme Court (CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi) dismissed Jitender Singh v Union of India (W.P.(C) 460/2026), a PIL by a man seeking gender parity in Section 13(2)(iii), saying special provisions for women are constitutionally permitted (reported; verify).

p: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce · Family Law
x: The court grants relief only if: (a) the petitioner is not taking advantage of his or her own wrong (the bar of ‘own wrong’); (b) the petitioner has not been accessory to or connived at the act complained of; (bb) no condonation (forgiveness with restoration to former marital status; revives if the condoned offence repeats); (c) not collusive; (d) no unnecessary or improper delay; (e) no other legal ground for refusing relief. Section 23(2): court must try to reconcile where possible. Section 14: no divorce petition within one year of marriage unless exceptional hardship or exceptional depravity. Section 15: remarriage after decree allowed once the time for appeal lapses or the appeal is dismissed (Section 28). Section 21B: trial day-to-day; Section 21A: transfer of petitions; Section 19: jurisdiction: place of marriage, where respondent resides, where parties last resided together, or where the wife resides (inserted 2003).

p: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce · Family Law
x: 13B(1): a joint petition on the ground that they have been living separately for one year or more, have not been able to live together and have mutually agreed to dissolve the marriage. 13B(2): the second motion not earlier than six months and not later than eighteen months after the petition; if the petition is not withdrawn, the court after inquiry grants a decree. Consent must continue until decree: Sureshta Devi v Om Prakash (1991); the Supreme Court in Hitesh Bhatnagar v Deepa Bhatnagar (2011) reaffirmed that one party can withdraw consent before the decree; Anil Kumar Jain v Maya Jain (2009) held that only the Supreme Court, under Article 142, could waive the statutory period, a rigid view later softened by Amardeep Singh (2017). Cooling-off period is directory: Amardeep Singh v Harveen Kaur (2017): it can be waived by the Family Court if the statutory one-year separation is over, efforts at mediation have failed, the parties have settled alimony and custody, and waiting would only prolong agony. Shilpa Sailesh v Varun Sreenivasan (2023, five judges) also approved this. Recent: A Supreme Court bench in S v State of Odisha (Justices Nagarathna and Mahadevan, 28 September 2026, reported) invoked Article 142 to grant divorce by mutual consent, awarded alimony and quashed 18 pending civil and criminal cases between the parties, observing that Section 13B does not limit its power (verify; 2026 INSC 1060 appears in a report).

p: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce · Family Law
x: Shilpa Sailesh v Varun Sreenivasan (2023) : Constitution Bench of Justices Kaul, Khanna, Oka, Vikram Nath and Maheshwari. Held: the Supreme Court may dissolve a marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown under Article 142(1) to do ‘complete justice’, even though it is not a statutory ground; it is not a matter of right, but a discretion to be exercised with care; it may also quash related criminal proceedings; it can waive the 6-month period; the Court laid down factors such as period of separation (a long separation, often six years or more, is relevant), efforts at reconciliation, nature of allegations, number of proceedings, the interest of children and financial security of the wife, but refused to fix a rigid rule. High Courts cannot use Article 142; family courts cannot treat irretrievable breakdown as a ground. Earlier cases: Naveen Kohli v Neelu Kohli (2006) recommended amendment; Vishnu Dutt Sharma v Manju Sharma (2009) said courts cannot add a ground; Samar Ghosh listed long separation as indicating irretrievable breakdown. 2026 applications (reported; verify): Neha Lal v Abhishek Kumar (2026 INSC 73, 20 January 2026): marriage dissolved over the husband’s objection after only 65 days of cohabitation and over ten years of separation with more than forty proceedings; judgment of 2 June 2026 dissolving a marriage of two government doctors separated for fifteen years (‘stale and frozen’ marriages); 27 May 2026 (Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta) dissolved an Army officer and doctor’s marriage with large permanent alimony.

p: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce · Family Law
x: Section 24: interim maintenance and expenses of proceedings to the spouse with no independent income sufficient for support (either wife or husband); to be decided within 60 days of service. Section 25: permanent alimony and maintenance (gross sum or monthly), modifiable if circumstances change; it ceases on remarriage or unchastity (wife) or if the husband has sex outside marriage (husband). Section 26: custody, maintenance and education of minor children; welfare is paramount. Section 27: disposal of property presented at or about the time of marriage that belongs jointly to both spouses. Rajnesh v Neha (2020) mandates an affidavit of disclosure of assets and liabilities in all maintenance cases; interim maintenance from the date of application; no fixed formula (reaffirmed in 2026 decisions: verify). Anamika Jain (28 January 2026, Section 25 HMA): a working wife can still be entitled to alimony; maintenance enhanced from Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000 per month (verify).

t: Overview: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce
p: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce · Family Law
x: Core idea: The Hindu Marriage Act gives six matrimonial reliefs: restitution of conjugal rights (Section 9), judicial separation (Section 10), nullity (Sections 11–12), divorce (Section 13), divorce by mutual consent (Section 13B) and ancillary reliefs (Sections 24–27: maintenance, alimony, custody, property). The philosophy has moved from the fault theory (guilty spouse) to consent and, through Article 142, towards irretrievable breakdown .

t: Memory Capsule: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce
p: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce · Family Law
x: Desertion period is two years under HMA (Section 13(1)(ib)); judicial separation or restitution non-compliance is one year under Section 13(1A). Section 13(2) grounds are for the wife only; Section 13(1) grounds are for both. Conversion is a ground for the other spouse to seek divorce; it does not dissolve the marriage automatically. Section 13B requires a joint petition; Section 14 bar (one year) applies to Section 13, and Section 13B has its own one-year separation condition. ‘Irretrievable breakdown’ is NOT a statutory ground under HMA; the Supreme Court uses Article 142 (not High Courts). Cruelty burden of proof: preponderance, not ‘beyond reasonable doubt’ (Dastane).

t: Analysis Angle: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce
p: Matrimonial Remedies: Divorce and Theories of Divorce · Family Law
x: Recent trend: The Supreme Court is trying to shorten matrimonial litigation (Article 142, mediation, quashing of cross-FIRs), while insisting on adequate permanent alimony and on settling custody and visitation at the same time. Statutory amendment to introduce irretrievable breakdown remains pending.

p: Changing Dimensions of Marriage: Live-in Relationships · Family Law
x: Not an offence: S. Khushboo v Kanniammal (2010): living together is part of the right to life; premarital sex and live-in relationships are not criminal. Lata Singh v State of UP (2006): consenting adults may live together. Presumption of marriage: Where a man and a woman have lived together as husband and wife for a long period, the law presumes a valid marriage: Gokal Chand v Parvin Kumari (1952); Badri Prasad v Dy. Director of Consolidation (1978): a strong presumption in favour of marriage; S.P.S. Balasubramanyam v Suruttayan (1993): cohabitation as husband and wife raises a presumption of marriage and the children are legitimate; Tulsa v Durghatiya (2008); Dhannulal v Ganeshram (2015). The presumption is rebuttable and cannot be raised for a ‘walk-in, walk-out’ relationship. Maintenance: Chanmuniya v Virendra Kumar Singh Kushwaha (2010) read ‘wife’ in Section 125 CrPC widely to include a woman in a long relationship of marriage-like nature; referred a question to a larger bench (whether a strict proof of marriage is needed). Lalita Toppo v State of Jharkhand (2018) held a live-in partner entitled to maintenance under the DV Act (not necessarily under Section 125) and noted the DV Act protects ‘relationships in the nature of marriage’. Domestic Violence Act 2005: Section 2(f): ‘domestic relationship’ includes a relationship between two persons who live or have lived together in a shared household when they are related by consanguinity, marriage, a relationship in the nature of marriage , adoption or joint family. Reliefs: Section 18 (protection orders), 19 (residence orders), 20 (monetary relief), 21 (custody), 22 (compensation).

p: Changing Dimensions of Marriage: Live-in Relationships · Family Law
x: Case Holding D. Velusamy v D. Patchaiammal (2010) Four conditions for ‘relationship in the nature of marriage’: (1) couple must hold themselves out to society as spouses; (2) must be of legal age to marry; (3) must be qualified to enter into a legal marriage including being unmarried; (4) must have voluntarily cohabited and held themselves out as spouses for a significant period. A ‘keep’ or mistress, a weekend or one-night relationship is not covered Indra Sarma v V.K.V. Sarma (2013) Guidelines: duration of relationship, shared household, pooling of resources, domestic arrangements, sexual relationship, children, socialisation, intention and conduct. A relationship with a married man knowingly is not ‘in the nature of marriage’ and the woman may not get DV Act protection (the court suggested legislative reform) Nandakumar v State of Kerala (2018) Two adults can live together even if the man is below the marriageable age of 21; the couple’s live-in cannot be broken Shafin Jahan v Asokan (2018) (Hadiya) Choice of partner is part of Articles 19 and 21; courts cannot annul a marriage by exercising parens patriae over an adult Shakti Vahini v Union of India (2018) Khap or family interference in adult marriages is illegal; guidelines for preventive, remedial and punitive measures Bharatha Matha v R. Vijaya Renganathan (2010) Child of a live-in or void relationship is legitimate under Section 16 HMA but takes only parents’ self-acquired property (before Revanasiddappa 2023) Revanasiddappa v Mallikarjun (2023) Children of void and voidable marriages are entitled to parents’ property including ancestral share; the logic extends to children of long-term relationships Lokesh B.H. v State of Karnataka (3 August 2026, reported) Section 498A IPC (now Section 85 BNS) can apply to a live-in relationship that qualifies as ‘in the nature of marriage’ and where the intention was to marry; mere cohabitation, casual or one-night arrangements do not qualify; arrest safeguards of Arnesh Kumar apply (verify) Supreme Court (April 2026, reported) A child born of a live-in relationship is not ‘illegitimate’ and retains rights; courts must distinguish consensual relationships from sexual offences (verify) Punjab and Haryana High Court (CRWP-2691-2026, 10 March 2026) and Delhi High Court (W.P.(CRL) 665/2026, 24 February 2026) Article 21 protection extends to live-in couples, including married adults who are in live-in with another person; protection from family threats without commenting on validity of the relationship (reported)

t: 4.3 Statutory live-in rules in State UCCs
p: Changing Dimensions of Marriage: Live-in Relationships · Family Law
x: Uttarakhand UCC Act 2024: Part on live-in relationships: compulsory registration with the Registrar for residents of the State (also those residing outside); parental consent for those under 21; registration of termination; penalties of imprisonment and fine for non-registration or false statements (amounts vary; do not memorise); children are legitimate; a woman abandoned by her live-in partner may claim maintenance. Gujarat UCC 2026: applies to marriage and divorce, succession and live-in relationships; includes registration of live-in relationships and their termination, a prohibition on bigamy, and a rule that a marriage is valid only if neither party has a living spouse; excludes Scheduled Tribes and certain groups with constitutionally protected customs; applies to residents of Gujarat even outside the State; received Presidential assent (reported on 5 October 2026), with rules to be notified before it takes effect (verify).

t: Overview: Changing Dimensions of Marriage: Live-in Relationships
p: Changing Dimensions of Marriage: Live-in Relationships · Family Law
x: Core idea: There is still no central statute on live-in relationships. Indian law protects them piecemeal: courts treat them as lawful between consenting adults (Article 21), presume marriage after long cohabitation (Section 114 Evidence Act, now Section 119 BSA), give some remedies under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 (DV Act), and recognise the legitimacy of children. State UCCs (Uttarakhand 2024; Gujarat 2026) are the first statutes to make live-in registration compulsory.

t: Memory Capsule: Changing Dimensions of Marriage: Live-in Relationships
p: Changing Dimensions of Marriage: Live-in Relationships · Family Law
x: Live-in relationship is not defined in any central statute; the DV Act uses ‘relationship in the nature of marriage’. Velusamy’s test requires both to be unmarried and of marriageable age, and to have cohabited for a significant period. A live-in partner is not automatically a ‘wife’ for Section 125 CrPC; courts apply a strictness test (Chanmuniya) and the DV Act gives alternative relief. Supriyo: no right to marry; SMA not struck; adoption by queer couples not recognised by the majority.

p: Recognition of Foreign Decrees on Marriage and Divorce · Family Law
x: Section 2(5) and 2(6) CPC: ‘foreign court’ and ‘foreign judgment’. Section 13 CPC: a foreign judgment is conclusive as to any matter directly adjudicated between the same parties, except where: (a) it has not been pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction; (b) it has not been given on the merits of the case; (c) it appears on the face of the proceedings to be founded on an incorrect view of international law or a refusal to recognise the law of India where applicable; (d) the proceedings in which it was obtained are opposed to natural justice; (e) it has been obtained by fraud; (f) it sustains a claim founded on a breach of any law in force in India. Memory aid: C-M-I-N-F-B (Competence, Merits, International law, Natural justice, Fraud, Breach of Indian law). Section 14 CPC: presumption that a foreign judgment was pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction (rebuttable). Section 44A CPC: a decree of a superior court of a ‘reciprocating territory’ (notified by the Central Government; e.g., the United Kingdom, Singapore, Bangladesh, UAE, Hong Kong, New Zealand, Trinidad and Tobago, Papua New Guinea, Fiji) is executable in India as if passed by an Indian District Court. The United States is not a reciprocating territory, so a US decree has to be sued on as a foreign judgment. Foreign Marriage Act 1969: applies to marriages of Indian citizens abroad solemnised before a Marriage Officer, and to registration of foreign marriages; its provisions also cover validity and jurisdiction. Section 19 HMA and Section 31 SMA: Indian courts’ jurisdiction in matrimonial causes (place of marriage; where the respondent resides; where parties last resided together; where the wife resides).

t: 5.2 Y. Narasimha Rao v Y. Venkata Lakshmi (1991)
p: Recognition of Foreign Decrees on Marriage and Divorce · Family Law
x: The Supreme Court held that a foreign matrimonial judgment will be recognised in India only if: Jurisdiction: the foreign court had jurisdiction according to the law under which the parties were married (the matrimonial law of the parties); the jurisdiction assumed by the foreign court and the ground on which relief was granted must accord with the Indian matrimonial law (for Hindus, the HMA). Grounds: the ground for relief must be available under that law. Submission: the respondent must have been duly served, voluntarily and effectively submitted to the jurisdiction and contested on merits. Consent: if the decree rests on the respondent’s consent, the consent must be freely given, unequivocal and without fraud or mistake. The Court rejected the rule that residence of the petitioner alone confers jurisdiction. Domicile and residence of the respondent matter; mere short stay of the petitioner in the foreign country is not enough. Ex parte decrees, or decrees on grounds (such as irretrievable breakdown) unknown to Indian personal law, are not recognised unless the respondent consented and submitted.

p: Recognition of Foreign Decrees on Marriage and Divorce · Family Law
x: Case Principle Satya v Teja Singh (1975) Divorce obtained from a Nevada court by a husband who falsely claimed domicile was a fraud on jurisdiction and not recognised Smt. Neerja Saraf v Jayant Saraf (1994) Indian court can decide whether to continue its proceeding when a foreign proceeding is pending; principle of forum non conveniens and comity Harmeeta Singh v Rajat Taneja (Delhi High Court, 2003) Anti-suit injunction against husband who sued in a foreign court to harass wife Veena Kalia v Jatinder Nath Kalia (Delhi High Court, 1996) Ex parte foreign decree not recognised where respondent was not heard Sondur Gopal v Sondur Rajini (2013) Indian court has jurisdiction in divorce where wife resides (in application of Section 19 HMA); foreign decrees do not shut out Indian proceedings if Narasimha Rao tests fail Ruchi Majoo v Sanjeev Majoo (2011) Welfare of the child is paramount; a foreign custody order is only a factor, not a bar Nithya Anand Raghavan v State (NCT of Delhi) (2017) Habeas corpus for custody of a child removed from foreign jurisdiction; Indian court may return the child under comity if it is in the child’s interest Prateek Gupta v Shilpi Gupta (2018) Court’s duty is to protect the child’s welfare; it is not bound to return a child to a foreign court Atul Jain (reported as 2026 LiveLaw (SC) 111, March 2026) Supreme Court (Justice Vikram Nath bench) set aside a High Court order dismissing a divorce petition in India because of a prior US divorce decree: the US decree on irretrievable breakdown is not recognised since that ground does not exist in the HMA and the husband had not effectively submitted to the foreign court; the Court itself granted divorce under Article 142 to end an eighteen-year separation (verify exact case title) International conventions (background): India is not a party to the 1980 Hague Convention on Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (the 2016 Law Commission 263rd Report recommended accession); India is party to the 1993 Hague Convention on Inter-country Adoption (ratified 2003). A Bill for compulsory registration of NRI marriages has been proposed but not enacted (verify).

p: Recognition of Foreign Decrees on Marriage and Divorce · Family Law
x: US ‘no-fault’ divorce decree against an Indian wife who did not appear: not recognised (ex parte, ground not recognised, no submission). Decree obtained by consent of both, after both appeared and contested: recognised if consent is real. Decree from a court in the country where both parties are domiciled and married, on grounds also valid under the personal law: likely recognised. Muslim talaq pronounced abroad: analysed according to the personal law and the 2019 Act when talaq-e-biddat is involved.

t: Overview: Recognition of Foreign Decrees on Marriage and Divorce
p: Recognition of Foreign Decrees on Marriage and Divorce · Family Law
x: Core idea: There is no special statute on foreign matrimonial decrees. Their recognition is governed by Section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (conclusiveness of foreign judgments), read with Sections 14 and 44A CPC, and interpreted for matrimonial causes by Y. Narasimha Rao v Y. Venkata Lakshmi (1991) . The aim is to prevent forum shopping and the ‘quickie’ divorces obtained abroad against an Indian spouse (often a wife left behind in India).

t: Memory Capsule: Recognition of Foreign Decrees on Marriage and Divorce
p: Recognition of Foreign Decrees on Marriage and Divorce · Family Law
x: Section 13 CPC lists six exceptions: (a)–(f). ‘Conclusive’ is the default. Section 44A applies only to decrees from reciprocating territories; the US and Canada are not (UK and Singapore are). Narasimha Rao looks to the respondent’s residence and submission; the petitioner’s short stay is not enough. Foreign decree on a ground unknown to HMA (irretrievable breakdown) is not binding on a Hindu spouse unless the spouse submitted.

p: Maintenance, Dower (Mahr) and Stridhan · Family Law
x: Section Subject Key points 18 Wife’s maintenance Entitled during her lifetime; entitled to live separately and still claim maintenance if husband is guilty of desertion, cruelty, has another living wife, keeps a concubine in the same house or habitually lives with one elsewhere, has converted, or on any other justifying cause (leprosy was also listed earlier; deleted 2019: verify). No maintenance if she is unchaste or ceases to be a Hindu 19 Widowed daughter-in-law Maintenance from father-in-law if she cannot maintain herself from her own earnings, property, her husband’s estate or from her children; obligation exists only if father-in-law has means out of coparcenary property; ceases on remarriage 20 Children and aged parents A Hindu is bound to maintain legitimate or illegitimate children (until minors) and aged or infirm parents and unmarried daughters who cannot maintain themselves 21 Dependants Father, mother, widow, son’s widow, minor sons and daughters of a deceased person etc. 22 Maintenance of dependants from estate Heirs who take the estate are bound to maintain the deceased’s dependants 23 Amount Discretion of court, considering position and status, number of claimants, reasonable wants, claimant’s own property, etc. 24–27 Disqualification, change of circumstances, debts, charge on property Interim and permanent alimony in matrimonial cases: Section 24 (pendente lite; either spouse; decided within 60 days of service of notice); Section 25 (permanent alimony; at the time of or after the decree; may be varied). No fixed formula; the Supreme Court says the amount depends on status, needs, income and conduct (Rajnesh v Neha, 2020; Vinny Parmvir Parmar v Parmvir Parmar, 2011; Kiran Jyot Maini v Anish Pramod Patel, 2024). Rajnesh v Neha (2020): all courts must require an affidavit of assets and liabilities; interim maintenance runs from the date of application; overlapping claims under different laws must be disclosed and adjusted; execution can be done through civil and criminal means. The Supreme Court in 2026 decisions on alimony (Deepa Joshi, Ruchika Rathi, Anju Jain; reported) repeated that there is no fixed formula and that the one-time settlement (‘clean break’) approach can be used with Article 142 (verify).

p: Maintenance, Dower (Mahr) and Stridhan · Family Law
x: Who can claim: wife (including a divorced wife who has not remarried), legitimate or illegitimate minor children, major children with physical or mental abnormality or injury, and father or mother, if unable to maintain themselves , from a person with sufficient means who neglects or refuses to maintain them. Ceiling: the earlier Rs 500 limit was removed in 2001; there is no ceiling now. Disqualification of wife (125(4)): living in adultery; refusing without sufficient reason to live with husband; living separately by mutual consent. Procedure: Magistrate First Class; interim maintenance allowed; Sections 126–128 CrPC: procedure, alteration and enforcement; BNSS: Section 144 (maintenance), Section 145 (procedure), Section 146 (alteration), Section 147 (enforcement). The Supreme Court (Gaurav Joshi, 16 April 2026, reported) held that EMIs and loan commitments cannot defeat a maintenance obligation (verify). Secular and religion-neutral: Bai Tahira v Ali Hussain Fissalli (1979), Fuzlunbi v K. Khader Vali (1980), Shah Bano (1985), Mohd. Abdul Samad v State of Telangana (2024). Vijaya Manohar Arbat v Kashirao Rajaram Sawai (1987): a married daughter with means has a duty to maintain her parents under Section 125.

t: 6.3 Maintenance under Muslim law and the 1986 and 2019 Acts
p: Maintenance, Dower (Mahr) and Stridhan · Family Law
x: During marriage: husband must maintain (nafaqa: food, clothing, lodging) even if the wife has means; the wife loses it if she is disobedient (nashiza) without lawful reason. After divorce (classical law): only during iddat (three months or three menstrual courses; until delivery if pregnant; for a widow four months and ten days). Shah Bano (Mohd. Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum, 1985, Constitution Bench, Chandrachud CJ): Section 125 CrPC applies to Muslim women; mahr is not a sum payable ‘on divorce’ in lieu of maintenance; maintenance of Rs 179.20 per month. The case also urged a UCC. Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986: Section 3: reasonable and fair provision and maintenance within the iddat period, mahr and property; Section 4: if no relatives, the State Waqf Board pays; Section 5: option of Section 125 by joint affidavit. Danial Latifi v Union of India (2001): upheld the 1986 Act but read it down: ‘reasonable and fair provision’ means a lump sum covering her future needs and may extend beyond iddat; Section 125 remains available. Iqbal Bano v State of UP (2007), Shabana Bano v Imran Khan (2010): divorced Muslim woman can claim under Section 125 even after iddat if she has not remarried and is unable to maintain herself. Mohd. Abdul Samad v State of Telangana (10 July 2024): Justices Nagarathna and Masih: a Muslim woman, including one illegally divorced by triple talaq, can seek maintenance under Section 125 CrPC; the remedy is in addition to the 1986 Act and the 2019 Act’s subsistence allowance; Section 125 is secular and religion-neutral. The All India Muslim Personal Law Board criticised it. 2019 Act, Section 5: subsistence allowance for the woman subjected to talaq-e-biddat, fixed by a Magistrate.

p: Maintenance, Dower (Mahr) and Stridhan · Family Law
x: Christians: Divorce Act 1869 Sections 36 (alimony pendente lite) and 37 (permanent alimony); Section 125 CrPC. Parsis: Parsi Act Sections 39 (pendente lite) and 40 (permanent alimony). SMA: Sections 36–37. DV Act 2005: monetary relief (Section 20), residence orders (Section 19). Satish Chander Ahuja v Sneha Ahuja (2020) overruled S.R. Batra v Taruna Batra (2006): a woman can claim residence in a house owned by in-laws if she has lived there in a domestic relationship; Hiral P. Harsora v Kusum Narottamdas Harsora (2016): ‘adult male’ struck from definition of respondent (women can be respondents); Prabha Tyagi v Kamlesh Devi (2022): actual residence at the time of filing not required. Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007: tribunal-based maintenance for parents and senior citizens. Dowry Prohibition Act 1961: Section 3 (giving or taking dowry: at least five years’ imprisonment and fine at least Rs 15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is more), Section 4 (demanding), Section 6 (dowry to be held in trust for the woman); BNS Section 80 (dowry death: minimum seven years); BSA Section 118 (presumption of dowry death).

p: Maintenance, Dower (Mahr) and Stridhan · Family Law
x: Definition: a sum of money or other property which the wife is entitled to receive from the husband in consideration of the marriage (Hedaya; Mulla). Mahmood J. in Abdul Kadir v Salima (1886): dower is not the price of consideration but an obligation imposed by law on the husband as a mark of respect for the wife. Classification Meaning Specified (mahr-i-musamma) Fixed by agreement before, at or after marriage Proper (mahr-i-misl) Not specified: assessed by reference to the dower of paternal female relatives of the wife (her father’s family: sisters, aunts), her own personal qualities and her husband’s status Prompt (muajjal) Payable on demand; wife can refuse cohabitation until it is paid; if marriage is not consummated she can refuse sexual relations Deferred (muwajjal) Payable on dissolution of marriage by death or divorce; it is not payable earlier unless agreed Amount: minimum under Hanafi law is 10 dirhams; Maliki 3 dirhams; Shia and Shafi’i: no fixed minimum. No maximum. If marriage is dissolved before consummation: half of the specified dower is due; if none was specified, a consolatory gift (mutah). Dower is a debt: the wife is an unsecured creditor of the husband’s estate ranking equally with other creditors; heirs are liable only to the extent of the estate in their hands, in proportion to their shares. Widow’s right of retention: if she is lawfully in possession of the husband’s property, she can retain it until her dower is paid, but she does not acquire title ( Maina Bibi v Chaudhri Vakil Ahmad , PC 1924; Kapore Chand v Kadar Unnisa , SC 1953). Remission: wife can remit (hiba-i-mahr) with free consent. Dower and the 1986 Act: mahr is to be paid at divorce in addition to maintenance (Section 3). Dower vs dowry: dower is the wife’s legal right in Muslim law and is not prohibited; dowry is illegal under the Dowry Prohibition Act 1961.

p: Maintenance, Dower (Mahr) and Stridhan · Family Law
x: Meaning: a woman’s absolute property over which she has full right of ownership and disposal. In classical Hindu law (Manu, Yajnavalkya, Narada, Katyayana) stridhan covers: gifts before the nuptial fire (adhyagni), at the bridal procession (adhyavahanika), gifts of affection (pritidatta, from in-laws), gifts at the time of leave-taking or obeisance (padavandanika), gifts from relatives (saudayika), subsequent gifts (anvadheyaka), and (in some texts) bridal price (sulka). The Mitakshara gives the widest meaning (including property by inheritance, partition, purchase, and her own earnings), the Dayabhaga narrower; the Bombay school (Vyavahara Mayukha) is in between. Section 14 HSA: any property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the Act, is held as full owner and not as limited owner; ‘property’ includes inheritance, devise, partition, maintenance or arrears, gift, own skill or exertion, purchase, prescription, and her stridhan. Section 14(2): property acquired by gift, will, instrument, decree or award which prescribes a restricted estate is excepted. V. Tulasamma v Sesha Reddy (1977): a widow’s right of maintenance converts a limited estate into an absolute estate under Section 14(1); Section 14(2) is a narrow exception. Eramma v Verrupanna (1966), Bai Vajia v Thakorbhai Chelabhai (1979): possession is a requirement. Husband’s position: he has no right over stridhan during marriage except in an emergency, and must restore it ( Pratibha Rani v Suraj Kumar , 1985: stridhan is the wife’s sole property; refusal to return it is criminal breach of trust under Section 406 IPC, now BNS Section 316). Rashmi Kumar v Mahesh Kumar Bhada (1997) reaffirms. The Supreme Court in 2024–25 judgments (reported; for instance Maya Gopinathan v Anoop S.B. , verify) again held that stridhan is exclusively the woman’s and that the husband and in-laws hold it only in trust. Section 27 HMA: court may pass orders about property presented at or about the time of marriage which belongs jointly to both parties. Succession to stridhan: Section 15 HSA (see topic 8 ): the pattern depends on the source (parents’ or husband’s family). Christians and Parsis: Married Women’s Property Act 1874 protects a married woman’s separate property (not applicable to Hindus, Muslims, Buddhists, Sikhs and Jains).

p: Maintenance, Dower (Mahr) and Stridhan · Family Law
x: Core idea: Maintenance is available through several overlapping routes: the personal law (Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act 1956; Muslim law and the 1986 Act), the matrimonial statutes (Sections 24–25 HMA and equivalents), the secular criminal-procedure provision (Section 125 CrPC, now Section 144 BNSS), and the DV Act 2005. Dower and stridhan are the wife’s own property rights.

t: Memory Capsule: Maintenance, Dower (Mahr) and Stridhan
p: Maintenance, Dower (Mahr) and Stridhan · Family Law
x: Section 125 CrPC ceiling of Rs 500 was removed in 2001. Section 144 BNSS corresponds to Section 125 CrPC; Section 144 CrPC is the old prohibitory order provision (do not confuse). Dower is a debt, not ‘consideration’ in the contractual sense; the widow’s lien is not ownership. Section 14(2) HSA is an exception; Section 14(1) is the general rule (Tulasamma). Shah Bano is a Section 125 case, and the 1986 Act partly overrode it; Danial Latifi upheld the 1986 Act as interpreted.

p: Maintenance, Dower (Mahr) and Stridhan · Family Law
x: Recent trend: Court decisions in 2024–2026 emphasise (a) full disclosure of income and assets, (b) maintenance as a means of dignity (not a bargaining tool), (c) no maintenance cap under Section 144 BNSS, (d) a wife’s qualification does not by itself bar alimony, and (e) stridhan as an enforceable right.

p: Adoption, Guardianship and Acknowledgement · Family Law
x: Section Content 5 Adoptions regulated by Chapter II; adoption made in contravention is void; an adoption not valid cannot create rights in anyone 6 Requisites of a valid adoption: (i) adopter has capacity and right to take in adoption; (ii) giver has capacity to give; (iii) the person adopted is capable of being adopted; (iv) adoption complies with other conditions 7 Capacity of a male Hindu: sound mind, not a minor; if he has a wife, her consent is necessary unless she has completely and finally renounced the world, ceased to be Hindu or been declared of unsound mind by a competent court; consent of all wives if more than one 8 Capacity of a female Hindu: sound mind, not a minor; unmarried, or married but marriage dissolved, or husband dead, or husband has completely and finally renounced the world, ceased to be Hindu, or been declared of unsound mind 9 Persons capable of giving in adoption: father or mother (father’s consent necessary unless he has completely and finally renounced the world, ceased to be Hindu or been declared of unsound mind; the mother can give if the father is dead or has renounced etc.; both can give together); guardian with court permission if both parents are dead, have abandoned the child, are of unsound mind or the child’s parentage is unknown 10 Persons who may be adopted: a Hindu; not already adopted; not married (unless custom allows); not completed fifteen years (unless custom allows) 11 Other conditions: (i) adopting a son: no Hindu son, son’s son or son’s son’s son (legitimate or adopted) living at the time; (ii) adopting a daughter: no Hindu daughter or son’s daughter living; (iii) if the adopter is a female and the adoptee a male, the adopter must be at least twenty-one years older; (iv) if the adopter is a male and the adoptee a female, he must be at least twenty-one years older; (v) the same child cannot be adopted simultaneously by two or more persons; (vi) the child must be actually given and taken in adoption with the intent to transfer the child from the family of birth to the adoptive family (datta homam is not essential) 12 Effects: from the date of adoption the child is deemed the child of the adoptive family for all purposes and ties with birth family are severed; provisos: marriage prohibitions in the birth family remain; property vested in the child before adoption continues to be hers or his (with obligations); the adopted child cannot divest any person of an estate vested before adoption 13 Adoptive parents retain right to dispose of property by transfer or will 14 Determination of adoptive mother when the adoptive father has more than one wife: the senior wife 15 A valid adoption cannot be cancelled by adopter or adoptee 16 Presumption in favour of a registered document recording an adoption signed by giver and taker unless disproved 17 Prohibition of payments in consideration of adoption; punishable Key point: Same-sex child restrictions: an adopter cannot adopt a child of the same sex as an existing living Hindu child of that sex (the ‘living child’ rule). Relation to JJ Act: Section 56(3) JJ Act 2015 excludes HAMA adoptions (Hindu adoptions continue under HAMA). The JJ Act (Amendment) Act 2021 transferred the power to issue adoption orders from courts to the District Magistrate (verify). Cases: Lakshmi Kant Pandey v Union of India (1984): guidelines for inter-country adoption and welfare of the child; CARA arose from it.

t: 7.2 Adoption under the JJ Act 2015 and Adoption Regulations 2022
p: Adoption, Guardianship and Acknowledgement · Family Law
x: Eligibility (Section 57): prospective adoptive parents (PAPs) must be physically fit, financially sound, mentally alert and highly motivated; a married couple must have two years of stable marital relationship and the consent of both spouses; a single woman can adopt a child of any sex; a single man cannot adopt a girl child. A person with three or more children is not eligible except for special-needs children and relatives’ children (as in CARA rules). Authority: CARA (Central Adoption Resource Authority) is a statutory body under the Ministry of Women and Child Development; the Child Care Institutions, Specialised Adoption Agencies and District Child Protection Units are the machinery; the Adoption Regulations 2022 (framed under Section 68) govern process; after the 2021 amendment, District Magistrates pass adoption orders. Section 2(2): adoption means the process through which the adopted child is permanently separated from biological parents and becomes the lawful child of the adoptive parents with all rights, privileges and responsibilities. Inter-country adoption: India ratified the 1993 Hague Convention on Inter-country Adoption in 2003; CARA is the Central Authority. Shabnam Hashmi v Union of India (2014): three-judge bench held that the right to adopt under the JJ Act is available to all, irrespective of religion, and that personal law cannot override this enabling law; the Court refused to declare adoption as a fundamental right. Muslims can therefore adopt under the JJ Act; personal law continues to apply to those who prefer it. In Shazia Aman Khan v State of Orissa (2024) the Supreme Court distinguished custody and guardianship from adoption in a Muslim family context (verify). Madras High Court (2025) held that the JJ Act prevails over Muslim personal law for registration of adoption of an intra-family child (reported; verify). Muslim law: no adoption (Quran 33:4–5: adopted child is not a real son); the nearest concepts are kafala (guardianship and sponsorship), custody and acknowledgement.

p: Adoption, Guardianship and Acknowledgement · Family Law
x: Section 4: minor is a person under 18; ‘guardian’ includes natural guardian, testamentary guardian, guardian appointed by court and guardian by court of wards; ‘natural guardian’ is a guardian in Section 6. Section 6 (natural guardians): (a) boy or unmarried girl: the father, and after him the mother, but the custody of a minor who has not completed five years shall ordinarily be with the mother; (b) illegitimate boy or unmarried girl: the mother and after her the father; (c) a married girl: the husband. No person is entitled to act as natural guardian if he has ceased to be a Hindu or has renounced the world. Gita Hariharan v Reserve Bank of India (1999): ‘after’ in Section 6(a) means ‘in the absence of’ for the father (due to his disinterest or incapacity); the mother may act during the father’s lifetime; avoided striking down the section by constitutional reading. Jijabai Vithalrao Gajre v Pathankhan (1970) is the earlier view of the father’s ‘absence’. ABC v State (NCT of Delhi) (2015): an unwed mother can be the sole guardian of her child without disclosing the father’s name. Section 7: natural guardianship of adopted son: adoptive father, then adoptive mother. Section 8: powers. The natural guardian may do all acts necessary or reasonable and proper for the benefit of the minor or for the realisation, protection or benefit of the minor’s estate, but cannot bind the minor by a personal covenant. Without prior permission of the court he cannot (a) mortgage, charge, or transfer by sale, gift, exchange or otherwise any immovable property of the minor; (b) lease for more than five years or for a term extending beyond a year after the minor attains majority. Alienation in breach is voidable at the minor’s instance (Section 8(3)); permission is given only for necessity or evident advantage (Section 8(4)). Section 9: testamentary guardian (the father or mother can appoint by will); Section 10: minor cannot be guardian; Section 11: de facto guardian cannot deal with the minor’s property; Section 12: no guardian for undivided interest in joint family property managed by karta; Section 13: welfare of the minor is the paramount consideration; Section 5: overriding effect. Custody cases: Nil Ratan Kundu v Abhijit Kundu (2008) and Gaurav Nagpal v Sumedha Nagpal (2009): welfare is paramount, not legal right; Roxann Sharma v Arun Sharma (2015): custody of a child under five with the mother; Vandana Shiva v Jayanta Bandhopadhyaya (2005). Orders under Section 26 HMA, Section 38 SMA and Section 41–43 Divorce Act apply in matrimonial proceedings.

p: Adoption, Guardianship and Acknowledgement · Family Law
x: Section 4(1): minor under 18 (Indian Majority Act 1875: 21 if a guardian is appointed by the court or the court of wards takes charge). Section 7: District Court may appoint or declare a guardian; Section 9: jurisdiction of the court where the minor ordinarily resides. Section 17: the court must consider the welfare of the minor, with reference to age, sex and religion; character and capacity of the proposed guardian; nearness of kin; wishes of the deceased parents; and existing or previous relations with the minor or the property. Section 19: no guardian can be appointed for a minor whose father is alive and not unfit; Section 25: return of ward to guardian custody; Section 29: a guardian appointed by court cannot mortgage, charge, sell, gift or lease for more than five years without court permission; Section 30: alienation in breach is voidable; Section 47: appeals.

p: Adoption, Guardianship and Acknowledgement · Family Law
x: Concept Meaning Wilayat-i-nikah Guardianship in marriage (father, then paternal relatives) Wilayat-i-mal (property) Father is the natural guardian; after him his executor (wasi), then the paternal grandfather; the mother is not a guardian of property (Imambandi v Mutsaddi, 1918) Hizanat (custody of person) The mother has the right to custody of a boy until age seven (Hanafi) and of a girl until puberty; Shia: boy two years, girl seven; Maliki: boy until puberty, girl until marriage; the father then takes over Loss of custody Mother remarries a stranger (a person not related within prohibited degrees to the child), leads an immoral life, neglects the child, or lives far from the father’s residence; welfare of the child is paramount in modern case law (the Muslim law rule yields to welfare)

p: Adoption, Guardianship and Acknowledgement · Family Law
x: Muslim law: acknowledgement of paternity is a declaration by a man that a child is his legitimate child. Conditions: (a) the parentage of the child must be unknown (not known to be the child of another man); (b) the age difference must be such that the acknowledger could be the father (traditionally, he must be at least 12½ years older than the acknowledged); (c) the child must not be known as the offspring of zina or of another man; (d) the child must not be the child of a woman whom the acknowledger could not have lawfully married at the time of conception; (e) if the acknowledged is an adult, he or she must confirm; (f) the acknowledger must be of sound mind and majority. Effect: legitimacy, inheritance rights, and a presumption that cannot be revoked once made ( Ashrufood Dowlah v Hyder Hossein Khan , PC 1867; Habibur Rahman Chowdhury v Altaf Ali Chowdhury , PC 1921: acknowledgement of legitimacy does not apply where illegitimacy is apparent). Presumption in other laws: Section 112 Evidence Act (now Section 116 BSA 2023): birth during marriage or within 280 days after its dissolution, mother remaining unmarried, is conclusive proof of legitimacy unless non-access is proved ( Goutam Kundu v State of West Bengal , 1993: DNA test cannot be ordered routinely; Nandlal Wasudeo Badwaik v Lata Nandlal Badwaik , 2014: scientific evidence prevails over presumption, in the facts; Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v Ajinkya Arun Firodia , 2023: DNA only in exceptional cases). Hindu law: the HAMA adoption route replaces earlier ‘dattaka’ and ‘kritrima’ forms; there is no separate concept of acknowledgement, but Section 16 HMA and presumption of marriage secure legitimacy.

p: Adoption, Guardianship and Acknowledgement · Family Law
x: Core idea: Only Hindus (including Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs) have a codified adoption law with the effect of severing the child from the birth family: the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act 1956 (HAMA). For everyone else, adoption is through the secular Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015 (JJ Act), as upheld in Shabnam Hashmi v Union of India (2014). Muslim law does not recognise adoption but has guardianship (wilayat), custody (hizanat) and acknowledgement (iqrar). Guardianship is governed by the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956 (HMGA) and the secular Guardians and Wards Act 1890 (GWA).

x: Section 6 HMGA: the mother is ordinarily entitled to custody of a child under five years, but that is not a rule of absolute entitlement. Section 8(2) HMGA: the need for prior court permission covers immovable property only; dealings in movables are tested by the necessity or benefit of the minor under Section 8(1) . Under HAMA datta homam is not essential; actual giving and taking is. Hindu male adopting a girl or Hindu female adopting a boy: the age gap must be at least twenty-one years. A single man cannot adopt a girl child under the JJ Act regime.

p: Succession and Inheritance · Family Law
x: Application (Section 2): Hindus in the extended sense (as in HMA); not Scheduled Tribes unless notified; not Muslims, Christians, Parsis or Jews. Overriding effect (Section 4): HSA overrides any text or custom on matters it deals with. Mitakshara coparcenary and Section 6 (as amended in 2005) Before 2005, only male members were coparceners. The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 (in force from 9 September 2005 ) made the daughter a coparcener by birth ‘in the same manner as the son’, with the same rights and liabilities (Section 6(1)). Section 6(3): on the death of a Hindu after the amendment, his interest in coparcenary property devolves by testamentary or intestate succession (not by survivorship), on the basis of notional partition ; daughter gets the same share as a son; the share of a pre-deceased child goes to his or her surviving child or grandchild. Section 6(1) proviso and 6(5): not applicable to a partition effected before 20 December 2004 (a registered deed or a court decree). Cases: Prakash v Phulavati (2015): amendment prospective: only living daughters of living coparceners on 9 September 2005. Danamma @ Suman Surpur v Amar (2018): daughters entitled even if father died before 2005 (partly contrary). Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma (11 August 2020, three-judge bench of Justices Arun Mishra, S. Abdul Nazeer and M.R. Shah): the right of a daughter is by birth; it is not necessary that the father was alive on 9 September 2005; the provision is ‘retroactive’ in the sense that it applies to rights arising from birth; oral partition and unregistered family settlements cannot defeat the right unless proved by public documents or a court decree; overruled Prakash and part of Danamma. Ganduri Koteshwaramma v Chakiri Yanadi (2011): benefit of the amendment extended to pending partition suits before final decree. Arunachala Gounder v Ponnusamy (2022): a Hindu male’s self-acquired property devolves by succession; if he dies intestate without a male heir the daughter inherits, even for deaths before 1956, and the daughter’s right is superior to collaterals. Dayabhaga: sons do not acquire an interest by birth; coparcenary in the Mitakshara sense does not exist, so Section 6 mostly concerns Mitakshara. Notional partition and Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v Hirabai (1978): the interest of a deceased coparcener is determined by assuming a partition immediately before death; widow’s share added. Repealed by 2005: Section 4(2) (agricultural holdings), Section 23 (daughter’s limited right in dwelling house), Section 24 (certain widows’ disqualification on remarriage). Heirs of a Hindu male (Sections 8–13) Class Members Rule Class I (16 heirs after 2005) Son; daughter; widow; mother; son of predeceased son; daughter of predeceased son; son of predeceased daughter; daughter of predeceased daughter; widow of predeceased son; son of predeceased son of predeceased son; daughter of predeceased son of predeceased son; widow of predeceased son of predeceased son; and (added 2005) son of predeceased daughter of predeceased daughter; daughter of predeceased daughter of predeceased daughter; daughter of predeceased son of predeceased daughter; daughter of predeceased daughter of predeceased son Take simultaneously and to the exclusion of all others Class II (9 entries) I: father; II: son’s daughter’s son, son’s daughter’s daughter, brother, sister; III: daughter’s son’s son, daughter’s son’s daughter, daughter’s daughter’s son, daughter’s daughter’s daughter; IV: brother’s son, sister’s son, brother’s daughter, sister’s daughter; V: father’s father, father’s mother; VI: father’s widow, brother’s widow; VII: father’s brother, father’s sister; VIII: mother’s father, mother’s mother; IX: mother’s brother, mother’s sister An entry excludes the later entries; those in one entry take together Agnates Related wholly through males Preference by degrees (Section 12) Cognates Related not wholly through males After agnates Government If no heirs Escheat (Section 29), subject to liabilities Distribution among Class I (Section 10): Rule 1: widow (or widows together) takes one share; Rule 2: surviving sons, daughters and the mother one share each; Rule 3: the heirs of a predeceased son or daughter take together one share; Rule 4: within each branch, the division is per stirpes. Other sections: Section 14 (female’s absolute ownership), 15–16 (female’s property), 18 (full blood preferred over half blood), 19 (per capita; tenants in common), 20 (child in womb is treated as born), 21 (simultaneous deaths: the younger is presumed to survive), 22 (preferential right to acquire the property of the intestate), 25 (murderer disqualified), 26 (descendants of a convert disqualified unless Hindus at the time of opening succession), 27 (disqualified person treated as predeceased), 28 (disease or defect is not a disqualification), 29 (escheat), 30 (testamentary succession: a Hindu may dispose of his coparcenary interest by will). Property of a Hindu female (Sections 15–16) 15(1): order: (a) sons, daughters (including children of predeceased children) and husband together; (b) heirs of the husband; (c) mother and father; (d) heirs of the father; (e) heirs of the mother. 15(2): exceptions (the ‘source’ rule): (a) property inherited from her father or mother: if no son, daughter or their children, goes to the father’s heirs; (b) property inherited from her husband or father-in-law: if no son, daughter or their children, goes to the husband’s heirs. Section 16: rules for distribution among heirs. Pending challenge: the Supreme Court is hearing petitions challenging Sections 15 and 16 as discriminatory against women; the Court indicated it would proceed cautiously (reported; verify status).

p: Succession and Inheritance · Family Law
x: Principles: inheritance arises only on death; no birth-right; no primogeniture; no distinction between self-acquired and ancestral property; no right of representation in Sunni law (nearer in degree excludes the remoter; a grandchild whose father predeceased is excluded by the deceased’s son; the Shia school allows a form of representation); the estate first pays funeral expenses, then debts, then bequests up to one-third, and the balance is divided among heirs; the female heir gets half of the male heir’s share in the same degree. Sunni (Hanafi) heirs: (1) Sharers (Quranic heirs, ashab al-furud): husband, wife, daughter, son’s daughter, father, true grandfather, mother, true grandmother, full sister, consanguine sister, uterine sister, uterine brother; (2) Residuaries (asaba): those who take the residue (son, father, brother etc., and females made residuaries by males: daughter with son); (3) Distant kindred (dhawul arham): everyone else related by blood, in four classes. Heir Share Husband 1/2 if no child or child of son; 1/4 if there is a child Wife (or wives together) 1/4 if no child; 1/8 if there is a child Daughter 1/2 if the only child; 2/3 for two or more; with son she becomes a residuary and takes half of the son’s share Mother 1/6 if there is a child or two or more brothers or sisters; otherwise 1/3 Father 1/6 if there is a child; otherwise a residuary Uterine brother or sister 1/6 for one; 1/3 for two or more, shared equally Doctrine of Aul (increase): if the total of the sharers’ fractions exceeds unity, each share is proportionately reduced. Doctrine of Radd (return): if there is a surplus and no residuary, the surplus returns to the sharers (except husband and wife in Hanafi law). Shia law rejects Aul and the concept of taasib; it classifies heirs in three classes (parents and children; grandparents, brothers and sisters; paternal and maternal uncles and aunts), allows representation and gives a childless widow no share in land (restricted share in immovable property). Disqualifications: homicide, difference of religion (but Caste Disabilities Removal Act 1850 and Section 28 HSA principles limit this in India: convert not excluded), illegitimacy limitations, slavery (obsolete). Posthumous child: counted as an heir if born within the maximum period of gestation (Hanafi 2 years; Shia 10 months). Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937: applies Muslim law to intestate succession notwithstanding custom (agricultural land included since 1943).

t: 8.3 Christians and Parsis: Indian Succession Act 1925
p: Succession and Inheritance · Family Law
x: Christians (Part V, Chapter II, Sections 31–49): where the intestate leaves a widow and lineal descendants, the widow takes one-third and the descendants two-thirds (Section 33); where there are no descendants but kindred, the widow takes one-half and the kindred the rest; if there are no kindred, the widow takes the whole (Section 33 and 34 pattern). A widower takes his wife’s intestate estate on a footing similar to a widow’s (Section 35: verify the exact share). Order of kindred: father, then mother and siblings, etc. (Sections 36–48). Sons and daughters take equally. Parsis (Part V, Chapter III, Sections 50–56): a widow and each child take equal shares and each parent of the intestate takes half the share of a child (Section 51), with parallel rules for a female Parsi intestate (Section 52). John Vallamattom v Union of India (2003): Section 118 ISA (restriction on a Christian’s bequest for religious or charitable purposes) struck down as violating Article 14 (the Court also urged a UCC). Special Marriage Act: Section 21 (ISA applies) and Section 21A (HSA applies when the spouses are Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jain).

t: 9.1 Will under the Indian Succession Act 1925 (applies to Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs, Jains, Christians, Parsis)
p: Will, Gift and Wakf · Family Law
x: Definition (Section 2(h)): legal declaration of the intention of a testator with respect to his property which he desires to be carried into effect after his death. A will is ambulatory (revocable), operates only on death, and requires no consideration. Capacity (Section 59): every person of sound mind and not a minor may make a will. A married woman can bequeath property she can alienate. A deaf, dumb or blind person can make a will if he knows what he does. Will by a person who is intoxicated, ill or otherwise unable to know what he is doing is void. Will obtained by fraud, coercion or importunity is void (Section 61). Execution (Section 63): (a) testator signs or affixes his mark, or another signs in his presence and by his direction; (b) signature or mark so placed as to appear to give effect to the writing as a will; (c) attested by two or more witnesses, each of whom has seen the testator sign or has received from him a personal acknowledgement of his signature; each witness signs in the presence of the testator (not necessarily in each other’s presence). Registration is not mandatory. Privileged wills (Sections 65–66): soldiers employed in an expedition or actually engaged in warfare, airmen and mariners at sea may make an unwritten (nuncupative) will before two witnesses; no formal attestation. Revocation: Section 70: an unprivileged will is revoked only by another will or codicil, by a writing declaring an intention to revoke it executed like a will, or by burning, tearing or otherwise destroying it with that intention. Section 62 states that a will is liable to be revoked or altered by the maker at any time when he is competent. Codicil (Section 2(b)) is an instrument supplementing the will. Probate: Probate of a will is the copy certified under the seal of a court of competent jurisdiction; compulsory (Section 213) for wills made by Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs and Jains in the territories of the former Presidency towns (Bombay, Calcutta and Madras) (Section 57(c)) and for Parsi and Christian wills in India. Letters of administration are for intestacy or for wills without executors (Section 218). Succession certificate for debts (Section 370 ISA, now Section 372). Proof of will: H. Venkatachala Iyengar v B.N. Thimmajamma (1959) set out the principles: the propounder must prove due execution and the testator’s sound disposing mind; suspicious circumstances must be explained; Jaswant Kaur v Amrit Kaur (1977), Rabindra Nath Mukherjee v Panchanan Banerjee (1995) and Meenakshiammal v Chandrasekaran (2005) apply it. Hindu coparcener’s will: Section 30 HSA allows a Hindu to dispose by will of his coparcenary interest (Explanation to Section 30). Muslim will (wasiyat) rules: The testator must be an adult of sound mind and a Muslim of free consent; a will of a suicidal act (a will made after taking poison or injury) is void in Hanafi law. One-third rule: a bequest cannot exceed one-third of the net estate (after funeral expenses and debts) unless the heirs consent after the testator’s death (Sunni) or at any time (Shia). No bequest to an heir without the consent of the other heirs (Sunni; Shia allows bequest to an heir within one-third). The legatee must be in existence at the testator’s death (a child in the womb who is born within six months qualifies); a legatee who causes the testator’s death is disqualified. A will may be oral; no writing, no registration, no witness required; may be revoked expressly or by implication. Part VI of the Indian Succession Act does not apply to Muslim wills (Section 58), and the Shariat Act 1937 originally left wills outside its scope unless a person declared under Section 3, so Muslim will law is largely uncodified (Hedaya, Fatwa-i-Alamgiri). Death-bed gifts (marz-ul-maut) are treated like wills (limited to one-third and requiring consent for more).

p: Will, Gift and Wakf · Family Law
x: Hindu gift: TPA Sections 122–129 Section Content 122 Gift is the transfer of certain existing movable or immovable property made voluntarily and without consideration by one person (the donor) to another (the donee) and accepted by or on behalf of the donee. Acceptance must be made during the lifetime of the donor and while he is still capable of giving 123 Mode: for immovable property, a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses ; for movables, either by a registered instrument or by delivery 124 Gift comprising existing and future property is void as to the future 125 Gift to several donees where one does not accept: void as to that donee’s share 126 Suspension and revocation: by agreement upon the happening of a specified event not depending on the donor’s will; not revocable at will; can be revoked for any cause (other than want of consideration) that would justify rescission of a contract 127 Onerous gifts: donee takes the benefit and the burden of a gift of several things 128 Universal donee: liable for the debts of the donor existing at the time of the gift 129 Exceptions: gifts of movables in contemplation of death (donatio mortis causa) and Muslim law rules Acceptance: need not be express; can be inferred from conduct ( Asokan v Lakshmikutty , 2007). A gift is complete when accepted; possession is not essential for a registered immovable gift ( K. Balakrishnan v K. Kamalam , 2004; Renikuntla Rajamma v K. Sarwanamma , 2014: a gift deed cannot be treated as valid without proof of acceptance and attestation). Karta’s gifts: a Hindu karta cannot gift ancestral immovable property except small gifts for pious purposes. Muslim gift (hiba) Definition: an immediate and unconditional transfer of the ownership of the substance of a thing, without any return. Essentials: (1) declaration (ijab) by the donor; (2) acceptance (qabul) by the donee, express or implied; (3) delivery of possession (qabza) : actual or constructive, appropriate to the property. Registration is not required for validity (Section 129 TPA keeps Muslim gifts out of Section 123; Mohammad Abdul Ghani v Fakhr Jahan Begam , PC 1922; Hafeeza Bibi v Shaikh Farid , SC 2011: oral gift valid if all three requirements are satisfied; writing alone is not sufficient). Capacity: donor must be a Muslim, major, of sound mind, and the owner; donee may be any person, including a minor (accepted by guardian), an unborn child (invalid except if born within six months). Mushaa (undivided share): a gift of an undivided share in property capable of division is invalid under Hanafi law unless exceptions apply; the Indian courts require division except in the case of shares in a freehold property in large buildings, shares in a company, etc.. Shia law has no objection. Contingent and future gifts: a gift to take effect in future is void; a condition repugnant to absolute ownership is void though the gift itself may stand, while use of property without ownership is the separate transaction of ariyat. Kinds: Hiba-bil-iwaz (gift for an exchange or consideration; it is a sale in effect); Hiba-ba-shart-ul-iwaz (with a stipulation for return); Sadaqah (gift for religious merit; cannot be revoked after delivery); Ariyat (loan of the use of property); Hiba of mushaa (as above). Revocation: before delivery, the donor can withdraw; after delivery, only by a decree of court or consent of the donee; a gift becomes irrevocable on the donee’s death, the donor’s death, the donee being a relative within prohibited degrees, a spouse, on the donee’s alienation, when consideration has been given (hiba-bil-iwaz), when the gift is sadaqah, and when the subject is lost or increased. Death-bed gift (marz-ul-maut): treated as a will; valid only up to one-third of the estate unless the heirs consent. Mahr in lieu: hiba-i-mahr; wife’s remission of dower. Hindu gift vs Muslim gift Point Hindu (TPA) Muslim (hiba) Writing and registration for immovables Registered deed attested by two witnesses Not required Delivery of possession Not essential if registered Essential (qabza) Revocability Not at will Revocable before delivery; limited after delivery Undivided share Allowed Mushaa invalid (Hanafi) except exceptions Governing law TPA Sections 122–129 Muslim law (Section 129 TPA saves it)

p: Will, Gift and Wakf · Family Law
x: Definition (Waqf Act 1995, Section 3(r), as amended by the Waqf (Amendment) Act 2025): the permanent dedication of any movable or immovable property for any purpose recognised by Muslim law as pious, religious or charitable. The 2025 amendment replaced the earlier open definition (any person could create a wakf) with a requirement that the person showing or demonstrating that he is practising Islam for at least five years and has ownership of the property may create a waqf, removed the category of ‘waqf by user’ prospectively, and provided that a waqf-alal-aulad (family waqf) shall not deny inheritance rights of female heirs and other heirs; the Supreme Court stayed the five-year practice condition until rules are framed (see below). The principal Act was also renamed (the Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development Act 1995: verify). Essentials: (1) a person competent to dedicate (a Muslim of sound mind, major and owner); (2) permanent dedication (a wakf cannot be for a limited time); (3) property capable of dedication, movable or immovable; (4) a pious, religious or charitable purpose; (5) the dedication must be unconditional and irrevocable (Hanafi law: according to Abu Yusuf’s view followed in India a wakf is complete by declaration without delivery to the mutawalli; Imam Muhammad requires delivery; Abu Hanifa treats it as revocable until a judicial decree). Wakf vs trust: in a wakf the ownership vests in the Almighty; the mutawalli is a manager (not owner); a wakf is irrevocable and perpetual; a trust vests ownership in the trustee. Types: wakf-ul-ahli or wakf-alal-aulad (family wakf; valid under the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act 1913 if the ultimate benefit is for the poor); wakf-khairi (public wakf); wakf by user (long public religious use; abolished prospectively by the 2025 amendment, SC said the abolition is not arbitrary); wakf by declaration, instrument or by dedication. Management: Mutawalli (Section 3(i) of the 1995 Act); State Waqf Boards (supervision, registration of wakfs, powers under Sections 32–33); Central Waqf Council (advisory body to the Central Government; Section 9); Waqf Tribunal (Section 83) decides disputes relating to waqf property; Section 85 bars civil court jurisdiction; Section 51 (alienation of wakf property without Board’s sanction is void); registration (Section 36); survey by a Survey Commissioner (Sections 4–6). Waqf (Amendment) Act 2025 and In re: Waqf (Amendment) Act 2025 (Supreme Court, 15 September 2025): Issue Position in the interim order (CJI B.R. Gavai and Justice A.G. Masih) Whole Act Court refused to stay the Act as a whole; held that no case was made out for staying the entire provisions Five years’ practice of Islam to create a waqf Stayed until rules to prove the practice are framed (risk of arbitrary power in the absence of a mechanism) Collector or designated officer to decide whether property is government land (Section 3C) Core provision stayed on separation-of-powers grounds; property is not to be treated as non-waqf during inquiry; no dispossession or change of revenue or Board records until the Tribunal or court decides; no third-party rights to be created meanwhile Waqf by user Deletion not stayed : court held it was not arbitrary and that fears of State seizure were unfounded (and said omission takes effect prospectively from the Act’s date) Non-Muslim members Not struck; the Central Waqf Council should not have more than four non-Muslim members and State Waqf Boards no more than three ; ex-officio chairperson ‘strive’ to be Muslim (reported); the CEO can be a non-Muslim but ‘as far as possible’ a Muslim Limitation Act Applicability to waqf property not stayed (consistency with other property) Registration Not interfered with; mandatory Other provisions not stayed Protected monuments (ASI), restrictions in scheduled areas Final adjudication on the constitutional challenge was pending at last reliable report; check whether the Constitution-level or final judgment has been delivered before the exam (verify). Other cases: M. Siddiq v Mahant Suresh Das (2019) on a mosque as wakf by user in the Ayodhya case; Pramatha Nath Mullick v Pradyumna Kumar Mullick (PC, 1925) (Hindu idol as a juristic person; contrast with wakf); Hindu endowments: debuttar property vests in the deity; the shebait is a manager.

p: Will, Gift and Wakf · Family Law
x: Core idea: Will (testamentary succession), gift (inter vivos transfer without consideration) and wakf (permanent dedication of property for pious, religious or charitable purposes) are the three main tools of voluntary disposition. Hindu wills and gifts are governed by the Indian Succession Act 1925 (ISA) and the Transfer of Property Act 1882 (TPA); Muslim wills (wasiyat) and gifts (hiba) by uncodified Muslim law; wakf by Muslim law as modified by the Waqf Act 1995 (as amended in 2013 and 2025) and the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act 1913.

Under Section 63 ISA: two attesting witnesses, but no registration. p: Uniform Civil Code (UCC) · Family Law
x: Constituent Assembly (23 November 1948): Draft Article 35 (now 44) was debated; Muslim members sought a proviso protecting personal laws; Dr. Ambedkar, K.M. Munshi and others supported the provision; it was adopted as a Directive Principle on the understanding that it would be enacted when society was ready. Related provisions: Article 25(2)(b) (State may regulate social welfare and reform), Article 13, Entry 5 of List III, Article 254 (a State UCC that conflicts with a Central law needs Presidential assent), Article 371A and Sixth Schedule (tribal customs). Goa: the Goa, Daman and Diu Administration Act 1962 continued the Portuguese Civil Code 1867 as the Goa Civil Code; the Supreme Court in Jose Paulo Coutinho v Maria Luiza Valentina Pereira (2019) described Goa as a shining example of a State with a uniform civil code, while noting that the Goa code recognises some religion-based exceptions (verify).

p: Uniform Civil Code (UCC) · Family Law

t: 10.4 Uttarakhand Uniform Civil Code Act 2024 (first State UCC)
p: Uniform Civil Code (UCC) · Family Law
x: Process: committee headed by Justice (retd.) Ranjana Prakash Desai; Bill passed by the State Assembly in February 2024 ; Presidential assent in March 2024 ; brought into force in January 2025 after rules were notified (reported; verify exact dates). Scope: applies to residents of Uttarakhand (also residents living outside the State) and excludes Scheduled Tribes and persons whose customary rights are protected by the Constitution; covers marriage and divorce, succession (wills and intestate), live-in relationships, and miscellaneous provisions. Key features: equal marriage age (21 for men, 18 for women); monogamy (bigamy prohibited); mandatory registration of marriages and divorces; equal grounds of divorce for men and women; prohibition of practices such as triple talaq, halala and iddat; marriages and divorces by religious customs allowed as to ceremonies but not to substance; equal inheritance rights for sons and daughters; children of void or voidable marriages and live-in relationships treated as legitimate; adopted and biological children treated alike; live-in relationships to be registered and terminated with notice. Challenge: petitions have been filed in the High Court against the live-in registration and other provisions (verify status).
