Reported features: registration of live-in relationships and of their termination; prohibition of bigamy (a marriage is valid only if neither party has a living spouse); all separations must be through civil courts (reportedly ending extra-judicial or customary divorce); compulsory registration of marriages; common succession framework. As of 2026 there is still no national UCC; Goa has a historic common code, and Uttarakhand (2024) and Gujarat (2026) have enacted State UCCs.

t: 11.5 Frequent confusions (MCQ traps in one place)
p: Revision Toolkit: Cases, Numbers, Timelines and Traps · Family Law
x: Void vs voidable: HMA Sections 11 (void) and 12 (voidable); child is legitimate in both (Section 16). Judicial separation vs divorce: marriage subsists after judicial separation. Mutual consent vs irretrievable breakdown: 13B is statutory; irretrievable breakdown is Article 142 only. Dower vs dowry; mahr vs mutah (gift on divorce) vs muta (temporary marriage). Hizanat (custody) vs wilayat (guardianship): mother has hizanat; father has wilayat. Guardian and Wards Act (secular) vs HMGA (Hindu). Hiba (gift) vs wasiyat (will): hiba effective immediately with delivery; wasiyat after death. Aul vs Radd: Aul reduces shares; Radd returns the surplus. Wakf vs trust: ownership in God; mutawalli is not owner. Section 125 CrPC vs Section 144 BNSS: same subject; do not confuse with Section 144 CrPC (prohibitory orders). Natural guardian of a married Hindu girl: her husband.

p: Exam Pattern, Trends and Study Method · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Direct fact: "The term of a patent in India is…", "The Biological Diversity Act was enacted in…" Multi-statement (I, II, III, IV): "Which of the statements is/are correct?" This is the commonest style. Examiners plant one subtle error, such as 60 instead of 50 years, or Section 43 instead of Section 66. Match the following: Cases ↔ principles; Conventions ↔ subjects; Sections ↔ offences; Institutions ↔ locations. Assertion–Reason: usually on theories (Locke/Hegel/utilitarian), on why Section 3(d) exists, or on the Shreya Singhal reasoning. Chronological order: Paris → Berne → UCC → Rome → TRIPS → WCT; or the IT Act 2000 → 2008 amendment → Shreya Singhal → DPDP Act. "Which is NOT" / odd one out: items not patentable under Section 3, offences not in the IT Act, bodies not part of the three-tier biodiversity structure.

Natco (compulsory licence), Shreya Singhal (Section 66A), Puttaswamy (privacy), Amar Nath Sehgal (moral rights), Eastern Book Company (originality), Toyota v. Prius (territoriality), Cadila (deceptive similarity). Recent legislative churn is a favourite: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 (IPAB abolished); Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023; Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and DPDP Rules 2025 (verify commencement status); Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (in force 1 July 2024), which change the IPC/CrPC/Evidence Act references in cyber law; Patents (Amendment) Rules 2024; the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025; WIPO Treaty on IP, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (May 2024); WIPO Riyadh Design Law Treaty (November 2024). Cross-over topics: GI vs trademark; TK vs patents; intermediary liability under Section 79 IT Act vs copyright infringement; Section 81 IT Act (proviso protecting copyright/patent rights). Trap words: "only", "always", "all", "must", "exclusively". IPR rules usually have exceptions, so extreme words often signal a wrong option.

x: Exam format (UGC NET Law, Subject Code 58). Paper 2 has 100 MCQs of 2 marks each (200 marks). Paper 1 (General) and Paper 2 are taken in one continuous 3-hour sitting, and there is no negative marking, so never leave a question blank. The syllabus has 10 units, and Unit IX is one of the most fact-dense and statute-driven units. Marks here come from precision: section numbers, years, durations, penalties, institution names and case holdings. Typically this unit contributes somewhere around 8–12 questions (my estimate from past-paper patterns, not an official figure), spread across IPR (about 60–65%) and IT law/cyber law (about 35–40%).

p: Concept and Meaning of Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Intellectual property (IP) refers to creations of the human intellect to which the law grants exclusive, time-bound (or, in some cases, renewable) rights that allow the creator or owner to exclude others from exploiting the creation without permission. The property is intangible (incorporeal): the right is not in the physical object but in the idea-expression, invention, mark or know-how embodied in it. Buying a book gives you ownership of the copy, not the copyright; buying a patented machine does not give you the patent. The classic definition is in Article 2(viii) of the WIPO Convention 1967 , which lists IP as rights relating to: literary, artistic and scientific works; performances of performing artists, phonograms and broadcasts; inventions in all fields of human endeavour; scientific discoveries; industrial designs; trademarks, service marks and commercial names and designations; protection against unfair competition; and all other rights resulting from intellectual activity in the industrial, scientific, literary or artistic fields.

t: 1.2 Categories of IP and Indian statutes
p: Concept and Meaning of Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: IP right Protects Main Indian law Typical term Copyright (and related rights) Original literary, dramatic, musical, artistic works, films, sound recordings Copyright Act 1957 Life + 60 years (author works); 60 years (films, sound recordings, photographs) Patent New, inventive, industrially applicable inventions Patents Act 1970 20 years from filing Trademark Distinctive signs for goods/services Trade Marks Act 1999 10 years, renewable indefinitely Industrial design Aesthetic features of shape, pattern, configuration applied to an article Designs Act 2000 10 years + 5 years extension (total 15) Geographical indication Goods whose quality or reputation is attributable to place of origin GI of Goods (Registration & Protection) Act 1999 10 years, renewable indefinitely Semiconductor IC layout-design Layout-designs of integrated circuits Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act 2000 10 years Plant varieties and farmers' rights New, distinct, uniform, stable (NDUS) varieties Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act 2001 15 years (18 for trees/vines) Trade secrets / confidential information Undisclosed information No separate statute; contract, equity, tort (TRIPS Art. 39) As long as secrecy is maintained Biological resources and associated TK Access and benefit sharing Biological Diversity Act 2002 Not a term-based right Industrial property vs copyright. Industrial property (patents, trademarks, designs, GIs, unfair competition) is governed internationally by the Paris Convention ; copyright and related rights by the Berne Convention and the Rome Convention.

p: Concept and Meaning of Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Intangible and incorporeal: the same creation can be used simultaneously by many people, which is why law must create artificial scarcity. Territorial: rights exist only in the country that grants them (an Indian patent has no effect in the US). The Paris and Berne principles of national treatment reduce the harshness of this. Exclusive but limited: limited in time (except trademarks, GIs and trade secrets), in scope (fair dealing, compulsory licences, the Bolar exception) and by public interest. Negative right: primarily a right to exclude , not a right to practise. You may hold a patent on an improvement whose use still infringes someone else's earlier patent. Freely transferable (assignment, licence, mortgage), except GI rights (Section 24 GI Act) and moral rights. Registration: mandatory for patents, designs, registered trademarks and GIs; optional for copyright (Section 45 registration is only prima facie evidence under Section 48).

t: 1.4 Constitutional and institutional framework in India
p: Concept and Meaning of Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Entry 49, List I (Union List): "Patents, inventions and designs; copyright; trade-marks and merchandise marks." Parliament has exclusive power over these subjects. Article 300A (right to property) has been held to include IP. In Entertainment Network (India) Ltd v. Super Cassette Industries Ltd (2008, SC), the Court recognised the balance between the copyright owner's property right and the public interest in access. Article 21 (health) and Article 39(b) (distribution of material resources) are invoked to justify limits on pharmaceutical patents (the Section 3(d) and compulsory licensing debate). Article 51(c) and Entry 14, List I: treaty-making and implementing international obligations (TRIPS compliance). Administration: the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce) is the nodal department. The Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM) , headquartered in Mumbai , oversees the patent offices (Kolkata, Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai), the Trade Marks Registry (Mumbai, with branch offices including Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Ahmedabad) and the Geographical Indications Registry ( Chennai ). The Copyright Office and the Registrar of Copyrights are in New Delhi (Department-level administration under DPIIT). National IPR Policy 2016 (slogan "Creative India; Innovative India" ): seven objectives including IPR awareness, creation of IPRs, legal framework, administration, commercialisation, enforcement and human capital. CIPAM (Cell for IPR Promotion and Management) implements it. Dispute forums: The Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB), established under the Trade Marks Act 1999, was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 . Appeals formerly heard by IPAB now go to the High Courts (Delhi High Court has a dedicated IP Division , 2021). Infringement suits go to the District Court/High Court and are commercial disputes under the Commercial Courts Act 2015 .

p: Concept and Meaning of Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: The doctrine of exhaustion (first-sale doctrine) says that once the owner sells a product lawfully, the right to control its further resale ends. Three models: national (only sales within the country exhaust the right), regional (e.g. EU) and international (sale anywhere exhausts the right). India follows international exhaustion for patents (Section 107A(b), parallel imports) and, through Section 30(3)–(4) of the Trade Marks Act, for trademarks ( Kapil Wadhwa v. Samsung Electronics , Delhi HC 2012). Parallel imports in copyright are restricted under Section 51(b)(iv) (import of infringing copies). TRIPS Article 6 leaves exhaustion to each member.

p: Theories of Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: In his Second Treatise of Government (1690), Locke argued that God gave the world to humankind in common, but a person owns his body and therefore his labour. When labour is mixed with a thing in the common, it becomes the labourer's property. Applied to IP, the author who labours to compose a work or the inventor who toils to create an invention deserves ownership. Two limits are famous: the "enough and as good" proviso (appropriation is justified only if enough and as good is left in common for others) and the spoilage limitation . Critics say ideas are not scarce, so the proviso is hard to apply, and that labour theory cannot justify a time-limited right. The theory underlies the old UK "sweat of the brow" standard ( University of London Press v. University Tutorial Press , 1916), later displaced in India by the "modicum of creativity" standard ( Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak , 2008).

p: Theories of Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Kant treated a book as an act of speech by the author to the public, an expression of personality that cannot be fully alienated. Hegel argued that property is the embodiment of the will and personality of the owner. Radin's "personhood" version distinguishes personal property (closely tied to self-development) from fungible property. This theory explains moral rights : the rights of paternity and integrity that survive assignment of copyright (Section 57, Copyright Act; Article 6bis Berne). It is dominant in civil-law countries (France, Germany), where author's rights ( droit d'auteur ) are central, while the common-law tradition leans utilitarian.

p: Theories of Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Bentham's maxim "the greatest happiness of the greatest number" supports IP only where benefits of creativity exceed the costs of monopoly. The economic form is the incentive theory : information is a public good (non-rival: my use does not diminish yours; non-excludable: hard to stop copying), so without legal exclusivity the creator cannot recover costs and too little will be created. This theory explains why terms are limited, why fair dealing and compulsory licences exist, and why the US Constitution grants Congress power "to promote the progress of science and useful arts." TRIPS Article 7 (objectives: "mutual advantage of producers and users of technological knowledge") is explicitly utilitarian. Criticisms: it rests on assumptions that are hard to measure, and it cannot explain moral rights.

t: 2.4 Social planning theory and the commons
p: Theories of Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Fisher's social planning theory asks that IP be used as a tool to achieve a just culture, giving weight to democratic participation, diversity and access. It underpins public-interest limits : Sections 31–31D (compulsory/statutory licences) and Section 52 (fair dealing) of the Copyright Act, and Sections 84 and 92 (compulsory licences) of the Patents Act. The commons and anticommons arguments warn that over-protection harms follow-on innovation.

p: Theories of Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Idea–expression dichotomy: copyright protects expression, not ideas ( R.G. Anand v. Delux Films , SC 1978). Originality tests: sweat of the brow (UK, old) vs modicum of creativity (US Feist v. Rural , 1991; India Eastern Book Company , 2008). Rights vs welfare: natural-law and personality theories are rights-based (deontological); utilitarian and economic theories are consequence-based . Public domain: works whose protection has expired or never existed, free for all to use.

x: Theories justify why the law should grant exclusive rights over intangible creations. UGC NET asks mainly: which thinker, which theory, and what is its core idea (and sometimes which theory best explains a particular doctrine). Learn the table first, then read the explanations. Mill IP rights give incentive to create and invest; maximises social welfare Patents, limited-term copyright, TRIPS rationale Economic/Public goods theory Modern law and economics (Landes & Posner) Creations are non-rival and non-excludable, so free-riding destroys incentives unless law creates exclusivity Why IP exists at all; why terms are limited Social planning theory William Fisher IP should be used to build a just and attractive culture Fair use, compulsory licences, public interest limits Prospect theory Edmund Kitch Patent grant is like a mining claim that lets the patentee coordinate development of a technology Early patent filing, scope of claims Contract / Social bargain theory Classical patent theory Inventor discloses the invention; society grants a temporary monopoly in exchange Disclosure requirement, sufficiency of specification, term limit Reward theory Associated with natural-law tradition Society owes the creator a reward for benefit conferred Remuneration claims, royalties Tragedy of the anticommons Michael Heller Too many overlapping exclusive rights block use of resources Patent thickets, licensing bottlenecks
