p: International Conventions on Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: The Paris Convention is the foundation of industrial property law. Its core principles are: National treatment (Art. 2): foreigners from member states get the same protection as nationals. Right of priority (Art. 4): an applicant who first files in one member state has 12 months (patents, utility models) or 6 months (industrial designs, trademarks) to file in other member states and claim the first filing date. Commonly tested: 12 vs 6 months. Independence of patents (Art. 4bis): a patent in one country is independent of patents for the same invention elsewhere. Well-known marks (Art. 6bis): protection against registration or use of marks that conflict with well-known marks even if unregistered. Art. 10bis: protection against unfair competition ; Art. 10: false indications of source. Art. 5A: compulsory licence only after 4 years from filing or 3 years from grant (the basis of Section 84(1) of Indian Patents Act: three years from grant).

p: International Conventions on Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Berne rests on three basic principles : (1) national treatment ; (2) automatic protection (no formalities such as registration or notice); (3) independence of protection (protection does not depend on protection in the country of origin). Other points: minimum term life of the author + 50 years (Art. 7); moral rights (Art. 6bis); minimum rights of translation, reproduction, public performance, adaptation; the Appendix gives developing countries compulsory licences for translation and reproduction. The latest text is the Paris Act 1971 . TRIPS (Art. 9) incorporates Berne (Arts. 1–21) except Article 6bis (moral rights) . India implements Berne through the Copyright Act 1957 and the International Copyright Order.

p: International Conventions on Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Sponsored by UNESCO, designed to bring countries that did not join Berne (notably the USA) into a copyright system. It requires only a notice ( ©, name of owner, year ) as a formality, and sets a minimum term of life + 25 years. After the US joined Berne (1989), UCC lost importance; Berne prevails over UCC among Berne members.

p: International Conventions on Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Protects performers (minimum 20 years), producers of phonograms (20 years) and broadcasting organisations (20 years) as "neighbouring rights". India is not a party , but protects these rights domestically (Sections 37–39A Copyright Act; Section 13 for sound recordings). WPPT 1996 later updated rights of performers and phonogram producers for the digital environment.

p: International Conventions on Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: The most comprehensive IP treaty, administered by the WTO , binding on all WTO members. Key features: Minimum standards (members may give more protection, Art. 1.1). National treatment (Art. 3) and Most Favoured Nation (Art. 4), a new principle in IP law. Objectives and principles: Arts. 7 and 8 (public health, nutrition, public interest measures). Copyright (Arts. 9–14): incorporates Berne (except moral rights); computer programs as literary works (Art. 10); rental rights (Art. 11); term of at least 50 years where not based on life (Art. 12); performers/phonogram producers 50 years; broadcasters 20 years (Art. 14). Trademarks (Arts. 15–21): registrable subject matter, initial registration and each renewal at least 7 years ; compulsory licensing of trademarks not allowed (Art. 21). GIs (Arts. 22–24): general protection (Art. 22) and additional protection for wines and spirits (Art. 23). India has been seeking extension of Art. 23 to all products. Industrial designs (Arts. 25–26): at least 10 years. Patents (Arts. 27–34): patents available for inventions in all fields of technology (Art. 27(1)) that are new, involve an inventive step and are capable of industrial application; exclusions in Art. 27(2)–(3) (including plants and animals other than micro-organisms, and the option of sui generis plant variety protection, the basis of India's PPVFR Act); term 20 years from filing (Art. 33); compulsory licensing conditions (Art. 31); burden of proof in process patents (Art. 34). Layout-designs of integrated circuits (Arts. 35–38): 10 years. Undisclosed information (Art. 39): protection against unfair competition and test data protection. Enforcement (Part III), dispute settlement through the WTO DSB. Transition: developing countries had until 2000 (general), plus a further 5 years (to 2005) for product patents in new fields; least-developed countries have longer transition periods. India introduced product patents in pharmaceuticals/agrochemicals through the Patents (Amendment) Act 2005 , after the 1999 and 2002 amendments. Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health (14 November 2001): TRIPS "can and should be interpreted and implemented in a manner supportive of WTO members' right to protect public health"; each member has the right to grant compulsory licences and determine what constitutes an emergency. The 30 August 2003 Decision (Paragraph 6 system) allows export of medicines made under compulsory licence to countries lacking manufacturing capacity; it was made permanent as Article 31bis (in force 23 January 2017 ). India's counterpart is Section 92A of the Patents Act. At the WTO's 12th Ministerial Conference (June 2022), members adopted a limited TRIPS decision on COVID-19 vaccines (a temporary waiver-like flexibility for vaccine patents).

t: 3.7 WIPO and the WIPO Internet Treaties
p: International Conventions on Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: WIPO (World Intellectual Property Organization) was established by the 1967 Convention (in force 1970) and became a specialised agency of the UN in 1974 ; headquarters Geneva . It administers about 26 treaties including Paris, Berne, PCT, Madrid, Hague and Lisbon. WCT 1996 protects computer programs and compilations of data (databases) as literary works, grants a right of distribution, rental and right of communication to the public , and requires protection against circumvention of technological protection measures (TPMs) and removal of rights management information (RMI) . WPPT 1996 gives performers moral rights and economic rights in fixed performances and phonogram producers economic rights. India's Copyright (Amendment) Act 2012 added Sections 65A (TPMs) and 65B (RMI) to align with these treaties.

p: International Conventions on Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: One international application filed with a receiving office has effect in all designated PCT states. Stages: international phase (search report, written opinion, publication at 18 months, optional international preliminary examination) and national phase (entry into each country within 30 months from priority date; India's period is 31 months , Rule 20(4)(i)). PCT does not grant an "international patent"; each national office grants the patent. The Indian Patent Office acts as a Receiving Office, International Searching Authority (ISA) and International Preliminary Examining Authority (IPEA).

p: International Conventions on Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: The Madrid Agreement (1891) and Madrid Protocol (1989) create a single international registration administered by WIPO. India joined the Protocol (not the Agreement) in 2013 . A basic application or registration in the home country is required, and the international registration is dependent on it for five years ( central attack ). India uses the Nice Classification (45 classes: 1–34 goods, 35–45 services).

t: 3.10 Convention on Biological Diversity, Nagoya Protocol, UPOV and ITPGRFA
p: International Conventions on Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: CBD 1992 (Rio Earth Summit) recognises national sovereignty over biological resources , and sets three goals: conservation, sustainable use, and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources. Article 8(j) requires respect for traditional knowledge of indigenous and local communities. Nagoya Protocol (2010) operationalises access and benefit sharing (ABS). Cartagena Protocol (2000) covers biosafety. UPOV (International Union for Protection of New Varieties of Plants): India is not a member ; it chose a sui generis system under TRIPS Art. 27(3)(b), balancing breeders' and farmers' rights under the PPVFR Act 2001. ITPGRFA (International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture, 2001): farmers' rights and a multilateral benefit-sharing system; India is a party. WIPO GRATK Treaty (24 May 2024): requires patent applicants to disclose the country of origin or source of genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge used in claimed inventions. It enters into force after a threshold number of ratifications (verify current ratification count).

p: International Conventions on Intellectual Property · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Marrakesh Treaty 2013: India was the first country to ratify (2014); reflected in Section 52(1)(zb) (accessible formats for persons with disabilities). Beijing Treaty on Audiovisual Performances 2012: performers' rights in audiovisual fixations. Hague Agreement: international registration of industrial designs. Riyadh Design Law Treaty (2024) harmonises design formalities. Lisbon Agreement 1958 and Geneva Act 2015: appellations of origin and geographical indications. Patent Law Treaty 2000 (formalities harmonisation); India is not a party. Budapest Treaty 1977: a deposit of a micro-organism with an International Depositary Authority satisfies the disclosure requirement. Quick facts for revision (Section 3). Priority: 12 months (patents) / 6 months (designs, marks). Berne term: life + 50 . India's term: life + 60 (more than Berne). Rome Convention: India not a member. PCT national phase: 30 months generally, 31 in India . Madrid Protocol: India 2013. WCT/WPPT: India 2018. TRIPS in force: 1 January 1995 . TRIPS patent term: 20 years . UPOV: India not a member.

p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: The Copyright Act 1957 (in force 21 January 1958) replaced the Indian Copyright Act 1914 (which extended the UK Copyright Act 1911). It has been amended in 1983, 1984, 1991, 1994, 1999 and, most importantly, in 2012 (in force 21 June 2012; the Copyright Rules 2013 followed). The Copyright Board was merged into the IPAB (2017) and, after the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 , its functions passed to the High Court / Commercial Court. A Registrar of Copyrights maintains the Register (Section 44, 45). Registration is optional ; the certificate is prima facie evidence (Section 48). Copyright subsists automatically on creation (Berne principle).

t: 4.2 Nature of copyright: what is protected
p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Copyright protects expression, not ideas, procedures, methods of operation or mathematical concepts (idea–expression dichotomy: R.G. Anand v. Delux Films , 1978; the test of substantial similarity is how the ordinary observer/lay viewer sees the two works). Section 13 lists the classes of work in which copyright subsists: Original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works Cinematograph films Sound recordings Key definitions (Section 2): Literary work (2(o)) includes computer programmes, tables and compilations including computer databases . Dramatic work (2(h)) includes recitation, choreographic work or entertainment in dumb show, scenic arrangement (the acting form); it does not include a cinematograph film. Musical work (2(p)) : music and any graphical notation; it does not include words or action intended to be sung, spoken or performed with the music (lyrics are a separate literary work). Artistic work (2(c)) : painting, sculpture, drawing (including diagram, map, chart or plan), engraving, photograph, work of architecture, and any other work of artistic craftsmanship ; the artistic quality of the work is irrelevant for paintings/sculptures/drawings/engravings/photographs. Cinematograph film (2(f)) : any work of visual recording on any medium, including a sound recording accompanying it, and any work produced by video or any similar process. Sound recording (2(xx)) : recording of sounds from which sounds can be produced, regardless of the medium. Author (2(d)) : literary/dramatic – the author; musical – the composer; artistic – the artist; photograph – the photographer; cinematograph film and sound recording – the producer ; computer-generated work – the person who causes the work to be created . Communication to the public (2(ff)) : making a work available to the public by any means of display or diffusion, other than by issuing copies. Originality. India moved from the English "sweat of the brow" standard ( University of London Press v. University Tutorial Press , 1916) to the "modicum of creativity" standard in Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak (2008, SC) : copy-edited judgments and headnotes of law reports qualify only if the editorial inputs show a minimum degree of creativity and skill, not mere labour. The US analogue is Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone (1991). Photographs, translations, compilations and adaptations are protected as derivative works if original. No copyright in: ideas, titles and slogans (generally, as insufficient), news facts, works of the Government that are statutory (but Government works carry copyright under Section 17(d)), and works not original. A "work" must also be fixed or expressed; copyright does not subsist in unpublished works of foreign authors unless the author is a qualified person (Section 13(2)–(3); International Copyright Order).

p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: The author is the first owner (Section 17), subject to exceptions in the absence of a contrary agreement: Journalist employed by a newspaper/magazine under a contract of service: the proprietor owns copyright for publication in the paper, but the journalist keeps the right for book publication (Section 17(a)). Commissioned photographs, paintings, portraits, engravings (for valuable consideration): the commissioner (Section 17(b)); cinematograph film made for valuable consideration – the producer is the author under Section 2(d)(v). Employment (contract of service or apprenticeship): the employer (Section 17(c)); contract for service (independent contractor) leaves ownership with the contractor unless assigned. Government work : the Government (Section 17(d)); public undertaking (Section 17(dd)); international organisation (Section 17(e)); public lecture/address : the person delivering (Section 17(cc)). Authors of literary/musical works in a film: the 2012 proviso to Section 17 states that nothing in clauses (b) or (c) affects the right of the author in works incorporated in a cinematograph film, other than as part of the film. The producer cannot take over lyricists' and composers' separate rights.

t: 4.4 Rights of the owner: economic rights (Section 14)
p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Section 14 gives exclusive rights , which differ by class of work: Literary, dramatic, musical works: reproduce; issue copies to the public (not already in circulation); perform in public/communicate to the public; make a cinematograph film or sound recording; make translations and adaptations. For computer programmes , also sell or give on commercial rental . Artistic works: reproduce (including in 3D from 2D and vice versa); communicate; adapt; issue copies. Cinematograph films: make a copy (including a photograph of any image); sell/hire; communicate to the public. Sound recordings: make any other recording; sell/hire; communicate. Moral rights (Section 57), Special rights of the author: independent of the author's economic rights and survive assignment. They comprise: Right of paternity: claim authorship of the work. Right of integrity: restrain or claim damages for any distortion, mutilation, modification or other act prejudicial to honour or reputation. They can be enforced by the author or, after death, by the legal representatives . Cases: Amar Nath Sehgal v. Union of India (Delhi HC, 2005) , destruction/neglect of a bronze mural at Vigyan Bhavan violated the integrity right, with relief granted; Mannu Bhandari v. Kala Vikas Pictures (Delhi HC, 1987) , a film adaptation of a novel that mutilated it infringed integrity right (the right is not limited by the assignment). Performer's moral rights are in Section 38B (2012).

p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Work Term Section Published literary, dramatic, musical, artistic work (original) Author's life + 60 years (from the beginning of the calendar year after death; for joint authors, from death of the last author) 22 Anonymous / pseudonymous work 60 years from publication 23 Posthumous work 60 years from publication 24 Photographs 60 years from publication 25 Cinematograph films 60 years from publication 26 Sound recordings 60 years from publication 27 Government works; public undertaking; international organisations 60 years from publication 28–30 Broadcast reproduction right 25 years 37 Performer's right 50 years from the beginning of the calendar year after performance 38 The term is computed from the beginning of the calendar year following the relevant event. India's life + 60 exceeds the Berne minimum of life + 50.

p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Assignment (Sections 18–19): the owner may assign the existing or future copyright (a future work: assignment takes effect on coming into existence). The assignment must be in writing signed by the assignor , and identify the work, the rights assigned, the duration and the territorial extent . If duration is not stated, it is deemed 5 years ; if territory is not stated, India ; if the assignee does not exercise the rights within one year , the assignment is deemed to lapse (unless otherwise specified). The 2012 proviso: authors of literary and musical works in films cannot assign the right to receive royalties except to legal heirs or a copyright society. Licence (Sections 30–30A): the owner can grant exclusive or non-exclusive licences in writing. Licences are not assignments of ownership. Section 19A: disputes about assignment or licence (Copyright Board earlier; now the High Court under the 2021 Act). Compulsory licences: Section 31 (works withheld from the public), 31A (unpublished or orphan works; Indian works where author is dead/unknown/untraceable), 31B (for persons with disabilities , 2012), 31C (cover versions of sound recordings, after 5 years), Section 31D ( statutory licence for broadcasting organisations for literary and musical works and sound recordings, on payment of royalty fixed by the Appellate Board / High Court). Tips Industries v. Wynk Music (Bombay HC, 2019) held that Section 31D covers radio and television broadcasts, not internet streaming; the point remains debated, following a DPIIT 2016 memorandum that extended it to internet broadcasting. Section 32 covers compulsory licence for translation. Copyright societies (Section 33–36A): associations of authors/owners that collect and distribute royalties: IPRS (Indian Performing Right Society, 1969, music composers/lyricists), PPL (Phonographic Performance Ltd), IRRO (Indian Reprographic Rights Organisation), ISRA (Indian Singers' Rights Association). Section 33: no person may carry on the business of issuing or granting licences in respect of a work without being registered/authorised as a copyright society.

p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Primary infringement (51(a)): a person infringes if, without a licence from the owner or the Registrar of Copyrights, he does anything the exclusive right to do which is conferred on the owner; or he permits for profit any place to be used for communication of the work to the public where such communication constitutes infringement (unless he was unaware and had no reasonable ground to believe it was infringement). Secondary infringement (51(b)): making for sale or hire, selling or letting for hire, distributing for the purpose of trade, exhibiting in public by way of trade, or importing infringing copies (except two copies for private use, 2012). Test of infringement: access plus substantial similarity of expression; the quantity and quality of what is taken are considered ( R.G. Anand ; Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon , SC 1996, "Bandit Queen"). Reproduction in a different medium is infringement. Authorising infringement is also an infringement ( Super Cassette Industries v. Myspace , Delhi HC DB 2016: an intermediary with actual knowledge of infringing content may be liable; safe harbour under Section 79 IT Act is limited by Section 81 proviso).

t: 4.8 Limitations and exceptions: fair dealing and other free uses (Section 52)
p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Section 52 lists acts that are not infringement . Indian law uses the closed-list fair dealing model (unlike the open-ended US fair use). Main items: Fair dealing for private or personal use including research; criticism or review; reporting of current events and current affairs including lectures delivered in public (52(1)(a)). Not applicable to computer programmes (except as in (aa)). Cases: India TV Independent News Service v. Yashraj Films (Delhi HC 2013); Wiley Eastern v. Indian Institute of Management (Delhi HC 1996). Computer programmes: making backup copies, adaptation for the lawful use, observation/study/testing, and reverse engineering for interoperability (52(1)(aa)–(ad)). Transient or incidental storage for technological process, and for providing electronic links, access or integration , where not expressly prohibited by the right holder (52(1)(b)–(c), 2012). Judicial proceedings , reports of legislatures and committees; certified copies of public records. Educational: reproduction by a teacher or pupil in the course of instruction; as questions in an examination; performance in an educational institution (52(1)(i)–(j)). Chancellor, Masters & Scholars of the University of Oxford v. Rameshwari Photocopy Services (Delhi HC 2016) , a single judge upheld photocopying of course packs for students as covered by Section 52(1)(i); the Division Bench (2017) set aside the order and remanded; the underlying issue remains in the exam-relevant discussion. Persons with disabilities (52(1)(zb)): conversion to accessible formats, aligned with the Marrakesh Treaty. Religious ceremonies and amateur club performances (52(1)(za), (z)) , certain architectural works, public art in sites, and sound recording of literary/musical works under compulsory conditions (cover versions).

p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Civil remedies (Chapter XII, Section 55): injunction (including interim, Anton Piller order for search and seizure and Mareva -type orders, and John Doe orders for unknown infringers), damages , account of profits , delivery up of infringing copies and plates (Section 58). Innocent infringement: no damages where defendant proves he was unaware and had no reasonable ground to believe copyright subsisted (Section 55(2)), but injunction/account still available. Jurisdiction (Section 62(2)): suit may be filed where the plaintiff actually and voluntarily resides, carries on business or personally works for gain ; see Indian Performing Right Society v. Sanjay Dalia (SC 2015). Section 60: relief against groundless threats of infringement proceedings. Criminal remedies (Chapter XIII): Section 63: knowingly infringing or abetting: imprisonment 6 months to 3 years and fine ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh . Section 63A: enhanced penalty on second or subsequent conviction: imprisonment 1 to 3 years and fine ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh . Section 63B: knowing use of an infringing copy of a computer programme: imprisonment 7 days to 3 years , fine ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh . Section 65A: circumvention of technological protection measures : imprisonment up to 2 years and fine. Section 65B: tampering with rights management information : up to 2 years and fine. Section 64: police may seize infringing copies without a warrant (officer not below Sub-Inspector). Section 53: the Registrar may ban import of infringing copies (Customs Act).

p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Rights related to copyright, protecting those who interpret, record or broadcast works: Broadcast reproduction right (Section 37): every broadcasting organisation has this right: re-broadcast, record, reproduce or sell/hire the broadcast. Term 25 years. Performer's right (Section 38–38B): a performer ( Section 2(qq) includes actor, singer, musician, dancer, acrobat, juggler, conjurer, snake charmer, a person delivering a lecture or any other person who makes a performance) has exclusive rights to make a sound/visual recording, reproduce, broadcast and communicate the performance. Term 50 years. Section 38A(2): once a performer consents to incorporation of the performance in a cinematograph film, he may not object to its exploitation, but is entitled to royalties for other uses; Section 38B gives moral rights (paternity and integrity in respect of performance). Phonogram producers (sound recording producers) have rights under Section 13/14 as authors of sound recordings (60 years). Section 39: acts that do not infringe performers' and broadcasters' rights. Cases: Fortune Films International v. Dev Anand (Bombay HC, 1979) on performer's rights; the 2012 Act brought performers' royalties into the statute.

p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Introduced performers' moral rights and made rights of performers and broadcasters TRIPS/WPPT-compliant. Authors' right to royalties in films (non-assignable except to heirs/copyright societies). Section 31B, 52(1)(zb) for persons with disabilities; Section 31D (statutory licence for broadcasting); Section 31C (cover versions). Sections 65A and 65B on TPMs and RMI; ISP/transient storage exceptions in Section 52(1)(b)–(c). Sections 19(4)–(10) : clear time/territory defaults and the one-year non-exercise rule. Section 33 : copyright societies regulated, with owners' governance rights.

p: Copyright and Neighbouring Rights · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Generative AI and copyright: ANI Media v. OpenAI (Delhi HC, filed 2024) on whether training on news content infringes; DPIIT expert committee working papers on AI training and licensing (2025) – verify current status . The Act has no "text and data mining" exception. Authorship of AI works: under Section 2(d)(vi) the author of a computer-generated work is the person who causes it to be created; the Copyright Office's registration of an AI co-authored work (RAGHAV) and its withdrawal remain a discussion point. Dynamic injunctions and website blocking for piracy: UTV Software Communication v. 1337X.to (Delhi HC 2019) allowed injunctions extending to mirror/redirect websites; Star India v. Moviemaza continues the line. Personality rights and voice cloning: Delhi and Bombay High Courts (e.g. Anil Kapoor v. Simply Life India , 2023; Arijit Singh v. Codible Ventures , Bombay HC 2024) granted injunctions against AI voice/image misuse. Statutory licensing for internet broadcasting and OTT royalties for lyricists remain contested. Quick facts for revision (Section 4). Act: 1957 ; big amendment 2012 . Term: life + 60 ; films/sound recordings/photographs 60 ; broadcast reproduction 25 ; performers 50 . Default assignment: 5 years, India, lapse after 1 year of non-exercise . Moral rights: Section 57 . Infringement: Section 51 ; fair dealing: Section 52 ; criminal: Sections 63–63B (6 months–3 yrs / ₹50,000–₹2 lakh). Orphan works licence: 31A . Disability: 31B / 52(1)(zb) . Jurisdiction: 62(2) . Copyright societies: 33–36 .

p: Law of Patents · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: The Patents Act 1970 (in force 20 April 1972) replaced the Indian Patents and Designs Act 1911. It was modelled on the Ayyangar Committee Report (1959) and originally allowed only process patents for food, medicines and chemicals (Section 5). TRIPS compliance came in three steps: the Patents (Amendment) Act 1999 (mailbox facility and exclusive marketing rights), the 2002 Amendment (term extended to 20 years, Sections 3(p), 25 and TK/biological-material disclosure provisions) and the 2005 Amendment ( product patents in all fields of technology; Section 5 omitted; Section 3(d) strengthened; Section 92A added). The Patents Rules 2003 (amended 2016, 2019, 2021 and 2024 ) govern procedure. The Patents (Amendment) Rules 2024 (March 2024) among other changes relaxed the Form 27 (working statement) to a three-financial-year cycle (verify exact current text). A patent is a statutory monopoly , not a natural right: Bishwanath Prasad Radhey Shyam v. Hindustan Metal Industries (SC 1978) explained that a patent is a reward for the inventor's disclosure, and that the grant of a monopoly must not be broader than the invention.

p: Law of Patents · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Invention (Section 2(1)(j)): a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application . New (2(1)(l)): not anticipated by prior publication, prior use or otherwise, anywhere in the world ( absolute novelty ) before the date of filing/priority. Inventive step (2(1)(ja)): a feature involving technical advance compared to existing knowledge, or having economic significance or both, and making the invention not obvious to a person skilled in the art ("PSITA"). Capable of industrial application (2(1)(ac)): the invention is capable of being made or used in an industry. Subject matter excluded: Section 3 ("What are not inventions"). This is the single most tested provision in patent law. Learn all of 3(a)–(p): Clause Not an invention 3(a) Frivolous inventions or claims contrary to well-established natural laws 3(b) Inventions whose commercial exploitation would be contrary to public order or morality , or cause serious prejudice to human, animal, plant life or health, or the environment 3(c) Discovery of a scientific principle , formulation of an abstract theory, or discovery of any living thing or non-living substance occurring in nature 3(d) Mere discovery of a new form of a known substance that does not result in enhancement of known efficacy ; mere discovery of a new property or new use of a known substance; mere use of a known process unless it results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant. Salts, esters, polymorphs, isomers, combinations are the same substance unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy. 3(e) Mere admixture resulting only in the aggregation of properties of components (e.g. a combination of known drugs with no synergistic effect) 3(f) Mere arrangement, rearrangement or duplication of known devices functioning independently 3(g) (Omitted by the 2002 Amendment) 3(h) Method of agriculture or horticulture 3(i) Any process for the medicinal, surgical, curative, prophylactic, diagnostic, therapeutic or other treatment of human beings or of animals to render them free of disease or to increase their economic value 3(j) Plants and animals in whole or in any part , including seeds, varieties and species, and essentially biological processes for production or propagation of plants and animals (micro-organisms are patentable) 3(k) Mathematical or business method or a computer programme per se or algorithms 3(l) Literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work or any other aesthetic creation (including cinematographic works and television productions) 3(m) A mere scheme, rule or method of performing a mental act , or a method of playing a game 3(n) Presentation of information 3(o) Topography of integrated circuits 3(p) An invention which, in effect, is traditional knowledge , or is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known component(s) Section 4: inventions relating to atomic energy (Atomic Energy Act 1962, Section 20) are not patentable. Section 3(d) and Novartis. Novartis AG v. Union of India (SC, 1 April 2013) is the leading case. Novartis sought a patent on the beta crystalline form of imatinib mesylate (Glivec) for cancer. The Supreme Court held that the beta crystalline form was a new form of a known substance (imatinib free base, disclosed in the Zimmermann patent) and that the claimed increase in bioavailability did not show enhanced therapeutic efficacy ; the explanation to Section 3(d) requires that "efficacy" means therapeutic efficacy for medicines. The Court read 3(d) as a standard setting a higher threshold for incremental innovations to prevent evergreening (extending monopoly by trivial changes), and held it consistent with TRIPS and Article 21. It also said that Section 3(d) is not a limit on patentability of true innovations . Computer-related inventions (CRI). Section 3(k) excludes software per se . CRI Guidelines 2017 (revised) allow patents where the claim shows a technical effect or technical contribution and is not merely software. Ferid Allani v. Union of India (Delhi HC 2019) held that software with technical effect is patentable; Microsoft Technology Licensing LLC v. Assistant Controller of Patents (Delhi HC 2023) applied the same approach. Biotechnology. Dimminaco AG v. Controller of Patents (Calcutta HC 2002): a vaccine containing a live virus was patentable as the claimed process produced a manufacture, rejecting the Controller's "living organism" refusal. Micro-organisms are patentable ( Diamond v. Chakrabarty , US 1980, is the global reference; the Budapest Treaty deposit is required where the invention uses a micro-organism not publicly available). Plant varieties are under the PPVFR Act 2001 .

t: 5.3 Who can apply (Section 6) and forms of application
p: Law of Patents · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: A patent application may be made by: the true and first inventor ; the assignee of the right to apply; or the legal representative of a deceased person who was entitled before death. Applications are made in Form 1 with Form 2 (specification: provisional or complete ), plus Form 3 (Section 8: statement and undertaking on foreign filing), Form 5 (declaration of inventorship, for convention/PCT applications) and Form 26 (authorisation of patent agent). The specification must fully and particularly describe the invention and the best method of performing it known to the applicant (Section 10(4)), and the claims define the scope of protection. A provisional specification secures a priority date, with the complete specification due within 12 months (Section 9).

t: 5.4 Procedure for grant: step by step
p: Law of Patents · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Filing (Section 7) at the appropriate Patent Office (determined by the applicant's/inventor's residence or place of business). Publication (Section 11A) automatically 18 months from the filing/priority date; early publication can be requested (Rule 24A, within about a month). Request for examination (Section 11B) in Form 18 within 48 months from the earlier of the priority/filing date ( expedited examination, Rule 24C, Form 18A for startups, small entities, women applicants, applications where India was the ISA and some others). Examination by an examiner (Section 12): the First Examination Report (FER) is issued; the applicant must comply within 6 months (extendable by 3 months; total 9 months from FER) (Section 21). Search for anticipation by previous publication and prior claiming (Section 13). Pre-grant opposition (Section 25(1)): any person, after publication and before grant , may file a representation. Grounds include: wrongful obtaining; prior publication; prior claiming; public knowledge/use; obviousness; not an invention or not patentable (Sections 3, 4); insufficient description; failure to disclose Section 8 information; convention-date non-compliance; non-disclosure or wrong mention of source/geographical origin of biological material (25(1)(j)); anticipation by knowledge available within a local or indigenous community in India or elsewhere (25(1)(k)). (Rule 55: within 6 months of publication or before grant, whichever is later.) Grant (Section 43) and sealing : the patent is granted if all requirements are met, entered in the Register, and published in the Patent Office Journal . The date of the patent is the date of filing (Section 43(4)). Where it is a PCT application, the international filing date. Post-grant opposition (Section 25(2)): by any person interested , within 12 months from the date of publication of grant , before an Opposition Board , then decided by the Controller. Grounds are the same list as pre-grant (with the wording "person interested" and no "public knowledge/use" difference of note). A revocation petition (Section 64) can be filed before the High Court or as a counterclaim in an infringement suit. Renewal (Section 53(2)): annual renewal fee from the second/third year onwards (the patent lapses on non-payment but may be restored, Sections 60–61). Other key provisions Section 8: the applicant must furnish information about corresponding foreign applications; failure is a ground for opposition and revocation. Section 16: divisional applications where the application claims more than one invention (before grant). Section 54: patent of addition (an improvement or modification of the main invention); term coterminous with the main patent. Section 35–39: secrecy directions for inventions relevant to defence; Section 39: an Indian resident must obtain prior written permission (or wait 6 weeks ) before filing abroad. Section 138 / Rule 20: PCT national-phase entry (31 months). Priority: Convention applications within 12 months (Section 135). Fees: reduced for startups, small entities and educational institutions (80% rebate for startups since 2021 Rules; 2024 Rules extended educational-institution benefits – verify).

p: Law of Patents · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Subject to the Act, a patent grants: For a product patent : the exclusive right to prevent third parties without consent from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the product in India. For a process patent : the exclusive right to prevent others from using the process , and from using, offering for sale, selling or importing the product directly obtained by the process (Section 48(b)). Section 104A: burden of proof shifts to the defendant in process patent suits where the product is new, or where there is a substantial likelihood that the product was made by the patented process and the patentee has been unable to determine the process used. Term (Section 53): 20 years from the date of filing of the application (for PCT, from the international filing date), for all patents. Assignment and licence: must be in writing and registered (Sections 68–70); co-owners have rights under Sections 50–51; Section 70: a co-owner may work the patent but cannot assign/license without the others' consent (subject to agreement). Working of the patent: patentees/licensees must file Form 27 statements on commercial working (Section 146).

t: 5.6 Limitations and exceptions to patent rights
p: Law of Patents · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Government use (Section 47): the Government may import or make patented products for its own use, for research, or for distribution in dispensaries, hospitals and medical institutions. Sections 99–103: use of inventions for the purposes of Government , with notice and payment of royalty/compensation and the Central Government's power of acquisition (Section 102) . Research and experimental use (Section 47(3)): a patented process/product may be used for research or instruction. Bolar provision (Section 107A(a)): any act of making, constructing, using, selling or importing a patented invention solely for uses reasonably related to the development and submission of information required under any law that regulates manufacture/sale/import of any product (so generics can seek regulatory approval before patent expiry). 107A(b): parallel importation of patented products from a person duly authorised to sell them – international exhaustion. Compulsory licences (Sections 84–92): Section 84: any person interested may apply after 3 years from the date of grant on grounds that (a) the reasonable requirements of the public have not been satisfied; (b) the invention is not available at a reasonably affordable price ; (c) the invention is not worked in the territory of India . Bayer Corporation v. Union of India and Natco Pharma (Controller 2012; IPAB 2013; Bombay HC 2014; SC dismissed SLP 2014) is India's first (and best-known) compulsory licence : sorafenib tosylate (Nexavar) , for kidney/liver cancer, granted to Natco on all three grounds, with royalty of 6% of net sales. Section 92: compulsory licence at any time after grant in circumstances of national emergency, extreme urgency or public non-commercial use , by notification of the Central Government. Section 92A: compulsory licence for export of patented pharmaceutical products to countries with insufficient manufacturing capacity (TRIPS Para 6 system; Art. 31bis). Section 83: general principles applicable to working of patented inventions: patents are granted to encourage inventions and secure that they are worked on a commercial scale in India without undue delay and not merely for importation; they should not impede protection of public health and nutrition. Section 90: terms and conditions of CL (reasonable royalty, non-exclusive, non-assignable, with the main aim of supply in India). Section 66: revocation of a patent in the public interest by the Central Government. Patent linkage rejected: Bayer Corporation v. Union of India (Delhi HC 2010) held that the drug regulator cannot refuse marketing approval merely because a patent exists; India does not follow patent linkage. Traditional knowledge protection (Section 3(p)) and disclosure of biological source (Section 10(4)(d)(ii)(A)); Section 64(1)(p)–(q) grounds for revocation.

p: Law of Patents · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: On petition of a person interested or the Central Government (or counterclaim in an infringement suit) to the High Court . Grounds (Section 64(1)) include: patent granted to a person not entitled; already claimed in an earlier Indian patent (prior claiming) ; invention published before the priority date or publicly known/used in India ( prior publication/use ); obvious or lacking inventive step; not an invention under the Act or not patentable ; insufficient/ambiguous description ; wrong Section 8 information; secrecy directions contravened; failure to disclose the source of biological material (64(1)(p)); and anticipation by traditional knowledge (64(1)(q)).

p: Law of Patents · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: What is infringement? Unauthorised making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the patented product, or using the patented process (and its direct products), in India , during the term of the patent. Test: the claims are construed purposively; the court looks at the "pith and marrow" of the invention ( Raj Prakash v. Mangat Ram Chowdhary , Delhi HC 1977); equivalents are considered under the doctrine of equivalents/purposive construction (Indian courts have also applied Catnic ). Infringement and revocation are decided on the claims as granted . Jurisdiction (Section 104): suits lie in the District Court ; where the defendant counterclaims for revocation, the suit is transferred to the High Court . After the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021, appeals from the Controller go to the High Court (Section 117A). Reliefs (Section 108): injunction (interim and final), damages or account of profits (against the infringer; innocent infringer exception, Section 111), delivery up . Section 106: relief against groundless threats of infringement proceedings . Section 109: an exclusive licensee may sue (patentee as co-plaintiff); Section 110: the right of a licensee/assignee. Standard-essential patents (SEPs): Telefonaktiebolaget LM Ericsson v. Lava International (Delhi HC 2024) awarded approx. ₹244 crore in damages for SEP infringement of 2G/3G patents, an important recent decision on FRAND (fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory) licensing. Offences (Chapter XX): falsification of Register (Section 123), unauthorised claim of patent rights (Section 120), wrongful claim of being a patent agent, breach of secrecy directions (Section 118), refusal to supply information; with penalties of imprisonment (up to 6 months in some provisions) and fines, though many criminal provisions were decriminalised or reduced under the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act 2023 (verify provisions).

p: Law of Patents · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: IPAB abolition (2021): appeals now lie to the High Court ; the Delhi High Court's IP Division deals with Patent Office appeals. Section 3(d) litigation continues (e.g. disputes on drugs such as risdiplam and linagliptin). Standard-essential patents and FRAND damages (Ericsson v. Lava, 2024). Increasing use of the 2021–2024 Rules to reduce fees and timelines (startups, educational institutions, expedited examination). Patent grants by the Indian Patent Office have risen sharply since 2020 (CGPDTM annual reports). Genome/AI inventions and CRI Guidelines; disclosure of origin under the WIPO GRATK Treaty (2024) and Section 10(4)(d)(ii)(A). Patents (Amendment) Rules 2024: Form 27 once in three years (verify), changes to Form 3 timeline and divisional applications. Quick facts for revision (Section 5). Act: 1970 (in force 1972). Term: 20 years from filing . Publication: 18 months . RFE: 48 months . FER reply: 6 + 3 months . Pre-grant opposition: Section 25(1) ; post-grant: 25(2) within 12 months of publication of grant. Revocation: Section 64 . Compulsory licence: Section 84 (after 3 years ), Section 92 (emergency, any time), Section 92A (export). Bolar: 107A . Product patents: 2005 . Not inventions: Section 3 ; atomic energy: Section 4 . Novartis: 2013 (3(d), "therapeutic efficacy"). First CL: Natco (Bayer's sorafenib), 2012 . Burden of proof in process patents: Section 104A . Foreign filing permission: Section 39 (6 weeks) .

p: Law of Trademarks · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: The Trade Marks Act 1999 (in force 15 September 2003 ) replaced the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act 1958 and brought Indian law in line with TRIPS. The Trade Marks Rules 2017 (in force 6 March 2017) replaced the 2002 Rules and streamlined forms (single Form TM-A for all applications, e-filing fee concessions). The Registrar of Trade Marks works from the Trade Marks Registry (HQ Mumbai ; offices at Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Ahmedabad). Classification follows the Nice Classification: 45 classes (classes 1–34 goods; 35–45 services). Functions of a trademark: indication of origin, guarantee of quality, advertising and investment function . Definitions (Section 2(1)): Trade mark (zb): a mark capable of being represented graphically and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others, and may include the shape of goods, their packaging and combination of colours . ( Sound marks can be represented graphically through musical notation, and the 2017 Rules allow an MP3 file; the first Indian sound mark was the Yahoo! yodel (2008).) Mark (m): includes a device, brand, heading, label, ticket, name, signature, word, letter, numeral, shape of goods, packaging or combination of colours, or any combination. Well-known trade mark (zg): a mark that has become so to the substantial segment of the public which uses the goods/receives the services that its use on other goods/services would likely be taken as indicating a connection with the proprietor. Certification trade mark (e) , collective mark (g) , service (z) , permitted use (r) , deceptively similar (h) (a mark that so nearly resembles another as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion).

p: Law of Trademarks · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Kind Notes Provisions Product/word/device marks Words, logos, labels, devices Sec 2(1)(zb) Service marks Marks for services (banking, airlines, telecom) Sec 2(1)(z) Collective marks Owned by an association; members use it (e.g. trade association emblem) Sec 2(1)(g), 61–68 Certification marks Certify origin, material, mode of manufacture, quality (e.g. AGMARK, ISI, Woolmark ) Sec 2(1)(e), 69–78 Well-known marks Protected across classes even if unregistered in India; Registrar's list under Rule 124 Sec 2(1)(zg), 11(6)–(9), 29(4) Shape, colour and trade dress marks 3-D shapes, packaging, colour combination Sec 2(1)(zb), 9(3); Colgate Palmolive v. Anchor Health (Delhi HC 2003, red-and-white colour combination); Christian Louboutin v. Abubaker (Delhi HC 2018, red sole) Sound marks Jingle/audio logo (Yahoo! 2008) 2017 Rules Series marks Several marks that resemble each other in material particulars Sec 15 Associated marks Marks of the same proprietor that are identical/similar and used for same/similar goods Sec 16 Domain names Protected via passing off when they function as source identifiers Yahoo! Inc v. Akash Arora (Delhi HC 1999); Satyam Infoway v. Sifynet Solutions (SC 2004) Note: defensive registration (Section 47, TMMA 1958) was abolished by the 1999 Act; protection of well-known marks in dissimilar goods replaces it.

p: Law of Trademarks · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Absolute grounds (Section 9): a mark shall not be registered if it: is devoid of any distinctive character (not capable of distinguishing); consists exclusively of marks or indications that may serve to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, values, geographical origin, time of production or other characteristics of goods or services ( descriptive ); consists exclusively of marks which have become customary in the current language or in bona fide and established practices of trade ( generic ); is of such nature as to deceive the public or cause confusion ; is likely to hurt the religious susceptibilities of any class; contains scandalous or obscene matter; or is prohibited under the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act 1950 ; Section 9(3): a mark that consists exclusively of the shape of goods resulting from the nature of the goods , or necessary to obtain a technical result , or which gives substantial value to the goods . Proviso to 9(1): acquired distinctiveness (a mark that has become distinctive through use before the application date, or is a well-known mark, is registrable). Spectrum of distinctiveness: generic \< descriptive \< suggestive \< arbitrary \< fanciful (coined) marks; fanciful/arbitrary marks get the strongest protection. Relative grounds (Section 11): Registration is refused where, because of identity or similarity with an earlier trade mark and identity or similarity of goods/services , there exists a likelihood of confusion , including likelihood of association (11(1)). Section 11(2): a mark identical or similar to an earlier mark with a reputation in India shall not be registered for dissimilar goods where use would take unfair advantage of, or be detrimental to, the distinctive character or repute of the earlier mark. Section 11(3): prohibited where use is liable to be prevented by the law of passing off or copyright . Section 11(6)–(9): factors in determining a well-known mark : knowledge in the relevant sector of the public (including as a result of promotion), duration, extent and geographical area of use, promotion, registration or applications, record of successful enforcement. Section 11(9): it is not necessary that the mark has been used in India, registered in India, or is well known to the public at large in India. Section 12: honest concurrent use and special circumstances allow registration of identical or similar marks.

p: Law of Trademarks · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Search the register (optional but advisable) and file the application (Section 18): by a person claiming to be the proprietor of a mark used or proposed to be used ; one application for a single class (multi-class permitted in a single application now). Examination by the Registrar (Section 19, 20): objections raised by an examination report ; the applicant replies and may be heard. Acceptance and advertisement in the Trade Marks Journal (Section 20). Opposition (Section 21): any person may oppose within three months from the advertisement, extendable by one month (maximum 4 months); notice of opposition in Form TM-O ; counterstatement within two months. Registration (Section 23): if no opposition or opposition fails, the mark is registered and a certificate issued. The date of registration is the date of application. Duration and renewal (Section 25): registration is for 10 years and renewable for 10-year periods indefinitely ; renewal is due before expiry; a lapsed mark can be restored with surcharge (within one year after expiry, Section 25(3)). Appeal (Section 91): appeals from the Registrar's orders lie to the High Court (earlier the IPAB, abolished in 2021). Removal for non-use (Section 47): a registration can be removed on the ground that the mark was registered without a bona fide intention to use it, and has not been used for a continuous period of 5 years and 3 months from the date of registration. Section 57: rectification of the register. Assignment, transmission and use by others: Section 37–45: a registered/unregistered trademark is assignable with or without goodwill (Section 38); an assignment creating overlapping exclusive rights in different places is restricted (Sections 40–42). Registered users (Sections 48–55) and permitted use: the use of a mark by a registered user or permitted user is deemed use by the proprietor (licensing with quality control). Section 28: registration gives the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods/services and to obtain relief for infringement. Section 31: registration is prima facie evidence of validity; Section 32: protection of registration on ground of acquired distinctiveness; Section 33: acquiescence for five years bars the proprietor of an earlier mark from objecting to later use (unless registration was applied for in bad faith).

p: Law of Trademarks · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Infringement is a statutory wrong : a person who, not being a registered proprietor or permitted user, uses in the course of trade a mark identical or deceptively similar to the registered mark, in a way likely to be taken as use as a trademark, infringes. Under Section 29: 29(1): the mark is identical/deceptively similar and goods/services are those for which the mark is registered. 29(2): (a) the mark is identical and goods are similar ; (b) the mark is similar and goods are identical ; (c) both are similar; in each case with likelihood of confusion . 29(3): the court presumes confusion where the mark and goods are both identical . 29(4): dilution : infringement even for dissimilar goods if the registered mark has a reputation in India and use takes unfair advantage of, or is detrimental to, the distinctive character or repute of the mark. 29(5): use of the registered mark as a trade name or part of a trade name of the defendant's business. 29(6)–(9): forms of "use" (affixing, selling, importing, using on business papers, advertising, spoken use ); infringement by advertising that takes unfair advantage or is contrary to honest practices. Limits on the effect of registration (Section 30): use of the mark that is in accordance with honest practices in industrial or commercial matters is not infringement, including: use of one's own name or place of business; indications of kind, quality, quantity, geographical origin ( descriptive/nominative fair use ); use to indicate the intended purpose of goods (spare parts); exhaustion of rights after lawful sale (Section 30(3)–(4), subject to impairment of condition of goods); and Section 34 : prior user rights (continuous use from before the registration/use of the registered proprietor). Tests for deceptive similarity (Indian case law): Amritdhara Pharmacy v. Satya Deo Gupta (SC 1963): the test is how the mark would strike a person of average intelligence and imperfect recollection ; the marks are compared as wholes ("Amritdhara" vs "Lakshmandhara"). Corn Products Refining Co. v. Shangrila Food Products (SC 1960): "Gluvita" vs "Glucovita"; overall structural and phonetic similarity. Parle Products v. J.P. & Co. (SC 1972): the question is whether a person acquainted with the original would be deceived; Cadila Health Care v. Cadila Pharmaceuticals (SC 2001): in pharma cases, courts apply stricter standards (nature of the goods, the consumers, the risk of harm); factors include nature of marks, degree of resemblance, nature of goods, class of purchasers, mode of purchase and surrounding circumstances. Ruston & Hornsby v. Zamindara Engineering (SC 1969): infringement is a statutory remedy, passing off is a common-law remedy, and the plaintiff in an infringement action need not prove actual deception where the marks are identical. Territoriality: Toyota Jidosha Kabushiki Kaisha v. Prius Auto Industries (SC 2017) reaffirmed the territoriality principle (reputation in India is required; a foreign mark's spillover reputation must be proved in India) and distinguished earlier cases like N.R. Dongre v. Whirlpool and Milmet Oftho Industries v. Allergan (SC 2004) , where transborder reputation was accepted. Dilution: Daimler Benz v. Hybo Hindustan (Delhi HC 1994) ("Benz" on underwear); Tata Sons v. Manoj Dodia (Delhi HC 2011) on well-known marks and dilution.

p: Law of Trademarks · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Passing off is a common-law tort preserved by Section 27(2) (no action lies for infringement of an unregistered trade mark, but the right of action for passing off is unaffected). It protects goodwill . Classical trinity (Reckitt & Colman v. Borden, "Jif Lemon", House of Lords 1990): (1) goodwill or reputation in the plaintiff's goods/services; (2) misrepresentation by the defendant (leading or likely to lead the public to believe the goods are the plaintiff's); (3) damage (or likelihood) to the plaintiff. Indian cases: Laxmikant V. Patel v. Chetanbhat Shah (SC 2002) (injunction against passing off even without proof of actual damage; honest adoption is not a defence); Cadbury India v. Neeraj Food Products (Delhi HC 2007) ; S. Syed Mohideen v. P. Sulochana Bai (SC 2015) (registration is not a defence to passing off by a prior user). Infringement Passing off Source Statute (Trade Marks Act, Section 29) Common law tort (Section 27(2) preserves it) Mark Registered mark Registered or unregistered; goodwill is the basis Proof Use of identical/deceptively similar mark; confusion presumed in some cases Goodwill + misrepresentation + damage Defence of honest adoption Limited Not a defence Forum District Court / High Court (Section 134) Same court as the suit may combine both causes of action

p: Law of Trademarks · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Civil (Section 135): injunction (including interim injunction, Anton Piller (search/seizure) and John Doe orders ), damages or account of profits , delivery up of infringing labels and marks for destruction. Section 134: the suit shall be instituted in a District Court not inferior to the court having jurisdiction, and the plaintiff can sue where he actually and voluntarily resides, carries on business or personally works for gain (the plaintiff-friendly jurisdiction clause). Section 142: relief against groundless threats. Criminal (Chapter XIII): Section 103: applying a false trademark or false trade description: imprisonment 6 months to 3 years and fine ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh . Section 104: selling goods with false trade marks; Section 105: enhanced penalty for repeat offences; Section 107: falsely representing a trade mark as registered (up to 3 years or fine, as amended). Section 115(4): police officers of the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police or above may search and seize without a warrant after obtaining the Registrar's opinion on facts involved. Offences by companies: Section 114 ; Customs: the Registrar may stop importation of infringing goods (Section 11 of the Customs Act read with IPR Rules 2007).

p: Law of Trademarks · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Madrid Protocol (2013) has increased international filings; sound mark and shape mark registrations are growing. E-commerce intermediaries: Christian Louboutin v. Nakul Bajaj (Delhi HC 2018) and Amazon Seller Services v. Modicare (Delhi HC DB 2020) discuss the "active role" of marketplaces and safe harbour under Section 79 IT Act in trademark cases. Well-known marks: Registrar's list under Rule 124 and judicial declarations (Delhi High Court has declared many marks well known). Keyword advertising and meta-tags ( Google India v. Vishwa Bharti ; Consim Info v. Google India , Madras HC 2013) and domain-name disputes (INDRP, .IN registry). Dilution of famous marks in unrelated goods; trade dress disputes (shape and packaging). Abolition of IPAB : High Courts hear all trademark appeals. Quick facts for revision (Section 6). Act: 1999 (in force 2003 ); Rules 2017 . Classes: 45 (Nice). Registration: 10 years , renewable. Opposition: 3 months + 1 . Non-use removal: 5 years 3 months . Absolute grounds: Section 9 ; relative grounds: Section 11 . Infringement: Section 29 ; limits: Section 30 ; passing off preserved: Section 27(2) . Appeals: Section 91 (High Court). Suit jurisdiction: Section 134 . Penalties: Sections 103–107 (6 months–3 years; ₹50,000–₹2 lakh). Certification marks: Sections 69–78 ; collective marks: 61–68 . Well-known mark: Section 2(1)(zg) .

p: Geographical Indications · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999 (in force 15 September 2003 ; GI Rules 2002) is India's sui generis GI law, enacted to comply with TRIPS Articles 22–24 . The Geographical Indications Registry is at Chennai , under the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (who is also the Registrar of GIs ). The first Indian GI was Darjeeling Tea (registered 2004–05). Definition (Section 2(1)(e)): an indication which identifies such goods as agricultural goods, natural goods or manufactured goods as originating, or manufactured in the territory of a country, or a region or locality in that territory , where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin , and in the case where such goods are manufactured goods , one of the activities of either the production, processing or preparation takes place in such territory, region or locality.

p: Geographical Indications · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Who may apply (Section 11): any association of persons or producers , or any organisation or authority established by or under any law representing the interests of the producers of the goods concerned. An individual cannot apply. Register (Section 6): Part A (registered geographical indications) and Part B ( authorised users ). A producer of the goods can apply to be registered as an authorised user (Section 17). Procedure: application; preliminary scrutiny; Examination by a Consultative Group of Experts ; show-cause notice; publication in the GI Journal ; opposition (within three months , extendable); registration. Duration (Section 18): registration is for 10 years , renewable indefinitely (like trademarks). Grounds of refusal (Section 9): a GI is not registrable if its use would deceive or confuse ; is contrary to law ; contains scandalous or obscene matter; may hurt religious susceptibilities ; would otherwise be disentitled to protection in a court ; is a generic name or has ceased to be protected, or has fallen into disuse, in its country of origin; or, although literally true as to origin, falsely represents to the public that the goods originate elsewhere. GI logo and tagline ("Geographical Indication of India"), introduced to promote GI-tagged products.

p: Geographical Indications · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Section 21: registration gives authorised users the exclusive right to the use of the GI and the right to obtain relief for infringement . Section 20: no action lies for infringement of an unregistered GI, though passing off remains available. Infringement (Section 22): (a) use of any means in the designation or presentation of goods that indicates or suggests that the goods originate in a geographical area other than the true place of origin in a manner that misleads the public; (b) use that constitutes an act of unfair competition including passing off ; (c) use of another GI even where the true origin is indicated , or where the GI is used in translation or accompanied by expressions like " kind ", " style ", " imitation " (thus India gives wine-and-spirits type protection broadly). Section 24: a right to a GI cannot be assigned, transmitted, licensed, pledged or mortgaged ; on the death of an authorised user, the right devolves on the successor in title. This is the major difference from trademarks. Offences: falsifying a GI , falsely applying a GI to goods and selling goods with false GIs are punishable by imprisonment of 6 months to 3 years and fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh (offences chapter of the Act). Appeals: formerly to the IPAB; now to the High Court after the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021.

p: Geographical Indications · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Tea Board India v. ITC Ltd (Calcutta HC 2011): Darjeeling tea (certification mark and GI); ITC's "Darjeeling Lounge" use at its hotels was challenged.
