t: 8.1 Why this topic exists: the IPR–biodiversity link
p: Biodiversity and Traditional Knowledge · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Biological resources and the knowledge of communities about them are valuable inputs for pharmaceuticals, agriculture and cosmetics. Before the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) 1992 , genetic resources were treated as the "common heritage of mankind" and freely accessible; patents on products derived from them were granted without sharing benefits. The CBD changed this by recognising sovereign rights of states over biological resources (Article 15) and requiring prior informed consent (PIC) and mutually agreed terms (MAT) for access, and fair and equitable benefit sharing . Biopiracy means unauthorised commercial exploitation of biological resources or associated traditional knowledge (TK), usually through patents granted to foreign companies/institutions without consent or benefit sharing.

p: Biodiversity and Traditional Knowledge · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Enacted to implement the CBD (to which India is a party since 1994). The Biological Diversity Rules 2004 supplement the Act. The BD Act sets up a three-tier institutional structure : Tier Body Location / key feature National National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) (Section 8) Chennai ; statutory body established in 2003; regulates access and benefit sharing; advises Government State State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) (Section 22) Regulates commercial utilisation by Indian citizens/companies; advises state governments Local Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) (Section 41) Constituted by local bodies; prepare People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs) documenting local biological resources and knowledge Key provisions Section 3: foreign nationals, non-resident Indians and foreign-controlled companies/organisations (non-Indian participation in share capital or management) require prior approval of the NBA to obtain any biological resource occurring in India, or knowledge associated with it, for research, commercial utilisation, bio-survey or bio-utilisation. Section 4: prior approval of NBA for transfer of results of research relating to biological resources occurring in/obtained from India to any foreigner. Section 6: approval of NBA is required before applying for any IPR in or outside India for an invention based on biological resources obtained from India (the original Act allowed approval after acceptance of an Indian patent application but before sealing). Section 6(3): NBA may impose benefit-sharing conditions or royalties . Section 7: Indian citizens/companies must give prior intimation to the SBB before obtaining biological resources for commercial utilisation (not for local people and vaids/hakims who have been practising indigenous medicine, and exemptions for normally traded commodities). Section 18, 21: functions of NBA; benefit sharing may be monetary or non-monetary : joint ownership of IPR, technology transfer, research and development, capacity building, royalties. Section 36: Government to develop national strategies for conservation ; Section 37: declaration of Biodiversity Heritage Sites (BHS) by the State Governments in consultation with local bodies; Section 38: notification of threatened species ; Section 36(5): Central Government protects traditional knowledge of local people. Section 41: BMCs; Section 55 (as originally enacted): penalties for contravention of Sections 3, 4 and 6: imprisonment up to 5 years , or fine up to ₹10 lakh , or both. Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023. Passed by Parliament in July–August 2023 and brought into force in phases. Main changes: Decriminalisation: imprisonment replaced by monetary penalties for most offences (penalties ranging from about ₹1 lakh up to ₹50 lakh, higher for serious breaches; verify the exact figures); adjudication by an Adjudicating Officer . Exemptions for codified traditional knowledge , cultivated medicinal plants , and AYUSH practitioners and local communities (including the earlier exemption of vaids/hakims); and fast-track approvals for research, patent applications and transfer of research results. Prior approval for IPR now required before grant (not before application) – aimed at easing patent filings (verify exact stage). Benefit-sharing now tied to commercial utilisation ; Indian companies (including those with limited foreign shareholding) treated more favourably; foreign-owned entities remain regulated. Wider definition of " access " and addition of "codified TK" , and requirement for the BMCs and Local Bodies to be consulted.

t: 8.3 Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights (PPVFR) Act 2001
p: Biodiversity and Traditional Knowledge · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Enacted under TRIPS Art. 27(3)(b) option for a sui generis system, rather than joining UPOV. Authority: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority (PPVFRA) , New Delhi; Registry ; Plant Varieties Protection Appellate Tribunal . Registrable varieties: new, distinct, uniform and stable (NDUS) ; extant varieties and farmers' varieties are also registrable. Varieties with genetic use restriction technologies ("terminator") are not registrable. Term (Section 24(6)): 15 years from the date of registration for most crops; 18 years for trees and vines ; 15 years from the date of notification for extant varieties. Breeders' rights: exclusive right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import or export the variety. Farmers' rights (Section 39): a farmer may save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share or sell his farm produce including seed of a protected variety, but cannot sell branded seed of a protected variety. Also: farmers are not required to pay fee in proceedings; Further: registration of farmers' varieties and recognition and reward through the Gene Fund ; Section 26 and the National Gene Fund for benefit sharing ; Liability: compensation if the variety fails to perform as claimed. Compulsory licensing of protected varieties is possible after 3 years if the seed isn't available to the public at a reasonable price (Section 47). Related case/current affairs: PepsiCo India Holdings v. Registrar/PPV&FR Authority (Delhi HC; FL-2027 potato variety – breeders' rights vs. farmers' rights, litigation 2021–2024; verify latest status). Monsanto Technology v. Nuziveedu Seeds (SC 2019): Bt cotton patents; Section 3(j) Patents Act and the interface with PPVFR.

p: Biodiversity and Traditional Knowledge · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Meaning. TK is knowledge, know-how, skills and practices developed, sustained and passed from generation to generation within a community, often forming part of its cultural or spiritual identity. It includes agricultural, medicinal (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Yoga), ecological knowledge, and traditional cultural expressions (folklore) . It is typically collective, oral, cumulative and not novel in the patent-law sense (it is already in the public domain, so the patent system tends to fail to protect it and invites misappropriation). Biopiracy and landmark cases (very high yield) Turmeric (haldi) patent: US Patent No. 5,401,504 (1995) was granted to the University of Mississippi Medical Center for use of turmeric in wound healing. India's CSIR challenged it with ancient Sanskrit texts and a 1953 JAMA paper ; the USPTO revoked the patent in 1997 – the first successful challenge by a developing country to a biopiracy patent. Neem patent: European Patent No. 436,257 (granted 1994) to the US Department of Agriculture and W.R. Grace & Co. for a fungicidal neem-oil method; opposed in Europe by Indian and international organisations (including Vandana Shiva, the Research Foundation for Science, Technology and Ecology and the European Greens ); revoked by the EPO in 2000 and the revocation was upheld on appeal in 2005 for lack of inventive step (no novelty because of prior use of neem in India). Basmati rice: RiceTec Inc. obtained US Patent No. 5,663,484 (1997) claiming Basmati lines and grains; after India's challenge (via APEDA/Government) the USPTO narrowed the claims (2001) , and RiceTec withdrew the Basmati-named claims; this led to Basmati's GI registration in India (2016) . Others: Hoodia (San people, South Africa) and Kava , Ayahuasca , Hoodia are international examples of benefit-sharing disputes. India's legal measures to protect TK Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) : established in 2001 by CSIR and the Department of AYUSH , a searchable database of Indian systems of medicine (Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Yoga, Sowa-Rigpa). Information is classified using the Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification (TKRC) , modelled on the International Patent Classification, and made available in English, French, German, Japanese and Spanish . Access agreements allow patent examiners at the EPO, USPTO, JPO, UKIPO and other offices to search TKDL as prior art , preventing erroneous patents. Patents Act (2002 Amendment): Section 3(p) (TK is not an invention); Section 10(4)(d)(ii)(A) (disclosure of the source and geographical origin of biological material); Section 25(1)(j)–(k) and 25(2)(j)–(k) (pre-grant and post-grant opposition on non-disclosure and on anticipation by TK); Section 64(1)(p)–(q) (revocation). Biological Diversity Act 2002: PIC/MAT , benefit sharing (Sections 3, 6, 21), BMCs and People's Biodiversity Registers (to document local knowledge and prevent misappropriation), Section 36(5) . GI Act 1999: protects collective indigenous products linked to place (handlooms, handicrafts). Copyright: folklore as traditional cultural expressions is only indirectly protected (works whose authors are unknown; the Copyright Act has no sui generis TCE right, although Sections 22–23 deal with anonymous works). PPVFR Act 2001: farmers' varieties and farmers' rights. International developments CBD Article 8(j) (respect and maintain TK, innovations and practices of indigenous and local communities and promote their wider application with their approval and involvement, with equitable benefit sharing) and Nagoya Protocol 2010 (access to genetic resources and associated TK , benefit sharing, compliance measures). WIPO IGC (Intergovernmental Committee on IP and Genetic Resources, Traditional Knowledge and Folklore, established 2000 ): led to the WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge, adopted 24 May 2024 , the first WIPO treaty directly addressing TK. It requires patent applicants to disclose the country of origin or source of genetic resources, and the Indigenous Peoples or local community providing associated TK. Enters into force after ratification by 15 contracting parties (verify current status). TRIPS Council debate on a mandatory disclosure of origin (proposed amendment to TRIPS Art. 29bis, supported by India, Brazil and others). ITPGRFA 2001: a multilateral system for access and benefit sharing for plant genetic resources for food and agriculture, and farmers' rights . Analysis points (for conceptual MCQs). (i) TK is not patentable because it lacks novelty (public domain) and an identifiable inventor. (ii) The defensive approach (databases like TKDL preventing wrongful patents) is distinct from positive protection (granting rights to communities). (iii) Disclosure of origin is a linking mechanism between patent law and the CBD. (iv) The 2023 amendment's exemption for codified TK is criticised for weakening community benefit sharing. Quick facts for revision (Section 8). BD Act: 2002 ; NBA: Chennai (2003) ; SBBs; BMCs; PBR; Section 3 (foreigners), 4 (transfer), 6 (IPR), 7 (Indian users), 41 (BMC). Amendment: 2023 . PPVFR Act: 2001 ; term 15/18 years ; Section 39 farmers' rights. TKDL: 2001 ; CSIR + AYUSH. Turmeric: US patent revoked 1997 ; Neem: EPO revoked 2000 (upheld 2005); Basmati: RiceTec 1997 claims narrowed 2001 . CBD: 1992 ; Nagoya: 2010 ; WIPO GRATK Treaty: 2024 .

t: 9.1 Background and objectives of the IT Act 2000
p: Information Technology Law: Digital Signature, E-Governance and Electronic Records · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: The Information Technology Act 2000 (Act 21 of 2000) was enacted on 9 June 2000 (assent) and came into force on 17 October 2000 . It is based on the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce 1996 (adopted by UN General Assembly Resolution 51/162 of 30 January 1997) and was amended by the Information Technology (Amendment) Act 2008 (in force 27 October 2009 ), which introduced electronic signatures (technology neutral), Section 66A–66F, 67A–67C, 69A–69B, 70A–70B , Section 43A , Section 79 (intermediary) and the "reasonable security practices" regime. Objectives (preamble): to provide legal recognition for transactions carried out by electronic data interchange and other means of electronic communication ("electronic commerce"), to facilitate electronic filing of documents with Government agencies , and to amend the IPC, the Indian Evidence Act 1872, the Bankers' Books Evidence Act 1891 and the RBI Act 1934 . Extent and application (Section 1): extends to the whole of India and, Section 75 , applies also to any offence or contravention committed outside India by any person if the act involves a computer, computer system or computer network located in India . Section 1(4) + First Schedule: the Act does not apply to: (a) a negotiable instrument other than a cheque ; (b) a power of attorney ; (c) a trust ; (d) a will ; (e) a contract for the sale or conveyance of immovable property . Important definitions (Section 2(1)): access (a) ; addressee (b) ; adjudicating officer (c) ; affixing electronic signature (d) ; asymmetric crypto system (f) ; Certifying Authority (g) ; computer (i) ; computer network (j) ; computer resource (k) ; computer system (l) ; Controller (m) ; cyber cafe (na) ; cyber security (nb) ; data (o) ; digital signature (p) ; Digital Signature Certificate (q) ; electronic form (r) ; electronic record (t) ; electronic signature (ta) ; electronic signature certificate (tb) ; information (v) ; intermediary (w) (any person who on behalf of another receives, stores or transmits that record or provides any service with respect to it, including telecom service providers, network service providers, ISPs, web-hosting service providers, search engines, online payment sites, online-auction sites, online marketplaces and cyber cafes); key pair (x) ; originator (za) ; private key (zc) ; public key (zd) ; secure system (ze) ; security procedure (zf) ; subscriber (zg) .

p: Information Technology Law: Digital Signature, E-Governance and Electronic Records · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Digital signature (Section 2(1)(p), Section 3): authentication of any electronic record by a subscriber by means of an electronic method or procedure in accordance with Section 3. A digital signature is created using an asymmetric crypto system and a hash function : the subscriber's private key transforms (encrypts) the hash (message digest) of the record; the public key (certified in a Digital Signature Certificate ) is used by the recipient to verify both authenticity (who signed) and integrity (record unchanged). It is technology-specific (PKI-based). Electronic signature (Section 2(1)(ta), Section 3A, inserted by the 2008 Amendment): authentication of any electronic record by a subscriber by means of the electronic technique specified in the Second Schedule , and includes a digital signature. It is technology neutral and reflects the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Signatures 2001 . Conditions for a reliable electronic signature (Section 3A(2)): (a) the signature creation data are, within the context in which they are used, linked to the signatory and to no other person ; (b) the data were, at the time of signing, under the exclusive control of the signatory ; (c) any alteration to the electronic signature after affixing is detectable ; and (d) any alteration to the information authenticated after affixing is detectable . The Second Schedule was amended in 2015 to include e-KYC/Aadhaar-based e-Sign ("Aadhaar e-Sign"). Aspect Digital signature (Sec. 3) Electronic signature (Sec. 3A) Nature Technology-specific ( asymmetric crypto + hash function ) Technology neutral (techniques in Second Schedule) Certificate Digital Signature Certificate by a Certifying Authority Electronic Signature Certificate where applicable Introduced 2000 (original Act) 2008 Amendment (the original Act's term was only "digital signature") Examples PKI-based USB-token DSC (Class 1/2/3) Aadhaar-based e-Sign, OTP-based signatures Relationship A species of electronic signature The genus that includes digital signature Legal recognition: Section 4: where any law requires information to be in writing/typewritten/printed, the requirement is satisfied if it is in electronic form and accessible for subsequent reference. Section 5: where any law requires information or a document to be authenticated by affixing a signature , the requirement is satisfied by a digital/electronic signature . Section 10A (2008): contracts formed through electronic means are valid and enforceable (proposals, acceptance and revocation expressed in electronic form). Sections 11–13: attribution, acknowledgement and the time and place of dispatch and receipt of electronic records (dispatch occurs when the record enters a computer resource outside the control of the originator; receipt occurs when it enters the designated computer resource; the place of dispatch/receipt is the place of business of the originator/addressee). Sections 14–16: secure electronic records and secure electronic signatures , and the security procedure prescribed by the Central Government.

p: Information Technology Law: Digital Signature, E-Governance and Electronic Records · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) (Section 17): appointed by the Central Government (under MeitY); functions in Section 18 (supervising CAs, certifying public keys, laying down standards and conditions, specifying qualifications of CAs, maintaining the Repository , resolving conflicts of interest). The CCA operates the Root Certifying Authority of India (RCAI) , the root of trust for the Indian PKI. Licence (Sections 21–24): a CA must hold a licence from the Controller (application with CPS, security documents, fees); licence valid for a prescribed period (renewable) and suspended or revoked (Sections 25–26) for contravention. Section 19: recognition of foreign Certifying Authorities (by the Controller with Central Government approval). Duties of Certifying Authorities (Sections 30–34): use hardware/software and procedures secure from intrusion and misuse ; provide a reasonable level of reliability; adhere to security procedures ; ensure compliance with the Act and rules ( Section 31 ); display the licence (Section 32); surrender the licence on suspension/revocation (Section 33); disclose the CPS, certificate, revocation notice, and any event materially affecting its operation (Section 34). Digital Signature Certificate (Chapter VII): Section 35: CA issues DSC on application (with fee and a certification practice statement) after satisfying itself that the applicant holds the private key and the corresponding public key; Section 36: representations upon issuance (the CA certifies it has complied with the Act, the subscriber holds the private key, etc.); Section 37: suspension of DSC (on request, or in public interest, for not more than 15 days without hearing); Section 38: revocation of DSC (on request, death, dissolution of company, or when a material fact is false); Section 39: notice of suspension or revocation.

p: Information Technology Law: Digital Signature, E-Governance and Electronic Records · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Section 40: Generating key pair: where any DSC the public key of which is to be listed in the certificate has been accepted by the subscriber, the subscriber must generate the key pair by applying the security procedure . Section 40A (2008): duties of subscribers of Electronic Signature Certificate : to comply with the prescribed requirements and exercise due diligence and reasonable care to retain control of the signature creation data . Section 41: Acceptance of Digital Signature Certificate: the subscriber accepts a DSC if he publishes or authorises its publication to one or more persons or in a repository, or otherwise demonstrates approval. By acceptance, the subscriber certifies to all who reasonably rely on it that (a) he holds the private key corresponding to the public key listed; (b) all representations made to the CA and all material relevant to the certificate are true ; and (c) all information in the certificate that is within his knowledge is true . Section 42: Control of private key: every subscriber shall exercise reasonable care to retain control of the private key corresponding to the public key listed in his DSC and take all steps to prevent its disclosure to a person not authorised to affix his digital signature. If the private key has been compromised , he must communicate the same without any delay to the Certifying Authority in the manner specified by regulations. He is liable until he has informed the CA. Penalties linked to subscriber/CA conduct: Section 71 (misrepresentation to the Controller/CA: up to 2 years or fine up to ₹1 lakh or both); Section 73 (publishing a DSC with false particulars; up to 2 years or fine up to ₹1 lakh); Section 74 (publication for fraudulent purpose: up to 2 years or fine up to ₹1 lakh).

p: Information Technology Law: Digital Signature, E-Governance and Electronic Records · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Electronic record (2(1)(t)): data, record or data generated, image or sound stored, received or sent in an electronic form or micro film or computer-generated micro fiche . Section 7: Retention of electronic records: where a law requires documents/records/information to be retained, the requirement is met if the electronic record is accessible for later reference , retained in the format in which it was originally generated, sent or received (or a format that accurately represents it), and the details of origin, destination and date/time of despatch or receipt are retained. Section 7A: audit of documents maintained in electronic form. Section 8: publication of rules, regulations and notifications in the Electronic Gazette (legally valid, if published also in the official Gazette in the prescribed manner). Section 6: Use of electronic records and electronic signatures in Government and its agencies: the appropriate Government may (permissive, not mandatory) allow filing of forms/applications, issue of licences/permits, receipt/payment of money in electronic form. Section 6A (2008): delivery of services by service providers (e.g. through Common Service Centres ) on behalf of the Government. Section 9: no right to insist that any Ministry/Department/Government agency must accept, issue, create, retain or preserve documents in electronic form. Section 10: power of the Central Government to make rules on digital signatures (type, manner, format, procedure, control of processes). Section 87: rule-making power. Electronic evidence: the Indian Evidence Act 1872 (amended by the IT Act): Section 3 ("evidence" includes electronic records), Section 65B (admissibility of electronic records with a certificate). Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (in force 1 July 2024 ), the corresponding provision is Section 63 (certificate in Part A and Part B , including hash value and expert's certification). Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (SC 2014) held the certificate mandatory for secondary electronic evidence; Shafhi Mohammad v. State of H.P. (2018) relaxed it; Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (SC 2020) overruled Shafhi and restored the mandatory certificate requirement. Section 79A IT Act: Central Government may notify Examiner of Electronic Evidence . E-governance in India: National e-Governance Plan (NeGP) (2006), Digital India (2015) , e-Courts , Aadhaar , DigiLocker , UMANG , e-Sign . Types: G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E . Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017, 9-judge bench) recognised the right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21 ; Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) (2018) upheld the Aadhaar Act (with Section 57 struck down and limited private use). Data protection: Section 43A (compensation for failure to protect sensitive personal data) and the IT (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules 2011 are being replaced by the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (assent 11 August 2023), which makes consent the principal basis for processing digital personal data, creates Data Fiduciary / Data Principal / Data Protection Board of India , and provides penalties up to ₹250 crore ; the DPDP Rules 2025 (notified November 2025) bring the Act into force in phases (verify current commencement status). Section 44(2) of the DPDP Act omits Section 43A of the IT Act.

p: Information Technology Law: Digital Signature, E-Governance and Electronic Records · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Section 79 (safe harbour): an intermediary is not liable for third-party information, data or communication link made available or hosted by it if (a) its function is limited to providing access to a communication system ; (b) it does not initiate the transmission, select the receiver or select or modify the information; and (c) it observes due diligence and the Central Government's guidelines. The protection is lost if the intermediary conspires, abets, aids or induces the unlawful act, or on receiving actual knowledge (or being notified by the appropriate Government) fails to expeditiously remove or disable access . Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (SC, 24 March 2015): the Court read down Section 79(3)(b) and the Intermediary Guidelines Rules 2011 (Rule 3(4)) : "actual knowledge" means a court order or notification by the appropriate Government relating to Article 19(2) matters. (It also struck down Section 66A and upheld Section 69A with the Blocking Rules 2009.) Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021 (notified 25 February 2021; amended 2022 and 2023): due diligence, significant social media intermediaries (SSMIs) ( 5 million registered users ) must appoint a Chief Compliance Officer, Nodal Contact Person and Resident Grievance Officer (resident in India), enable first originator identification (Rule 4(2)) for messaging services, and comply with a three-tier grievance mechanism for digital media/OTT platforms; Grievance Appellate Committees (from 2022). Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025 (assent 22 August 2025): prohibits online money games , creates a regulatory authority; promotes e-sports (verify implementing rules). Quick facts for revision (Section 9). IT Act: 2000 (in force 17 Oct 2000 ); Amendment 2008 (in force 27 Oct 2009 ). Model Law: UNCITRAL 1996 . Digital signature: Sections 2(1)(p), 3 ; electronic signature: 3A ; legal recognition: 4, 5 ; contracts: 10A ; retention: 7 ; e-Gazette: 8 ; e-governance: 6, 6A ; CCA: Section 17 ; CA duties: 30–34 ; DSC: 35–39 ; Subscriber duties: 40–42 ; First Schedule exclusions (5 items) ; Act applies abroad: Section 75 ; Shreya Singhal (2015) .

t: 10.1 Concept and classification of cyber crime
p: Cyber Crimes, Penalties and Adjudication · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: The IT Act does not define "cyber crime" as such. Conceptually, a cyber crime is an unlawful act where a computer or communication device is the target, the tool, or the incidental medium of the offence. Common classifications: (i) crimes against individuals (cyber stalking, identity theft, online harassment, voyeurism, sextortion, defamation); (ii) crimes against property (hacking, data theft, ransomware, phishing, online banking fraud, software piracy); (iii) crimes against organisations/government (cyber terrorism, attacks on critical information infrastructure , unauthorised access to protected systems); (iv) crimes against society (obscenity, child sexual abuse material, hate speech, fake news). The Act draws a distinction between civil contraventions (Sections 43–47: compensation/penalty, adjudicated by an Adjudicating Officer) and criminal offences (Sections 65–78: prosecuted in a criminal court).

t: 10.2 Civil liability: penalties and compensation (Chapter IX, Sections 43–47)
p: Cyber Crimes, Penalties and Adjudication · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Section 43 (penalty and compensation for damage to computer, computer system, etc.): if any person without permission of the owner or any other person in charge of a computer, computer system or computer network does any of the following, he is liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person so affected : (a) accesses or secures access to the computer/system/network/resource; (b) downloads, copies or extracts any data, database or information, including information held or stored in any removable storage medium; (c) introduces or causes to be introduced any computer contaminant or computer virus ; (d) damages or causes damage to any computer, system, network, data, database or programmes; (e) disrupts or causes disruption; (f) denies or causes denial of access to any authorised person (denial-of-service); (g) provides any assistance to any person to facilitate access in contravention of the Act; (h) charges the services availed of by a person to the account of another person by tampering or manipulating; (i) destroys, deletes or alters any information residing in a computer resource, or diminishes its value or utility , or affects it injuriously by any means; (j) steals, conceals, destroys or alters any computer source code used for a computer resource with an intention to cause damage. (Since the 2008 Amendment there is no cap on compensation under Section 43; the ₹1 crore cap was removed.) Section 43A (2008): a body corporate possessing, dealing or handling sensitive personal data or information in a computer resource that it owns, controls or operates, which is negligent in implementing and maintaining reasonable security practices and procedures , is liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person affected (the 2011 SPDI Rules prescribe standards, e.g. ISO/IEC 27001). This provision is to be omitted by the DPDP Act 2023 upon commencement (Section 44(2) of the DPDP Act). Section 44: penalty for failure to furnish information, return or books : up to ₹1.5 lakh for failure to furnish document/return/report to the Controller or CA; ₹5,000 per day for failure to file return within the time; ₹10,000 per day for failure to maintain books of account/records. Section 45 (residuary penalty): contravention of any rule/regulation for which no penalty is provided: compensation not exceeding ₹25,000 to the affected person (or penalty not exceeding ₹25,000). Section 47: factors the adjudicating officer considers: amount of gain of unfair advantage (where quantifiable), amount of loss caused to any person, and the repetitive nature of the default .

p: Cyber Crimes, Penalties and Adjudication · Intellectual Property Rights and IT Law
x: Section 46: the Central Government appoints an Adjudicating Officer (AO) for contraventions under Chapter IX. The AO must be of the rank of Director in the Government of India or equivalent (State Government: Secretary of IT Department) , and must possess IT and legal experience . Section 46(1A): the AO's jurisdiction extends to claims for injury or damage not exceeding ₹5 crore ; above that, the civil court has jurisdiction. The AO exercises the powers of a civil court (summons, discovery, evidence) and proceedings are deemed judicial proceedings. Section 48 (Cyber Appellate Tribunal) and Section 57: an appeal from the AO's order lies to the Cyber Appellate Tribunal (CAT) , within 45 days . The CAT was merged into the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) by the Finance Act 2017 ; TDSAT now hears these appeals. Section 62: appeal to the High Court from the Tribunal's decision within 60 days on any question of fact or law. p: How to Use These Notes and What the Exam Looks Like · Jurisprudence
x: The question formats that appear repeatedly in Law Paper 2 are: Direct memory questions: who wrote which book, who propounded which theory, which case laid down which principle, which Article says what. Statement-based questions: two or more statements are given and you must choose the correct combination (Statement I true and II false, and so on). These test whether you know the nuance, not just the name. Match the list (List I with List II): jurist with theory, jurist with book, case with principle, concept with definition. This is the single most common format in Jurisprudence. Assertion and Reason: you must decide whether the reason correctly explains the assertion. Chronological or sequence questions: for example, arranging schools or thinkers in order of appearance. 'Which is NOT correct' questions: these reward careful reading of exceptions and common mix-ups, such as confusing Austin with Bentham or Hart with Kelsen.

p: How to Use These Notes and What the Exam Looks Like · Jurisprudence
x: Questions are increasingly applied : the examiner gives a situation or a proposition and asks which jurist or school it matches, instead of asking only for names. Indian Supreme Court and High Court judgments on legal personality (rivers, animals, idols, religious books), privacy , constitutional morality and liability appear far more often than they used to. Modern and contemporary thinkers (Rawls, Dworkin, Amartya Sen, Martha Nussbaum, Thomas Pogge, Foucault, Derrida, Lyotard) now get regular representation, alongside the classical names (Austin, Salmond, Savigny, Pound). Topics 8 , 9 and 10 (Law, poverty and development; Global justice; Modernism and post-modernism) are comparatively newer in the syllabus and are very predictable: a handful of thinkers and books decide almost every question. The Hart–Devlin, Hart–Fuller and Hart–Dworkin debates, the distinction between 'is' and 'ought', and the contrast between 'rights' (Hohfeld, Salmond) and 'duties' keep recurring.

p: Nature and Sources of Law · Jurisprudence
x: The word jurisprudence comes from the Latin juris prudentia , meaning 'knowledge of law' or 'skill in law'. Jurisprudence is the study of the fundamental principles on which law rests, as distinct from the study of a particular statute or branch of law. It asks questions such as what law is, why it binds, how it differs from morality, and what ends it should serve. Definitions of jurisprudence (frequently asked): Ulpian (Roman jurist): knowledge of things divine and human, the science of the just and the unjust. John Austin: the philosophy of positive law. Salmond: the science of the first principles of the civil law. Holland: the formal science of positive law. Roscoe Pound: the science of law, using the word 'law' in the juridical sense of the body of principles recognised or enforced by public and regular tribunals. Julius Stone: the lawyer's extroversion, that is, the lawyer's examination of the precepts, ideals and techniques of the law in the light of present-day knowledge from other disciplines. Gray: the science of law, that is, the statement and systematic arrangement of the rules followed by courts and the principles involved in those rules. Dias: the study of legal theory in the widest sense (he preferred a wide, multi-purpose approach). Divisions of jurisprudence: Bentham divided it into expositorial (what the law is) and censorial (what the law ought to be). Bentham also coined the term 'international law'. Austin divided it into general (principles common to all legal systems) and particular (a given system of law). He treated only the general, analytical part as true jurisprudence and excluded 'legislation' (what ought to be) from its province. Salmond speaks of legal theory in the widest sense and recognises three main approaches: analytical , historical and ethical . Salmond also distinguishes jurisprudence in the wider sense (the whole of legal theory) from jurisprudence in the narrow sense (the science of the first principles of civil law). Method of jurisprudence (modern view): analytical (breaking concepts into parts), historical (tracing origin and growth), sociological (law in society), philosophical or ethical (justice and values), and comparative (across legal systems).

t: 1.2 Nature of Law: Definitions and Characteristics
p: Nature and Sources of Law · Jurisprudence
x: There is no single universally accepted definition of law. Each definition reflects the school of the thinker. Learn them as pairs: jurist and one key phrase . Jurist Definition or key idea Austin Law is the command of the sovereign backed by sanction Blackstone A rule of civil conduct prescribed by the supreme power in a state, commanding what is right and prohibiting what is wrong Salmond The body of principles recognised and applied by the State in the administration of justice Holmes The prophecies of what the courts will do in fact, and nothing more pretentious John Chipman Gray What the judges declare, not the source of law but law itself Savigny An expression of the common consciousness of the people ( Volksgeist ) Ihering The form of the guarantee of the conditions of life of society, assured by the State's power of constraint Kelsen A primary norm which stipulates a sanction; a coercive order, a hierarchy of norms Hart The union of primary rules of obligation and secondary rules (recognition, change, adjudication) Dworkin An interpretive concept: law as integrity, comprising rules and principles Fuller The enterprise of subjecting human conduct to the governance of rules (inner morality of law) Roscoe Pound A social institution to satisfy social wants, a tool of social engineering Cicero Highest reason implanted in nature (the natural law idea) Aquinas An ordinance of reason for the common good, made by one who has care of the community, and promulgated Henry Maine Law develops from status to contract (a historical generalisation) Essential characteristics of law (as most schools accept them): Normative: it prescribes conduct, it does not merely describe it. General: it applies to classes of persons and acts, not to a single named individual. Prospective: it generally operates for the future (retrospective penal laws are restricted by Article 20(1) of the Indian Constitution). Public and certain: it must be promulgated and knowable. Coercive or backed by sanction: this is emphasised by positivists and denied as the sole feature by Hart, who stresses the internal point of view of those who accept the rules. Institutional: it is made, applied and enforced through institutions such as legislatures, courts and administrative bodies. Fuller's eight desiderata (inner morality of law) from The Morality of Law (1964): generality, promulgation, non-retroactivity, clarity, non-contradiction, possibility of compliance, constancy through time, and congruence between declared rule and official action. Fuller's story of 'King Rex' illustrates the eight ways of failing to make law. Remember: Fuller says a system that fails entirely on these cannot be called law. Functions of law: social control; dispute settlement; protection of rights; social change and engineering (Pound, and in India the Constitution's transformative aims); allocation of power and authority; maintenance of order and security; and providing a framework for economic and social life. Classification of law (common textbook divisions): Substantive and procedural law: substantive law defines rights and duties (for example the Indian Penal Code or its successor), procedural law prescribes how they are enforced (for example the Code of Criminal Procedure). Salmond calls the law of procedure the law of the remedy . Public and private law: public law governs the relationship between the State and individuals (constitutional, administrative, criminal), private law governs relations among individuals (contract, tort, property, family). Municipal and international law: Austin said international law is merely 'positive international morality' because it lacks a sovereign command, while Salmond, Oppenheim and the modern view regard it as true law. Civil and criminal law, and common law and equity. Salmond's classification of law: imperative law, physical or scientific law, natural or moral law, conventional law, customary law, practical or technical law, and international law.

t: 1.3 Austin's Command Theory (The Core of Analytical Positivism)
p: Nature and Sources of Law · Jurisprudence
x: John Austin (1790 to 1859), the first Professor of Jurisprudence at the University of London, delivered the lectures later published as The Province of Jurisprudence Determined (1832) . His programme was to separate law as it is (positive law) from law as it ought to be (morality, ethics). Austin's classification of laws: Laws properly so called: (a) divine laws (set by God to men), and (b) human laws (set by men to men). Human laws divide into positive law (set by political superiors to political inferiors, and by persons acting in pursuance of legal rights) and positive morality (set by men who are not political superiors, such as rules of clubs, and also the 'law of fashion' and international law). Laws improperly so called: laws by analogy (rules of fashion, honour, international law) and laws by metaphor (laws of nature, like the law of gravity). Elements of law in Austin's theory: Command: the expression of a wish by a determinate person that something be done, with the power and purpose to inflict evil (sanction) if the wish is not complied with. Duty: the obligation to obey the command, existing because of the likelihood of the sanction. Sanction: the evil that will be inflicted if the command is disobeyed. Sovereign: a determinate human superior who receives habitual obedience from the bulk of the society and who does not himself habitually obey any other like superior. Sovereignty is, in Austin's view, indivisible, illimitable (legally unlimited) and determinate . Examples used by Austin and his critics: Maine pointed out that Ranjit Singh of the Punjab was a good example of an Austinian sovereign (an absolute ruler issuing commands), but even he did not make general laws, he mostly made specific orders and left custom largely undisturbed. Criticisms (high yield): Hart says Austin's model is the 'gunman situation writ large' and cannot explain power-conferring rules (for example how to make a will or contract) which do not command anything, they only confer powers. Austin cannot explain customary law (law that existed before and independently of any sovereign command) or international law or constitutional law (the sovereign is bound by the constitution). His idea of an indivisible sovereign does not fit federal systems where sovereignty is shared (as in India or the USA). Law's binding force rests on acceptance (Hart's internal point of view), not just fear of sanction. He ignored the law-making role of judges and the difference between obligation and being obliged . Natural lawyers criticise the total separation of law and morality. Austin's defenders: Austin's contribution was the clear analytical method and the insistence on distinguishing law as it is from law as it ought to be. Even Hart's own project is built on revising Austin. Bentham versus Austin (a common confusion): Bentham's Of Laws in General (published only in the twentieth century by H.L.A. Hart as Of Laws in General , 1970) is richer than Austin's version: Bentham recognised that a law can be a complex of commands and accepted permissions and powers , and he allowed the sovereign to be limited by public opinion and popular acceptance. Bentham's An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789) is the source of utilitarianism (the greatest happiness of the greatest number, with the hedonic or felicific calculus).

t: 1.4 Sources of Law: Concept and Classification
p: Nature and Sources of Law · Jurisprudence
x: The expression 'sources of law' is ambiguous, so examiners often test the classification. Salmond's classification (the most commonly asked): Formal source: the will of the State, which gives the rule its validity and force as law. Law gets its legal validity from this. Material sources: the places from which the matter (content) of law is drawn, not the validity. These are of two kinds: Legal sources: those which the law itself recognises as authoritative (gateways through which new principles enter the law). They are legislation, precedent, custom, agreement (conventional law) and, to a lesser extent, professional or juristic opinion and equity. Historical sources: those which influence the law only indirectly, such as legal literature, foreign law, and writings. They are not authoritative until a legal source adopts them. Other classifications: Austin treated legislation (sovereign command) as the real source and the others as 'sources' only in a loose sense. Allen in Law in the Making concentrates on legislation, precedent and custom as the main 'sources', and treats the study of how the law is made as the study of its sources. Gray lists statutes, judicial precedents, opinions of experts, customs and principles of morality. Keeton distinguishes binding sources (legislation, precedent, custom) from persuasive sources (books of authority, foreign decisions, principles of morality). Hart uses the rule of recognition , a social rule used by officials to identify valid law, as the ultimate criterion of validity within a legal system, so the 'source thesis' says legal validity depends on social facts (pedigree) and not on moral merit. Kelsen traces validity upward to the Grundnorm (basic norm), a presupposed norm. Sources of Indian law (for applied questions): the Constitution of India; statutes enacted by Parliament and State legislatures; ordinances (Articles 123 and 213); delegated legislation (rules, regulations, bye-laws); judicial precedent (Article 141); custom and usage (Article 13(3)(a) treats custom or usage having the force of law as 'law'); personal laws (partially, by religion); and international treaties as implemented through Article 253 and, increasingly, as guiding principles (for example Vishaka v State of Rajasthan , 1997, which read international conventions into fundamental rights where domestic law is silent).

p: Nature and Sources of Law · Jurisprudence
x: Meaning: legislation is the declaration of legal rules by a competent authority , and it is the most important source in modern states. Salmond says that legislation is that source of law which consists in the declaration of legal rules by a competent authority. Kinds (Salmond): Supreme legislation: that which emanates from the sovereign power and cannot be repealed, annulled or controlled by any other legislative authority. In Salmond's day, the British Parliament. In India, Parliament is not supreme in this sense because of the written Constitution and judicial review. Subordinate legislation: made by an authority subordinate to the supreme legislature. Salmond lists five forms: colonial (legislatures of colonies), executive (the executive's power to make rules and regulations by delegation), judicial (rules of court made by judges), municipal (bye-laws by local authorities) and autonomous (laws by private bodies like universities or railway companies, with the State's permission). Delegated legislation in India (concept and cases): In re Delhi Laws Act (1951): the legislature cannot delegate its essential legislative function , but may delegate non-essential functions. Conditional legislation is valid. Hamdard Dawakhana v Union of India (1960): the legislature must lay down the policy and legal principle, leaving only details to the delegate. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co v Asst. Commissioner of Sales Tax (1973): the legislature must declare the policy; excessive delegation is unconstitutional. Indian Express Newspapers v Union of India (1985): delegated legislation can be challenged for being manifestly arbitrary and unreasonable under Article 14. Chintaman Rao ? Not required; focus on the three above. Codification and consolidation: codification arranges existing law systematically in a code (Bentham's wish; the Indian Contract Act 1872 and the older Penal Code are examples), consolidation merges many statutes on one subject without changing substance. Bentham was a strong advocate of codification and rejected 'judge-made law' as 'dog law'. Merits of legislation over precedent: it is deliberate, prospective, systematic, can create new law quickly, is made by representatives, and is accessible. Demerits: it can be rigid, may lag behind facts, can be poorly drafted, and may be rendered uncertain by interpretation. Interpretation of statutes (rules the examiners like): Literal rule: words are given their plain ordinary meaning. Golden rule: depart from the literal meaning only to avoid absurdity. Mischief rule (Heydon's case, 1584): ask what the common law was, what the mischief was, what remedy Parliament appointed, and the true reason of the remedy. Purposive approach: the court looks to the legislative purpose, which is now the preferred approach in India and in most modern systems. Ejusdem generis, noscitur a sociis, expressio unius est exclusio alterius are the commonest maxims.

p: Nature and Sources of Law · Jurisprudence
x: Meaning: a judicial decision to which authority is attributed in the later decisions of the courts. The doctrine of stare decisis ('stand by what has been decided') provides that like cases should be decided alike. Salmond defines precedent as the decision of a court of justice treated as an authority in later cases. Two parts of a judgment: Ratio decidendi: the principle of law on which the decision rests, the binding part. Obiter dicta: remarks made by the way, not necessary for the decision. They are persuasive only (although the Indian Supreme Court has said considered obiter of the Supreme Court deserves great weight). Tests for finding the ratio: Wambaugh's inversion test: reverse the proposition; if the decision would still stand, the proposition is not the ratio. Goodhart's test: the ratio is found by taking into account the material facts treated as material by the judge, and the decision based on them. Goodhart rejected the idea that the ratio is simply the judge's stated reasoning. Halsbury's view (Quinn v Leathem, 1901): a case is only an authority for what it actually decides, not what logically follows from it. Kinds of precedent (Salmond): Authoritative and persuasive precedents. Authoritative precedents must be followed even if the judge disagrees with them. Persuasive precedents (foreign decisions, decisions of lower courts, obiter) are only considered. Declaratory and original precedents. A declaratory precedent merely applies existing law; an original precedent creates and applies new law. Salmond notes that original precedents are the real law-making ones. Absolutely authoritative and conditionally authoritative: absolutely authoritative precedents bind the court and cannot be disregarded in any circumstances ; conditionally authoritative precedents may be disregarded if they are wrong in a certain way (for example if decided per incuriam ). Departing from precedent: Distinguishing: the later court finds a material difference in facts. Overruling: a higher court (or in some cases the same court, or a larger bench) declares the earlier decision wrong. Reversing: a higher court on appeal in the same case sets aside the decision of the lower court. Per incuriam: a decision given in ignorance of a binding statute or binding authority. See Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co (1944). Sub silentio: a point passed without argument or consideration is not binding. Prospective overruling: a decision is declared wrong but applies only to the future, not to past transactions. The doctrine was adopted in India in Golak Nath v State of Punjab (1967) (borrowed from American practice, Linkletter v Walker ). Indian position on precedent: Article 141: the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India. It does not bind the Supreme Court itself. Article 129 and Article 215: the Supreme Court and High Courts are courts of record. Bengal Immunity Co v State of Bihar (1955): the Supreme Court is not bound by its own earlier decisions and may depart from them in appropriate cases. Keshav Mills Co v CIT (1965): the Court can reconsider an earlier decision only if there are compelling reasons, the settled law should not be lightly disturbed. Union of India v Raghubir Singh (1989): a classic statement by Chief Justice Pathak on the need for certainty and the proper approach to precedent. Central Board of Dawoodi Bohra Community v State of Maharashtra (2005): a bench of the Supreme Court is bound by a decision of a coordinate or larger bench; if it disagrees, it must refer the matter to a larger bench . A smaller bench cannot overrule a larger bench. Article 145(3): the minimum bench of five judges for constitutional questions (Constitution Bench). High Court decisions bind subordinate courts in that State, and are persuasive in other States. English position (for comparison): The House of Lords in London Tramways v LCC (1898) held itself absolutely bound by its earlier decisions, which was relaxed by the Practice Statement of 1966 (the Lords may depart from previous decisions 'when it appears right to do so'). The Supreme Court of the United Kingdom has inherited this approach. Merits of precedent: certainty, predictability, equality, efficiency, and gradual growth of law through experience. Demerits: rigidity, danger of bad decisions being perpetuated, complexity because of a vast mass of cases, and artificial distinctions.

p: Nature and Sources of Law · Jurisprudence
x: Meaning: custom is a rule of conduct which has been observed over a long time by a community, and is accepted by that community as binding. Salmond calls custom the embodiment of those principles which have commended themselves to the national conscience as principles of justice and public utility. The historical school (Savigny, Puchta) treated custom as the primary form of law, the direct expression of the Volksgeist. Requisites of a valid custom (the classical tests, often framed in MCQs): Antiquity: it must be ancient, in English law traditionally from 'time immemorial' (1189). In India, courts accept customs of long usage, but there is no fixed period; it must be of such age as to be taken as having been always observed. Continuity: it must have been observed continuously without interruption. Peaceable enjoyment: it must have been exercised without force or secrecy. Certainty: it must be definite in its nature and scope. Reasonableness: it must be reasonable (it can be contrary to the common law but not contrary to the fundamental principles of justice). Obligatory force: it must be regarded by those who follow it as binding, not merely optional. Consistency: it must not conflict with another custom. Conformity with statute law and public policy: a custom cannot override an express statute or public morality. Generality or locality: a general custom applies to the whole community, a local one only to a particular place or group. Kinds of custom (Salmond): Legal custom: one that has the force of law in itself (further divided into local and general ). The two kinds are local custom (a particular locality) and general custom (the whole kingdom, which is part of the common law). Conventional custom (usage): binds only because the parties have agreed to it, expressly or by implication, as part of their contract (for example, trade usages). Austin and Holland on custom: Austin treated custom as a mere 'positive morality' until the courts adopt it, at which point it becomes law by judicial recognition ( custom is transmuted into law by judicial decision ). Holland and Salmond say that custom is law before judicial recognition because it is accepted as such in the community. Indian law on custom: Article 13(3)(a): 'law' includes custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law, so a custom can be tested for violation of fundamental rights (although the courts have been cautious in applying this to personal law). Collector of Madura v Mootoo Ramalinga Sethupathy (1868): the Privy Council famously held that clear proof of usage will outweigh the written text of the law. This is the leading authority on the priority of custom over the Smritis in Hindu law. Section 13 of the Indian Evidence Act (now in the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023) allows custom to be proved by showing specific instances. Hindu Marriage Act 1955 section 3(a) defines 'custom and usage' as a rule which has been continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, is certain and not unreasonable or opposed to public policy, and in the case of a rule applicable only to a family, has not been discontinued by the family. (The same wording is used in the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act 1956.) Custom and statute today: legislation has largely displaced custom in modern states, but custom remains alive in personal laws, tribal laws (for instance the Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas), constitutional conventions and international law (custom is a source under Article 38(1)(b) of the ICJ Statute, which requires state practice and opinio juris ).

t: 1.8 Other Sources: Agreement, Juristic Writings, Equity, Constitution
p: Nature and Sources of Law · Jurisprudence
x: Agreement (conventional law): private agreements create law inter partes, and treaties create law between states. Juristic writings: in the common law system, books of authority (Coke, Blackstone, Glanville) can be authority; in Roman, Hindu and Muslim law, the writings of jurists were primary sources (for example the Dharmashastras and Manusmriti, Yajnavalkya Smriti and the commentaries Mitakshara and Dayabhaga ). Equity: developed in the English Court of Chancery as a corrective to the rigidity of common law (maxims such as 'equity follows the law' and 'he who seeks equity must do equity'). In India, equity operates under 'justice, equity and good conscience'. Constitution: in written-constitution systems, it is the supreme source from which all other legal authority derives, and under Article 13 laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void.

t: Memory Capsule: Nature and Sources of Law
p: Nature and Sources of Law · Jurisprudence
x: Austin: Province of Jurisprudence Determined (1832); command, duty, sanction, sovereign; law improperly so called includes international law and laws of fashion. Bentham: expositorial and censorial; utilitarian; coined 'international law'. Salmond: formal source versus material sources; legal versus historical sources; author of Jurisprudence (1902). Holmes: 'prophecy of what courts will do'; 'The life of the law has not been logic, it has been experience'. Fuller: eight desiderata; The Morality of Law . Hart: The Concept of Law (1961), union of primary and secondary rules. Precedent: ratio versus obiter; Wambaugh's inversion test; Goodhart's material facts test; Articles 141 and 145(3); Bengal Immunity ; Dawoodi Bohra ; prospective overruling in Golak Nath . Custom: antiquity, continuity, certainty, reasonableness, obligatory force; Collector of Madura ; Article 13(3)(a). Common confusions: (1) Bentham is the source of 'expositorial and censorial', Austin is not; (2) Savigny is the historical school, Ihering is the sociological/teleological precursor; (3) Kelsen's law is a coercive order of norms, Hart's is rules, Austin's is commands; (4) per incuriam is not the same as obiter.

p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: School Core idea Key thinkers Key works Natural law Law is based on reason, nature or divine order; an unjust law is defective Aristotle, Cicero, Aquinas, Grotius, Locke, Fuller, Finnis Summa Theologica ; De Jure Belli ac Pacis ; Two Treatises ; Morality of Law ; Natural Law and Natural Rights Analytical positivism Law is a command or a system of rules made by human authority; separate from morality Bentham, Austin, Hart, Raz Province of Jurisprudence Determined ; Concept of Law Pure theory Law is a hierarchy of norms cleansed of politics, ethics and sociology Kelsen General Theory of Law and State ; Pure Theory of Law Historical Law grows out of the spirit of the people and cannot be made at will Savigny, Puchta, Maine, Montesquieu Of the Vocation of Our Age ; Ancient Law Sociological Law is a social phenomenon, to be studied by its effects and to be used to serve social ends Comte, Durkheim, Ihering, Ehrlich, Duguit, Pound, Weber Law as a Means to an End ; Living Law ; Scope and Purposes of Sociological Jurisprudence Realist (American and Scandinavian) Law is what courts and officials actually do Holmes, Gray, Llewellyn, Frank; Hagerstrom, Olivecrona, Ross Path of the Law ; Bramble Bush ; Law and the Modern Mind ; On Law and Justice Marxist Law is part of the superstructure and serves the dominant economic class Marx, Engels, Pashukanis, Vyshinsky Communist Manifesto ; General Theory of Law and Marxism Economic analysis Law should be understood and shaped by efficiency Coase, Posner, Calabresi Problem of Social Cost ; Economic Analysis of Law Critical, feminist, post-modern Law is indeterminate and political; it reproduces power Unger, Kennedy, MacKinnon, Foucault, Derrida (see Topic 10 ) Mnemonic for the order of the major schools: Natural (ancient) then Positivist (nineteenth century) then Historical (early nineteenth, a reaction to codification) then Sociological (late nineteenth and twentieth) then Realist (early twentieth) then Critical (late twentieth).

p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: Basic position: there exists a higher law, derived from nature, reason, God or human nature, which is superior to man-made law and provides the standard by which the justice of positive law is measured. The slogan associated with it is lex iniusta non est lex (an unjust law is no law), which comes from St Augustine and is developed by Aquinas. Stages of development (very important for chronological questions): (a) Greek natural law Heraclitus and the Sophists debated physis (nature) against nomos (convention). Socrates, Plato and Aristotle: Plato's Republic describes justice as each class performing its proper function. Aristotle (in Nicomachean Ethics and Politics ) distinguished natural justice (valid everywhere with the same force) from legal or conventional justice , and divided justice into distributive and corrective (rectificatory) justice. He said man is a political animal. The Stoics (Zeno, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius) taught that the universe is governed by reason ( logos ), and that all men, being rational, are subject to a universal law of nature. (b) Roman natural law Cicero in De Re Publica described true law as right reason in agreement with nature, of universal application, unchanging and everlasting. Roman jurists developed the jus naturale , the jus gentium (law of nations) and jus civile (civil law). Gaius and Ulpian explained these categories. (c) Medieval natural law (the theological phase) St Augustine ( City of God ): an unjust law does not seem to be law. St Thomas Aquinas ( Summa Theologica ) gives the most famous classification of law, a four-fold scheme: Lex aeterna (eternal law): the divine reason governing the whole universe. Lex divina (divine law): the revealed law of Scripture. Lex naturalis (natural law): man's participation in the eternal law through reason. Lex humana (human law): the rules made by human authorities, derived from natural law, and valid only if consistent with it . Aquinas defines law as an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by one who has care of the community, and promulgated . (d) The Renaissance and the age of reason (the secular, rationalist phase) Hugo Grotius (1583 to 1645), the 'father of international law', in De Jure Belli ac Pacis (1625) argued that natural law would exist even if God did not exist , because it rests on human reason and man's social nature ( appetitus societatis ). He separated natural law from theology. Thomas Hobbes ( Leviathan , 1651): in the state of nature life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short'; men surrender their rights to an absolute sovereign through a social contract for security. John Locke ( Two Treatises of Government , 1689): in the state of nature men have natural rights to life, liberty and property ; government exists by consent to protect these, and may be resisted if it breaches the trust. Locke influenced the American Declaration of Independence and constitutionalism. Jean-Jacques Rousseau ( The Social Contract , 1762): 'Man is born free and everywhere he is in chains'; sovereignty rests in the general will of the people. Immanuel Kant ( Metaphysics of Morals , Rechtslehre ): the categorical imperative ; law is the sum of conditions under which the freedom of one can co-exist with the freedom of all according to a universal law of freedom. (e) Decline in the nineteenth century: the natural law approach was attacked by the historical school (Savigny), utilitarians (Bentham called natural rights 'nonsense upon stilts') and positivists (Austin). It was seen as vague and subjective. (f) Revival in the twentieth century: two World Wars, the Nazi regime and the Nuremberg trials revived the idea that there are limits to the validity of positive law . Rudolf Stammler ( Theory of Just Law ): natural law with a variable content . The form of just law is constant, the content changes with time and place. He proposed the social ideal of a community of free-willing men, and two principles of respect and participation . Josef Kohler: law as an evolving civilisation; 'jurisprudence of culture' (neo-Hegelian). Giorgio del Vecchio: natural law as the inherent consciousness of justice in man. Gustav Radbruch: after WWII, advanced the Radbruch formula : a positive law, even if duly enacted, must yield to justice where the contradiction is intolerable (extreme injustice is not law). Lon Fuller ( The Morality of Law , 1964): the procedural natural law of eight desiderata (see Topic 1 ) and the claim that law has an inner morality . Fuller's argument in the Hart–Fuller debate ( Harvard Law Review , 1958) is the classic 'natural law reply' to positivism. John Finnis ( Natural Law and Natural Rights , 1980): a new natural law approach drawn from Aquinas, setting out the basic goods : life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability (friendship), practical reasonableness and religion . Finnis argues that law's moral force is a central case matter: unjust laws are law in a defective sense. Ronald Dworkin: principles in law (see Dworkin below) and his 'moral reading' of the Constitution, a neo-natural law element although he does not use the label. John Rawls ( A Theory of Justice , 1971): a modern social-contract account of justice (see Topic 9 ). The Hart–Fuller debate (1958) in detail: Context: the post-war German informer case : a woman denounced her husband under a Nazi statute for insulting remarks about Hitler; after the war, she was prosecuted for illegally depriving him of liberty. The question was whether the Nazi statute was 'law'. Hart (positivist): the Nazi statute was law, but it was so evil that it should not be obeyed . The right solution is to pass a retrospective statute and say openly that it is a departure from the principle against retroactivity, and to separate the question of 'what law is' from 'what it ought to be'. Fuller (natural law): a system so flawed that it fails to meet the inner morality of law is not law at all; such a regime is incompatible with the idea of legality. The court should have refused to apply the statute. Hart's reference to the core and penumbra: a rule has a core of settled meaning and a penumbra of uncertainty , the standard example being a rule that bans vehicles in a park (does it ban roller skates?). Fuller answered that interpretation involves purpose, not merely words. Features of natural law thinking (for 'which of the following' questions): Law and morality are necessarily connected . Law has a moral validity test , unjust rules are defective or void. Law is discovered by reason, not merely made. It supplies a critical standard for judging and reforming positive law. It has been used both to support revolution (Locke, American and French Revolutions) and to justify the status quo (feudal order under medieval theology). Indian connection: the Indian concept of Dharma has features of natural law (a universal order). In constitutional adjudication, the Supreme Court's use of basic structure ( Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala , 1973), the reading of natural justice and 'due process' into Article 21 ( Maneka Gandhi v Union of India , 1978), and the expansion of fundamental rights are often analysed as natural-law-flavoured reasoning. In Golak Nath (1967), fundamental rights were treated as 'natural rights' beyond amendment, although that decision was later overruled in Kesavananda . Criticisms: vagueness and subjectivity (whose reason? whose nature?); confusion between is and ought ; has been used to justify contradictory positions; Hume's guillotine says one cannot derive an 'ought' from an 'is'; and the failure to explain why an immoral rule can still be valid (because validity and justice are different).

p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: Basic position: law is a matter of social fact , not moral merit. The separation thesis is that there is no necessary connection between law and morality, and the sources thesis is that the existence of law depends on social sources (who made it, how), not its content. Bentham (1748 to 1832): Founder of utilitarianism : the principle of utility requires that the right act or law is the one which produces the greatest happiness of the greatest number. He measured pleasure and pain through the hedonic (felicific) calculus with seven factors: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (nearness), fecundity, purity and extent. Works: A Fragment on Government (1776), An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), Of Laws in General , Limits of Jurisprudence Defined . Rejected natural rights and the social contract; supported codification ; classified law into expositorial and censorial; and coined the terms international law, codification and utilitarian . John Stuart Mill: Utilitarianism (1863), On Liberty (1859): introduced a qualitative distinction among pleasures ('better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied') and the harm principle (power may be rightfully exercised over an individual against his will only to prevent harm to others). The harm principle is central in the law and morality debate (Topic 3 ). John Austin: see Topic 1 .3. H.L.A. Hart (1907 to 1992) The Concept of Law (1961): the leading modern positivist, Professor of Jurisprudence at Oxford. Criticism of Austin: the gunman analogy shows the 'command and threat' model cannot account for obligation ; the model cannot explain power-conferring rules , continuity of legislative authority, customary law, or the self-binding nature of the legislature. Distinction between 'being obliged' and 'having an obligation': a gunman obliges you to hand over money, but you are not under an obligation to do so. Law as the union of primary and secondary rules: Primary rules impose duties (what people must or must not do). They solve the problem of static rules. Secondary rules are rules about rules. They are of three types: the rule of recognition (identifies valid rules; solves the problem of uncertainty ), rules of change (provide for making and altering rules; solve the static quality), and rules of adjudication (empower courts to decide breaches; solve the inefficiency of social pressure). The rule of recognition is the ultimate rule of the system. It is not itself 'valid' or 'invalid', it simply exists as a matter of fact (accepted by officials). It is the key to the concept of legal validity . Internal and external point of view: the internal point of view is that of someone who accepts the rule as a standard of conduct (the participant ), and the external point of view is that of an observer who only records regularities. Law cannot be understood from the external viewpoint alone. Open texture of law: because language is general, every rule has a core of settled meaning and a penumbra of doubt where judges exercise discretion . Minimum content of natural law: Hart accepted that there are certain truisms about human nature which give law a minimum moral content: human vulnerability, approximate equality, limited altruism, limited resources, and limited understanding and strength of will. Hence rules protecting persons, property and promises are present in all societies. This is often tested as 'Hart's concession to natural law'. Hart's theory of justice and morality: he distinguishes legal obligation from moral obligation , and recognises that morals can influence law, but does not require it for validity. Hart versus Devlin (1959 onwards): see Topic 3 . Hart on punishment: Punishment and Responsibility (1968): the justifying aim of punishment is general deterrence , but it is limited by retributive principles of who may be punished and how much (a mixed theory). Joseph Raz (1939 to 2022): developed exclusive (hard) legal positivism : legal validity depends only on sources (social facts), never on moral criteria. His works include The Authority of Law (1979) and The Morality of Freedom (1986). He developed the 'service conception of authority'. In contrast, inclusive (soft) positivism (Hart's Postscript , Jules Coleman, W.J. Waluchow) allows that a legal system may incorporate moral criteria in its rule of recognition (for example, a constitutional bill of rights). Key differences within positivism: Point Bentham/Austin Hart Raz Nature of law Command backed by sanction Union of primary and secondary rules Authoritative directives; exclusive sources thesis Sovereign Needed Replaced by rule of recognition Law claims authority Validity Source in sovereign Rule of recognition Social sources only Morality Separate Minimum content of natural law Strictly separate

t: 2.4 Ronald Dworkin and the Hart–Dworkin Debate
p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: Ronald Dworkin (1931 to 2013): Taking Rights Seriously (1977), Law's Empire (1986), A Matter of Principle (1985), Justice for Hedgehogs (2011), Justice in Robes (2006), Freedom's Law (1996). Attack on positivism: a legal system contains not only rules but also principles (standards observed because they are a requirement of justice, fairness or morality) and policies (standards setting a goal for community welfare). Rules apply in an all or nothing fashion , principles have weight and can be balanced against each other. Hart's rule of recognition cannot identify principles by pedigree alone. Hard cases and the rights thesis: in hard cases the judge does not have strong discretion ; the judge must find the right answer by constructing the theory that best fits and justifies the existing legal materials. Judges decide on principle (rights) , not on policy, which belongs to the legislature. Hercules: the ideal, superhumanly learned and patient judge who can construct such a theory. Law as integrity: in Law's Empire , law is an interpretive concept ; the judge is a writer of a chain novel , adding a chapter that fits the earlier chapters, and showing the practice in its best moral light. Integrity combines fit and justification . Law's Empire opposes conventionalism and pragmatism . Cases cited by Dworkin: Riggs v Palmer (1889, New York: a murderer cannot inherit from his victim under the will, the principle that no man may profit from his own wrong) and Henningsen v Bloomfield Motors (1960, on freedom of contract and unequal bargaining power). Rights as trumps: individual rights trump collective goals. Hart's reply (Postscript to The Concept of Law, 1994): principles can be identified by the rule of recognition if the system uses inclusive criteria; Dworkin's theory misunderstands the descriptive nature of Hart's project.

p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: Hans Kelsen (1881 to 1973) , Austrian jurist and the principal drafter of the 1920 Austrian Constitution. Works: Pure Theory of Law (1934, revised 1960), General Theory of Law and State (1945). Aims and the idea of purity: Methodological purity: law should be studied as it is, not as it ought to be morally. Kelsen wanted to purge jurisprudence of psychology, sociology, ethics and political theory . This is a science of law , not a theory of justice. Is and ought: a norm is an 'ought' proposition. Natural science deals with causality ( is ), legal science with imputation (if X then ought to follow Y). A legal norm is valid if it belongs to a legal order which is, on the whole, efficacious. Validity comes from a higher norm, not from the facts. The hierarchy of norms (Stufenbau): every lower norm derives validity from a higher norm: individual decision then statute then constitution then Grundnorm (basic norm). The Grundnorm is not enacted , it is a presupposition of juristic thinking: 'one ought to obey the historically first constitution'. It is a transcendental-logical presupposition (borrowed from Kant), not a moral or natural-law norm. Other features: Law is a coercive order : it attaches sanctions to conduct. State and law are identical: the State is merely the personification of the legal order; Kelsen rejected the dualism of state and law. Static and dynamic systems of norms: in a static system norms are valid because of their content (as in morality), in a dynamic system norms are valid because they were created in a particular way, which is the character of law. Public and private law distinction: Kelsen rejected it as ideological. Rights and duties: a right is merely a reflex of a duty. International law: Kelsen advocated the primacy of international law (monism). Grundnorm and revolutions: when a revolution succeeds and the new regime becomes effective, the Grundnorm changes . This explains the following decisions, often asked: State v Dosso (1958, Pakistan): Munir CJ applied Kelsen to hold that the successful coup of 1958 created a valid legal order. This was overruled in Asma Jilani v Government of Punjab (1972) . Uganda v Commissioner of Prisons, ex parte Matovu (1966): the Ugandan High Court held that the 1966 revolution had created a new legal order with a new Grundnorm. Madzimbamuto v Lardner-Burke (1968) (Rhodesia): the court considered the Unilateral Declaration of Independence and the Grundnorm. The Privy Council held the illegal regime had no legal authority, whereas the General Division of the High Court in Rhodesia had recognised the new regime on the basis of Kelsen's reasoning. ( Rhodesia: also R v Ndhlovu , 1968.) Criticisms: the Grundnorm is a fiction and is not needed; the theory is too formal and ignores the content of law and justice; the dependence on 'efficacy' compromises purity; Hart said it is wrong to see the rule of recognition as presupposed rather than a social fact; Julius Stone said the theory is 'empty'; and Kelsen's thesis that every legal norm is a conditional sanction-rule is oversimplified.
