Kelsen versus Austin versus Hart (a standard comparative table): Issue Austin Kelsen Hart Law is Command of sovereign Hierarchy of norms Union of primary and secondary rules Source of validity Sovereign Grundnorm Rule of recognition (a social fact) Sanction Essential Essential (coercive order) Not essential for each rule Law versus morality Separate Separate Separate, with minimum content of natural law Approach Analytical Normative and formal Analytical and descriptive sociology

p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: Basic position: law is not a product of deliberate legislation or abstract reason. It is a gradual, organic growth , rooted in the history, customs and genius ( Volksgeist ) of a people, in the same way as language. The school arose in Germany as a reaction against the French Revolution, natural law rationalism and the movement for codification . Precursors: Montesquieu ( The Spirit of the Laws , 1748): laws are shaped by climate, soil, religion, customs, commerce and the form of government. He is often called a precursor of both the historical and sociological schools and of the doctrine of separation of powers . Edmund Burke: a conservative who stressed continuity, tradition and slow reform in opposition to the French Revolution. Gustav Hugo: a German jurist who taught that law is the product of the nation's growth and that positive law need not be rationalised. Friedrich Karl von Savigny (1779 to 1861): the chief exponent. Controversy with Thibaut (1814): Thibaut, a Heidelberg professor, urged a uniform civil code for the German states. Savigny replied in his pamphlet Of the Vocation of Our Age for Legislation and Jurisprudence (1814) that Germany was not ready for a code: the science of law was undeveloped, and a code would freeze and distort what ought to evolve. The result was a delay of codification until the German Civil Code (BGB) of 1900. Volksgeist (the spirit of the people): law, like language, originates in the common consciousness of the people. It is found , not made . Law grows with the people, strengthens with them, and finally dies when the nation loses its individuality. Custom as the first source: law first appears as custom, then as juristic law (developed by lawyers as representatives of the people), and finally legislation, which should merely give effect to the popular will. Principal works: System of Modern Roman Law ( System des heutigen romischen Rechts , 1840 to 1849), and The Law of Possession ( Das Recht des Besitzes , 1803), a work that made his early reputation. Georg Friedrich Puchta , a pupil of Savigny, extended the idea in his work on customary law ( Das Gewohnheitsrecht ) and claimed that custom stands above statutes and that the jurist is a mediator between the Volksgeist and the law. Sir Henry Maine (1822 to 1888): the English historical jurist and a member of the Viceroy's Council in India (the Law Member in 1862 to 1869), who applied the historical method to comparative legal history, including India. Works: Ancient Law (1861), Village Communities in the East and West (1871), Early History of Institutions (1875), Early Law and Custom (1883), Dissertations on Early Law and Custom . From status to contract: 'the movement of the progressive societies has hitherto been a movement from Status to Contract .' In early societies a person's rights and duties derived from family status; in progressive societies they derive from freely made contracts. Static and progressive societies: only the progressive societies develop their law beyond early customary stages. Stages in the development of law: (1) law by Themistes (judgments dictated by the king under divine inspiration, as in Homer); (2) customary law , held by an aristocratic minority; (3) codes (the Twelve Tables of Rome, the Laws of Manu in India, the Code of Draco in Athens); (4) instruments of legal change : legal fictions, equity and legislation , in that order. Patriarchal theory: primitive society was composed of patriarchal families, not individuals. Indian dimension: Maine's discussion of the Indian village community and of the Hindu law of caste and joint family has had a lasting influence on colonial legal studies. Merits of the historical school: it introduced the idea of evolution , gave a scientific, comparative understanding of law, showed the role of custom, and warned against hasty legislation. Criticisms: the Volksgeist is vague and unprovable; the school overstates the role of custom and undervalues legislation; it ignores the role of deliberate reform and conscious legal planning (as in modern welfare states); the idea of one 'national spirit' ignores the diversity of groups; it was misused by Nazi ideology to glorify race and nation; and ironically, Savigny's own work is based on Roman law , a foreign import.

p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: Basic position: law is a social phenomenon and an instrument of social control. It must be studied in its actual working and its effects on society (not just as an abstract rule), and it should be a tool to satisfy social interests. The approach is functional. Forerunners: Auguste Comte (1798 to 1857): founder of positivism and of sociology ; the 'law of three stages' (theological, metaphysical and positive). Herbert Spencer: an organic analogy of society and 'survival of the fittest'; wrote Social Statics . Montesquieu (see above). Emile Durkheim (1858 to 1917): The Division of Labour in Society (1893). Law is the visible index of social solidarity . Mechanical solidarity (found in simple societies, based on likeness) is sustained by repressive law (penal), while organic solidarity (in complex societies with division of labour, based on interdependence) is sustained by restitutive (cooperative) law (civil, commercial, administrative). Law is a social fact; crime offends the collective conscience. Rudolf von Ihering (1818 to 1892): a German jurist, one of the main founders of the sociological and teleological approach, who moved from conceptual jurisprudence to a purposive theory. Works: Law as a Means to an End ( Der Zweck im Recht , 1877 to 1883), The Struggle for Law ( Der Kampf ums Recht , 1872), Spirit of Roman Law . Law is the sum of the conditions of social life assured by the State through external compulsion. Law is created for a purpose (the interest of society), and 'purpose is the creator of the entire law'. Social utilitarianism: he combined the idea of social interest with the individual's interest; he held that rights are legally protected interests . The struggle for law: it is an individual's moral duty to assert and defend his rights, and the sum of such struggles creates law. Eugen Ehrlich (1862 to 1922): Austrian jurist, the founder of the sociology of law (a free law thinker). Work: Fundamental Principles of the Sociology of Law ( Grundlegung der Soziologie des Rechts , 1913). Living law: the true centre of gravity of legal development 'lies not in legislation, nor in juristic science, nor in judicial decision, but in society itself'. The living law is the law which dominates life even though not posited in legal propositions, as against the state law (norms for decision), which is made by the State. Studied the actual customs of the Bukovina region (then in Austria) for evidence. Leon Duguit (1859 to 1928): French jurist, a leader of the solidarism approach. Works: Law in the Modern State , Les Transformations du droit public , Traite de droit constitutionnel . Law is based on social solidarity (interdependence of men, an idea he took from Durkheim). Social function , not rights, is the basic concept: property is a social function; there are no natural or subjective rights , only duties of each person to contribute to social interdependence. The State is not a sovereign commanding, but a cooperative of public services . The public service is the key concept of public law. Roscoe Pound (1870 to 1964): Dean of Harvard Law School, the main American sociological jurist. Works: The Scope and Purpose of Sociological Jurisprudence (1911 to 1912), An Introduction to the Philosophy of Law (1922), Interpretations of Legal History (1923), Social Control through Law (1942), Jurisprudence (five volumes, 1959). Law as social engineering: law is a social institution to satisfy social wants, to the maximum extent with the minimum friction and waste. Jurisprudence is a social engineering of balancing competing interests, as an engineer builds a structure. Interests protected by law (three categories): Individual interests: personality, domestic relations, interests of substance (property, succession, freedom of industry and contract). Public interests: interests of the State as a juristic person, and as guardian of social interests. Social interests: general security, security of social institutions, general morals , conservation of social resources , general progress and individual life (the social interest in the individual's human life). Jural postulates: the statements about what should be in a given civilisation, for example that people must be able to assume that others will not commit intentional aggression, and that men must act with due care. Law in books and law in action: the gap between the formal rule and how it works in practice. He urged the study of the working of law and the effects of legal doctrines on society. Theory of social control: law is a developed form of social control, among religion and morality, as the society gets more complex. Criticisms: the theory of 'interests' is vague and has no principle for ranking them; the 'engineering' metaphor suggests a technocratic, uncritical approach; and the theory gives the judge too much room. Max Weber (1864 to 1920): Economy and Society . Three types of legitimate authority: traditional, charismatic and legal-rational . Weber analysed the rationalisation of law, identifying formal rationality as characteristic of modern capitalist legal systems (as against substantive or irrational types). Benjamin Cardozo (1870 to 1938): The Nature of the Judicial Process (1921). Judges legislate in the gaps ( interstitially ) and use four methods: logic (philosophy), history (evolution), custom (tradition) and sociology (social welfare) . Cardozo's method of sociology means deciding in view of public welfare. Julius Stone: The Province and Function of Law (1946), who distinguished the functions of law and wrote on the lawyers' extroversion . Indian application: the sociological approach is at the heart of the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV), and the Preamble , which makes law an instrument of social and economic justice. The Supreme Court's Public Interest Litigation (PIL) and the idea of social-action litigation are examples ( Hussainara Khatoon v State of Bihar , 1979; S.P. Gupta v Union of India , 1981 (on locus standi )). The Maneka Gandhi and Olga Tellis decisions illustrate purposive reading. Also associated is Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer , who often used the sociological approach to justice.

p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: Basic position: law is what courts and officials actually do , not what is written in rules. The focus is on judicial behaviour , the psychological, social and personal influences on decision, and on law in action. There are two strands. American Realism: Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. (1841 to 1935): a forerunner; The Common Law (1881) ('The life of the law has not been logic: it has been experience') and 'The Path of the Law' (1897), which proposed the 'bad man' theory : 'If you want to know the law and nothing else, you must look at it as a bad man, who cares only for the material consequences which such knowledge enables him to predict.' Law is a prediction of the incidence of public force through the courts . John Chipman Gray: The Nature and Sources of the Law (1909): law is what the judges declare; statutes are only sources of law, because they become law only when interpreted by judges. Karl Llewellyn (1893 to 1962): The Bramble Bush (1930, lectures to law students), The Common Law Tradition: Deciding Appeals (1960); the principal drafter of the Uniform Commercial Code . He stressed 'law in action' , the study of what officials do, and distinguished 'paper rules' from 'real rules'. He was a rule-sceptic . He listed the law-jobs (such as conflict resolution, channelling conduct and allocating authority). Jerome Frank (1889 to 1957): Law and the Modern Mind (1930), Courts on Trial (1949). A fact-sceptic (the uncertainty of law lies mainly in the uncertainty of facts and in the personality of the judge and the jury), who held that legal certainty is a myth (the 'basic legal myth') . He criticised the idea that law can be fully predictable (what he called the 'quest for certainty' or 'father-substitute'). Rule scepticism (Llewellyn) versus fact scepticism (Frank) is a common test point. Scandinavian Realism: Axel Hagerstrom (Uppsala): rejected metaphysical concepts like 'duty' and 'right' as meaningless , 'non-natural' facts. Karl Olivecrona: Law as Fact (1939): law is a set of 'independent imperatives'; the binding force of law is a psychological illusion. Vilhelm Lundstedt: Legal Thinking Revised (1956): social welfare method, rejecting the idea of justice. Alf Ross: On Law and Justice (1953): law is the body of rules actually effective in the minds of judges, which they feel socially bound to follow; 'Tu-tu' (an invented word to show that a legal concept like 'ownership' is an empty word used merely for convenience of speech). Criticisms: exaggerates the unpredictability of law; ignores normative element; judges do follow rules in most cases; cannot explain how to distinguish a rule from a habit; and is a theory about adjudication , not about the whole of law.

p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels: law belongs to the superstructure that rests on the economic base (the relations of production). In a class society, law is an instrument of class domination, reflecting the interests of the ruling class. Bourgeois law is the will of the bourgeois class 'made into a law for all'. Withering away of the state and law: with a classless communist society, there will be no need for law and coercive state. Lenin: law is the will of the ruling class; during the transition, the dictatorship of the proletariat needs 'proletarian' law. E.B. Pashukanis ( General Theory of Law and Marxism , 1924): the commodity-exchange theory , according to which the legal form arises from the relations of commodity exchange; thus legal form will disappear with capitalism. He was executed in the Stalinist purges. A.Y. Vyshinsky: the Stalinist view that law is the aggregate of rules of conduct expressing the will of the ruling class , established by legislation, and backed by the coercive force of the State. He rejected the Pashukanis approach. Antonio Gramsci: hegemony ; law helps to secure the consent of the governed. Criticisms: economic determinism; neglect of the autonomy of law; the rule of law as a real constraint; its predictions of the withering away of law were falsified by the experience of Soviet states. Relevance in India: Marxist ideas on law and development, class, and labour influence the thinking of writers like Upendra Baxi and the idea of social justice in the Constitution.

t: 2.10 Economic Analysis of Law (Law and Economics)
p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: Ronald Coase: The Problem of Social Cost (1960), the Coase theorem : if transaction costs are zero, parties will bargain to an efficient outcome regardless of the initial allocation of legal entitlements; if transaction costs are positive, the law should allocate rights to minimise costs. Richard Posner: Economic Analysis of Law (1973): the common law is efficient; the goal of law is wealth maximisation . Guido Calabresi: The Costs of Accidents (1970); property rules and liability rules (with Melamed, 1972, 'One View of the Cathedral'). The approach is criticised for treating efficiency as the only value and for the 'ability to pay' problem (as in Dworkin's critique of wealth maximisation).

p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: Dharma is the central concept: the cosmic and social order, righteous conduct, duty. It is a wider concept than law . The sources of Dharma according to Manu ( Manusmriti ) are the Vedas (Sruti), Smriti, the conduct of the virtuous (Sadachara) and one's own conscience (Atmatushti) . Kautilya's Arthashastra names the four sources (or legs) of law: Dharma (sacred law), Vyavahara (evidence or transactions), Charitra (history or custom) and Rajasasana (edict of the king) . In case of conflict, each later one overrides the earlier, with Rajasasana having the final authority. Danda (punishment) is essential for the maintenance of order; the king is under the law (Dharma). Mimamsa (Jaimini) contributed principles of interpretation, which are still used in Hindu law. Commentaries: Mitakshara (Vijnaneshwara; birth-right in the joint family property) and Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana; Bengal school, no birth right). Modern Indian thinkers: Mahatma Gandhi (truth, non-violence, Satyagraha and trusteeship), B.R. Ambedkar (constitutional morality, social democracy), Jawaharlal Nehru , Upendra Baxi ( The Crisis of the Indian Legal System , human rights, Bhopal).

t: 2.12 Topic 2: Revision Box and Common Confusions
p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: Author-and-work pairs (highest frequency): Austin: Province of Jurisprudence Determined (1832). Bentham: Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789). Hart: The Concept of Law (1961). Kelsen: General Theory of Law and State (1945); Pure Theory of Law . Savigny: Of the Vocation of Our Age for Legislation and Jurisprudence (1814). Maine: Ancient Law (1861). Ihering: Law as a Means to an End and Struggle for Law . Ehrlich: Fundamental Principles of the Sociology of Law (1913), 'living law'. Pound: social engineering , interests, jural postulates. Duguit: social solidarity ; law as public service. Holmes: 'The Path of the Law' (1897); Llewellyn: The Bramble Bush ; Frank: Law and the Modern Mind . Ross: On Law and Justice ; Olivecrona: Law as Fact . Fuller: The Morality of Law ; Finnis: Natural Law and Natural Rights ; Dworkin: Taking Rights Seriously and Law's Empire ; Rawls: A Theory of Justice . Stammler: Theory of Just Law ('natural law with variable content'). Grotius: De Jure Belli ac Pacis ; Hobbes: Leviathan ; Locke: Two Treatises ; Rousseau: The Social Contract ; Aquinas: Summa Theologica . Frequent traps: Natural law with a variable content is Stammler , not Kohler (Kohler is the 'jurisprudence of culture'). Social engineering belongs to Pound , whereas social solidarity belongs to Duguit (and Durkheim). Ihering is a sociological jurist (not historical), though he began in the Roman-law tradition. Rule-scepticism = Llewellyn; fact-scepticism = Frank. Gunman situation is Hart on Austin; obliged versus obligation is also Hart. Rule of recognition is Hart ; Grundnorm is Kelsen ; Law as integrity is Dworkin . Status to contract is Maine ; mechanical and organic solidarity is Durkheim . Hercules belongs to Dworkin .

p: Schools of Jurisprudence · Jurisprudence
x: This is the heaviest topic of the unit for MCQs. Every school asks the same five questions about law: What is law? Where does its authority come from? What is its relation to morality? What is its relation to society? Who makes it and who finds it? If you can answer these five for each school in one line, almost any match-the-list question becomes easy.

t: 3.1 The Core Question and the Vocabulary
p: Law and Morality · Jurisprudence
x: The central question is whether there is a necessary connection between law and morality and, a separate question, whether the law should enforce morality . Examiners test (a) which school takes which view, (b) the Hart–Devlin and Hart–Fuller debates, and (c) Indian cases in which 'constitutional morality' was set against 'public' or 'social' morality. Key terms: Positive (or conventional) morality: the moral beliefs actually held by a society. Critical (or ideal) morality: the moral principles by which social practices, including law, can be criticised (Hart's terms). Legal moralism: the view that conduct may be legally prohibited simply because it is immoral (Devlin). Legal paternalism: the law may restrict a person's liberty for the person's own good (for example seat-belt laws). Harm principle: the law may restrict liberty only to prevent harm to others (Mill). Offence principle: the law may prohibit conduct that is seriously offensive to others even if not harmful (Joel Feinberg, The Moral Limits of the Criminal Law , four volumes, 1984 to 1988: Harm to Others, Offense to Others, Harm to Self, Harmless Wrongdoing ). Constitutional morality: adherence to the core values of the Constitution (liberty, equality, dignity, fraternity, rule of law) as against popular or majoritarian morality.

t: 3.2 Differences Between Law and Morality (Concept Table)
p: Law and Morality · Jurisprudence
x: Basis Law Morality Source Made by the State or recognised by it (statute, precedent, custom) Conscience, religion, society, reason Sanction External, organised, coercive (fine, imprisonment) Internal (guilt) and social disapproval Concern Mainly external conduct; mental state only as element (mens rea) Includes inner motives, intentions and thoughts Certainty Relatively definite and written Often vague and varying Universality Differs between states; territorial Claimed to be universal (in natural law view) Change Changes by formal process Changes slowly by social evolution Scope Does not cover all moral duties (such as ingratitude) Wider; includes duties not enforced by law Enforcement Courts and police Conscience and public opinion Where they overlap: crimes such as murder, theft and fraud; duty of care in tort; good faith in contract; maintenance and child-protection laws. Where law is morally neutral: traffic rules, limitation periods, company formalities.

t: 3.3 Views of the Schools on Law and Morality
p: Law and Morality · Jurisprudence
x: Natural law: a necessary connection . An unjust law lacks full legal status (Augustine, Aquinas, Radbruch, Fuller, Finnis). Analytical positivism: separation thesis . Austin: 'The existence of law is one thing; its merit or demerit is another.' Hart accepts a minimum content of natural law but insists on conceptual separation. Raz: strict source thesis. Kelsen: the validity of law is independent of morality; justice is an irrational ideal outside legal science. Historical school: law and morality both come from the Volksgeist. Sociological school: law serves social interests which include morals (Pound listed 'general morals' as a social interest). Realists: morality matters only in so far as it influences judges. Marxists: both are ideological reflections of the economic order. Dworkin: law includes moral principles; the best interpretation of legal practice involves moral judgment (law as integrity). Fuller: the internal morality of law (the eight desiderata) is the necessary morality of legality, and law has a moral dimension essential to its existence. Hart's description: the existence of law is a matter of fact; but it is the minimum content of natural law, the union of rules and the internal point of view that links law to morality in practice.

p: Law and Morality · Jurisprudence
x: See Topic 2 .2 for the details of the informer case. In outline: Hart, 'Positivism and the Separation of Law and Morals' ( Harvard Law Review , 1958): even an evil rule may be law; the right response is to say 'this is law, but too evil to be obeyed', so as to keep moral criticism honest. Fuller, 'Positivism and Fidelity to Law: A Reply to Professor Hart' (1958): the internal morality of law; the idea of law cannot be separated from the idea of fidelity to law, and a system of extreme injustice cannot be law. Outcome: both views remain influential; many cite the Radbruch formula as a middle position.

t: 3.5 The Hart–Devlin Debate: Should Law Enforce Morality?
p: Law and Morality · Jurisprudence
x: Background: the Wolfenden Report (1957). The Committee on Homosexual Offences and Prostitution, chaired by Sir John Wolfenden , recommended that homosexual behaviour between consenting adults in private should no longer be a criminal offence . It said the function of criminal law is to preserve public order and protect citizens from what is offensive or injurious, and 'there must remain a realm of private morality and immorality which is, in brief and crude terms, not the law's business.' It was implemented by the Sexual Offences Act 1967 (England and Wales). Lord Patrick Devlin ( The Enforcement of Morals , the Maccabaean Lecture, 1959): Society is held together by a shared morality ; a society has a right to protect itself from threats, including moral threats, just as against treason. The suppression of vice is as much the law's business as the suppression of subversive activities. Disintegration thesis: if society's shared morality is flouted, society may disintegrate; hence the law may punish immorality as such. The test of the reasonable man (the 'man in the jury box' or 'man on the Clapham omnibus'): the limits of tolerance are those of the right-minded person . The marks of a public morality are ' intolerance, indignation and disgust '. Where there is a real feeling of 'reprobation', the law may act, but it must always have regard for the privacy of the individual, and tolerate as much as is consistent with the integrity of society. H.L.A. Hart ( Law, Liberty and Morality , 1963; The Morality of the Criminal Law , 1965): Rejects the disintegration thesis as lacking empirical evidence: society does not disintegrate because of changes in sexual morality; the idea that a change in morality is like treason is incorrect. Distinguishes positive morality from critical morality . Devlin's argument, Hart says, confuses social acceptance with moral rightness . Mere moral outrage, disgust and intolerance cannot justify the use of criminal law. Supports Mill's harm principle , while recognising certain justifiable cases of paternalism (for example, to protect people from exploitation or when consent is unreal). Called Devlin's view 'a moral populism', and said that to enforce morality merely because it is shared is an unjustified form of moral tyranny of the majority. Also noted that the Wolfenden position was consistent with utilitarian liberalism . Other contributions: J.S. Mill, On Liberty (1859): the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others . His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant. James Fitzjames Stephen ( Liberty, Equality, Fraternity , 1873): an early critic of Mill who argued that law may enforce morality; Devlin's views are close to his. Ronald Dworkin ('Lord Devlin and the Enforcement of Morals', Yale Law Journal , 1966) criticised Devlin for treating popular reaction as the same as moral conviction . Case law (English and American) often used as illustrations: Shaw v DPP (1962): the House of Lords recognised a common-law offence of conspiracy to corrupt public morals (the 'Ladies' Directory' case), accepted by commentators as Devlin's view in action. Knuller v DPP (1973): the Lords reaffirmed the offence of outraging public decency. R v Brown (1993): the Lords upheld convictions for consensual sadomasochistic acts (a paternalism and public-morality case); the Mill and Hart view would have favoured the defendants. Bowers v Hardwick (1986, US Supreme Court) upheld a Georgia sodomy law, but this was overruled by Lawrence v Texas (2003) , which emphasised liberty and privacy. Obergefell v Hodges (2015, US) recognised same-sex marriage.

t: 3.6 Indian Cases on Law, Morality and Constitutional Morality (Highest Recent Yield)
p: Law and Morality · Jurisprudence
x: The Indian Supreme Court's recent judgments have been drawn on repeatedly in questions. Learn the name, year, and the one-line holding . (a) Homosexuality and Section 377 IPC Naz Foundation v Government of NCT of Delhi (2009): the Delhi High Court (A.P. Shah CJ) read down Section 377 IPC to exclude consensual adult sexual acts in private; it relied on constitutional morality and said popular morality or public disapproval cannot justify limits on fundamental rights. Suresh Kumar Koushal v Naz Foundation (2013): the Supreme Court reversed that decision, holding that the question was for Parliament and that LGBT persons were a 'miniscule fraction'. National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) v Union of India (2014): recognised the right of transgender persons to self-identify their gender and held that they are entitled to fundamental rights, and are a 'third gender'. K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017): a nine-judge bench unanimously held that privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21 (and Part III as a whole), overruling M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) in part. Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India (2018): a five-judge Constitution Bench read down Section 377 and decriminalised consensual same-sex acts between adults, overruling Koushal . It emphasised constitutional morality over social morality , dignity, and the transformative character of the Constitution. Bestiality and non-consensual acts remain punishable. Note: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (in force from 1 July 2024) has replaced the IPC and has no counterpart of Section 377; check the statutory mapping if the exam gives section-numbered questions. (b) Adultery: Joseph Shine v Union of India (2018): Section 497 IPC (adultery) was struck down as violating Articles 14, 15 and 21; it treated a wife as the property of the husband and was based on outdated morality. (c) Religion, gender and constitutional morality Indian Young Lawyers Association v State of Kerala (Sabarimala) (2018): by a 4:1 majority, the Court held the exclusion of women of menstruating age from the Sabarimala temple violated Articles 14, 15, 17 and 25; constitutional morality must prevail over religious practices that violate dignity. Justice Indu Malhotra dissented, saying courts should not interfere with essential religious practices. Kantaru Rajeevaru v Indian Young Lawyers Association (2020): review petitions were referred to a larger bench to consider the broader questions of the scope of religious freedom and essential religious practices. (Check the latest status of the nine-judge bench.) Shayara Bano v Union of India (2017): by 3:2 the Court struck down instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) as arbitrary and unconstitutional. (d) Obscenity and public morality (Section 292 IPC, now Section 294 BNS) Ranjit D. Udeshi v State of Maharashtra (1965): adopted the English Hicklin test ( R v Hicklin , 1868), asking whether the material tends to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such immoral influences. K.A. Abbas v Union of India (1970): on censorship of films, upheld pre-censorship as a reasonable restriction. Bobby Art International v Om Pal Singh Hoon (1996): Bandit Queen ; the context and the message of the film matter. Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal (2014): rejected the Hicklin test and adopted the 'community standards' test (from the US Roth approach), holding that a picture of Boris Becker with his fiancee, published for an anti-racism message, was not obscene. (e) Dignity, death and autonomy Aruna Shanbaug v Union of India (2011): allowed passive euthanasia under judicial supervision. Common Cause v Union of India (2018): recognised the right to die with dignity under Article 21 and allowed 'living wills' (advance directives) with safeguards. (f) Constitutional morality in other contexts: Manoj Narula v Union of India (2014) on appointment of tainted persons as ministers, where the Court explained constitutional morality as conformity with the norms of the Constitution; the concept was invoked by Dr B.R. Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly (borrowing from the historian George Grote ) as the 'effective co-ordination between conflicting interests'; it is not a natural sentiment and must be cultivated.

t: 3.7 Law, Morality and Other Normative Orders
p: Law and Morality · Jurisprudence
x: Law and religion: historically fused (Dharma, Sharia, canon law); modern states separate them, though personal laws persist (Article 25 and the debate on the Uniform Civil Code under Article 44). Law and ethics of profession: Bar Council rules on professional misconduct. Law and justice: justice is a moral value that law aims to achieve; for Aristotle, justice includes distributive and corrective aspects; for Kelsen, justice is outside the 'pure' science; for Rawls, justice is 'the first virtue of social institutions'. Civil disobedience (Thoreau; Gandhi's Satyagraha ; Rawls, Dworkin): the claim that an unjust law may justify non-violent, public, conscientious breach.

p: Law and Morality · Jurisprudence
x: Wolfenden Report (1957): private morality is not the law's business . Devlin : The Enforcement of Morals (1959): shared morality; disintegration; intolerance, indignation, disgust . Hart : Law, Liberty and Morality (1963): Mill's harm principle; positive versus critical morality. Mill : On Liberty ; Fuller : eight desiderata; Dworkin : moral reading; Feinberg : harm and offence. Indian anchors: Naz (2009), Koushal (2013), NALSA (2014), Puttaswamy (2017), Joseph Shine (2018), Navtej Johar (2018), Sabarimala (2018), Shayara Bano (2017), Common Cause (2018), Aveek Sarkar (2014). Trap: Hicklin test was replaced by the community standards test in Aveek Sarkar ; Naz (Delhi HC) was reversed in Koushal and finally restored in substance by Navtej .

t: 4.1 Meaning and Definitions of a Legal Right
p: Concept of Rights and Duties · Jurisprudence
x: A legal right is an interest or claim that the law recognises and protects, and the violation of which is a legal wrong, while the respect for which is a legal duty. Unlike a mere moral claim, a legal right can be enforced by the courts. Jurist Definition Salmond An interest recognised and protected by a rule of right; any interest respect for which is a duty and the disregard of which is a wrong Austin A faculty which resides in a determinate party or parties by virtue of a given law, and which avails against a party or parties other than the party or parties in whom it resides Holland A capacity residing in one man of controlling, with the assistance of the State, the actions of others Gray A power which a man has to make a person or persons do or refrain from doing something, so far as the power is derived from the law Ihering A legally protected interest Bentham Rights are the creatures of law and arise from it; there is no right without a corresponding duty Kant, Hegel, Savigny A right is the power or sphere of free will Pound An interest recognised by law, whether an individual, public or social interest Hohfeld A right strictly is a claim ; correlatives are duties

p: Concept of Rights and Duties · Jurisprudence
x: Will (choice) theory: a right is a protected sphere of individual will or choice , such that the right-holder has control over the corresponding duty (for example, to waive or enforce it). Associated with Kant, Hegel, Savigny, Puchta, Windscheid ; in modern times H.L.A. Hart (choice theory). Criticism: it cannot explain the rights of infants, mentally ill persons, and unborn children, or inalienable rights. Interest (benefit) theory: a right is a legally protected interest . Associated with Ihering, Bentham, Salmond, Austin (partly) and Joseph Raz ('X has a right if X's well-being is a sufficient reason for holding another to be under a duty'; Raz in The Morality of Freedom ). Criticism: third-party beneficiaries have interests but not rights; trust beneficiaries. Hybrid theories: MacCormick and others combine will and interest. Rights as trumps (Dworkin): individual rights override collective goals. Social function theory (Duguit): rights are replaced by social functions and duties. Kelsen: a right is a reflex of a duty ; the 'right' is the legal duty seen from the standpoint of the person entitled.

p: Concept of Rights and Duties · Jurisprudence
x: The subject or owner of the right (the person who has the benefit). The person of incidence , or the person against whom the right is available (the person bound by the duty). The content of the right , or the act or forbearance which the person bound must do or abstain from doing. The object of the right , the thing or subject matter over which the right is exercised. The title of the right , the facts or events by which the right is vested in the owner (for example, a contract or purchase).

t: 4.4 Hohfeld's Analysis of Fundamental Legal Conceptions
p: Concept of Rights and Duties · Jurisprudence
x: Wesley Newcomb Hohfeld (American jurist, 1879 to 1918) published Fundamental Legal Conceptions as Applied in Judicial Reasoning (articles of 1913 and 1917, published as a book in 1919). He argued that the term 'right' is used loosely and in at least four different senses. He identified eight jural conceptions in two sets of four: jural opposites and jural correlatives . Jural opposites Jural correlatives Right (claim) ↔ No-right Right ↔ Duty Privilege (liberty) ↔ Duty Privilege ↔ No-right Power ↔ Disability Power ↔ Liability Immunity ↔ Liability Immunity ↔ Disability Definitions: Right (claim, right in the strict sense): a claim that another must do or not do something. Correlative: duty . (If A has a right that B not trespass on his land, B has a duty not to trespass.) Privilege (liberty): the freedom of the holder to do something without being under a duty not to . Correlative: no-right (others cannot claim that he should not do it). Opposite: duty . Power: the ability of a person, by his own act, to change legal relations (his own or another's). Examples: the power to make a will or contract, or to sell property. Correlative: liability . Opposite: disability . Immunity: freedom from the power of another to change one's legal position. Correlative: disability (in the other). Opposite: liability . (Example: the immunity of diplomats from jurisdiction; judges' immunity.) Liability: the position of being subject to another's power to change one's legal relations (for example, a debtor's liability to be sued; a mortgagor's liability to a power of sale). Disability: the absence of a power (for example, a minor's incapacity to make a binding contract). Duty: being legally bound to act or forbear. No-right: the absence of a claim. Key exam trap: correlatives are two sides of the same relation and exist in different persons (right in A is duty in B); opposites are the negation of a conception in the same person (a person who has a right does not have a no-right). Hohfeld called the four conceptions of right, privilege, power and immunity the 'advantages' , and the other four the 'disadvantages' .

p: Concept of Rights and Duties · Jurisprudence
x: Perfect and imperfect rights: a perfect right is one that is both recognised and enforceable (for example, the right to recover a debt); an imperfect right is recognised but not enforceable (for example, a time-barred debt). Positive and negative rights: a positive right corresponds to a duty to do something (to pay a debt); a negative right corresponds to a duty to forbear (not to trespass). Real rights ( in rem ) and personal rights ( in personam ): a right in rem is available against the world at large (the right of ownership, the right to reputation); a right in personam is available against a determinate person or persons (contractual rights). Salmond notes that rights in rem are generally negative and rights in personam generally positive , but there are exceptions. Proprietary and personal rights: proprietary rights relate to a person's estate or property and are valuable (ownership, debts, shares), whereas personal rights relate to a person's status or condition (right to liberty, reputation, family rights). Rights in re propria and rights in re aliena : the right of ownership over one's own property, or jura in re propria , and encumbrances on the property of another, jura in re aliena . The four categories of encumbrances are leases, servitudes (easements), securities (mortgages, pledges and liens) and trusts . Principal and accessory rights: an accessory right is subordinate to a principal one (for example, a mortgage securing a debt). Vested and contingent rights: a vested right is fully acquired, while a contingent right depends on a future event. Primary (antecedent) and secondary (sanctioning or remedial) rights: a primary right exists independently of any wrong (the right to bodily integrity); a secondary right arises from a violation (the right to damages). Legal and equitable rights; public and private rights; municipal and international rights; rights against the State. Human rights and fundamental rights: a human right is a claim recognised by international law and moral theory, and a fundamental right is a human right incorporated into the Constitution and enforceable under Articles 32 and 226 . Salmond's and Austin's views on 'rights without correlative duties': Austin said that there are absolute duties (those not correlative to any right), such as duties owed to oneself, to God, to the lower animals and to the public. Salmond argues that every right has a duty , but not every duty has a right (absolute duties exist but are rights of the State). Hohfeld says the correlative of right is duty, but privileges have no-right as correlatives. Key maxims: ubi jus ibi remedium (where there is a right there is a remedy); damnum sine injuria (loss without legal injury is not actionable, Gloucester Grammar School case , 1410; Bradford Corporation v Pickles , 1895); injuria sine damno (violation of right without loss is actionable, Ashby v White , 1703; the right to vote).

p: Concept of Rights and Duties · Jurisprudence
x: Meaning: a duty is an act of forbearance that the law obliges a person to perform in the interest of another, and the neglect of which is a wrong. Salmond: duty is an obligatory act, the opposite of which is a wrong. Austin: the idea of duty is prior to the idea of right, and the duty is the basic concept (the right is only the other side). Kelsen: the right is a reflex of the duty. Duguit: only duties exist, as everyone has the duty to perform a social function. Kinds of duties: Positive and negative duties. Primary (or antecedent) and secondary (or sanctioning) duties: the duty to pay compensation after a wrong is secondary. Absolute and relative duties: relative duties correspond to rights in a determinate person; absolute duties have no corresponding right in an individual (for example, duties towards the public or the State). Duties in rem and in personam. Legal and moral duties. Penal and remedial (civil) duties. Fundamental duties in India (Part IV-A, Article 51A): Introduced by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 , on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee , and inspired by the USSR Constitution . Originally ten duties; an eleventh (duty of a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child between the ages of six and fourteen) was added by the Eighty-sixth Amendment Act, 2002 . They include respect for the Constitution, the national flag and anthem; cherishing the ideals of the freedom struggle; upholding sovereignty and integrity; defending the country; promoting harmony and renouncing practices derogatory to the dignity of women; preserving the composite culture; protecting the natural environment; developing the scientific temper and humanism; safeguarding public property and abjuring violence; and striving for excellence. Not directly enforceable by writ, but useful in interpreting laws and in determining the reasonableness of restrictions on rights. See Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v State of UP (1985); AIIMS Students' Union v AIIMS (2002) (fundamental duties are not enforceable by writ but the court can use them to interpret); and Bijoe Emmanuel v State of Kerala (1986) (national anthem and the right not to sing). Duties of the State (in the Constitution): the Directive Principles (Part IV) impose duties on the State, but are non-justiciable (Article 37). The Court has expanded fundamental rights to read in many directive principles (for example, Unni Krishnan v State of AP , 1993, on the right to education, which led to Article 21A by the 86th Amendment).

p: Concept of Rights and Duties · Jurisprudence
x: Most theorists (Salmond, Holland, Hohfeld, Bentham) treat right and duty as correlatives : no right without a duty in someone else. Austin and Kelsen see duty as the primary notion. Duguit and the sociological school see duty (social function) as the basic concept. Hohfeld's contribution is to show that the word 'right' hides four different relations: claim, liberty, power and immunity.

t: 4.8 Indian Rights Jurisprudence: Landmark Cases for Recent Trends
p: Concept of Rights and Duties · Jurisprudence
x: Kharak Singh v State of UP (1962) and Gobind v State of MP (1975): early recognition of privacy. Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978): the 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 must be just, fair and reasonable ; the 'golden triangle' of Articles 14, 19 and 21. Olga Tellis v Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985): the right to livelihood is part of the right to life. Francis Coralie Mullin v Administrator, Delhi (1981): the right to live with human dignity. Vishaka v State of Rajasthan (1997): guidelines on sexual harassment at the workplace, drawing on international conventions (CEDAW). K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017): privacy; Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) (2018): limited validity of Aadhaar. Mohini Jain v State of Karnataka (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993): the right to education; Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 . Property: the right to property was removed from fundamental rights by the 44th Amendment (1978) and made a constitutional right under Article 300A . PUCL v Union of India (2001): the right to food (Article 21). Subhash Kumar v State of Bihar (1991) and M.C. Mehta cases: the right to a wholesome environment.

t: Memory Capsule: Concept of Rights and Duties
p: Concept of Rights and Duties · Jurisprudence
x: Will theory : Savigny, Kant, Hegel, Hart; interest theory : Ihering, Bentham, Salmond, Raz. Hohfeld: eight conceptions; correlatives (right–duty; privilege–no-right; power–liability; immunity–disability); opposites (right–no-right; privilege–duty; power–disability; immunity–liability). Salmond's five elements of a right: subject, person bound, content, object, title. Encumbrances: leases, servitudes, securities, trusts. Article 51A: 11 duties; added by 42nd Amendment (1976) on Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation; the eleventh added by 86th Amendment (2002). Trap: Austin said duty without right can exist; Hohfeld's privilege is not the same as a right .

p: Legal Personality · Jurisprudence
x: The word person comes from the Latin persona , the mask worn by actors in the Roman theatre, hence a role or character played in the legal drama. In law, a person is any being, real or imaginary, to which the law attributes legal rights and duties . Legal personality is the capacity to be the holder of rights and duties. Salmond: a person is any being whom the law regards as capable of rights or duties. Any being that is so capable is a person, whether a human being or not, and no being that is not so capable is a person, even though he be a man. John Chipman Gray: a person is an entity to which rights and duties may be attributed. Kelsen: the legal person is not a real entity; it is the personification of a unity of legal norms (a complex of rights and duties), an auxiliary concept of legal thinking. Paton: legal personality is a technique to attribute rights and duties to a subject. Two classes of persons: Natural persons: human beings. Not every human being has been a legal person in history (slaves in Roman law were things, not persons, and the 'civil death' of convicts existed in old English law). Today all human beings are persons, but capacity may vary (minors, persons of unsound mind). Legal (juristic, artificial) persons: entities other than human beings which the law treats as persons: corporations, institutions, funds, idols, and, in some recent decisions, rivers and animals.

t: 5.2 Status of Natural Persons in Special Situations
p: Legal Personality · Jurisprudence
x: The unborn child (nasciturus): Salmond says an unborn child is not a person in the full sense, but the law protects the child's contingent rights , for example, in property and inheritance. A child en ventre sa mere is regarded as born for the purposes of beneficial rights, if it is subsequently born alive. Indian law: Section 13 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (a transfer for the benefit of an unborn person, with a prior life interest in a living person, is valid, subject to conditions); Section 20 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (a child in the womb who is later born alive has the same right of inheritance as if born before the death of the intestate). Tort: Montreal Tramways v Leveille (1933, Supreme Court of Canada) and the Congenital Disabilities (Civil Liability) Act 1976 (UK) allowed claims for pre-natal injury once the child was born alive. Salmond's classic approach is that the unborn child's rights are suspended until birth; an unborn child cannot sue in its own right but its interests can be protected by trustees or guardians. The dead person: Salmond and Austin say that a dead man has no legal personality , though the law respects wishes expressed in a will (the 'posthumous' will); the dead have an interest in reputation (Explanation 1 to the defamation provision allows prosecution if the imputation would harm the reputation of the deceased if he were living and hurts the feelings of his family) and in decent burial . Pt. Parmanand Katara v Union of India (1989): the right to dignity and fair treatment under Article 21 extends not only to a living man but also to his body after death . Ashray Adhikar Abhiyan v Union of India (2002): the dignity of the dead extends to the homeless dead, who are entitled to a decent funeral. Minors, persons of unsound mind, convicts, alien enemies: have personality but limited capacity (see the Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 11, and the Indian Majority Act, 1875: majority at 18). A minor's agreement is void ab initio ( Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose , 1903, Privy Council).

p: Legal Personality · Jurisprudence
x: (a) Corporations Corporation aggregate: a body of persons united to form a single legal person (a company, a registered society, a university or a municipal body). The members change but the corporation continues, with perpetual succession . Corporation sole: a series of successive individuals holding an office , treated as a single person (the Crown, a bishop, the President of India, the Administrator-General, the Official Trustee, the Public Trustee). The office, not the individual, is the person. Salmond's conception: a corporation is a group or series of persons which is treated by law as a person. (b) Institutions: a charitable fund, a hospital, a church or a temple endowed with property may be treated as a legal person, for example the idol in Hindu law. (c) Funds and estates: a trust fund , the estate of a deceased person or a bankrupt's estate may be treated as juristic person for purposes of administration (in India, the trust is not a person ; the trustee holds the property). (d) The State: the Union and the States are juristic persons capable of suing and being sued ( Article 300 ). Local authorities and statutory corporations are also persons (for example, LIC, SBI, Municipal Corporations). (e) Entities that are not legal persons in India: a partnership firm (it is not a separate legal entity under the Partnership Act, 1932, although it is recognised as a unit under some statutes, such as Income Tax), a Hindu undivided family (HUF), a trust , and an unregistered association . By contrast, a company (Companies Act, 2013; Section 9 deals with the effect of registration: the company is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal) and a limited liability partnership (LLP Act, 2008, Section 3: an LLP is a body corporate and a legal entity separate from its partners) are legal persons.

t: 5.4 Theories of Corporate Personality (Essential for MCQs)
p: Legal Personality · Jurisprudence
x: Theory Main proponents Core idea Fiction theory Savigny, Salmond, Pope Innocent IV ( persona ficta ), Coke Only human beings are real persons; the corporation is an artificial person created by the law through a legal fiction Concession (grant) theory Savigny (with fiction), Dicey, Austin A corporation exists only because the State grants it recognition; the State may withdraw it Realist (organic, group-personality) theory Gierke, Maitland, Zitelmann The group is a real entity with a real will of its own, existing before and independently of State recognition; the State only recognises it Bracket (symbolist) theory Ihering, Hohfeld, Holland The corporation is a convenient bracket for the real persons (members) behind it; only human beings have rights Purpose (Zweckvermogen) theory Brinz, Bekker There is no person, only property devoted to a purpose; the rights belong to nobody but the assets are bound to a specific purpose Kelsen's normative theory Kelsen The legal person is merely the personification of a set of norms; there is no difference between natural and juristic persons Hohfeldian/Procedural device Hohfeld, Frederick Hallis (later writers) Corporate personality is only a technical device for convenience of legal handling (Textbooks differ somewhat on exact labels, but for exam purposes: Fiction: Savigny/Salmond; Concession: Savigny/Dicey; Realist: Gierke/Maitland; Bracket: Ihering; Purpose: Brinz; Normative: Kelsen .) Key points: Gierke ( Das deutsche Genossenschaftsrecht ) argued that a group has a Gesamtperson with its own will; F.W. Maitland translated part of his work and popularised it in England. Realist theory supports the claim that associations (such as trade unions) have rights independent of the State's grant , and was used in discussing the Taff Vale case (1901). Salmond's view: for the sake of convenience law treats the corporate body as a person, even though it is only a fiction; the rights and liabilities belong to the corporation , which are quite distinct from those of its members. Duguit denies the reality of personality of corporations, but he did not espouse the fiction approach either: he thought the idea of 'person' was metaphysical , and replaced it by 'social function'.

p: Legal Personality · Jurisprudence
x: Separate legal entity from its members: Salomon v A. Salomon & Co Ltd (1897, House of Lords): a company is a separate person, even if one man holds virtually all its shares, and the shareholder-creditor Salomon was not liable to the company's creditors. Perpetual succession: the death, insolvency or retirement of members does not affect the existence of the company. Common seal and capacity to sue and be sued in its own name. Limited liability (for companies limited by shares). Separate property: Macaura v Northern Assurance Co (1925): a shareholder has no insurable interest in company property. Capacity limited by its objects (the ultra vires doctrine, Ashbury Railway Carriage Co v Riche , 1875), though the Companies Act, 2013 has diluted its effect. Rights of a corporation: a company is a person under Article 14 but is not a citizen and so cannot claim Article 19 rights ( Tata Engineering and Locomotive Co v State of Bihar , 1964). In R.C. Cooper v Union of India (1970) (the Bank Nationalisation case) and Bennett Coleman v Union of India (1973) the Court allowed shareholders to challenge the infringement of their own rights when the company's action also affected them.

p: Legal Personality · Jurisprudence
x: Courts sometimes disregard the separate personality of the company and look at the real persons behind it ( lifting the veil ). Grounds (judicial and statutory): Fraud or improper conduct: Gilford Motor Co v Horne (1933) (a company formed to evade a restrictive covenant was a mere cloak); Jones v Lipman (1962) (a company was a 'device' or 'sham' to avoid specific performance). Determination of character (enemy character): Daimler Co v Continental Tyre & Rubber Co (1916): a company registered in England but controlled by enemy aliens was regarded as an enemy. Tax evasion: Juggilal Kamlapat v CIT (1969); Dinshaw Maneckjee Petit (1927) (a person who made himself a company to evade super-tax). Agency or trust and Group enterprises: DHN Food Distributors v Tower Hamlets (1976), later qualified, Adams v Cape Industries (1990), which narrowed veil lifting. Protection of revenue and public interest: State of UP v Renusagar Power Co (1988); Life Insurance Corporation of India v Escorts Ltd (1986) (the court may look behind the corporate form where necessary to see the real transaction); Delhi Development Authority v Skipper Construction Co (1996) (fraud; the court lifted the veil to reach the property of directors and their families). Corporate groups and Foreign investment: Vodafone International Holdings BV v Union of India (2012) (the Supreme Court respected separate corporate personality and looked at the 'substance' of the transaction as a whole). Prest v Petrodel Resources (2013, UK Supreme Court): distinguishes concealment from evasion principles; veil piercing is available only when a person is under an existing legal obligation or liability which he deliberately evades by interposing a company. Statutory instances under the Companies Act, 2013: Section 7(7) (incorporation by false information), Section 34 and 35 (misstatement in the prospectus), Section 339 (fraudulent conduct of business) and Section 447 (punishment for fraud), and Section 2(60) (officer in default). Also 'trading with fewer than the statutory minimum members' (earlier legislation). Alter ego: Bacha F. Guzdar v CIT (1955): a shareholder is not the owner of the corporation's assets; the shareholder has only a right to a share of profit in the form of dividend.

p: Legal Personality · Jurisprudence
x: A corporation has no body to imprison or a mind to be guilty, yet it may be liable for crimes under the doctrine of identification (the 'directing mind and will' of the company is the company). See Lennard's Carrying Co v Asiatic Petroleum Co (1915); Tesco Supermarkets v Nattrass (1972); H.L. Bolton (Engineering) Co v T.J. Graham & Sons (1957) (Lord Denning's 'brain and nerve centre' analogy). Indian position: Standard Chartered Bank v Directorate of Enforcement (2005): a company can be prosecuted even for offences that require mandatory imprisonment, and fine can be imposed in such cases. Iridium India Telecom Ltd v Motorola Inc (2011): a company can be liable for offences requiring mens rea (cheating), the knowledge of the directing officers being attributed to it. Sunil Bharti Mittal v CBI (2015): the principle of attribution ; directors are not automatically liable for the company's acts and a company can be liable only under the 'alter ego' principle.

t: 5.8 Legal Personality of Idols, Religious Books, Rivers, Animals (High-Yield Indian Material)
p: Legal Personality · Jurisprudence
x: Idols and religious texts Pramatha Nath Mullick v Pradyumna Kumar Mullick (1925, Privy Council): a Hindu idol is a juristic person capable of holding property; the shebait acts as its manager and representative. The idol's ownership is ideal , the shebait's powers are real. Yogendra Nath Naskar v Commissioner of Income Tax (1969): the idol, a juristic person, is assessable to income tax as an 'individual'. Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, Amritsar v Som Nath Dass (2000): the Guru Granth Sahib is a juristic person ; the Court recognised it as a legal entity capable of owning property. The Ram Janmabhoomi (Ayodhya) judgment ( M. Siddiq v Mahant Suresh Das , 2019) also discussed the deity as a juristic person that can sue through a next friend; read its treatment of the deity and the 'asthan' carefully before relying on it in an exam. A mosque is not a juristic person in Indian law. Rivers and natural entities Mohd. Salim v State of Uttarakhand (2017): the Uttarakhand High Court declared the rivers Ganga and Yamuna and their tributaries as legal and living entities with the status of a legal person, and appointed the Director NAMAMI Gange, the Chief Secretary and the Advocate General as 'persons in loco parentis' to protect them. The Supreme Court stayed the decision in State of Uttarakhand v Mohd. Salim (2017) on grounds of practical difficulties (for example, liability for floods). Lalit Miglani v State of Uttarakhand (2017): the same High Court extended this status to the Himalayan glaciers (Gangotri and Yamunotri) , streams, rivulets, lakes, air, meadows, dales, jungles, forests and springs. Sukhna Lake case ( Court on its Own Motion v Union Territory of Chandigarh , 2020): the Punjab and Haryana High Court declared Sukhna Lake a 'living entity' with legal personality. Foreign comparisons: the Whanganui River in New Zealand ( Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act, 2017 ) and Te Urewera Act 2014 ; the Constitution of Ecuador (2008) recognises the rights of nature ( Pachamama ); Bolivia 's Law of Mother Earth (2010); and the Atrato River case of Colombia (2016). Animals Animal Welfare Board of India v A. Nagaraja (2014): the Jallikattu case: the Supreme Court held that animals have a right to live with dignity , extended the idea of Article 21 'life' to animals, and listed the 'five freedoms' of animals: freedom from hunger, thirst and malnutrition; from fear and distress; from physical and thermal discomfort; from pain, injury and disease; and freedom to express normal patterns of behaviour. It also invoked Article 51A(g) (compassion for living creatures) and the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 . Narayan Dutt Bhatt v Union of India (2018): the Uttarakhand High Court declared the entire animal kingdom , including avian and aquatic species, as legal entities having the status of legal persons, and citizens as their guardians. Karnail Singh v State of Haryana (2019): the Punjab and Haryana High Court declared the animal kingdom a legal entity (the Supreme Court stayed this in 2019). Comparative note: in the US, the New York Court of Appeals (2022, Nonhuman Rights Project v Breheny , the elephant 'Happy') refused to treat an elephant as a legal person for habeas corpus. Artificial intelligence and other emerging entities: in 2017 the European Parliament debated a proposal on 'electronic personhood' for sophisticated autonomous robots, which many criticised; Saudi Arabia symbolically granted 'citizenship' to the robot Sophia in 2017. Indian law has no concept of AI personhood. The debate centres on liability gaps and whether legal personality is a pragmatic device.

p: Legal Personality · Jurisprudence
x: Persona = mask. Salmond: any being capable of rights and duties. Kelsen: personification of norms. Theories: Fiction (Savigny, Salmond), Concession (Dicey), Realist (Gierke, Maitland), Bracket (Ihering), Purpose (Brinz), Normative (Kelsen). Corporation sole (office) versus aggregate (group). Salomon (1897); Lee v Lee's Air Farming (1961); Macaura (1925); lifting the veil (Gilford, Jones v Lipman, Daimler, Skipper, LIC v Escorts, Vodafone). Idol: Pramatha Nath Mullick (1925); Guru Granth Sahib: Som Nath Dass (2000); Rivers: Mohd. Salim (2017) (stayed by the Supreme Court); Animals: A. Nagaraja (2014) and Narayan Dutt Bhatt (2018). A company is a 'person' but not a 'citizen' ( Tata Engineering , 1964); partnership firms, HUFs and trusts are not juristic persons in India.

p: Concepts of Property, Ownership and Possession · Jurisprudence
x: Meaning in different senses (Salmond): All legal rights of a person , proprietary and personal (this is the widest sense, used by Locke and in the older writers). Proprietary rights only (the right of ownership, and rights in the estate, as distinguished from personal rights, rights of status). Material things that are the subject-matter of proprietary rights (land and chattels). Corporeal property in the sense of material things (land or goods), and incorporeal property (rights such as copyright, patents, debts, shares, goodwill). Kinds of property: Movable and immovable property; real and personal property (English law distinction based on the type of action available). Corporeal (tangible) and incorporeal (intangible) property: intangible includes intellectual property (patent, copyright, trademark, design), goodwill and choses in action. Private, public, and common property. Public trust doctrine: M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath (1997): natural resources like the rivers, forests and the seashore are held by the State as a trustee for the public. Theories of property (important for conceptual and match-the-following questions): Theory Thinker Idea Labour (natural rights) John Locke ( Two Treatises ) Property arises when a man mixes his labour with what is held in common, subject to the proviso that 'enough and as good' be left for others Occupation Grotius, Kant (in a limited sense) First occupation gives title Utilitarian Bentham, Hume Property is a creation of law; 'property and law are born together and die together'; it creates security of expectation Personality Hegel, Kant Property is the embodiment of personality; needed for self-development Marxist Marx, Engels; Proudhon Private property is the basis of class exploitation; Proudhon: 'property is theft' ( What is Property? , 1840) Social function Duguit Property is not a right but a social function Economic efficiency Demsetz, Posner Property rights internalise externalities and promote efficient use Historical Maine, Savigny Property evolves from collective to individual ownership Natural law Aquinas, Blackstone Property is derived from natural law; Blackstone called it 'that sole and despotic dominion' over external things Indian constitutional position on property: The right to property (Articles 19(1)(f) and 31) was a fundamental right until the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978 deleted these provisions and inserted Article 300A in Part XII: no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law . It is now a constitutional right (not a fundamental right) and a human right ( Vidya Devi v State of Himachal Pradesh , 2020). Article 31A, 31B and 31C protect agrarian reform and the Directive Principles (Articles 39(b) and (c)); the Ninth Schedule (inserted by the First Amendment, 1951) immunises listed laws, but I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu (2007) held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda Bharati ) are open to challenge on the ground of violation of the basic structure or fundamental rights. Cases: Kameshwar Singh v State of Bihar (1952); State of West Bengal v Bela Banerjee (1954) (compensation must be a just equivalent); R.C. Cooper (1970) (rejected the argument that the compensation was non-justiciable); Kesavananda Bharati (1973); K.T. Plantation v State of Karnataka (2011) (Article 300A requires public purpose and authority of law, though not necessarily compensation); Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v State of Gujarat (1995). The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 replaced the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.

p: Concepts of Property, Ownership and Possession · Jurisprudence
x: Definitions: Austin: a right indefinite in point of user , unrestricted in point of disposition and unlimited in point of duration over a determinate thing. Salmond: ownership, in its most comprehensive signification, denotes the relation between a person and any right that is vested in him. A person's owner is the person in whom the right is vested; ownership of a material thing is the greatest possible interest in it, the entirety of the powers of use and enjoyment, a right in rem. Holland: the plenary control over an object. Hibbert: ownership is a bundle of rights ; a plenary right of dominion over a thing. Hohfeld: ownership is a bundle of Hohfeldian relations (claims, privileges, powers, immunities). Blackstone: 'that sole and despotic dominion which one man claims and exercises over the external things of the world, in total exclusion of the right of any other individual in the universe.' A.M. Honore's 'Ownership' (1961) gives the modern standard incidents of ownership : (1) the right to possess , (2) the right to use , (3) the right to manage , (4) the right to the income , (5) the right to the capital (the power to alienate, consume or destroy), (6) the right to security (immunity from expropriation), (7) transmissibility , (8) absence of term (indefinite duration), (9) the prohibition of harmful use , (10) liability to execution (for debt), and (11) residuary character (the right to what remains when lesser interests lapse). Essential characteristics of ownership (Salmond/Austin): it is indeterminate in extent (the owner has all the rights over the thing not given to others), it is residuary (rights left after lesser interests are carved out), it is permanent (it outlasts the owner by inheritance), and it is a right in rem (good against everybody). Kinds of ownership (Salmond): Corporeal and incorporeal ownership: over a material thing and over an intangible right (a patent, a copyright, a debt). Sole ownership and co-ownership: two or more persons may own a thing together ( joint tenancy with the right of survivorship; tenancy in common with undivided shares; in India, co-ownership in joint Hindu family property, and the Transfer of Property Act). Trust and beneficial ownership: the trustee holds legal title while the beneficiary has the equitable (beneficial) interest ( Section 3 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 ). Legal and equitable ownership. Vested and contingent ownership: vested where the title is complete; contingent where it depends on a future event. Absolute and limited ownership; ownership limited by encumbrances (leases, easements, mortgages). Modes of acquisition of ownership (Salmond): Original acquisition: by absorption (taking things not owned: occupation, finding, accession), by prescription (the long enjoyment of a right). Derivative acquisition: by transfer (alienation by agreement, voluntary), by inheritance (succession on death, involuntary), by execution or bankruptcy ( forced transfer ). Prescription (positive and negative): under Indian law, Section 27 of the Limitation Act, 1963 , extinguishes the right to property when the limitation period for suing for possession has expired. Adverse possession: Article 65 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963 (12 years for private property and 30 years for property of the Government, Article 112). Landmark cases: Karnataka Board of Wakf v Government of India (2004); Hemaji Waghaji Jat v Bhikhabhai Khengarbhai Harijan (2009) (the Court expressed unease with adverse possession); Ravinder Kaur Grewal v Manjit Kaur (2019) (a person claiming adverse possession may use it as a sword as well as a shield, with a plaintiff able to seek a declaration of title). Modern limitations on ownership: planning and zoning laws, environmental regulations, land ceiling laws, rent control, eminent domain (compulsory acquisition), taxation, and the public trust doctrine .

p: Concepts of Property, Ownership and Possession · Jurisprudence
x: Meaning: possession is the de facto relationship between a person and a thing, the effective control over a thing with the intention to hold it to the exclusion of others. It is a notoriously elusive concept in law. Definitions and theories: Salmond: possession is the continuing exercise of a claim to the exclusive use of a thing . He distinguishes possession in fact and possession in law . Savigny (subjective theory): possession has two elements: corpus possessionis (the physical control, or the power to deal with the thing) and animus domini (animus possidendi) (the intention to hold the thing as an owner, to the exclusion of all others). If there is corpus without animus , the person only has detention ( detentio ), as in a tenant, servant or bailee who recognises another's ownership. Ihering (objective theory): animus is not an independent element; it is merely the intention to deal with the thing as an ordinary man would deal with his own (corpus alone is enough, subject to the law's exceptions). Possession is protected by law as the 'outpost' (outer defence) of ownership , and its protection serves ownership . Pollock and Holmes: possession is power to exclude others with the intention to do so. Holmes ( The Common Law , 1881): the protection of possession follows from the idea of preventing breaches of the peace and of the person's will; Pollock emphasises effective control . Pollock and Wright's Possession in the Common Law (1888) is the standard work. Kant and Hegel: the 'intelligible possession' arises from will and is connected to right and not just to physical control. Elements in Salmond's view: an intention (animus) and a corpus (a degree of physical power or control). Kinds of possession: Corporeal (possession of things) and incorporeal (possession of rights , such as an easement or a way, sometimes called quasi-possession ). Mediate and immediate possession: an owner who lets another hold the thing for him (a bailee, a tenant) retains mediate possession, while the bailee has immediate possession. Possession in fact and in law (constructive possession). Concurrent possession: different persons have possession of the same thing in different ways (a pledgor and pledgee). Adverse possession: possession that is hostile to the true owner's title, with the intention to claim ownership. Joint and sole possession. Acquisition of possession: by taking (with or without the consent of the previous possessor), by delivery (actual or constructive), and by operation of law . Leading cases on possession and finders (frequent MCQs): Armory v Delamirie (1722): a chimney-sweep's boy who found a jewel acquired a title good against everybody except the true owner ; the jeweller was liable for refusing to return it. Bridges v Hawkesworth (1851): a customer who found banknotes on the floor of a shop was entitled to them against the shopkeeper, since the notes were never in the shopkeeper's possession. South Staffordshire Water Co v Sharman (1896): the owner of land has a better claim than the finder to things found embedded in the land (the rings found in a pool); the occupier, having a greater degree of control, has possession. Hannah v Peel (1945): the finder of a brooch in a requisitioned house was entitled to it against the occupier who had never lived there. Parker v British Airways Board (1982): the occupier's superior claim exists only if he manifested an intention to control the premises and things on them; the finder's rights were set out. Merry v Green (1841): the buyer of a bureau with a secret drawer who found money in it was guilty of larceny, as the property had not passed to him. Indian statutes: Sections 71 and 168 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (the finder of goods is a bailee and has a right to retain and to sue for reward only in some conditions); Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (a person dispossessed of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law can recover possession by a summary suit within six months , regardless of title, and no appeal lies from the order); Section 110 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (possession as prima facie proof of ownership), now carried into the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 . Importance of possession: possession is prima facie evidence of ownership (the maxim possession is nine points of law ), possession is protected even against the true owner who takes the law into his own hands, a person in possession can sue trespassers, and possession is a root of title for prescription and adverse possession .

p: Concepts of Property, Ownership and Possession · Jurisprudence
x: Basis Ownership Possession Nature A right de jure (legal title) A fact de facto (effective control) Duration Permanent, indefinite May be temporary Extent The totality of rights over the thing A limited relationship with the thing (control and enjoyment) Protection Remedies for recovery and declaration of title Protected by summary remedies, and against wrongdoers Transmissibility Inheritable and alienable Not always transferable as a right Relation A thief has possession without ownership; an owner who loses a thing retains ownership but has lost possession Ihering's remark: possession is the outer fortress of ownership . Savigny: possession is a mere fact, but with legal consequences. The two are separate concepts that usually coincide, hence the usual case of an owner in possession; Salmond treats ownership as an ideal and possession as the visible relationship.

t: Memory Capsule: Concepts of Property, Ownership and Possession
p: Concepts of Property, Ownership and Possession · Jurisprudence
x: Austin's ownership: indefinite user, unrestricted disposition, unlimited duration. Honore: 11 incidents. Locke: labour theory; Bentham: property and law born together; Hegel: personality; Proudhon: property is theft; Duguit: social function. Possession: corpus and animus ; Savigny (subjective, animus domini) versus Ihering (objective, protection of ownership); Salmond: continuing exercise of a claim to exclusive use. Cases: Armory v Delamirie (1722), Bridges v Hawkesworth (1851), South Staffordshire v Sharman (1896), Hannah v Peel (1945), Parker v British Airways (1982). Constitution: Article 300A, deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 (44th Amendment, 1978); I.R. Coelho (2007). Specific Relief Act, Section 6 (six months); Limitation Act, Article 65 (12 years) and Article 112 (30 years for government).

t: 7.1 Meaning and Nature of Legal Liability
p: Concept of Liability · Jurisprudence
x: Liability is the condition of being legally answerable for an act or omission. If a right is violated, the person who violated it incurs liability, and the law supplies a remedy (compensation, punishment or restoration). Salmond: liability or responsibility is the bond of necessity that exists between the wrong-doer and the remedy of the wrong . It is the vinculum juris (bond of law) that links the wrongdoer to the remedy. Austin: liability is the condition of being exposed to a sanction as a consequence of a wrongful act or omission. Kelsen: liability is the sanction attaching to the delict; a person is liable when a sanction can be directed against him (a person is responsible if he is the one against whom the sanction is directed, whether or not he is the wrongdoer). Hart ( Punishment and Responsibility , 1968): distinguishes four senses of responsibility: role-responsibility , causal-responsibility , liability-responsibility and capacity-responsibility . Hohfeld's 'liability' is a different, technical idea: the correlative of a power (a person who may have his legal position changed by another's act). Do not confuse it with Salmond's liability. The foundation of liability: the maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea (an act does not make one guilty unless the mind be guilty).
