Under the traditional approach, liability requires (a) a wrongful act (or omission), and (b) a blameworthy state of mind , except where the law imposes strict liability.

t: 7.2 The Wrongful Act and Its Elements (Salmond's Analysis)
p: Concept of Liability · Jurisprudence
x: A wrong is an act contrary to the rule of right and justice. Wrongs are civil (redressed by compensation or restitution, as in tort or breach of contract) or criminal (redressed by punishment). Elements of a wrongful act: (1) an act or omission (the actus reus ), (2) a mental element ( mens rea : intention, recklessness, negligence), (3) damage or injury in the legal sense (not always required), and (4) a causal link between act and harm. Maxims: damnum sine injuria (damage without violation of a right is not actionable) and injuria sine damno (violation of a legal right is actionable even without loss) (see Topic 4 ). Mental states: Intention: the foresight of an act or consequence together with the desire for it (Salmond: intention is the purpose or design with which an act is done ). Oblique intention (virtual certainty of consequence) is relevant in murder: R v Woollin (1998). Motive: the ultimate end or reason behind the intention. Motive is generally irrelevant to liability ( Bradford Corporation v Pickles , 1895; Allen v Flood , 1898), though it can be relevant to sentencing and in some torts (malicious prosecution, nuisance, conspiracy). Malice: malice in law (wrongful act done intentionally without just cause or excuse) versus malice in fact (actual ill will). Negligence (Salmond's view): a state of mind, being inadvertence ( subjective theory). Winfield and modern law treat it as a breach of duty (an objective standard of the reasonable man). Recklessness: conscious taking of an unjustified risk.

p: Concept of Liability · Jurisprudence
x: (a) Civil and criminal liability: Basis Civil liability Criminal liability Purpose Redress for the wronged person (compensation, restitution) Punishment of the wrongdoer in the public interest Who initiates The injured party The State Standard of proof Balance of probabilities Beyond reasonable doubt Parties Plaintiff and defendant Prosecutor and accused Outcome Damages, injunction, specific performance Fine, imprisonment, death Compromise Generally possible Only for compoundable offences (b) Remedial and penal liability (Salmond): Penal liability: the wrongdoer is punished (imprisonment, fine); the law aims at deterrence or retribution . Remedial liability: the law merely enforces the right which has been violated, as when a debtor is compelled to pay, specific performance is ordered, or a trespasser is required to restore possession. The purpose is restitution . Salmond notes that criminal liability is penal, and civil liability may be penal (exemplary damages) or remedial. (c) Vicarious liability: liability of one person for the wrong of another, arising from a relationship such as master and servant, principal and agent, partners, or employer and employee. The maxims are respondeat superior and qui facit per alium facit per se (he who does through another does through himself). Rationale: the employer controls the enterprise and benefits from it; the employer is in a better position to compensate and insure. Requirements: relationship, and a wrong committed in the course of employment (the Salmond test : an act authorised by the master, or an unauthorised mode of doing an authorised act). Lloyd v Grace, Smith & Co (1912): the employer liable for the solicitor's clerk's fraud; Limpus v London General Omnibus Co (1862) (the driver's unauthorised racing was an unauthorised mode of an authorised act). Employer and independent contractor: generally not liable for an independent contractor, with exceptions (non-delegable duties, hazardous activities). Vicarious liability of the State: under Article 300 of the Constitution, the Union and the State may sue and be sued in relation to their affairs 'in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the Provinces'. The old distinction between sovereign and non-sovereign functions ( P. & O. Steam Navigation Co v Secretary of State for India , 1861) was applied in Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v State of UP (1965) (the State was not liable for the loss of gold seized by police, as the police acted in sovereign functions). State of Rajasthan v Vidyawati (1962) held the State liable for the negligence of a government driver, treating the State as an employer in the same way as a private person. The modern trend has moved to compensation for violation of fundamental rights as a public law remedy , independent of sovereign immunity ( Rudul Sah v State of Bihar , 1983; Bhim Singh v State of J&K , 1985; Nilabati Behera v State of Orissa , 1993; D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal , 1997). Vicarious criminal liability: generally not recognised in the Penal Code except where a statute provides (for example, Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 , for companies and persons in charge; Sunil Bharti Mittal v CBI , 2015). (d) Strict and absolute liability: liability without proof of mens rea or negligence. Strict liability in tort: Rylands v Fletcher (1868): a person who for his own purposes brings on his land and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes must keep it at his peril, and is prima facie answerable for all damage which is the natural consequence of its escape. Exceptions: act of God, consent of plaintiff, plaintiff's default, act of a stranger, statutory authority, and common benefit. Absolute liability (India): M.C. Mehta v Union of India (1987) (the Oleum gas leak case, Delhi): the Supreme Court said the Rylands v Fletcher rule is too narrow for modern hazardous industries and laid down the rule of absolute liability : an enterprise engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activity is strictly and absolutely liable to compensate those harmed, and none of the exceptions applies . The enterprise's capacity to pay determines the quantum of damages (the 'deep pocket' principle: the larger and more prosperous the enterprise, the greater the amount of compensation). Union Carbide Corporation v Union of India (1989): the Bhopal Gas Tragedy settlement. The Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985 made the Union the sole representative of the victims. Related legislation: Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 , and National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 (Section 17: no-fault liability ). Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v Union of India (1996) (Bichhri, Rajasthan): the polluter pays principle ; Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v Union of India (1996): adopted the precautionary principle and polluter pays principle as part of Indian law and as part of sustainable development. Statutory strict liability: Workmen's Compensation (now Employees' Compensation Act, 1923), the Motor Vehicles Act (no-fault liability, Section 140, and Section 164), and the Consumer Protection Act (product liability under the 2019 Act). Strict liability in criminal law: Sherras v De Rutzen (1895) (presumption of mens rea may be displaced); R v Prince (1875); State of Maharashtra v Mayer Hans George (1965) (offences under FERA/customs: mens rea not required where the statute so requires); Nathulal v State of MP (1966) (the Court reaffirms the presumption of mens rea ); Sweet v Parsley (1970) (presumption of mens rea is strong in 'truly criminal' offences). (e) Joint and several liability, contributory liability, and liability of the corporation (see Topic 5 ).

p: Concept of Liability · Jurisprudence
x: Donoghue v Stevenson (1932): the neighbour principle ; a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer. Elements of the tort of negligence: duty of care, breach, and damage caused by the breach, which is not too remote. Bolton v Stone (1951): a risk which is very small does not require precautions; Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks Co (1856): negligence is the omission to do something which a reasonable man would do. Remoteness: Re Polemis (1921) (directness test) replaced by The Wagon Mound (No. 1) (1961) (reasonable foreseeability). Res ipsa loquitur: the thing speaks for itself ( Byrne v Boulton , 1863; Scott v London & St Katherine Docks , 1865). Criminal negligence in India (medical negligence): Jacob Mathew v State of Punjab (2005): for a criminal prosecution of a doctor, gross negligence or recklessness must be shown, not mere lack of care; civil negligence is the standard of the Bolam test ( Bolam v Friern Hospital , 1957), accepted in India. Indian Consumer Protection Act and medical negligence: Indian Medical Association v V.P. Shantha (1995): medical services come within the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.

p: Concept of Liability · Jurisprudence
x: Insanity: M'Naghten's case (1843): the accused must show that at the time of the act he was labouring under such a defect of reason from disease of the mind as not to know the nature and quality of the act or that it was wrong. India: Section 84 IPC (now Section 22 BNS). Infancy: a child under seven is doli incapax (Section 82 IPC; Section 20 BNS); between seven and twelve it depends on maturity (Section 83 IPC; Section 21 BNS). Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. Necessity: R v Dudley and Stephens (1884): necessity is no defence to murder. Self-defence, consent, accident, mistake of fact (and not of law), duress, and act of God (in tort). Statutory exceptions in the Penal Code (General Exceptions, Chapter IV IPC; Chapter III BNS). Note: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (2023) came into force on 1 July 2024 , replacing the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act; the exam may use either set of section numbers during the transition.

t: 7.6 Theories of Punishment (Closely Linked to Penal Liability)
p: Concept of Liability · Jurisprudence
x: Theory Thinker Core idea Criticism Retributive Kant, Hegel, Bradley Punishment is deserved; the offender must suffer in proportion to the wrong ('an eye for an eye'); looking backward Does not reduce crime; can be vengeful Deterrent Bentham, Beccaria, Paley, Salmond Punishment prevents others (general deterrence) and the offender (specific deterrence) by fear; looking forward Ineffective if offenders do not calculate; can justify excessive penalties Preventive (incapacitation) Plato, modern penologists Remove the offender from society (imprisonment, death) Does not reform; costly Reformative (rehabilitative) Modern penology; Indian reformists Punishment aims to reform the offender; prison as a correctional institution May not deter; difficult to assess reform Expiatory Religious thought Punishment atones for guilt Hard to defend in a secular state Utilitarian Bentham, Mill Punishment is justified only if it produces more good (happiness) than evil Might punish the innocent for deterrence Mixed (Hart) H.L.A. Hart General justifying aim is deterrence, subject to distribution principles based on responsibility and proportionality -- Restorative Victimology, Howard Zehr Repair the harm; reconcile offender, victim and community Limited for serious crimes Salmond's view: punishment is an evil inflicted on the wrongdoer for his wrong ; deterrence is the primary purpose, with retribution, prevention and reform as secondary. Indian cases on punishment: Capital punishment: Jagmohan Singh v State of UP (1973) (the death penalty is constitutional); Rajendra Prasad v State of UP (1979); Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980) (the Constitution Bench upheld constitutionality of the death penalty and laid down the 'rarest of rare' doctrine, requiring a balance of aggravating and mitigating circumstances); Machhi Singh v State of Punjab (1983) (guidelines); Mithu v State of Punjab (1983) (the mandatory death penalty under Section 303 IPC was struck down); Shatrughan Chauhan v Union of India (2014) (undue delay in disposal of mercy petitions is a ground for commutation). The 262nd Law Commission Report (2015) recommended abolition of the death penalty for all crimes other than terrorism-related offences. Reformative approach: Mohd. Giasuddin v State of Andhra Pradesh (1977) (Justice Krishna Iyer, the need to humanise punishment and use reform); the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 ; Santosh Kumar Satishbhushan Bariyar v State of Maharashtra (2009) (sentencing in death cases must consider the possibility of reform). Beccaria's On Crimes and Punishments (1764) opposed torture and the death penalty and favoured certain, swift punishment.

p: Concept of Liability · Jurisprudence
x: Salmond: liability is the bond of necessity between the wrongdoer and the remedy of the wrong; penal and remedial liability. Maxims: actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea ; respondeat superior ; qui facit per alium facit per se . Strict liability: Rylands v Fletcher (1868); absolute liability: M.C. Mehta (1987) (Oleum gas); polluter pays: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996); precautionary principle: Vellore Citizens (1996). State liability: Kasturi Lal (1965) (sovereign immunity); Vidyawati (1962); Nilabati Behera (1993) and Rudul Sah (1983) (compensation under Article 32). Death penalty: Bachan Singh (1980) (rarest of rare); Mithu (1983). Trap: Salmond's remedial liability is not the same as civil liability; Hohfeld's liability is the correlative of power .

t: 8.1 Why This Topic Matters for the Exam
p: Law, Poverty and Development · Jurisprudence
x: This is one of the newer additions to the Jurisprudence syllabus, so questions are drawn from a small and predictable pool : Amartya Sen (entitlements, capabilities, freedoms), Nussbaum's central capabilities , the Right to Development (1986) , the MDGs and SDGs , the law and development movement (and its critics), Hernando de Soto's legal empowerment idea, and Indian Supreme Court decisions on the rights of the poor . Memorise names, books, dates and numbers.

p: Law, Poverty and Development · Jurisprudence
x: Absolute poverty: inability to afford the minimum basket of goods and services needed for survival (the poverty line). Relative poverty: deprivation measured against the average standard of living in a society. Multidimensional poverty: poverty measured by deprivations in health, education and living standards, not only by income. The Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) was introduced in 2010 by the UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI) (Sabina Alkire and James Foster developed the method). It has three dimensions (health, education, living standards) and ten indicators. India's poverty measurement: the Lakdawala method; the Tendulkar Committee (2009); the Rangarajan Committee (2014). NITI Aayog's National MPI (first report 2021; the 2023 report) showed a sharp fall in multidimensional poverty (roughly from about 25 per cent in 2015-16 to about 15 per cent in 2019-21). Check the latest figures, as they are updated. World Bank's international poverty line: updated in 2022 to US\$ 2.15 a day (2017 prices) and, in 2025, to US\$ 3.00 a day (2021 prices), so verify the current figure if it appears in your exam. Human Development Index (HDI): introduced in 1990 in the first Human Development Report by Mahbub ul Haq with Amartya Sen's contribution; it measures health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and standard of living (GNI per capita).

p: Law, Poverty and Development · Jurisprudence
x: Amartya Sen (Nobel Prize in Economics, 1998; Bharat Ratna, 1999): Poverty and Famines: An Essay on Entitlement and Deprivation (1981): famines are caused not only by a shortage of food but by a failure of entitlements (the means by which people command food: production, trade, labour, inheritance). The Bengal famine of 1943 is his example, where food supply was not much lower than in previous years. Commodities and Capabilities (1985) , Development as Freedom (1999) : development is the expansion of the real freedoms that people enjoy ; poverty is capability deprivation (not just low income). He identified five instrumental freedoms : political freedoms, economic facilities, social opportunities, transparency guarantees, and protective security . The capability approach: the focus is on what people are actually able to do and to be (their functionings and capabilities ), instead of resources or utility. He criticised both utilitarianism and Rawls's focus on primary goods. The Idea of Justice (2009): a critique of 'transcendental institutionalism' (the Rawlsian search for perfectly just institutions) in favour of a realisation-focused comparative approach to reduce manifest injustice. He draws a distinction in Sanskrit between niti (rules, institutions, organisation) and nyaya (realised justice in the lives of people), and the images of the three children and the flute (Anne, Bob, Carla). He values public reasoning and the impartial spectator (from Adam Smith). Also: Collective Choice and Social Welfare (1970), Inequality Reexamined (1992), The Argumentative Indian (2005), Development and Participation . Martha Nussbaum: a philosopher who developed the capabilities approach, with a more specific, universal list. Works: Women and Human Development (2000), Frontiers of Justice (2006), Creating Capabilities (2011). Ten central human capabilities: (1) life; (2) bodily health; (3) bodily integrity; (4) senses, imagination and thought; (5) emotions; (6) practical reason; (7) affiliation; (8) other species; (9) play; (10) control over one's environment (political and material). Nussbaum says each citizen must have these to a minimum threshold; she ties them to constitutional guarantees. Difference from Sen: Sen does not give a fixed list (he leaves it to public reasoning); Nussbaum proposes a definite list. Mahbub ul Haq (the HDI) and Muhammad Yunus (Grameen Bank, microfinance; Nobel Peace Prize 2006) are associated with the practical side.

p: Law, Poverty and Development · Jurisprudence
x: Meaning: the study and practice of using law as a tool for economic and social development, especially in developing countries. First movement (1960s to 1970s): led mainly by American foundations (Ford Foundation) and law schools; it assumed that exporting Western legal institutions, legal education and 'modern' law to the Third World would speed up modernisation. Its failure was explained in David Trubek and Marc Galanter, 'Scholars in Self-Estrangement: Some Reflections on the Crisis in Law and Development Studies in the United States' (1974) . Second movement (1980s to 2000s): concentrated on the rule of law, property rights, judicial reform and market-friendly legal frameworks in support of the Washington Consensus (a term coined by John Williamson , 1989) and structural adjustment policies of the IMF and World Bank ; the World Bank's World Development Report 2002 and the Doing Business report (discontinued in 2021 after data irregularities) belong to this phase. Contemporary phase: the stress on institutions and governance , human rights-based approaches, and sustainable development . In 2024, the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded to Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity (see Acemoglu and Robinson, Why Nations Fail , 2012: inclusive versus extractive institutions). The 2019 Nobel went to Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer for an experimental approach to alleviating global poverty . Douglass North (Nobel 1993): institutions, including law, are the 'rules of the game' that shape economic performance. Hernando de Soto ( The Mystery of Capital , 2000): the poor hold vast assets as 'dead capital' because they lack formal, enforceable property titles; formalising property rights unlocks credit and capital. The Commission on Legal Empowerment of the Poor (co-chaired by Madeleine Albright and Hernando de Soto , report Making the Law Work for Everyone , 2008) identified four pillars: access to justice and the rule of law, property rights, labour rights, and business rights . Critics: Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL) scholars ( B.S. Chimni, Upendra Baxi, Antony Anghie ) see development law as a continuation of colonial hierarchies. Dependency theorists (Prebisch, Frank) see underdevelopment as a product of the global capitalist system. Others stress that legal transplants fail without local fit (the transplant effect ). New International Economic Order (NIEO, 1974) (UN General Assembly Resolution 3201 (S-VI)), the Charter of Economic Rights and Duties of States (1974) , and Permanent Sovereignty over Natural Resources (General Assembly Resolution 1803 (XVII), 1962) reflect the developing countries' demands.

t: 8.5 The Right to Development and Sustainable Development
p: Law, Poverty and Development · Jurisprudence
x: Declaration on the Right to Development (1986) (UNGA Resolution 41/128, 4 December 1986): Article 1 describes development as an inalienable human right by virtue of which every human person and all peoples are entitled to participate in, contribute to and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development. The human person is the central subject of development. It was reaffirmed in the Vienna Declaration (1993) as a universal and inalienable right and an integral part of fundamental human rights. Arjun Sengupta (an Indian economist) was Independent Expert on the right to development. Stockholm Conference (1972) , Brundtland Commission's report Our Common Future (1987) : sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs; Rio Declaration (1992) (Principle 3: right to development to be fulfilled so as to equitably meet developmental and environmental needs of present and future generations); Johannesburg (2002) ; Rio+20 (2012) . Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) (2000 to 2015): eight goals (including halving extreme poverty and hunger by 2015). Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (Agenda 2030, adopted in 2015): 17 goals and 169 targets . SDG 1: No Poverty ; SDG 2: Zero Hunger; SDG 3: Good Health; SDG 4: Quality Education; SDG 5: Gender Equality; SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities; SDG 16: Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions; SDG 17: Partnerships. Indian recognition: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum (1996) treated sustainable development as part of Indian law; Narmada Bachao Andolan v Union of India (2000) (the Sardar Sarovar Dam case; the Court balanced displacement and development and upheld the project with conditions for rehabilitation); Samatha v State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) (tribal land cannot be transferred to non-tribals; mining leases on scheduled-area land).

t: 8.6 Law as an Instrument of Social Change in India: Poverty and the Constitution
p: Law, Poverty and Development · Jurisprudence
x: Preamble: justice, social, economic and political; equality of status and opportunity. Directive Principles: Article 38 (social order for the promotion of welfare, minimising inequalities), Article 39(a) to (f) (adequate means of livelihood, distribution of resources, equal pay), Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976), Article 41 (right to work, education and public assistance), Article 43 (living wage), Article 46 (promotion of the educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and weaker sections), Article 47 (raising the level of nutrition and public health). Granville Austin ( The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation , 1966) described the Constitution as a social document and Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles as a 'seamless web' and the conscience of the Constitution. Fundamental rights and the poor: Hussainara Khatoon v State of Bihar (1979): speedy trial and free legal aid are part of Article 21 (undertrial prisoners' case). M.H. Hoskot v State of Maharashtra (1978); Khatri v State of Bihar (1981). People's Union for Democratic Rights v Union of India ( Asiad Workers' case , 1982): the denial of minimum wages is forced labour under Article 23 ; payment below the minimum wage is begar . Bandhua Mukti Morcha v Union of India (1984): bonded labour is violative of Articles 21 and 23. Olga Tellis v Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985): the right to livelihood is part of the right to life; pavement dwellers cannot be evicted without a fair procedure. Francis Coralie Mullin (1981): the right to live with dignity includes the minimum necessities of life. Shantistar Builders v Narayan Khimalal Totame (1990) and Chameli Singh v State of UP (1996): the right to shelter ('roti, kapda aur makaan') is part of Article 21. Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v State of West Bengal (1996): right to emergency medical aid ; Consumer Education and Research Centre v Union of India (1995): the right to health . People's Union for Civil Liberties v Union of India (2001, the right to food case): the Court monitored the mid-day meal scheme and public distribution to prevent starvation; later legislated through the National Food Security Act, 2013 . Unni Krishnan (1993) and Article 21A ; Right to Education Act, 2009 . Public Interest Litigation (PIL): S.P. Gupta v Union of India (1981) (the Judges' Transfer case ) broadened locus standi , allowing any public-spirited person to move court on behalf of the poor; the 'epistolary jurisdiction' (letters treated as writ petitions) and social action litigation were developed by Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer . Upendra Baxi 's Taking Suffering Seriously: Social Action Litigation in the Supreme Court of India (1985) is the classic scholarly treatment. Criticism: judicial overreach, lack of expertise in policy, and the 'PIL that serves the middle class'. Legislation for the poor: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (free legal aid; Lok Adalats); Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005 (a legal guarantee of 100 days of wage employment per rural household); Right to Information Act, 2005 ; Forest Rights Act, 2006 ; National Food Security Act, 2013 ; Right to Fair Compensation... Act, 2013 ; Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976; Minimum Wages Act (now the Code on Wages, 2019). Economic reservations: Indra Sawhney v Union of India (1992) held that reservation cannot be based on economic criteria alone, while the 103rd Constitutional Amendment (2019) inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6) giving up to 10 per cent reservation for economically weaker sections (EWS) , upheld by a 3:2 majority in Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India (2022).

t: 8.7 Law, Intellectual Property and Access to Essential Goods
p: Law, Poverty and Development · Jurisprudence
x: TRIPS Agreement (1994) and the Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health (2001) affirmed the right of countries to protect public health and promote access to medicines for all (flexibilities such as compulsory licensing). Novartis AG v Union of India (2013): the Supreme Court refused a patent for the beta crystalline form of imatinib mesylate (Glivec) under Section 3(d) of the Patents Act, 1970, as the new form did not show increased therapeutic efficacy; seen as pro-access.

t: Memory Capsule: Law, Poverty and Development
p: Law, Poverty and Development · Jurisprudence
x: Sen: Poverty and Famines (1981, entitlement), Development as Freedom (1999; five freedoms), The Idea of Justice (2009; niti and nyaya). Nussbaum: ten central capabilities. De Soto: The Mystery of Capital , 'dead capital'; Albright and De Soto Commission (2008). Right to Development Declaration: 1986 (Resolution 41/128). SDGs: 2015, 17 goals. MDGs: 2000 to 2015, 8 goals. Trubek and Galanter (1974): crisis in law and development. Indian cases: Hussainara (1979), Asiad (1982), Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984), Olga Tellis (1985), PUCL right to food (2001), Janhit Abhiyan (2022). Trap: Sen does not provide a fixed list of capabilities; Nussbaum does.

p: Global Justice · Jurisprudence
x: Global justice asks whether principles of justice (fairness, equality, rights and distribution of burdens and benefits) apply only within states or also across borders to all persons. It deals with global poverty and inequality, human rights, war and humanitarian intervention, climate change, trade, migration, and international institutions. The debate is between cosmopolitans , who hold that the same moral principles apply to all human beings wherever they live, and statists, nationalists or communitarians , who hold that principles of distributive justice arise only among members of a political community. Position Core view Key thinkers Cosmopolitanism Persons are the ultimate units of moral concern; borders are morally arbitrary; duties of justice are global Kant (cosmopolitan right), Beitz, Pogge, Singer, Barry, Nussbaum, Sen (in part) Statism or nationalism Distributive justice depends on shared institutions or co-nationality; only humanitarian duties exist across borders Nagel, Miller, Blake, Rawls (in Law of Peoples , in a qualified way) Communitarianism Justice is relative to the shared understandings of particular communities Walzer, MacIntyre, Sandel Realism (in international relations) States pursue interests; moral universals have little place Morgenthau, Waltz

p: Global Justice · Jurisprudence
x: A Theory of Justice (1971) is the starting point of modern theories of justice. The original position and the veil of ignorance: free and equal persons choose principles of justice behind a veil of ignorance (they do not know their class, race, talents, conception of the good). This device ensures impartiality ('justice as fairness'). The two principles of justice (in lexical order): Equal basic liberties: each person has an equal right to the most extensive scheme of equal basic liberties compatible with a similar scheme for others. Social and economic inequalities must (a) be attached to offices and positions open to all under conditions of fair equality of opportunity , and (b) be to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle , a 'maximin' idea). Primary goods: rights, liberties, opportunities, income, wealth and the social bases of self-respect. Reflective equilibrium: a method of adjusting principles and considered judgments until they cohere. Rawls versus utilitarianism: he rejects the sacrifice of the few for the greater good of the many; 'each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice'. Political Liberalism (1993): the idea of an overlapping consensus among reasonable comprehensive doctrines and public reason . The Law of Peoples (1999): Rawls's account of international justice. He extends the social contract idea to a 'second original position' among peoples (not individuals). He sets out eight principles : (1) peoples are free and independent and their freedom is to be respected; (2) peoples observe treaties; (3) peoples are equal and parties to the agreements that bind them; (4) peoples observe a duty of non-intervention ; (5) peoples have the right of self-defence but no right to instigate war; (6) peoples are to honour human rights ; (7) peoples are to observe certain specified restrictions in the conduct of war ; (8) peoples have a duty to assist other peoples living under unfavourable conditions that prevent their having a just or decent political and social regime. Five types of societies in The Law of Peoples : reasonable liberal peoples, decent (hierarchical) peoples, outlaw states, societies burdened by unfavourable conditions, and benevolent absolutisms. Duty of assistance, not global difference principle: Rawls holds that wealthy societies owe a duty of assistance to burdened societies until these can sustain just or decent institutions, but he rejects a global difference principle because (he argues) the wealth of a nation depends mostly on its political culture and not on the resources alone. This is the point on which cosmopolitan critics attack him.

p: Global Justice · Jurisprudence
x: Immanuel Kant: Perpetual Peace (1795): three 'definitive articles': (1) the civil constitution of every state should be republican ; (2) the law of nations should be founded on a federation of free states ; (3) cosmopolitan right shall be limited to conditions of universal hospitality . Charles Beitz: Political Theory and International Relations (1979), the first major cosmopolitan critique of Rawls. He argued that the global distribution of natural resources is arbitrary from a moral point of view, and proposed an international difference principle and a resource redistribution principle . The global economy shows enough interdependence to apply justice at the global level. Thomas Pogge: Realizing Rawls (1989), World Poverty and Human Rights (2002). Argues that the wealthy nations and the global institutional order (trade rules, borrowing privileges, resource privileges) contribute to severe poverty and thus violate a negative duty not to harm (not merely a positive duty to assist). Proposes the Global Resource Dividend (GRD) (a small tax on the use of natural resources, the proceeds to help the global poor) and the Health Impact Fund (to reward drug companies for health impact rather than patent monopoly). Holds that poverty is a human rights deficit ; the global order is institutional and the harm is foreseeable and avoidable . Peter Singer: 'Famine, Affluence and Morality' (1972), One World (2002), The Life You Can Save (2009). A utilitarian argument that if we can prevent something bad from happening without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do so; the drowning child analogy (the moral irrelevance of distance). He is a leading figure in the effective altruism movement. Brian Barry: Humanity and Justice in Global Perspective (1982), Why Social Justice Matters (2005): global egalitarianism. Martha Nussbaum: Frontiers of Justice (2006): the capabilities approach extended to disability, nationality and species membership ; every person is entitled to a threshold of central capabilities, no matter where they live. Amartya Sen: The Idea of Justice (2009): avoids a single blueprint of 'perfectly just institutions' and defends comparative, plural and open public reasoning, with 'open impartiality' (inviting perspectives from beyond the borders of one's community) as the way to reduce remediable injustice in the world. Onora O'Neill: Bounds of Justice (2000), a Kantian cosmopolitan approach; Henry Shue: Basic Rights: Subsistence, Affluence and U.S. Foreign Policy (1980), arguing that security and subsistence are basic rights since the enjoyment of every other right depends on them, and creating correlative duties on everyone . Nancy Fraser: Scales of Justice (2008): the problem of misframing (who counts as a subject of justice); three dimensions: redistribution, recognition and representation . Iris Marion Young: Responsibility for Justice (2011): the social connection model of responsibility, in which people who contribute through their actions to structural injustice share responsibility for remedying it.

p: Global Justice · Jurisprudence
x: Thomas Nagel , 'The Problem of Global Justice' (2005): demands of distributive justice arise only among those who are jointly subject to a sovereign state , which imposes coercive laws in their name; across states there are only duties of humanity and minimal justice . He regards the world as lacking a global sovereign, so global justice is 'not yet' applicable . David Miller , National Responsibility and Global Justice (2007): defends nationality and special obligations to compatriots, but accepts that basic human rights must be respected everywhere (a 'sufficiency' threshold). Michael Walzer , Spheres of Justice (1983): different social goods are distributed by different principles, internal to the shared understandings of each community; Just and Unjust Wars (1977): the modern account of just war theory and the moral reality of war . Michael Blake : justice is triggered by coercion and the state's claim to authority. Alasdair MacIntyre, Michael Sandel : communitarian critics of Rawls's 'unencumbered self'.

p: Global Justice · Jurisprudence
x: (a) Global poverty and economic justice: trade rules (WTO), foreign debt (the HIPC initiative ), tax havens, aid and the UN target of 0.7 per cent of GNI for official development assistance ; TRIPS and access to medicines (see Topic 8 ). (b) Human rights and international criminal justice: Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948); ICCPR and ICESCR (1966; in force 1976). Nuremberg (1945 to 1946) and Tokyo Tribunals; ICTY (1993) and ICTR (1994); the Rome Statute (1998; in force 2002) establishing the International Criminal Court (ICC) . India is not a party to the Rome Statute. Universal jurisdiction: the Eichmann case (Israel, 1961); R v Bow Street Metropolitan Stipendiary Magistrate, ex parte Pinochet (No. 3) (1999, House of Lords): a former head of state has no immunity for torture. Transitional justice: truth commissions (South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission), reparations and amnesties. (c) Humanitarian intervention and the Responsibility to Protect (R2P): The ICISS Report (2001) 'The Responsibility to Protect', commissioned by Canada, introduced the idea that sovereignty implies responsibility . The 2005 World Summit Outcome Document (paragraphs 138 and 139) adopted R2P: each state has a responsibility to protect its population from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity , and the international community must act through the UN Security Council if the state manifestly fails. Applied (controversially) in Libya (Resolution 1973, 2011). Just war theory: jus ad bellum (just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, last resort, proportionality, reasonable prospect of success), jus in bello (discrimination, proportionality) and jus post bellum . Sources: Augustine, Aquinas, Grotius, Walzer. (d) Climate justice: Stockholm (1972); Rio (1992) and UNFCCC (1992); Kyoto Protocol (1997); Paris Agreement (2015) (temperature limit well below 2 degrees Celsius, pursuing 1.5 degrees; Nationally Determined Contributions). Principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC) (Rio Principle 7): developed countries, which have contributed most to historical emissions, must take the lead. India has consistently argued for this principle and for climate finance and technology transfer . Loss and damage: a fund agreed at COP27 (Sharm el-Sheikh, 2022) and operationalised at COP28 (Dubai, 2023) . Henry Shue drew the distinction between subsistence emissions and luxury emissions . Courts: the ICJ delivered an advisory opinion on states' obligations in respect of climate change (July 2025) (verify the details for the exam); the Indian Supreme Court in M.K. Ranjitsinh v Union of India (2024) recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change as part of Articles 14 and 21. (e) Migration, refugees and statelessness: 1951 Refugee Convention and 1967 Protocol : the principle of non-refoulement (a refugee must not be returned to a place of persecution). India is not a party , but follows the principle in parts through the Constitution and customary law. Joseph Carens , 'Aliens and Citizens: The Case for Open Borders' (1987): argued for open borders on liberal-egalitarian grounds. Walzer defended the right of communities to decide on membership. Indian cases: National Human Rights Commission v State of Arunachal Pradesh (1996) ( Chakma refugees ; Article 21 protects non-citizens too); Mohammad Salimullah v Union of India (2021) (the Rohingya deportation case). (f) Global health and access to medicines: the TRIPS flexibilities and the Doha Declaration (2001) ; WHO ; the debate over vaccine equity in the Covid-19 pandemic ( COVAX ; TRIPS waiver proposals). (g) Indian constitutional links: Article 51 (promotion of international peace and security, respect for international law and treaty obligations); Article 253 (legislation to implement international agreements); Vishaka (1997) and Apparel Export Promotion Council v A.K. Chopra (1999) (international conventions read into domestic law where there is no conflict); Jolly George Varghese v Bank of Cochin (1980) (the ICCPR and imprisonment for debt).

p: Global Justice · Jurisprudence
x: Rawls: A Theory of Justice (1971), Political Liberalism (1993), The Law of Peoples (1999): no global difference principle ; duty of assistance ; eight principles ; five types of societies . Beitz: global resource redistribution; Pogge: negative duty and GRD; Singer: drowning child; Nagel: statism; Miller: nationality; Walzer: spheres of justice and just war; Nussbaum: capabilities across borders; Sen: The Idea of Justice . R2P: 2001 ICISS; 2005 World Summit; Libya 2011. CBDR: Rio Principle 7. Paris Agreement: 2015. Trap: the original position of Law of Peoples is among peoples (representatives of peoples), not individuals; Pogge builds on harm , Singer on beneficence .

p: Modernism and Post-Modernism · Jurisprudence
x: Modernism refers to the intellectual outlook that emerged from the Enlightenment (seventeenth and eighteenth centuries). Its main assumptions: Reason and rationality as the route to truth and progress. Objective, universal knowledge ; the existence of facts independent of observers. Grand narratives (metanarratives) of progress, emancipation and totalising explanation (liberalism, Marxism, science). The autonomous, rational subject (the Cartesian and Kantian individual). Law as a rational, neutral, coherent and autonomous system that can be systematised, codified and applied objectively (Bentham's codification, Austin's science, Kelsen's pure theory, Hart's concept of law; legal formalism and liberal legalism). Max Weber described modernity as the rationalisation and 'disenchantment' of the world; modern law is formally rational . Modern jurisprudential schools (natural law, positivism, historical, sociological, realist, Marxist) share the assumption that there is a coherent theory of law capable of explaining or justifying law. Even the realists and Marxists criticised law in the name of a better reason or science .

p: Modernism and Post-Modernism · Jurisprudence
x: Postmodernism is not a school with a single doctrine but a cluster of critical attitudes towards modernity. Main features: Incredulity towards metanarratives (Lyotard): suspicion of any single theory (including of justice, progress or reason) claiming universal truth. Knowledge is constructed through language, discourse and power , not discovered neutrally. Truth is local, contingent and plural. Decentring of the subject: the 'individual' is shaped by discourse and social forces (the 'death of the author' in Barthes). Rejection of foundations: no ultimate foundation for knowledge or morality. Deconstruction of binary oppositions (reason/emotion, public/private, male/female, law/politics, rule/exception). Indeterminacy of meaning: texts, including law, have no single fixed meaning. Pluralism and difference : emphasis on marginal voices, local knowledge and small narratives ( petits recits ). Law as power, discourse and text , not a neutral instrument of reason.

p: Modernism and Post-Modernism · Jurisprudence
x: Jean-Francois Lyotard (1924 to 1998): The Postmodern Condition: A Report on Knowledge (1979): defines the postmodern as 'incredulity towards metanarratives' ; language games (borrowed from Wittgenstein); knowledge legitimated through performativity . The Differend (1983): a differend is a conflict between two parties that cannot be resolved because no rule of judgment is applicable to both; the wrong suffered by the one who has no language to express it (this has been applied in law to the position of victims, minorities and indigenous peoples). Michel Foucault (1926 to 1984): Works: Madness and Civilization (1961), The Birth of the Clinic (1963), The Order of Things (1966), The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969), Discipline and Punish (1975), The History of Sexuality , Vol. I (1976), Society Must Be Defended (lectures 1975 to 1976), and lectures on governmentality . Power/knowledge: power and knowledge are inseparable; knowledge produces power and vice versa; power is productive , not merely repressive; and it is dispersed through society (capillary power), not located only in the state or sovereign. Sovereign (juridical) power versus disciplinary power: pre-modern power was exercised as sovereign command and spectacle (public execution, as in the opening of Discipline and Punish ), while modern power works through discipline , surveillance, examination and normalisation (prisons, schools, hospitals, barracks). Law has increasingly become one of many mechanisms of normalisation , and the legal 'subject' is produced by these practices. The Panopticon: Bentham's design for a prison, with a central tower from which inmates may be observed without knowing whether they are being watched; Foucault uses it as the metaphor of modern disciplinary society (self-regulation through the possibility of being watched). Biopower and biopolitics: the management of populations (births, health, sexuality) by the state. Genealogy: the historical analysis of how present practices and 'truths' emerged from contingent power struggles. Foucault urged political theory to 'cut off the king's head', that is, to look at the micro-physics of power rather than only at sovereign commands. Jacques Derrida (1930 to 2004): Deconstruction: the reading of texts to reveal the hidden hierarchies, contradictions and instabilities in their binary oppositions; differance (difference and deferral of meaning); logocentrism (the privilege given to speech and presence); aporia (an impasse); undecidability . Works: Of Grammatology (1967), Writing and Difference (1967), Dissemination , 'Force of Law: The Mystical Foundation of Authority' (1990). In Force of Law he argues that law is deconstructible (because it is a historical, constructed and changeable system), but justice is not deconstructible (it is an infinite, unconditional demand that law can never fully satisfy). The 'mystical foundation of authority': the founding act of law is itself neither legal nor illegal, a performative act of violence without prior legal justification. Justice is always 'to come' ( a venir ); a decision is just only when it passes through the ordeal of the undecidable . Others: Jean Baudrillard: Simulacra and Simulation (1981): hyperreality , where signs and simulations replace reality. Richard Rorty: Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature (1979), Contingency, Irony and Solidarity (1989): pragmatic anti-foundationalism ; liberal ironism . Stanley Fish: Is There a Text in This Class? (1980): meaning is produced by interpretive communities ; applied to legal interpretation ( Doing What Comes Naturally ). Fredric Jameson: Postmodernism, or the Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism (1991); David Harvey: The Condition of Postmodernity (1989). Zygmunt Bauman: Legislators and Interpreters (1987) and Liquid Modernity (2000); Anthony Giddens: The Consequences of Modernity (1990) (late or reflexive modernity); Ulrich Beck: Risk Society (1986). Jurgen Habermas: a defender of modernity: 'Modernity: An Unfinished Project' (1980); The Philosophical Discourse of Modernity (1985); Between Facts and Norms (1992): discourse theory of law and democracy , in which law's legitimacy rests on communicative rationality and the idea that norms are valid only if all those affected could agree in rational discourse. He criticised Foucault and Derrida for abandoning reason. Postmodern legal theorists: Costas Douzinas and Ronnie Warrington ( Postmodern Jurisprudence , 1991; Douzinas, The End of Human Rights , 2000); Peter Fitzpatrick ( The Mythology of Modern Law , 1992); Drucilla Cornell ( The Philosophy of the Limit , 1992); Jack Balkin (deconstruction and law); Boaventura de Sousa Santos ( Toward a New Legal Common Sense ; the idea of interlegality and the cartographic view of law); Dragan Milovanovic.

t: 10.4 Modernism versus Post-Modernism in Law: A Comparison
p: Modernism and Post-Modernism · Jurisprudence
x: Aspect Modernist jurisprudence Post-modern jurisprudence View of knowledge Objective, universal, rational Constructed, contextual, plural Law Coherent, neutral system; rule-bound Indeterminate, a discourse linked to power Subject Autonomous rational individual Decentred, produced by discourse Theory Grand theory (natural law, positivism, Marxism) Suspicion of grand theory; small narratives Justice Achievable by right reasoning or institutions Always deferred or undecidable (Derrida); a differend (Lyotard) Method Analysis, system-building, science Deconstruction, genealogy, narrative Power Sovereign, centred in the state Dispersed, productive, disciplinary (Foucault) Representative thinkers Kant, Bentham, Austin, Kelsen, Hart, Rawls, Habermas Lyotard, Foucault, Derrida, Baudrillard, Rorty

p: Modernism and Post-Modernism · Jurisprudence
x: Origins: CLS emerged in the United States in the late 1970s (a conference at the University of Wisconsin in 1977 is regarded as its founding event) among left-leaning law teachers influenced by legal realism, Marxism, the Frankfurt School, structuralism and later post-structuralism . Core tenets: Law is politics: legal doctrine is not neutral and reflects power relations, especially those of class, race and gender. Indeterminacy thesis: legal rules and precedents do not compel a single result; judges can reach opposite conclusions from the same material, and the apparent determinacy is produced by ideology. Contradiction: liberal legal thought contains deep contradictions between individualism and altruism (Kennedy's 'fundamental contradiction' ), rules versus standards, and so on. Legitimation: law reproduces social hierarchy by making it appear natural and necessary ( reification ); Gramsci's hegemony is used. Critique of rights: rights are indeterminate, reinforce individual isolation and are used by the powerful (Mark Tushnet, Peter Gabel). Trashing: the critical exposure of the contradictions of legal doctrine (Mark Kelman). Key figures and works: Roberto Mangabeira Unger: Knowledge and Politics (1975), The Critical Legal Studies Movement (1983), False Necessity (1987); he rejects 'false necessity' and proposes 'empowered democracy' and 'deviationist doctrine' . Duncan Kennedy: 'Form and Substance in Private Law Adjudication' (1976), The Rise and Fall of Classical Legal Thought , Legal Education and the Reproduction of Hierarchy (1983), A Critique of Adjudication (1997). Morton Horwitz: The Transformation of American Law, 1780 to 1860 (1977). Mark Tushnet, Karl Klare, Peter Gabel, Mark Kelman, Alan Hunt, Joseph Singer, Gerald Frug. Criticism: CLS offers a critique but no constructive programme; Owen Fiss ('The Death of Law?', 1986) and Paul Carrington ('Of Law and the River', 1984, who suggested that CLS scholars should resign); the indeterminacy thesis is exaggerated; and rights discourse has also served the oppressed (the response of critical race scholars).

p: Modernism and Post-Modernism · Jurisprudence
x: Liberal feminism: equal rights, equal opportunities, formal equality (Mary Wollstonecraft: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman , 1792; John Stuart Mill: The Subjection of Women , 1869; Betty Friedan; Ruth Bader Ginsburg's litigation). Cultural (difference) feminism: women have a distinct moral voice. Carol Gilligan , In a Different Voice (1982): the ethic of care versus the male-associated ethic of justice ; Robin West , 'Jurisprudence and Gender' (1988): the connection thesis (women are materially connected to others through pregnancy and nursing) versus the 'separation thesis' that underlies liberal legalism and male jurisprudence. Radical (dominance) feminism: Catharine MacKinnon , Sexual Harassment of Working Women (1979), Feminism Unmodified (1987), Toward a Feminist Theory of the State (1989): gender is a hierarchy of power and dominance , not merely difference; law is male because it is objective in the way that male power is objective; sexual harassment as sex discrimination; the campaign (with Andrea Dworkin ) for civil rights anti-pornography ordinances. Post-modern feminism: Judith Butler , Gender Trouble (1990): gender is performative (constituted by repeated acts), not a natural fact; Carol Smart , Feminism and the Power of Law (1989): law is a gendering strategy , and feminists should be careful about turning to law as the answer; Drucilla Cornell . Intersectionality: Kimberle Crenshaw , 'Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex' (1989): discrimination based on overlapping identities (race, sex, class) cannot be understood by looking at each category separately. Simone de Beauvoir , The Second Sex (1949): 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' Indian feminist legal landmarks: Mary Roy v State of Kerala (1986) (equal inheritance rights of Syrian Christian women under the Indian Succession Act); Mohd. Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum (1985) (maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 CrPC), followed by the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 , and Danial Latifi v Union of India (2001); Vishaka v State of Rajasthan (1997) and the POSH Act, 2013 ; Anuj Garg v Hotel Association of India (2008) (protective discrimination based on stereotypes is invalid); Shayara Bano (2017); Joseph Shine (2018); Independent Thought v Union of India (2017) (sexual intercourse with a wife under 18 is rape); Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma (2020) (daughters are coparceners by birth under the amended Hindu Succession Act, 2005); Sabarimala (2018). The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023 (the 106th Constitutional Amendment) provides one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies, to take effect after the next census and delimitation.

t: 10.7 Critical Race Theory, Queer Theory, Post-Colonial and TWAIL Approaches
p: Modernism and Post-Modernism · Jurisprudence
x: Critical race theory (CRT): Derrick Bell ( Faces at the Bottom of the Well , 1992; the interest-convergence thesis : progress for black Americans occurs only when it converges with white interests, as in Brown v Board of Education , 1954), Kimberle Crenshaw, Richard Delgado, Mari Matsuda, Patricia Williams ( The Alchemy of Race and Rights , 1991), Cheryl Harris ('Whiteness as Property', 1993). Methods: storytelling and counter-storytelling ; race as a social construct; critique of colour-blindness. Queer theory: Judith Butler , Michel Foucault , Eve Sedgwick ( Epistemology of the Closet , 1990): identity categories are social constructs; heteronormativity. Post-colonial theory: Edward Said , Orientalism (1978); Gayatri Spivak , 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988); Homi Bhabha ; the Subaltern Studies collective (Ranajit Guha). In law: Upendra Baxi , Ratna Kapur , and TWAIL scholars (B.S. Chimni, Antony Anghie) who show how international law carries colonial structures. Legal pluralism: the coexistence of more than one legal order in the same social field. Eugen Ehrlich (living law); John Griffiths , 'What is Legal Pluralism?' (1986) distinguishes strong (genuine, social) from weak (state-recognised) pluralism; Boaventura de Sousa Santos and Sally Engle Merry ( global and local law ); Gunther Teubner ('Global Bukowina', 1997). Niklas Luhmann and Teubner developed autopoiesis (law as a self-referential social system) as a late-modern account of law.

p: Modernism and Post-Modernism · Jurisprudence
x: Relativism and nihilism: it offers no basis to say that any legal arrangement is better than another. Performative contradiction (self-refutation): the claim that there are no universal truths seems itself a universal claim (Habermas). Political paralysis: rejection of metanarratives undermines the grounds for emancipatory politics, human rights and the rule of law. Obscurity of language and lack of empirical testing. Defenders reply that postmodernism does not abandon justice (Derrida), but demands more responsibility and attention to those whom 'universal' systems exclude (Lyotard's differend).

p: Modernism and Post-Modernism · Jurisprudence
x: Lyotard: The Postmodern Condition (1979): 'incredulity towards metanarratives'; differend ; language games . Foucault: power/knowledge; Discipline and Punish (1975); panopticon; biopower; genealogy. Derrida: deconstruction; differance ; Force of Law (1990): law deconstructible, justice not. Habermas: modernity an unfinished project; discourse theory; Between Facts and Norms (1992). CLS: Unger, Kennedy, Horwitz, Tushnet; indeterminacy thesis; 'law is politics'. Feminism: Gilligan ( In a Different Voice ), MacKinnon (dominance), Butler (performativity), Crenshaw (intersectionality), West (connection thesis). Trap: Bentham designed the panopticon; Foucault theorised it. Habermas defends modernity; Lyotard attacks metanarratives. Derrida says justice is undeconstructible , not law .

t: 11.3 Ten Exam-Day Strategies for Jurisprudence MCQs
p: Final Revision: Thinkers, Cases and Exam-Day Strategies · Jurisprudence
x: Do the match-the-list questions by elimination: pin down the two items you are sure of; the rest usually follow. Read 'NOT' and 'INCORRECT' twice ; the examiner often uses a minor swap (for example Bentham for Austin, Stammler for Kohler). For statement questions , look for absolute words ('always', 'only', 'never'); they usually signal a false statement. Remember who attacks whom: Hart attacks Austin; Dworkin attacks Hart; Fuller attacks Hart; Devlin versus Hart; Rawls versus utilitarians; Pogge and Beitz versus Rawls (on the global level); Habermas versus the postmodernists; Carrington and Fiss versus CLS. Years matter: Ancient Law 1861; Province 1832; Concept of Law 1961; Theory of Justice 1971; Law's Empire 1986; Development as Freedom 1999; Idea of Justice 2009; Declaration on the Right to Development 1986; SDGs 2015. Indian cases are favoured in applied questions: know the one-line holding of each landmark case, including whether it was later overruled or stayed. Distinguish similar concepts: ownership versus possession; right versus privilege (Hohfeld); fiction versus concession versus realist theory; strict versus absolute liability; legal versus moral duty. Use the schools' 'five questions' (nature, source of authority, law and morality, law and society, who finds the law) to place any unfamiliar proposition. Where news is involved (rivers, animals, EWS, privacy, climate), recall the court, year and outcome and any subsequent stay or reversal. Never leave a question blank , since there is no negative marking.

t: 0.1 BNS at a glance: high-yield numbers
p: Scope, Law Used and Exam Pattern · Law of Crimes
x: 358 sections in 20 Chapters; the IPC had 511 sections in 23 Chapters. Chapter I = preliminary and definitions (s.1-3; s.2 is the definitions section); Chapter II = punishments (s.4-13); Chapter III = general exceptions (s.14-44); Chapter IV = abetment, criminal conspiracy and attempt (s.45-62); Chapter V = offences against women and children (s.63-99); Chapter VI = offences affecting the human body (s.100-146); Chapter VII = offences against the State (s.147-158); Chapter VIII = offences relating to the Army, Navy and Air Force (s.159-168); Chapter IX = offences relating to elections (s.169-177); Chapter X = coin, bank notes, currency notes and Government stamps (s.178-188); Chapter XI = offences against public tranquillity (s.189-197); Chapter XVII = offences against property (s.303-334). New offences added: organised crime (s.111) , petty organised crime (s.112) , terrorist act (s.113) , mob lynching (s.103(2)) , snatching (s.304) , hit and run (s.106(2)) , sexual intercourse by deceitful means or false promise of marriage (s.69) , and acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India (s.152) . Removed or dropped: sedition (IPC 124A) (replaced in substance by s.152), adultery (IPC 497) (already struck down in Joseph Shine v. Union of India , 2018), unnatural offences (IPC 377) (consensual part read down in Navtej Singh Johar , 2018; BNS has no equivalent), and attempt to commit suicide (IPC 309) (replaced by a narrow s.226, attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain a public servant, punished with community service). Community service is a new punishment (s.4(f)), provided for small offences such as petty theft, defamation, attempted suicide to coerce a public servant and public intoxication. Rape (s.63) is still a male-offender, female-victim offence; the age of consent stays at 18 years.
