Motorola (2011); Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd (2006) (a civil dispute should not be dressed as a criminal case); Ram Jas v. State of U.P. (1970).

p: Offences Against Property · Law of Crimes
x: Mischief : intention or knowledge of likely to cause wrongful loss or damage to the public or any person, causing the destruction of any property or any such change in it that its value or utility is destroyed or diminished . Wrongful loss or gain need not be dishonest ; the ownership of the property is irrelevant (even the owner can commit mischief against a co-owner). Aggravated mischief : by fire or explosive (IPC 435-436), mischief to dwelling or a vessel , mischief by injury to public road, bridge , or inundation . Punishments rise from six months (simple) to ten years or life in the gravest forms.

p: Offences Against Property · Law of Crimes
x: Criminal trespass (s.329(1); IPC s.441) : entering into or upon property in possession of another with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy the person in possession, or remaining unlawfully with that intent. House-trespass (IPC 442): criminal trespass by entering into a building, tent or vessel used as a human dwelling , or as a place of worship or custody of property. Lurking house-trespass (IPC 443): taking precautions to conceal; house-breaking (s.331; IPC 445): six ways (e.g., through an opening made by the trespasser; by removal of a fastening). Lurking house-trespass or house-breaking by night (IPC 456-457) is punished more severely; by night means sunset to sunrise . Specific offences : house-trespass to commit an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment (s.332; IPC 449-451); house-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint (s.333; IPC 452); dishonestly breaking open a receptacle containing property (s.334; IPC 461). Illustration: entering another's house with intent to commit theft is house-trespass.

p: Offences Against Property · Law of Crimes
x: Making a false document (s.335; IPC s.464) : dishonestly or fraudulently making, signing, sealing or executing a document or electronic record, or part of it, with the intention of causing it to be believed that it was made by the authority of a person who did not make it, or by altering the document without lawful authority , or by causing a person of unsound mind or intoxicated to sign it. Forgery (s.336; IPC s.463) : making a false document or false electronic record with intent to cause damage or injury to the public or any person, or to support any claim or title, or to cause any person to part with property, or to enter into any express or implied contract, or with intent to commit fraud . Punishment : up to two years or fine or both (basic); forgery of a valuable security or will , for the purpose of cheating and record of a court attract higher punishments (up to seven years to life in some forms). Case : Mohammed Ibrahim v. State of Bihar (2009) (making a false document means making with the intention of forgery ; mere false statement in a sale deed is not forgery).

p: Offences Against Property · Law of Crimes
x: BNS Chapter XVII (ss.303-334) covers theft, snatching, extortion, robbery, dacoity, criminal misappropriation, criminal breach of trust, receiving stolen property, cheating, fraudulent deeds, mischief and criminal trespass. Chapter XVIII (ss.335-350) covers forgery and property marks. UGC NET repeatedly tests the distinctions among theft, extortion, robbery, dacoity, misappropriation, criminal breach of trust and cheating.

p: Offences Against Property · Law of Crimes
x: Theft : s.303; dishonest intention; movable; moving . Snatching : s.304; community service for small first-time theft. Extortion = delivery under fear ; Robbery = theft or extortion + instant fear ; Dacoity = five or more . Misappropriation = innocent possession, then dishonesty; CBT = entrustment first . Cheating needs dishonest intention from the start ; breach of contract alone is not cheating. Cases : Pyare Lal Bhargava (temporary taking = theft), K.N. Mehra , R.S. Nayak (extortion), Velji Raghavji Patel (partner), Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma (cheating vs breach), Mohammed Ibrahim (forgery). Punishment hooks : CBT by public servant/banker = life or ten years ; dacoity = life or ten years ; dacoity with murder = death/life/10+ years .

p: Offences Against Women and Children · Law of Crimes
x: A. Definition (s.63; IPC s.375) A man commits rape if he (a) penetrates his penis, to any extent, into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a woman or makes her do so with him or another person; (b) inserts, to any extent, any object or a part of the body, not being the penis , into the vagina, urethra or anus; (c) manipulates any part of the body of a woman so as to cause penetration; or (d) applies his mouth to the vagina, anus or urethra of a woman or makes her do so with him or another person, under any of seven descriptions : Against her will . Without her consent . With her consent obtained by putting her, or any person in whom she is interested, in fear of death or hurt . With her consent, when the man knows he is not her husband and her consent is given because she believes he is another man to whom she is or believes herself to be lawfully married. With her consent, when at the time of giving consent, by reason of unsoundness of mind or intoxication or the administration by him personally or through another of any stupefying or unwholesome substance , she is unable to understand the nature and consequences of that to which she gives consent. With or without her consent, when she is under eighteen years of age. When she is unable to communicate consent . Explanation 2 (consent) : unequivocal voluntary agreement by words, gestures or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication; mere lack of physical resistance is not consent. Exception 1 : a medical procedure or intervention is not rape. Exception 2 : sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his own wife , the wife not being under eighteen years of age, is not rape (the marital rape exception remains). Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017) read down the IPC exception to raise the age from 15 to 18 . A challenge to the exception itself ( RIT Foundation v. Union of India ) produced a split verdict in the Delhi High Court (2022) and is pending before the Supreme Court. B. Punishments (ss.64-71) BNS IPC Offence Punishment 64(1) 376(1) Rape Rigorous imprisonment not less than 10 years , may extend to life , and fine 64(2) 376(2) Aggravated rape (police officer, public servant, armed forces, jail or remand home or hospital staff, relative/guardian/teacher, during communal violence, pregnant woman , woman unable to give consent, person in a position of control, disabled woman , grievous hurt or maiming, repeated rape of the same woman ) Not less than 10 years , may extend to life (remainder of natural life) and fine 65(1) 376(3) Rape of a woman under 16 Not less than 20 years , may extend to life (natural life) and fine 65(2) 376AB Rape of a woman under 12 Not less than 20 years , life (natural life), or death 66 376A Rape causing death or a persistent vegetative state Not less than 20 years , life (natural life) or death 67 376B Sexual intercourse by husband upon wife during separation Two to seven years and fine 68 376C Sexual intercourse by a person in authority Five to ten years and fine 69 ( new ) none Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means (false promise of employment or promotion, inducement, marrying after suppressing identity ) Up to ten years and fine; this is not rape 70(1) 376D Gang rape Not less than 20 years , life (natural life) and fine 70(2) 376DA, 376DB Gang rape of a woman under 18 Life (natural life) or death 71 376E Repeat offenders Life (natural life) or death 72 228A Disclosure of identity of a rape victim Up to two years and fine 73 228A(2) Printing or publishing court proceedings without court permission Up to two years and fine Case law : Tukaram v. State of Maharashtra ( Mathura rape case , 1979) (acquittal on the ground of submission; led to the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1983 , which created custodial rape and the presumption of absence of consent , now in BSA s.120; Evidence Act s.114A); Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v. State of Gujarat (1983) (testimony of the victim needs no corroboration, as long as it is credible); State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh (1996) (sensitive approach to rape trials, in-camera trial); Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997); Lillu @ Rajesh v. State of Haryana (2013) (the two-finger test violates the right to privacy and dignity); State of Maharashtra v. Madhukar Narayan Mardikar (1991) (the character of a woman is irrelevant; even a woman of easy virtue is entitled to protection); Mukesh v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2017) ( Nirbhaya ); Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v. State of Maharashtra (2019) ( false promise of marriage versus breach of promise: consent given under a misconception of fact must be assessed; a promise that was false from the beginning vitiates consent); Uday v. State of Karnataka (2003); Deepak Gulati v. State of Haryana (2013). Legislative history : the Justice J.S. Verma Committee (2013) and the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013 (post- Nirbhaya ) added acid attack, stalking, voyeurism, sexual harassment, disrobing and trafficking; the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2018 (after the Kathua and Unnao cases) raised minimum punishment and introduced the death penalty for rape of girls under 12 .

t: 7.2 Sexual harassment and other offences against women (ss.74-79; IPC 354-354D, 509)
p: Offences Against Women and Children · Law of Crimes
x: BNS IPC Offence Punishment 74 354 Assault or criminal force to a woman with intent to outrage her modesty One to five years and fine 75 354A Sexual harassment : unwelcome physical contact and advances; demand or request for sexual favours; showing pornography against her will; sexually coloured remarks First three kinds: up to three years or fine or both; sexually coloured remarks: up to one year or fine or both 76 354B Assault or criminal force to a woman with intent to disrobe Three to seven years and fine 77 354C Voyeurism (watching or capturing the image of a woman engaging in a private act) First: one to three years ; repeat: three to seven years 78 354D Stalking (following, contacting despite clear disinterest, monitoring online) First: up to three years ; repeat: up to five years 79 509 Word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman Up to three years and fine Cases : Rupan Deol Bajaj v. K.P.S. Gill (1995) (outraging modesty; test of a reasonable person and the reaction of the woman); Raju Pandurang Mahale v. State of Maharashtra (2004) (modesty is an attribute associated with female sex); Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) and Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India (2013) ( Vishaka Guidelines for workplace sexual harassment, later enacted as the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH) ; Internal Committee needed at workplaces with ten or more employees; local committee at district level); Aureliano Fernandes v. State of Goa (2023) (the Court criticised delays in implementing the POSH Act).

p: Offences Against Women and Children · Law of Crimes
x: Cruelty by husband or relatives (s.85; IPC s.498A): husband or relative subjects a woman to cruelty : up to three years and fine. Cruelty (s.86) = (a) wilful conduct likely to drive the woman to suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (mental or physical); (b) harassment with a view to coercing her or any related person to meet an unlawful demand for property or valuable security . It is cognizable and non-bailable under the CrPC/BNSS schedule, and non-compoundable (in ordinary cases). Cases : Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) (no automatic arrest ; police must record reasons under the notice-of-appearance procedure); Sushil Kumar Sharma v. Union of India (2005) (upheld the constitutionality; the Court said misuse cannot invalidate the law); Rajesh Sharma v. State of U.P. (2017) ( Family Welfare Committees ; later modified in Social Action Forum for Manav Adhikar v. Union of India , 2018); Preeti Gupta v. State of Jharkhand (2010) (cautioned against exaggerated allegations against distant relatives); Kahkashan Kausar v. State of Bihar (2022) (omnibus allegations against in-laws should be examined carefully); in Dara Lakshmi Narayana v. State of Telangana (2024), the Supreme Court again warned of the misuse of s.498A and s.85 BNS. Dowry death (s.80; IPC 304B): see topic 4 . Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 : giving, taking or abetting dowry: five years and fine not less than ₹15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is more; demanding dowry: six months to two years. Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (civil remedies: protection, residence, monetary relief, custody); Hiral P. Harsora v. Kusum Narottamdas Harsora (2016) (the words "adult male" struck down so that women can also be respondents ); D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal (2010) (live-in relationship in the nature of marriage).

p: Offences Against Women and Children · Law of Crimes
x: Cohabitation by a man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage (s.81; IPC 493): up to ten years . Bigamy (s.82; IPC 494, 495): marrying again during the lifetime of the spouse: up to seven years and fine; concealing the former marriage: up to ten years . Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage (s.83; IPC 496): up to seven years . Enticing a married woman (s.84; IPC 498): up to two years . Exceptions to bigamy : the first marriage has been declared void by a court; the spouse has been continuously absent for seven years and not known to be alive. Cases : Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) (conversion to Islam only to contract a second marriage does not end the first marriage; bigamy is punishable); Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2000) (same). Adultery (IPC 497) was struck down by Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) and is absent from the BNS.

p: Offences Against Women and Children · Law of Crimes
x: Causing miscarriage (s.88; IPC 312): up to three years ; if the woman is quick with child : up to seven years . Without the woman's consent (s.89; IPC 313): life or up to ten years. Death caused by an act done with intent to cause miscarriage (s.90). Act done to prevent the child being born alive (s.91). Causing death of a quick unborn child by an act amounting to culpable homicide (s.92). Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 (amended 2021): termination allowed up to 20 weeks on the opinion of one registered medical practitioner and up to 24 weeks for special categories (survivors of rape or incest, minors, change of marital status during pregnancy, physically disabled women, mentally ill women, foetal malformation, emergency) on the opinion of two practitioners; no upper limit where a Medical Board diagnoses substantial foetal abnormalities . Cases : Suchita Srivastava v. Chandigarh Administration (2009) (reproductive choice is part of personal liberty ); X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department, Govt. of NCT of Delhi (2022) (the Court held that unmarried women are also entitled to 24-week abortion and that marital rape is relevant for the purposes of the MTP Act); K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) (right to privacy includes reproductive choices). Exposure and abandonment of a child under twelve by parent or person in charge (s.93; IPC 317): up to seven years . Concealment of birth by secret disposal of a dead body (s.94; IPC 318): up to two years .

t: 7.6 Offences against children in the BNS (ss.95-99; also s.139)
p: Offences Against Women and Children · Law of Crimes
x: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence (s.95; new ): three to ten years and fine. Procuration of a child (s.96; IPC 366A): up to ten years . Selling a minor for prostitution (s.98; IPC 372): five to fourteen years . Buying a minor for prostitution (s.99; IPC 373): seven to fourteen years . Kidnapping or maiming a child for begging (s.139; IPC 363A). Gang rape of a woman under 18 (s.70(2)): life (natural life) or death .

t: 7.7 POCSO Act, 2012 (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences)
p: Offences Against Women and Children · Law of Crimes
x: Child = any person below 18 (gender-neutral). Consent of a child is immaterial . Offences: penetrative sexual assault (ss.3-4: ten years to life ; under 16 : twenty years to life ); aggravated penetrative sexual assault (ss.5-6: twenty years to life or death , after the 2019 amendment ); sexual assault (ss.7-8: three to five years); aggravated sexual assault (ss.9-10: five to seven years); sexual harassment of a child (ss.11-12: up to three years); use of child for pornography (ss.13-14); storage of child pornography (s.15). Procedure : mandatory reporting (s.19; failure punishable under s.21), Special Courts (s.28), presumption of guilt (s.29, rebuttable), child-friendly procedure , in-camera trial , identity protection (s.23). Recent cases : Attorney General for India v. Satish Ekanathrao Ghoge (2021) (the " skin-to-skin " contact requirement of the Bombay High Court was set aside; sexual intent , not skin contact, is the test); Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish (2024) ( storing or viewing child pornography is an offence under POCSO s.15 and IT Act s.67B; the term "child pornography" should be replaced by child sexual exploitative and abuse material (CSEAM) ); Independent Thought (2017); Sakshi v. Union of India (2004) (rules for child witness trials). Child marriage : Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 (marriage of girls under 18 and boys under 21 is voidable at the option of the child; offenders face two years' rigorous imprisonment and fine up to ₹1 lakh ); Society for Enlightenment and Voluntary Action v. Union of India (2024) (guidelines for effective enforcement; personal laws cannot override the Act). Other laws : Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 ; Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986 ; Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 ; Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (amended 2016: prohibits employment of children under 14 in all occupations and adolescents in hazardous work).

t: Overview: Offences Against Women and Children
p: Offences Against Women and Children · Law of Crimes
x: Chapter V of the BNS (ss.63-99) gathers offences against women and children: rape and related sexual offences (ss.63-73) , sexual harassment and related offences (ss.74-79) , dowry death and cruelty (ss.80, 85-86) , marriage-related offences (ss.81-84) , miscarriage (ss.88-92) and offences against children (ss.93-99) . This is the most current-affairs-heavy topic: look for recent Supreme Court judgments and BNS changes.

t: Memory Capsule: Offences Against Women and Children
p: Offences Against Women and Children · Law of Crimes
x: Rape : seven descriptions; age of consent 18 ; marital exception only for wife 18 or above . Punishment ladder : rape 10 years to life; under 16 : 20 years to life; under 12 : 20 years to life or death; gang rape : 20 years to life; gang rape of a minor under 18 : life or death. s.69 BNS (deceitful means) is new and is not rape . Cases : Tukaram (Mathura) -> 1983 amendment; Vishaka -> POSH; Lillu (two-finger test); Pramod Pawar (false promise of marriage); Independent Thought (marital rape of minors); Arnesh Kumar (498A arrest); Joseph Shine (adultery); Satish Ghoge (skin-to-skin); Just Rights for Children Alliance (child pornography, 2024). POCSO : child = under 18; special courts ; reporting mandatory .

p: Drug Trafficking and Counterfeiting · Law of Crimes
x: Constitutional and treaty background : Article 47 (Directive Principle to prohibit intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health); India is a party to the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961 , the Convention on Psychotropic Substances, 1971 and the UN Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, 1988 . The Act replaced the Opium Act 1857, Opium Act 1878 and Dangerous Drugs Act 1930 . Definitions (s.2) : narcotic drug (coca leaf, cannabis (hemp), opium, poppy straw and all manufactured drugs); psychotropic substance (substances in the Schedule); cannabis ( charas , ganja (flowering or fruiting tops, excluding seeds and leaves when not accompanied by the tops) and any mixture); bhang (leaves and seeds) is excluded from the definition of cannabis in the Act and is regulated by State laws . Small quantity , commercial quantity and the in-between intermediate quantity are fixed by Central Government notification (2001 rationalisation). Key sections : s.8 : prohibition of cultivation, production, manufacture, possession, sale, purchase, transport, warehousing, use, consumption, inter-State import or export, import into or export from India of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances except for medical or scientific purposes and in accordance with the Act (licence or permit). ss.15-23 : specific offences (poppy straw s.15; coca s.16; prepared opium s.17; opium poppy and opium s.18; cannabis s.20; manufactured drugs and preparations s.21 ; psychotropic substances s.22 ; illegal import, export and transhipment s.23). s.24 : external dealings; s.25 : allowing premises to be used; s.27 : consumption ; s.27A : financing illicit traffic and harbouring offenders ( ten to twenty years , fine ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh); s.29 : abetment and criminal conspiracy ; s.30 : preparation; s.31 : enhanced punishment for subsequent offences; s.31A : death penalty for certain repeat offences; s.32A : no suspension, remission or commutation of sentence. s.35 : presumption of culpable mental state ; s.54 : presumption from possession of illicit articles; s.37 : offences are cognizable and non-bailable , with twin conditions for bail in cases involving commercial quantity; s.64A : immunity for addicts who volunteer for treatment. ss.41-43 : powers of search, seizure and arrest ; s.42 : entry, search, seizure and arrest without warrant (with recording of grounds and reporting to the superior within 72 hours ); s.50 : conditions for personal search (the person must be told of the right to be searched before a Gazetted Officer or Magistrate ); s.52A : disposal of seized drugs (inventory, sampling, magistrate certification); s.67 : power to call for information and examine persons; s.50A : controlled delivery . Authorities : Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) , Central Bureau of Narcotics , State Police, Customs, Revenue Intelligence (DRI). Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988 (PIT-NDPS) provides preventive detention of traffickers.

p: Drug Trafficking and Counterfeiting · Law of Crimes
x: Quantity Punishment (ss.15-24 type offences) Small quantity Rigorous imprisonment up to one year , or fine up to ₹10,000 , or both (for trafficking offences; consumption under s.27 is up to six months for non-cocaine type drugs , up to one year for specified hard drugs, with the fine of ₹10,000 or ₹20,000) More than small but less than commercial (intermediate) Rigorous imprisonment up to ten years and fine up to ₹1 lakh Commercial quantity Rigorous imprisonment of ten to twenty years and fine of ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh (the court may impose a higher fine for reasons recorded) Repeat offenders (s.31) One and a half times the punishment for the first offence s.31A Death for repeat offences involving specified very large quantities (made discretionary by the 2014 amendment after Indian Harm Reduction Network v. Union of India (Bombay High Court, 2011) read it down) (Old quantity limits were revised in 2001; the Act treats small and commercial quantities separately for each drug.) Illustrative quantities (from the 2001 notification; confirm in the schedule): heroin small 5 g / commercial 250 g; charas 100 g / 1 kg; ganja 1 kg / 20 kg; cocaine 2 g / 100 g; opium 25 g / 2.5 kg; morphine 5 g / 250 g; MDMA 0.5 g / 10 g; LSD 0.002 g / 0.1 g.

t: 8.3 Bail, presumptions and search procedure (the heart of NDPS case law)
p: Drug Trafficking and Counterfeiting · Law of Crimes
x: Twin conditions for bail (s.37) : for offences involving commercial quantity (and ss.19, 24, 27A), the accused shall not be released on bail unless (i) the Public Prosecutor has had an opportunity to oppose; and (ii) the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of the offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail . These conditions override the ordinary bail provisions. Presumption of culpable mental state (s.35) : the court presumes knowledge and intention and the accused must prove absence of such mental state beyond reasonable doubt (a reverse onus provision). s.54 : presumption from possession of illicit articles; Noor Aga v. State of Punjab (2008) upheld the validity of ss.35 and 54 but held that the prosecution must first establish the foundational facts beyond reasonable doubt before the presumption applies. Search and seizure compliance : State of Punjab v. Balbir Singh (1994): compliance with ss.42 and 50 is mandatory ; non-compliance can vitiate the conviction. State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh (1999) (Constitution Bench): s.50 is mandatory ; the accused must be informed of his right to be searched before a Gazetted Officer or Magistrate . Vijaysinh Chandubha Jadeja v. State of Gujarat (2011) (Constitution Bench): the informing of the right under s.50 is mandatory and should be substantial (proper compliance), with an oral explanation being enough. Union of India v. Mohanlal (2016) and Mohanlal v. State of Punjab (2018): importance of s.52A ; sampling must be done before a Magistrate ; non-compliance and delay can undermine the prosecution. Admissibility of statements : Tofan Singh v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020/2021): officers vested with powers of investigation under the NDPS Act (such as NCB officers ) are police officers within s.25 of the Evidence Act, so a confessional statement recorded under s.67 is inadmissible as evidence of guilt. (The same principle now falls under the BSA corresponding provisions.) Other constitutional rulings : Dadu @ Tulsidas v. State of Maharashtra (2000) struck down the bar on suspension of sentence in s.32A as unconstitutional; Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983) invalidated mandatory death under IPC s.303 and is cited for the policy against mandatory death sentences; the Supreme Court has repeatedly stressed proportionality in bail for small-quantity or addict cases. Treatment and rehabilitation : s.64A and the National Policy on Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances ; de-addiction under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 approach; the Narcotics policy balances harm reduction and deterrence. Interface with the BNS : organised crime (s.111) expressly includes trafficking in drugs, weapons or illicit goods by a syndicate, so a trafficking ring can be proceeded against under both the NDPS Act and BNS s.111.

t: 8.4 Counterfeiting: coin, currency notes and Government stamps
p: Drug Trafficking and Counterfeiting · Law of Crimes
x: The offences sit in BNS Chapter X (ss.178-188) , replacing IPC ss.230-263A (coin and stamps) and IPC ss.489A-489E (currency notes and bank notes). Offence IPC Punishment (IPC; BNS mirrors it) Counterfeiting Indian coin 232 Life or up to ten years and fine Counterfeiting other coin 231 Up to seven years and fine Making, buying or selling instruments for counterfeiting coin 233-234 Up to three years (Indian coin: up to ten years ) Possession of counterfeit coin, delivery of counterfeit coin 239-243 Varies (up to seven years) Counterfeiting currency notes or bank notes 489A Life or up to ten years and fine Using as genuine forged or counterfeit currency notes or bank notes 489B Life or up to ten years and fine Possession of forged or counterfeit notes knowing or having reason to believe them to be forged 489C Up to seven years , or fine, or both Making or possessing instruments or materials for forging or counterfeiting notes 489D Life or up to ten years and fine Making or using documents resembling currency notes 489E Fine up to ₹100 Counterfeiting Government stamps , using or possessing 255-263A Life or up to ten years in the gravest forms Key ingredients : the offender must know or have reason to believe that the note is counterfeit (for possession); the counterfeit must be capable of being passed as genuine (resemblance), but perfect imitation is not required . Case : Umashankar v. State of Chhattisgarh (2001): mere possession of forged notes without knowledge or reason to believe that they are counterfeit is not an offence under s.489C; mens rea must be established. R emember the mens rea rule . Terrorism link : the UAPA (s.15(1)(a)(iiia)) and BNS s.113 treat production, smuggling or circulation of high-quality counterfeit Indian currency that damages the monetary stability of India as a terrorist act . NIA investigates FICN (fake Indian currency notes) as a scheduled offence. Related laws : Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, s.31 (only the RBI may issue bank notes and currency notes); Coinage Act, 2011 ; Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (proceeds of NDPS and counterfeiting offences are scheduled offences ); Indian Stamp Act, 1899 .

p: Drug Trafficking and Counterfeiting · Law of Crimes
x: Trade Marks Act, 1999 : falsifying and falsely applying trade marks (s.103: imprisonment of six months to three years and fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh ), selling goods bearing a false trade mark (s.104), enhanced penalty for repeat offences (s.105); Copyright Act, 1957 : infringement as an offence (s.63: six months to three years and fine ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh ), possession of infringing copies (s.63B); Designs Act, 2000 ; Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999 . Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 : spurious and adulterated drugs (s.17B, s.13; punishment from three years to life ); Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 : unsafe food . BNS cheating by personation, forgery and making false trademarks and property marks (BNS ss.345-350; IPC 478-489) also address counterfeit goods.

p: Drug Trafficking and Counterfeiting · Law of Crimes
x: This topic has two parts : (1) drug trafficking under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS Act) ; (2) counterfeiting of coin, currency notes and Government stamps (BNS Chapter X, IPC Chapters XII), plus counterfeit goods under IP laws. Questions are mostly factual (quantities, punishments, sections, bail, seizure procedure) and from Supreme Court case law .

t: Memory Capsule: Drug Trafficking and Counterfeiting
p: Drug Trafficking and Counterfeiting · Law of Crimes
x: NDPS = 1985 ; s.37 = twin bail conditions ; s.35 = culpable mental state presumption ; s.50 = personal search ; s.42 = warrantless search ; s.52A = disposal ; s.27A = financing (10 to 20 years); s.31A = death for repeat large-quantity offenders (discretionary after 2014). Quantity bands : small (up to 1 year), intermediate (up to 10 years), commercial (10 to 20 years, fine ₹1 to 2 lakh). Cases : Balbir Singh and Baldev Singh (mandatory compliance, s.42 and s.50), Noor Aga (presumptions valid), Tofan Singh (NCB confessions inadmissible), Vijaysinh Jadeja (s.50), Dadu (s.32A), Mohanlal (s.52A). Counterfeiting : 489A-489E (IPC) now in BNS Chapter X ; life or ten years for counterfeiting; possession needs knowledge ( Umashankar ); high-quality counterfeit currency is a terrorist act (BNS s.113).

p: Offences Against Public Tranquillity · Law of Crimes
x: An assembly of five or more persons is designated an unlawful assembly if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is: to overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force , the Central or any State Government or Parliament or the Legislature of any State, or any public servant in the exercise of his lawful power; to resist the execution of any law , or of any legal process; to commit any mischief or criminal trespass , or other offence; by means of criminal force or show of criminal force , to take or obtain possession of property , or deprive any person of the enjoyment of a right of way, or of the use of water or other incorporeal right , or to enforce any right or supposed right ; by means of criminal force or show of criminal force , to compel any person to do what he is not legally bound to do , or to omit to do what he is legally entitled to do . Explanation : an assembly which was not unlawful when it assembled may subsequently become an unlawful assembly. Essentials : (1) five or more persons ; (2) a common object of the listed kind; (3) the common object must be unlawful , shared by all (or by a number sufficient to make five); (4) it need not be formed in advance ; it can form on the spot ( Lalji v. State of U.P. , 1989). Mere presence at the scene is not enough ( Masalti v. State of U.P. , 1965); active participation or sharing the common object is required, but overt act is not necessary for the liability under s.190. Punishments : being a member of an unlawful assembly (IPC 143): up to six months or fine or both; joining armed with deadly weapon (IPC 144): up to two years ; joining after being commanded to disperse (IPC 145): up to two years ; hiring or engaging persons for the assembly (s.192; IPC 150): same as a member of the assembly; knowingly joining or continuing in an assembly of five or more persons after it has been lawfully commanded to disperse (s.193; IPC 151): up to six months or fine or both; assaulting or obstructing a public servant when suppressing a riot (s.195; IPC 152): up to three years or fine or both. Dispersal : the BNSS (successor to CrPC ss.129-132 ) lays down the procedure for dispersal of unlawful assemblies by civil force, by armed forces , and protection for officers who act in good faith. Magistrate and police officers can order dispersal; the use of force must be the minimum necessary .

p: Offences Against Public Tranquillity · Law of Crimes
x: Liability of every member of an unlawful assembly for any offence committed by any member in prosecution of the common object , or such as the members knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. See topic 1 for the comparison with common intention and the cases ( Masalti , Lalji , Charan Singh , Yeshwant ).

p: Offences Against Public Tranquillity · Law of Crimes
x: Definition (s.191(1); IPC s.146) : whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly , or by any member thereof, in prosecution of the common object of such assembly, every member of such assembly is guilty of the offence of rioting . Punishment : rioting (s.191(2); IPC 147): up to two years or fine or both; rioting armed with a deadly weapon (s.191(3); IPC 148): up to five years or fine or both; rioting by a person armed with a deadly weapon or members aggravated (s.191(4)-(5)). Riot is an unlawful assembly that has used force. An unlawful assembly may exist without any violence ; a riot needs force or violence ( even slight force , such as pushing, may suffice). Liability for offences during the riot : members are liable under s.190 for offences in prosecution of the common object (e.g., murder, mischief by fire).

p: Offences Against Public Tranquillity · Law of Crimes
x: Definition : when two or more persons , by fighting in a public place , disturb the public peace , they are said to commit an affray . Punishment : up to one month , or fine up to ₹1,000 or both (the BNS raised the fine). Elements : (1) two or more persons ; (2) fighting ; (3) in a public place ; (4) disturbance of the public peace (the public nature distinguishes affray from an ordinary assault).

t: 9.6 Promoting enmity and national integration (ss.196-197; IPC 153A, 153B)
p: Offences Against Public Tranquillity · Law of Crimes
x: Promoting enmity between different groups (s.196; IPC 153A): words (spoken or written), signs, visible representations or electronic communication that promote or attempt to promote disharmony or feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between different religious, racial, language or regional groups or castes or communities , on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, caste or community ; also acts prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony and organising drills or exercises that involve criminal force. Punishment: up to three years , or fine, or both; in a place of worship or during religious ceremonies : up to five years and fine. Imputations and assertions prejudicial to national integration (s.197; IPC 153B): e.g., claims that any class of persons cannot bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution or denying citizens their rights on grounds of religion, etc. Punishment: up to three years or fine or both; in a place of worship : up to five years . Cases : Bilal Ahmed Kaloo v. State of A.P. (1997) (s.153A requires that at least two groups are involved and the intention to promote enmity must be shown; the offence cannot be based on a statement against one community alone); Manzar Sayeed Khan v. State of Maharashtra (2007) ( mens rea and intention to promote enmity are essential; mere publication of a statement is not enough); Ramesh v. Union of India (1988) (Tamil film on Rajiv Gandhi's assassination; test of the reasonable, strong-minded person ); Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan v. Union of India (2014) (hate speech; asked the Law Commission to study); Amish Devgan v. Union of India (2020) (hate speech, effect of speech on the targeted group ; the Court held speech must be judged by its effect on a reasonable person ); Patricia Mukhim v. State of Meghalaya (2021) ( no FIR under 153A and 505 where the Facebook post sought justice and did not promote enmity).

t: 9.7 Offences relating to religion (ss.298-302; IPC ss.295-298)
p: Offences Against Public Tranquillity · Law of Crimes
x: Offence BNS IPC Punishment Injuring or defiling a place of worship with intent to insult the religion of any class 298 295 Up to two years or fine or both Deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings by insulting religion or religious beliefs 299 295A Up to three years or fine or both Disturbing a religious assembly 300 296 Up to one year or fine or both Trespassing on burial places 301 297 Up to one year or fine or both Uttering words with deliberate intent to wound religious feelings 302 298 Up to one year or fine or both Ramji Lal Modi v. State of U.P. (1957): the Supreme Court upheld s.295A as a reasonable restriction on freedom of speech in the interest of public order , because it punishes only deliberate and malicious acts aimed at outraging religious feelings, not mere insult. Mere criticism or bona fide discussion is outside the section. Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) is the leading authority on the distinction between advocacy and incitement .

t: 9.8 Statements conducing to public mischief (s.353; IPC s.505)
p: Offences Against Public Tranquillity · Law of Crimes
x: Making, publishing or circulating any statement, rumour or report : (a) with intent to cause, or likely to cause, any officer, soldier, sailor or airman to mutiny or otherwise disregard or fail in his duty; (b) with intent to cause, or likely to cause, fear or alarm to the public , whereby any person may be induced to commit an offence against the State or against the public tranquillity ; (c) with intent to incite, or likely to incite, any class or community to commit any offence against any other class or community. Punishment : up to three years or fine or both; in a place of worship or at a religious assembly : up to five years and fine. The BNS includes electronic means and false or misleading information that endangers the sovereignty or security of India under s.353 (and related s.152).

t: 9.9 Public nuisance and orders to maintain peace
p: Offences Against Public Tranquillity · Law of Crimes
x: Public nuisance (s.270; IPC s.268) : an act or illegal omission which causes any common injury, danger or annoyance to the public, or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity, or which must necessarily cause injury, obstruction, danger or annoyance to persons who may have occasion to use any public right . A common nuisance is not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage . Punishment (s.292; IPC 290): fine up to ₹1,000 (older: ₹200). BNSS conditional order for removal of nuisance (CrPC s.133; BNSS s.152 ): the Magistrate can issue a conditional order to remove a public nuisance; Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand (1980) (Justice Krishna Iyer; the local authority must perform its statutory duty to remove nuisance; lack of funds is no excuse; s.133 is mandatory in effect). Orders under BNSS s.163 (CrPC s.144) : urgent orders in cases of nuisance or apprehended danger ; Madhu Limaye v. S.D.M. Monghyr (1970) (constitutional; reasonable restriction on rights); Babulal Parate v. State of Maharashtra (1961); Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) ( internet shutdown and s.144 orders must be necessary and proportionate , published and subject to judicial review ; indefinite orders are impermissible). Assembly and protest : Article 19(1)(b) (peaceful assembly without arms); Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018) (Jantar Mantar; the Court said protests must be regulated , not banned); Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police (2020) ( Shaheen Bagh ; public spaces cannot be occupied indefinitely ); Ramlila Maidan Incident, In Re (2012) ( right to sleep and right to assemble and police action at night); Destruction of Public and Private Properties v. State of A.P. (2009) (guidelines on compensation for property damage during protests and the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984 ). Disobedience to order duly promulgated by a public servant (s.223; IPC 188): if it causes obstruction, annoyance or injury : up to six months ; if it causes danger to human life, health or safety, or a riot or affray : up to one year and fine.

p: Offences Against Public Tranquillity · Law of Crimes
x: BNS Chapter XI (ss.189-197; IPC ss.141-160 and 153A, 153B) deals with unlawful assembly, rioting, affray and promoting enmity . Related topics: public nuisance (s.270; IPC 268), offences relating to religion (ss.298-302; IPC 295-298), statements conducing to public mischief (s.353; IPC 505) and disobedience of public servants' orders (s.223; IPC 188). The distinctions among unlawful assembly, riot and affray are an evergreen question .

p: Theories and Kinds of Punishment; Compensation to Victims of Crime · Law of Crimes
x: Theory Core idea Thinkers Key points Retributive Punishment is a just desert for the wrong done; the offender deserves suffering in proportion to the wrong Kant, Hegel ; the biblical "eye for an eye" ( lex talionis ) Looks backward ; proportionality ; supports the death penalty for the gravest crimes; criticised as vengeance Deterrent Punishment must frighten the offender ( individual deterrence ) and others ( general deterrence ) Jeremy Bentham, Beccaria, Paley Looks forward ; assumes rational choice ; exemplary punishment; criticised for ignoring offenders who are not rational and for the disproportionate punishment risk Preventive (incapacitative) Remove the offender from society so that he cannot repeat the crime Salmond (partly) Imprisonment, death , externment , preventive detention ; looks to protection of society Reformative (rehabilitative) Treat the offender as a patient ; aim is reform through education and training Gandhi (" hate the sin and not the sinner "); Justice Krishna Iyer Probation, parole, borstal, open prisons, juvenile justice ; individualised sentences; criticised as soft Expiatory The offender atones for the sin by suffering Religious thought Ancient Hindu law and canonical law Restorative Repair the harm to the victim and community through dialogue and compensation Howard Zehr Victim-offender mediation, plea bargaining, compensation Utilitarian / Mixed (eclectic) Combine deterrence, prevention and reformation Salmond: punishment is the instrument of deterrence, retribution and reformation Closest to Indian sentencing practice Indian judicial approach : courts apply a blend ( Mohd. Giasuddin v. State of A.P. , 1977; Justice Krishna Iyer stressed the reformative approach and the " hate the sin, not the sinner " principle); Dhananjoy Chatterjee v. State of W.B. (1994) ( deterrence and the society's cry for justice justified death); Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) ( reformative and retributive aims are balanced; death only in the rarest of rare cases); Soman v. State of Kerala (2013) (sentencing principles: proportionality ; the court must consider aggravating and mitigating factors). Committee reports : the Malimath Committee (2003) recommended a sentencing guideline ; Madhava Menon Committee (2007) proposed a National Policy on Criminal Justice . India has no statutory sentencing guideline ; discretion is judicial.

t: 10.2 Kinds of punishment (BNS s.4; IPC s.53)
p: Theories and Kinds of Punishment; Compensation to Victims of Crime · Law of Crimes
x: Death . Imprisonment for life . Imprisonment , of two descriptions: (i) rigorous (with hard labour ) and (ii) simple . Forfeiture of property . Fine . Community service ( new ). Other provisions of Chapter II (ss.4-13) : s.5 commutation of sentences (the appropriate Government may commute death to life imprisonment , etc., without the offender's consent ); s.6 fractions of terms ( life imprisonment is reckoned as twenty years for calculating fractions, unless otherwise provided); s.7 the sentence may be wholly or partly rigorous or simple ; s.8 amount of fine and default imprisonment ; s.9 limit of punishment for an offence made up of several offences; s.10 punishment where it is doubtful which of several offences was committed; s.11 solitary confinement ; s.12 limit of solitary confinement ; s.13 enhanced punishment after previous conviction. Life imprisonment : means imprisonment for the whole of the remaining natural life unless remitted or commuted by the appropriate Government ( Gopal Vinayak Godse v. State of Maharashtra , 1961; the twenty-year reckoning in s.6 is only for calculation of fractions ). Maru Ram v. Union of India (1981) upheld CrPC s.433A (a life convict must serve fourteen years before remission; the BNSS has an equivalent provision ); Swamy Shraddananda (2) v. State of Karnataka (2008) (the court may impose a fixed-term life sentence (no remission) as an alternative to death); Union of India v. V. Sriharan @ Murugan (2016) (Constitution Bench: the Constitutional Courts may impose a fixed term of life imprisonment beyond fourteen years , even for the whole natural life ; but no Government remission in that case). The BNS expressly uses " imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person's natural life " for certain aggravated sexual offences and for murder by a life convict . Rigorous imprisonment includes hard labour (grinding corn, digging, drawing water, wood-cutting); simple imprisonment has no hard labour. Prisoners' rights : Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration (1978, 1980) ( solitary confinement and bar fetters in jail violate Article 21 unless justified; prisoners retain fundamental rights ); Charles Sobraj v. Superintendent, Central Jail, Tihar (1978); Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration (1980) ( handcuffing is inhuman unless justified); Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979) ( speedy trial and legal aid for undertrials); Sheela Barse v. State of Maharashtra (1983) ( women and child prisoners). Solitary confinement (s.11-12; IPC 73-74): not more than three months in the whole; not more than fourteen days at a time , with intervals of equal length. Fine : if no sum is expressed, the fine is unlimited but not excessive (s.8); default imprisonment must not exceed one-fourth of the maximum imprisonment for the offence where the offence is punishable with both; fine is realisable within six years , and the offender's death does not discharge his property from liability. Community service (s.4(f)) : defined in BNS s.2 as work the court orders as punishment that benefits the community , for which the convict is not entitled to remuneration . Offences with community service (six): public servant unlawfully engaging in trade (s.202), non-attendance in obedience to an order from a public servant (s.209), attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain a public servant (s.226), theft of property valued under ₹5,000 by a first-time convict who returns the property (s.303(2)), misconduct in public by a drunken person (s.355), and defamation (s.356(2)). Mandatory minimum punishments : introduced for several offences (e.g., rape, dowry death, organised crime). Forfeiture and attachment of proceeds of crime: BNSS s.107 (new, attachment, forfeiture or restoration of property).

p: Theories and Kinds of Punishment; Compensation to Victims of Crime · Law of Crimes
x: Offences punishable with death in the BNS include murder (s.103) , murder by a life convict (s.104) , mob lynching (s.103(2)) , waging war (s.147) , abetment of mutiny and certain military offences, rape of a girl under 12 (s.65(2)) , rape causing death or persistent vegetative state (s.66) , gang rape of a woman under 18 (s.70(2)) , repeat rape offenders (s.71) , kidnapping for ransom (s.140(2): death or life), dacoity with murder (s.310(3)) , terrorist act causing death (s.113) , organised crime causing death (s.111) , and false evidence leading to the conviction of an innocent person for a capital offence . Special laws include POCSO (aggravated penetrative sexual assault), NDPS s.31A and UAPA s.16 . Landmark case law : Jagmohan Singh v. State of U.P. (1973): upheld the death penalty; sentencing discretion is guided by the procedure of a trial. Rajendra Prasad v. State of U.P. (1979): Justice Krishna Iyer limited death to cases of extraordinary nature ( extreme social danger ); overruled in Bachan Singh . Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980): Constitution Bench (4:1; Justice Bhagwati dissenting) upheld the constitutional validity of the death penalty (Article 21 and s.302 IPC); death can be imposed only in the "rarest of rare" cases when the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed ; the court must weigh aggravating and mitigating circumstances ; life imprisonment is the rule and death the exception ; CrPC s.354(3) requires special reasons for death. Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983): five categories to apply the rarest-of-rare test: manner of commission , motive , anti-social or socially abhorrent nature , magnitude , personality of the victim ; and a balance sheet of aggravating and mitigating factors. Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983): mandatory death under IPC s.303 is unconstitutional . Santosh Kumar Satishbhushan Bariyar v. State of Maharashtra (2009): crime test and criminal test ; the court must look at the offender as well as the offence ; not mechanical application of rarest-of-rare. Deena v. Union of India (1983): hanging is not a cruel, inhuman or degrading method (Article 21 upheld); T.V. Vatheeswaran v. State of T.N. (1983) and Triveniben v. State of Gujarat (1989): inordinate delay in execution; delay alone does not automatically entitle commutation unless unexplained and excessive . Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India (2014): undue and inordinate delay in deciding mercy petitions is a ground for commutation ; guidelines for the protection of death row convicts (e.g., mental illness , solitary confinement barred, legal aid ). Mohd. Arif @ Ashfaq v. Registrar, Supreme Court (2014): review petitions in death sentences must be heard in open court by a bench of at least three judges . Shabnam v. Union of India (2015): no execution without sufficient notice of 14 days after the mercy decision to allow remedies. Mukesh v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2017): Nirbhaya ; death confirmed. Yakub Memon v. State of Maharashtra (2015): curative petition heard at night before execution. Manoj v. State of M.P. (2022): the court must examine mitigating circumstances (psychological evaluation, jail conduct, probation report) before imposing death; a Constitution Bench reference was made in 2022 to frame guidelines on mitigating factors. Procedure : pre-sentence hearing (CrPC s.235(2); BNSS s.392(2)); confirmation of death sentence by the High Court (the BNSS chapter on confirmation, corresponding to CrPC ss.366-371); appeal to the Supreme Court ( Article 134 ); mercy petition to the Governor ( Article 161 ) and President ( Article 72 ; Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of A.P. , 2006: judicial review of mercy decisions is available on limited grounds ). Abolition debate : Law Commission 262nd Report (2015) recommended abolition for all crimes except terrorism-related offences ; Mithu and Bachan Singh remain the core precedents.

p: Theories and Kinds of Punishment; Compensation to Victims of Crime · Law of Crimes
x: Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 : courts may release first-time offenders on probation of good conduct (s.3: release after admonition for certain property offences and offences punishable with up to two years; s.4: release on probation of good conduct for offences not punishable with death or life ; s.6: restrictions on imprisonment of offenders under 21 ). Cases : Ratan Lal v. State of Punjab (1964) (probation to a young offender ; the Act is beneficial and retrospective ); Jugal Kishore Prasad v. State of Bihar (1972); Chhanni v. State of U.P. (2006) (probation to older offenders ; reasons must be recorded if not applied). Sentencing principles : proportionality , individualisation , consideration of both the crime and the criminal . Aggravating factors: premeditation , cruelty , vulnerable victim , abuse of position of trust , repeat offence . Mitigating factors: young age , no criminal history , remorse , provocation , mental condition , probability of reform . Plea bargaining (BNSS Chapter XXIII; CrPC Chapter XXIA introduced in 2005 ): available for offences with punishment up to seven years ; not for offences against women or children below 14 , socio-economic offences, or offences affecting the socio-economic condition of the country ; the court reduces the sentence (up to one-fourth of the minimum or one-half in some cases, depending on the stage). Compounding of offences (BNSS s.359; CrPC s.320): with or without court permission for the listed offences; non-compoundable serious offences. Juvenile justice : Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 ; no death or life imprisonment for children in conflict with law ; the maximum stay in a special home is three years ; heinous offences by 16-18 year-olds may be treated as adults . Parole and furlough : parole (temporary release for a specific purpose; not a right ), furlough (a reward for good conduct); State prison rules ; Maru Ram and Sunil Batra govern remission .

p: Theories and Kinds of Punishment; Compensation to Victims of Crime · Law of Crimes
x: Victimology : the UN Declaration of Basic Principles of Justice for Victims of Crime and Abuse of Power (1985) ; Indian reforms followed the Malimath Committee (2003) and the Law Commission 154th Report (1996) . Statutory provisions (BNSS; old CrPC in brackets): s.395 (CrPC 357) : order to pay compensation out of the fine or in addition to the fine; compensation to the victim for the loss or injury and costs ; courts may order compensation even when fine is not part of the sentence (357(3)). Hari Singh v. Sukhbir Singh (1988) (courts should liberally use the power); Ankush Shivaji Gaikwad v. State of Maharashtra (2013) (the court has a duty to consider compensation in every case ; the power is mandatory to consider); Suresh v. State of Haryana (2015) (the power is not ancillary to a sentence). s.396 (CrPC 357A) : Victim Compensation Scheme by every State, in coordination with the Central Government ; the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) or State Legal Services Authority decides the quantum where the court recommends compensation, even when the offender is not traced or identified or the trial ends in acquittal or discharge . ss.397 (CrPC 357B, 357C) : compensation for acid attack and sexual offences is in addition to fines (e.g., under s.124 (acid), s.65 (rape under 16), s.70 (gang rape)); free medical treatment (first-aid, diagnosis, hospitalisation and psychological counselling) in all hospitals , public or private, for victims of acid attack and rape . Right of appeal by the victim (proviso to CrPC s.372; BNSS s.413 ): Satya Pal Singh v. State of M.P. (2015). Victim participation and victim impact statements in sentencing and victim's right to be heard (BNSS ss.360, 230 etc.). Constitutional compensation (public law remedy) under Articles 32 and 226 : Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983) (compensation for illegal detention after acquittal); Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985); Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) ( custodial death ; compensation is public law and separate from private-law tort remedies); D.K. Basu v. State of W.B. (1997) ( arrest and detention guidelines ); Delhi Domestic Working Women's Forum v. Union of India (1995) ( Criminal Injuries Compensation Board for rape victims ; legal representation ); Bodhisattwa Gautam v. Subhra Chakraborty (1996) ( interim compensation to rape victims); Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das (2000) (compensation to a foreign national raped by railway employees); Laxmi v. Union of India (2014) and Parivartan Kendra v. Union of India (2015) ( acid attack : minimum ₹3 lakh ; free treatment); Nipun Saxena v. Union of India (2018) (a Model Victim Compensation Scheme for sexual offences and acid attack ; NALSA's 2018 scheme for women victims of sexual assault). Special statutes with compensation : Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 ; Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (monetary relief); Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (compensation, no-fault liability ); POCSO Rules, 2020 (interim compensation).
