Cases: Gloucester Grammar School v Bradford (teacher opening rival school; students left), Mogul Steamship Co v McGregor Gow & Co (lawful competition), Acton v Blundell and Chasemore v Richards (abstracting underground water), Bradford Corporation v Pickles (motive irrelevant when exercising a lawful right), Town Area Committee v Prabhu Dayal (Indian, demolition of unauthorized construction). Concept trap: Do not confuse damnum (loss) with injuria (legal wrong). Damnum sine injuria is the one that is NOT actionable.

p: Nature and Definition of Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Intention: the desire to bring about a consequence, or knowledge that it is substantially certain. Motive: the underlying reason; generally irrelevant in tort ( Bradford Corporation v Pickles ; Allen v Flood ), because a lawful act does not become unlawful merely because of a bad motive. Malice (in law: wrongful act done intentionally without just cause) matters in a few torts: nuisance ( Christie v Davey , deliberate banging to annoy neighbours; Hollywood Silver Fox Farm v Emmett ), malicious prosecution , conspiracy ( Quinn v Leathem ), defamation (defeats qualified privilege and fair comment), and malicious falsehood . Negligence: carelessness in breach of a duty; Recklessness: conscious disregard of risk.

t: 1.6 Theories of liability: pigeon-hole vs general principle
p: Nature and Definition of Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Salmond's "pigeon-hole" theory: Law of Torts . There are only specific named torts (assault, battery, defamation, nuisance etc.). If a wrong does not fit a recognised category, no liability. Winfield's general theory: Law of Tort . There is a general principle that every harm caused by wrongful conduct is actionable unless justified, so new torts can develop. Position today: The courts are closer to Winfield; the categories remain open, as shown by the growth of negligence ( Donoghue v Stevenson ), privacy-related claims, and constitutional torts in India.

p: Nature and Definition of Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Tort vs Crime Tort: private wrong; remedy is compensation; action by injured party; no necessity of mens rea in all torts; no codified list. Crime: public wrong; remedy is punishment; prosecution by State; mens rea normally required; defined in statute (now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023). Same act may be both (assault, defamation, negligent driving causing death, nuisance). Rule in Smith v Selwyn , once barred civil suits for felony until prosecution; not followed in modern law. Tort vs Breach of contract Contract: duty arises from agreement of parties, owed to specific person (privity), damages may be liquidated, and there is a right to enforce promised performance. Tort: duty fixed by law, owed to persons generally, damages unliquidated. Overlap: a doctor, carrier, or bailee may be liable in both. Donoghue v Stevenson removed the privity limitation that Winterbottom v Wright imposed. Tort vs Breach of trust: breach of trust is an equitable obligation remedied by equity; tort is a common law wrong. Tort vs Quasi-contract: quasi-contract (Sections 68–72, Indian Contract Act 1872) is based on unjust enrichment, not wrongdoing.

p: Nature and Definition of Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Judicial remedies Damages: nominal (right violated, no loss, e.g., Constantine v Imperial Hotels ), contemptuous (technical right but claim is worthless), substantial/compensatory , aggravated (injury to feelings), exemplary/punitive (only in limited categories laid down in Rookes v Devlin (1964): oppressive, arbitrary or unconstitutional action by government servants; conduct calculated to make profit exceeding compensation; where authorised by statute; confirmed in Cassell v Broome ). Injunction: temporary or perpetual, prohibitory or mandatory (nuisance, trespass, defamation). Specific restitution of property (recovery of goods or land). Extra-judicial remedies (self-help) Self-defence, prevention of trespass, re-entry on land, recaption of goods, abatement of nuisance , distress damage feasant (seizing trespassing cattle until compensation is paid), and expulsion of trespasser. Indian development: constitutional courts award public law compensation under Articles 32 and 226 for violation of Article 21 (e.g., Rudul Sah , Nilabati Behera ); this is distinct from private law tort damages (discussed in Topic 7 ).

t: 1.9 Discharge and survival of tort liability
p: Nature and Definition of Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Death: historical maxim actio personalis moritur cum persona (personal action dies with the person). In India, Section 306, Indian Succession Act 1925 provides that causes of action survive to the executor, except defamation, assault, and personal injuries not causing death of the party (and also where the party dies in other personal injury cases). Waiver / Accord and satisfaction / Release / Limitation (Limitation Act 1963 prescribes periods; for example, one year for defamation, malicious prosecution, false imprisonment; three years for general torts like conversion).

p: Nature and Definition of Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Expect: author–definition matching; damnum sine injuria vs injuria sine damno examples; which is NOT a tort remedy; effect of motive; Limitation Act definition; pigeon-hole vs general theory attribution; exemplary damages categories.

p: General Principles of Tortious Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The three general ingredients are (i) wrongful act or omission, (ii) legal damage, and (iii) a remedy. Within this, the courts also examine fault (intention, negligence), causation and remoteness , and defences . Liability may be: Fault-based (intention or negligence), the general rule. Strict liability ( Rylands v Fletcher ), where fault need not be proved but exceptions exist. Absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta ), no exceptions. Vicarious liability: one person liable for the tort of another.

p: General Principles of Tortious Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: An act is a positive wrong (battery, defamation). An omission is liable only when there is a legal duty to act (e.g., occupier's duty to make premises safe, parent's duty to child, a doctor's duty to a patient, a person who creates a danger). Mere moral duty (rescuing a stranger) generally gives no tort liability in English law, although rescuers who are injured can sue the wrongdoer ( Haynes v Harwood ).

p: General Principles of Tortious Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Actionable per se: trespass to person/land/goods, libel. Proof of loss is unnecessary. Actionable only on proof of special damage: negligence, public nuisance (special damage to plaintiff), slander (subject to exceptions), malicious prosecution.

t: 2.4 Parties: who can sue and who can be sued
p: General Principles of Tortious Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The State: liable under Article 300 of the Constitution, subject to the sovereign function distinction (Topic 7 ). Corporations: may sue and be sued; liable for torts committed by employees in the course of business ( Lennard's Carrying Co v Asiatic Petroleum , alter-ego theory; Citizens Life Assurance Co v Brown where the company was held liable for libel). Minors: liable for torts, but the court considers age and capacity to form intent (e.g., Walmsley v Humenick , young child not liable for intentional tort). Persons of unsound mind: liable if mental state is not such as to exclude the mental element ( Morriss v Marsden : an insane person who understood the nature of the act was liable). Husband and wife: in India married persons can sue each other as separate legal persons; interspousal immunity is not recognised in general. Trade unions: liable ( Taff Vale Railway v ASRS ), although later statute gave partial immunity in England. Foreign sovereigns and diplomats: immunity, subject to Section 86, CPC and the Diplomatic Relations (Vienna Convention) Act 1972. Joint tortfeasors: persons who act together in furtherance of a common design, or whose independent acts produce one damage, are jointly and severally liable. The plaintiff may sue any or all; release of one does not release others (in India, under Contribution rules, Merryweather v Nixan (no contribution) has been displaced in many jurisdictions; in exams, remember the classical rule and the modern right to contribution).

p: General Principles of Tortious Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Meaning: liability of one person for the wrong of another due to their relationship. Latin maxims: qui facit per alium facit per se (he who acts through another acts himself) and respondeat superior (let the master answer). Master and servant A master is liable for torts committed by the servant in the course of employment . Tests of a servant: control test, organisation/integration test, multiple/economic reality test. A servant is under control as to how work is done; an independent contractor only as to what is done. Course of employment: acts authorised, or unauthorised mode of doing an authorised act ( Limpus v London General Omnibus Co , driver racing to obstruct a rival bus; master liable). A prohibited act (not merely prohibited mode) is outside employment ( Conway v Wimpey , driver giving lift against orders; Twine v Beans Express ). But Rose v Plenty (milk float boy; master liable because the act was for the master's business despite prohibition). Acts of fraud/crime: Lloyd v Grace, Smith & Co (solicitor's managing clerk defrauded client; firm liable); Century Insurance v Northern Ireland Road Transport Board (tanker driver's smoking during petrol delivery; liable); Poland v Parr (force in defence of master's property). In modern English law the test is a close connection with the employment ( Lister v Hesley Hall , 2001; Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society ; Mohamud v Morrisons ). Loaned servants: Mersey Docks and Harbour Board v Coggins & Griffith — liability lies with the person having control at the time. Other relationships Principal and agent: principal liable for agent's torts within authority. Partners: liable jointly and severally for torts committed in the course of firm's business (Section 26–27, Indian Partnership Act 1932). Independent contractor: employer generally not liable, with exceptions : negligence in selecting contractor; non-delegable duties (e.g., hazardous operations, duty to maintain highway, strict liability torts); employer authorising the wrongful act; ultra-hazardous work ( Bower v Peate ). Indian illustrations: State of Rajasthan v Vidhyawati (vicarious liability of the State for the negligent driving of a government driver); Saheli v Commissioner of Police ; Municipal Corporation of Delhi v Subhagwanti . Rationale (memory): (i) deep pocket / better ability to pay, (ii) control over employee, (iii) the master benefits from the employee's work, (iv) deterrence and risk distribution through insurance.

t: 2.6 Strict, absolute and statutory no-fault liability (overview; details in Topics 6, 8, 9)
p: General Principles of Tortious Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Exceptional cases where liability arises regardless of fault: Rylands v Fletcher (1868), M.C. Mehta v UOI (1987) absolute liability for hazardous industries, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991, NGT Act 2010, Motor Vehicles Act (no-fault compensation), Employees' Compensation Act 1923, and CPA 2019 product liability.

p: General Principles of Tortious Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Indian courts have recognised a public law remedy of monetary compensation for violations of fundamental rights, particularly Article 21 (life and personal liberty), enforceable by the Supreme Court (Art. 32) and High Courts (Art. 226). Key cases: Rudul Sah v State of Bihar (1983), Bhim Singh v State of J&K (1985), Sebastian Hongray v UOI (1984), Nilabati Behera v State of Orissa (1993), D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal (1997). The Supreme Court holds that sovereign immunity is not a defence in public law proceedings, and that the compensation is without prejudice to a private law suit in tort.

p: General Principles of Tortious Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Expect: matching vicarious liability cases ( Limpus , Lloyd v Grace Smith , Century Insurance , Rose v Plenty , Mersey Docks ); identifying the correct test of servant; capacity of parties; exceptions to non-liability for independent contractors; the maxims respondeat superior , qui facit per alium facit per se ; assertion-reason on constitutional torts.

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Meaning: to a willing person, no injury is done. If the plaintiff voluntarily agrees to take the risk of harm, he cannot sue. Conditions: The plaintiff must have full knowledge of the risk (not merely that danger exists: Dann v Hamilton , passenger who got into car with a drunk driver; the House still considered volenti not established). The plaintiff must have freely and voluntarily agreed to the risk (not under compulsion or pressure of duty). The act must be within the scope of the consent (consent to a medical operation is not consent to a different operation). Cases: Hall v Brooklands Auto Racing Club — spectator at car race accepted the risk of cars leaving the track. Smith v Baker — employee's knowledge of danger is not by itself consent; knowledge is not assent . Nettleship v Weston — a driving instructor who checked insurance did not consent to the risk of negligent driving; volenti failed. Wooldridge v Sumner — sports participant accepts risks of a game played according to rules. Rescue cases: Haynes v Harwood ; Baker v T.E. Hopkins & Son (doctor who tried to rescue workers in a well; volenti rejected). The rule: rescuer's act is natural and probable and not voluntary assumption of risk. Exceptions: volenti does not apply in cases of statutory duty , rescue , and where the defendant's act is unlawful (e.g., consent to being unlawfully injured). Consent and medical treatment: Samira Kohli v Dr Prabha Manchanda (2008) — valid consent requires adequate information; consent for diagnostic procedure does not extend to therapeutic procedure unless emergency. Limits under CPA: exclusion clauses cannot defeat statutory consumer rights. Volenti vs contributory negligence: volenti is a complete defence (voluntary assumption of risk); contributory negligence is a partial defence (reduces damages).

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: An act done to prevent greater harm may be justified. Two forms: private necessity (to protect one's own interest) and public necessity (to protect the community). Cope v Sharpe — trespass to land to prevent a fire from spreading to the landlord's property justified. Leigh v Gladstone — force-feeding a prisoner on hunger strike held justified (preservation of life). Carter v Thomas — entering to extinguish a fire. Esso Petroleum v Southport Corporation — discharge of oil to save the ship. Kirk v Gregory — mere removal of jewellery to what the defendant thought a safer place was not necessity (unnecessary act causes loss). Medical necessity: treating an unconscious patient ( F v West Berkshire Health Authority , in a best-interest context). Under Indian law, necessity also appears in criminal law (BNS general exceptions); in tort, it must be reasonable and proportionate .

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Any person may use reasonable force to protect self, family, or property from unlawful aggression. The force must be proportionate ; excessive force is not a defence. Bird v Holbrook — spring-gun set to protect a garden; the defendant was liable because the danger was disproportionate and unannounced, also affecting an innocent person. Under criminal law, the right of private defence is codified in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (replacing IPC Sections 96–106); the tort rule parallels that.

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: A natural event, extraordinary and unforeseeable , without human intervention, so overwhelming that no reasonable human foresight or care could have prevented it. Nichols v Marsland (1876) — extraordinary rainfall breaking artificial lakes; defendant not liable. Greenock Corporation v Caledonian Railway — extraordinary rainfall; not Act of God because it could have been prevented by better works. Essentials: (i) natural forces, (ii) unforeseeable and extraordinary, (iii) no human agency, (iv) an incapacity to guard against it by reasonable care. It is an exception to strict liability ( Rylands v Fletcher ) but is not available in absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta ).

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: An accident that could not have been avoided by ordinary care, caution and skill . The burden of proof lies on the defendant. Stanley v Powell — a shot rebounded from a tree and injured a beater; the defendant was not liable. Brown v Kendall — accidental injury while separating fighting dogs. Holmes v Mather — a runaway horse. Key distinction: inevitable accident relates to a physical event not preventable with care, whereas Act of God is a specific natural event.

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Mistake of fact or law is generally not a defence in tort, although it can negate intention in rare cases, e.g., malicious prosecution (reasonable and probable cause). Consolidated Co v Curtis (an auctioneer sold goods of the wrong owner; liable for conversion); Hollins v Fowler (honest purchase for the principal was still conversion). Mistake is a defence in defamation only in a limited sense of unintentional defamation under statutory frameworks ( Hulton v Jones , the defendant was liable even though the mistake was innocent).

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Acts authorised by statute are not actionable if done within the powers and without negligence. Vaughan v Taff Vale Railway — sparks from a locomotive set fire to the plaintiff's woods; railway not liable because it used proper care and the statute authorised the engine. Hammersmith Rail Co v Brand — vibration damage from railway operation; no remedy under common law. Metropolitan Asylum District v Hill — hospital for smallpox patients; the statute was permissive , not mandatory, so nuisance was not justified. Rule: if the statute is mandatory , the defendant is protected even from inevitable nuisance; if permissive , the defendant must exercise powers without causing nuisance. Indian case: Municipal Corporation of Delhi v Subhagwanti (1966) — collapse of the clock tower; statutory authority does not excuse negligence.

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Where plaintiff's own negligence contributes to the harm, the damages are apportioned under the Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 (England); Indian courts follow the same principle of apportionment even without a statute (Motor Vehicles claims often apply it). Butterfield v Forrester (1809) — plaintiff riding fast, failed to see an obstruction; no recovery under the old law. Davies v Mann — the last opportunity rule ; the defendant who had the last clear chance to avoid the accident was liable. British Columbia Electric Railway v Loach — a modification of the last opportunity rule. Children: a child is judged by the standard of a child of that age ( Jones v Boyce , in the context of rescue and reasonable reaction). Standard: the plaintiff must also take reasonable care of himself (e.g., seat belts: Froom v Butcher , damages reduced by 15–25% for not wearing seat belts). Effect: partial defence (reduction of damages), not a complete bar in modern law.

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Judicial acts: a judge acting judicially is immune, even if erroneous or malicious, provided he acts within jurisdiction. In India, the Judicial Officers' Protection Act 1850 gives protection for acts done in good faith; Anderson v Gorrie ; Sirros v Moore . Executive acts: acts of the executive in the exercise of authorised statutory power are protected; if they are done in excess of authority, the officer is personally liable. Quasi-judicial acts: same protection when acting judicially.

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Parents, teachers and persons in loco parentis may inflict reasonable and moderate chastisement for the child's correction. The protection extends to teachers (in India, subject to the Right to Education Act 2009, Section 17 , which prohibits physical punishment and mental harassment). Excessive punishment is actionable and criminal.

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Expect: matching defence with case; "which is NOT a defence in tort"; difference between volenti, contributory negligence, inevitable accident, Act of God; essentials of Act of God; statutory authority (mandatory vs permissive); last opportunity rule; scope of rescue cases; Assertion–Reason on whether Nichols v Marsland applies to absolute liability.

p: General Defences in Tort · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: A defence is a justification or excuse that negates liability even when the elements of a tort are present. The classical list is: volenti non fit injuria, necessity, private defence, act of God, inevitable accident, mistake, statutory authority, plaintiff's default (contributory negligence), judicial and executive acts, parental/quasi-parental authority.

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Negligence has two senses: (i) a mental state (carelessness) and (ii) an independent tort (breach of a legal duty to take care resulting in damage). The classic definition is by Alderson B in Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks Co (1856): negligence is the omission to do something which a reasonable man, guided by considerations which ordinarily regulate human affairs, would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable man would not do. Winfield defines it as the breach of a legal duty to take care which results in damage, undesired by the defendant, to the plaintiff.

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Duty of care owed by the defendant to the plaintiff. Breach of that duty (failure to meet the standard of a reasonable person). Consequential damage caused by the breach and not too remote. The burden of proof is generally on the plaintiff (exception: res ipsa loquitur ).

t: 4.3 Negligence: Duty of care: development of the test
p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Donoghue v Stevenson (1932): a snail in a ginger beer bottle; Lord Atkin's neighbour principle : you must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour, meaning persons so closely and directly affected that you ought reasonably to have them in contemplation. This case created the modern tort of negligence and removed the need for privity of contract ( Winterbottom v Wright limited). Anns v Merton LBC (1978): a two-stage test (proximity/foreseeability; then policy considerations to negative or limit the duty). Later disapproved. Caparo Industries v Dickman (1990): the modern three-stage test : (i) damage must be reasonably foreseeable , (ii) there must be proximity between the parties, and (iii) it must be fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty. Auditors owed no duty to potential investors. Hedley Byrne v Heller (1964): liability for negligent misstatement causing pure economic loss where there is a special relationship and reliance (disclaimer protected the defendant there). Heaven v Pender : an early attempt at a general duty principle (Brett MR).

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The standard is that of the reasonable man ( Vaughan v Menlove : the hay-rick case, an objective standard regardless of the defendant's actual intellect). Factors: probability of harm, gravity of harm, cost of precautions, and social utility of the activity ( Bolton v Stone , a cricket ball hit out of the ground; Paris v Stepney Borough Council , a one-eyed worker owed greater care; Latimer v AEC ). Professionals: the standard of an ordinary skilled person in that profession. Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee (1957): a doctor is not negligent if he acts in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical opinion. ( Bolitho added that the opinion must withstand logical analysis.) Children: judged by a child of the same age ( Mullin v Richards ). Learners: Nettleship v Weston (objective standard of a competent driver). Specially skilled: the standard of one who professes that skill.

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Res ipsa loquitur ("the thing speaks for itself") is a rule of evidence by which negligence is inferred from the very occurrence when: (i) the thing causing damage was under the defendant's control, (ii) the accident would not ordinarily occur without negligence, and (iii) there is no explanation of the cause. It shifts the evidential burden to the defendant. Cases: Byrne v Boadle (1863) (a barrel of flour fell from a warehouse window), Scott v London & St Katherine Docks (sugar bags), Shyam Sundar v State of Rajasthan (1974) (SC applied the doctrine in a truck accident and held that the doctrine can apply in India), Pushpabai Purshottam Udeshi v Ranjit Ginning & Pressing Co (1977), Municipal Corporation of Delhi v Subhagwanti (1966). The doctrine does not apply where the facts themselves disclose the cause or where the defendant lacks control. It is a rule of evidence , not a rule of law that creates liability.

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Dr. Laxman Balkrishna Joshi v Dr. Trimbak Bapu Godbole (1969): a doctor owes the patient a duty to exercise a reasonable degree of skill and knowledge, deciding on treatment and administering it with care. Indian Medical Association v V.P. Shantha (1995): medical services (other than free services to all) fall under "service" in the Consumer Protection Act. Jacob Mathew v State of Punjab (2005): for criminal negligence of a doctor, gross negligence or recklessness must be shown (a higher threshold than civil negligence); the court approved Bolam and laid down guidelines for prosecution (a prior credible opinion from another competent doctor). Spring Meadows Hospital v Harjol Ahluwalia (1998): liability of hospital and doctors; parent as consumer for a child's treatment. Samira Kohli v Prabha Manchanda (2008): informed consent. Kusum Sharma v Batra Hospital (2010): guidelines on medical negligence; the standard is of an ordinary competent doctor. V. Kishan Rao v Nikhil Super Speciality Hospital (2010): expert evidence is not always mandatory; res ipsa loquitur may apply.

t: 4.7 Negligence: Damage, causation and remoteness (summary; details in Topic 5)
p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The plaintiff must prove that the breach caused the damage: the "but for" test ( Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington Hospital : poisoning case; the hospital's negligence did not cause death because the patient would have died anyway). If multiple causes, material contribution ( Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw ). Novus actus interveniens (new intervening act) may break the chain.

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Hambrook v Stokes (mother's fear for children); Bourhill v Young (a bystander who heard an accident was not owed a duty as she was not foreseeably affected); McLoughlin v O'Brian (1983) (mother saw injured family at hospital shortly afterwards). Alcock v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire Police (1992) (Hillsborough): for secondary victims, control mechanisms: a close tie of love and affection , proximity in time and space to the event or its immediate aftermath, and perception through one's own unaided senses (live television broadcasts were not enough). Page v Smith (primary victims: no need to prove foreseeable psychiatric injury if some physical injury was foreseeable).

t: 4.9 Negligence: Pure economic loss and omissions
p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Generally not recoverable in negligence unless a special relationship exists: Spartan Steel v Martin & Co (cable cut; loss of profit from the physical damage recoverable, but not purely economic loss); Murphy v Brentwood DC ; Hedley Byrne is the major exception. Omissions: no general duty to rescue; duty arises where a special relationship, control of a danger, or an assumption of responsibility exists ( Smith v Littlewoods ).

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Contributory negligence, volenti, inevitable accident, statutory authority (see Topic 3 ).

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Winfield: nuisance is an unlawful interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land, or some right over, or in connection with it. Two kinds: private nuisance (a tort) and public nuisance (a crime as well, and also a tort where special damage is shown).

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Unreasonable interference: with the use or enjoyment of land (not liability for mere inconvenience; the test is the standard of ordinary reasonable persons). Damage: either (a) physical injury to property (e.g., damage to trees, buildings) or (b) substantial interference with the comfort and enjoyment of land (smell, noise, vibrations, smoke). Nature of harm: continuous or recurrent, not a one-time event (though a single event may count if arising from a state of affairs on the land). Factors in reasonableness: locality ( St Helen's Smelting Co v Tipping , 1865: for material injury to property , locality is irrelevant; for personal discomfort , locality matters: "what would be a nuisance in Belgrave Square would not necessarily be so in Bermondsey"), duration and time , intensity , sensitiveness of the plaintiff ( Robinson v Kilvert : a person with abnormal sensitivity cannot complain; McKinnon Industries v Walker ), malice ( Christie v Davey ; Hollywood Silver Fox Farm v Emmett ), utility of the defendant's conduct (not a defence by itself). Who can sue: only those with a proprietary interest in the land (owner, tenant, occupier): Hunter v Canary Wharf (1997) ; mere residents without such an interest cannot. Who can be sued: the creator, the occupier, the landlord who authorised the nuisance, and in some cases the occupier who failed to abate a nuisance created by trespassers or natural causes ( Sedleigh-Denfield v O'Callaghan ; Leakey v National Trust , measured duty).

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: An act or omission that materially affects the reasonable comfort and convenience of a class of Her/His Majesty's subjects (earlier IPC Section 268, now BNS Section 270). Examples: obstructing a highway, polluting a river, operating a brothel or a gambling house. A private person can sue only if he suffers special damage (damage different in kind, not just degree, from that suffered by the public: Ricket v Metropolitan Railway ; Attorney General v PYA Quarries ). In India: Section 91 of the CPC allows a suit for public nuisance by the Advocate General, or by two or more persons with the leave of the court , without special damage; Section 133 CrPC (now BNSS equivalent) allows a Magistrate to order removal of public nuisance.

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Private: affects an individual's land; only a tort; remedy by the person injured; no need for special damage when interference is substantial. Public: affects a class of the public; a crime and a tort; the prosecution is by the State; a private plaintiff must show special damage.

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Valid defences: prescription (20 years' uninterrupted enjoyment as an easement: Sturges v Bridgman , the confectioner's noisy machinery against a doctor; the right begins when the nuisance becomes actionable; Indian Easements Act 1882, Section 15), statutory authority (Topic 3 ), consent/acquiescence , act of a stranger (limited), Act of God . Not defences: coming to the nuisance ( Sturges v Bridgman ), public benefit ( Adams v Ursell , a fried-fish shop), reasonable care , that the plaintiff's use was sensitive , others also contribute ( Lambton v Mellish ).

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Remedies: damages, injunction (the primary remedy), abatement (self-help, with notice generally required). St Helen's Smelting v Tipping (1865): physical vs comfort nuisance. Sturges v Bridgman (1879): locality and prescription. Cambridge Water Co v Eastern Counties Leather (1994): foreseeability of damage is a prerequisite for damages in nuisance. Coventry v Lawrence (2014): planning permission is not a defence per se. Indian cases: Municipal Council, Ratlam v Vardhichand (1980) (Justice Krishna Iyer; a municipality is obliged to provide drains; the public nuisance provisions are an instrument of social justice and a statutory duty can be enforced by a court); Ushaben v Bhagyalaxmi Chitra Mandir (1978, Guj) (the film Jai Santoshi Maa ; hurting religious sentiments is not a nuisance in tort). Nuisance vs trespass: trespass is a direct and immediate interference with possession (actionable per se); nuisance is indirect interference with enjoyment (actionable on proof of damage). Nuisance vs negligence: nuisance focuses on the result (the unreasonable interference), negligence on the conduct (breach of duty).

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Assault: an act creating in the plaintiff's mind a reasonable apprehension of immediate battery. Words alone are generally insufficient (but may qualify the act). Stephens v Myers (1830: a chairman advancing with a clenched fist; assault although stopped by others); Tuberville v Savage ("if it were not assize-time, I would not take such language from you": no assault, as the words negatived the intention); Read v Coker . Battery: the actual application of force (any physical contact without consent). The slightest touch can amount to battery. Cole v Turner (the least touching in anger is a battery); Wilson v Pringle (hostile touching; later criticised); F v West Berkshire and Collins v Wilcock (ordinary social contact is excepted). False imprisonment: the total restraint of a person's liberty without lawful justification (partial obstruction is not enough: Bird v Jones ). It is not necessary to know of the confinement ( Meering v Grahame-White Aviation ), but knowledge is relevant for damages. Herd v Weardale Steel (a miner's refusal to be taken to the surface was not false imprisonment because there was no obligation to provide an exit). Indian cases: Rudul Sah v State of Bihar (14 years of unlawful detention after acquittal), Bhim Singh v State of J&K , Sebastian Hongray . Malicious prosecution: the essentials, as set out by the Privy Council in Mohammed Amin v Jogendra Kumar Bannerjee (1947) : (i) the defendant prosecuted the plaintiff; (ii) the proceedings ended in the plaintiff's favour ; (iii) the defendant acted without reasonable and probable cause ; (iv) the defendant acted with malice ; (v) the plaintiff suffered damage. Defences: consent, self-defence, lawful authority, parental/quasi-parental authority, necessity.

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Unjustifiable interference with the possession of land. Possession (not ownership) is the basis for the suit. Forms: entering the land, remaining after a licence ends, placing objects on it, trespass ab initio ( Six Carpenters' Case : a lawful entry becomes a trespass from the start by a subsequent wrongful act). Airspace and subsoil: the owner's rights extend to such height and depth as are necessary for the ordinary use and enjoyment of the land ( Kelsen v Imperial Tobacco : an overhanging advertisement board; Bernstein v Skyviews : aerial photography at a height was not trespass). Leading cases: Entick v Carrington (1765) (the officers' warrantless entry was unlawful; the rule that the State must act within the law), Basely v Clarkson (a mistaken mowing of a neighbour's land was a trespass). Defences: licence, justification by law, necessity, self-help (re-entry), and the plaintiff's lack of possession. Remedies: damages, injunction, ejectment, re-entry, distress damage feasant .

t: 4.19 Trespass: Trespass to goods and conversion
p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Trespass to goods: direct interference with chattels in the plaintiff's possession. Conversion: a dealing with goods in a manner inconsistent with the owner's right, which deprives him of possession ( Fouldes v Willoughby : a ferry operator's removal of horses; a mere moving is not conversion unless exercising dominion; Hollins v Fowler ). Detinue: the wrongful detention of goods after a demand for return. (In England, detinue was abolished by the Torts (Interference with Goods) Act 1977; in India the action of detinue continues under general law and the Specific Relief Act.) Remedies: damages, recovery of the specific chattel (Specific Relief Act, 1963, Sections 7–8), recaption.

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Defamation is the publication of a false statement which tends to injure the reputation of a person by exposing him to hatred, contempt or ridicule, or which tends to lower him in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally, or to make them shun or avoid him ( Sim v Stretch ). It protects reputation (not feelings). The tort is in Indian law largely governed by English common law principles, while criminal defamation was in IPC Sections 499–500, now BNS Section 356 .

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Libel: a defamatory statement in a permanent form (writing, print, pictures, effigy; in some systems broadcasts). Actionable per se , and may also be a crime. Slander: in a transient form (spoken words, gestures). Generally actionable only on proof of special damage , except in four exceptions (slander per se ): (i) imputation of a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment, (ii) imputation of a loathsome disease , (iii) imputation of unchastity to a woman (Slander of Women Act 1891), and (iv) imputation of unfitness in office, profession, calling or trade . Indian position: the distinction is not strictly followed; a majority of Indian decisions treat both libel and slander as actionable without proof of special damage , though textbooks sometimes record the English rule. Exam answer: in India, the distinction is not recognised strictly and slander is also actionable per se (majority view); under English law, the distinction exists.

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The statement must be defamatory (judged by the right-thinking person test; innuendo: Tolley v Fry : a golfer's picture in an advertisement implying that he was paid). It must refer to the plaintiff ( Hulton v Jones : "Artemus Jones"; the test is whether reasonable persons would think that it refers to the plaintiff, so intention is irrelevant; Newstead v London Express ; Knupffer v London Express : no reference to an identifiable individual in a large class). A company can sue ( South Hetton Coal v North-Eastern News ), but a government body cannot. It must be published , i.e., communicated to at least one person other than the plaintiff ( Pullman v Hill : dictation to a stenographer; communication to the plaintiff alone is not publication; Mahendra Ram v Harnandan Prasad : a letter in Urdu sent to a person who could not read it; no publication). Malice is not an element in civil defamation (it matters for aggravated damages and defeating defences). The defendant's lack of intention does not excuse ( Hulton v Jones ).

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Justification (truth): a complete defence in civil law if the statement is substantially true (burden on the defendant). In criminal law, truth must also be for the public good (BNS exceptions). Fair comment: on a matter of public interest, an honest opinion based on true facts, without malice ( Merivale v Carson ; Kemsley v Foot ; the Indian provision in the exceptions to BNS Section 356). Privilege: Absolute: statements in Parliament, judicial proceedings, State communications, communications between spouses (in some systems), no liability regardless of malice. Qualified: a duty or interest to communicate ( Adam v Ward ), fair and accurate reports of proceedings, protection of one's own interests; defeated by malice . Reynolds v Times Newspapers (1999) developed a public-interest defence for responsible journalism. Apology and offer of amends: mitigating (in England under Defamation Act 1952/1996; in India, under general law, it mitigates damages). Consent ; innocent dissemination (distributors who exercise reasonable care).

t: 4.24 Defamation: Defamation and the Constitution (recent trend)
p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Subramanian Swamy v Union of India (2016): the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of criminal defamation (IPC Sections 499–500) as a reasonable restriction on freedom of speech under Article 19(2) and protecting the right to reputation as part of Article 21 . This is a very frequently tested case. R. Rajagopal v State of Tamil Nadu (1994): the right to privacy; the press may publish material from public records, but not private details without consent; public officials have limited protection against defamation claims unless they prove that the publication was made with reckless disregard of the truth. Under UK law, the Defamation Act 2013 introduced a serious harm threshold (not part of Indian law).

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Damages (including aggravated and in rare cases exemplary), injunction (quia timet to prevent publication, granted cautiously), and an apology. Limitation: one year for a suit for libel or slander under the Limitation Act 1963.

p: Specific Torts: Negligence, Nuisance, Trespass and Defamation · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Expect: Donoghue , Caparo , Bolam , Jacob Mathew , Alcock ; res ipsa loquitur cases; the St Helen's distinction; Hunter v Canary Wharf ; prescription period for nuisance; public nuisance procedure (CPC Section 91); Tuberville v Savage ; Bird v Jones ; ingredients of malicious prosecution; conversion vs detinue; libel vs slander; Hulton v Jones ; and Subramanian Swamy .

p: Remoteness of Damages · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Even if the defendant's breach caused the damage in fact (causation), the law refuses to hold him liable for every consequence, however unlikely. Remoteness of damage is the legal limit on the consequences for which a defendant is liable. Two stages: (1) causation in fact (but-for test) and (2) legal causation / remoteness (which of the consequences are recoverable).

p: Remoteness of Damages · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Facts: A stevedore's servant dropped a plank into the hold of a ship, which carried petrol vapour. A spark caused a fire that destroyed the ship. Held: the defendant was liable for all direct consequences of a negligent act, whether foreseeable or not. Some harm (damage by falling plank) was foreseeable, and the fire was a direct result. Rule: foreseeability of the kind of damage is irrelevant if the damage is a direct result of the negligent act.

p: Remoteness of Damages · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Facts: Oil negligently spilled from the ship Wagon Mound in Sydney harbour drifted to the plaintiff's wharf, where welding was carried on. Cotton waste floating on the oil caught fire from the molten metal, burning the wharf. The experts believed that oil on water would not ignite. Held (Privy Council, Viscount Simonds): Re Polemis was overruled ; the defendant is liable only for damage of a kind that is reasonably foreseeable . Fire was not foreseeable; no liability in negligence. Rule: reasonable foresight of the type of damage is the test of remoteness in negligence (although a person who is negligent is liable for all foreseeable consequences, even if the extent of damage is greater than expected).

p: Remoteness of Damages · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: In this separate action by the owners of ships damaged by the same fire, the court found that the risk of fire, though small, was real and a reasonable person in the position of the ship's engineer would not have disregarded it; liability was established in nuisance and negligence. Rule: a risk that is foreseeable and not far-fetched, and could be eliminated at no cost, must be guarded against.

p: Remoteness of Damages · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Hughes v Lord Advocate (1963): boys playing with an unattended paraffin lamp left near a manhole; the lamp exploded in an unforeseen manner and burned the child. Held: liable, since the kind of damage (burns) was foreseeable, though the exact manner of occurrence was not. Doughty v Turner Manufacturing (1964): an asbestos cover slipped into a cauldron, causing an eruption through a chemical reaction. The event was different in kind from the foreseeable risk (splash); defendant not liable. Egg-shell skull / thin skull rule: the defendant must take the plaintiff as he finds him . Smith v Leech Brain & Co (1962): a burn on the lip of a worker, who had a pre-malignant condition, caused cancer and death; the employer was liable since the burn was foreseeable. Vosburg v Putney (US). The rule applies to physical vulnerability and, in some cases, to psychological vulnerability. Bradford v Robinson Rentals (1967): foreseeable harm of cold (frost-bite) was recoverable even if its severity was not foreseen. Extent of harm: no need to foresee the exact extent ( Vacwell Engineering v BDH Chemicals : explosion of chemicals, the damage being of a different kind; held that damage was not foreseeable).

p: Remoteness of Damages · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: A new, independent act or event that breaks the chain of causation , so that the defendant is not responsible for the later damage. Act of a third party: the chain is broken if the act is unforeseeable and independent ( Knightley v Johns : the police inspector's negligent order; held the chain was broken). Scott v Shepherd (the squib case): a squib thrown into a market and tossed on by others; the first thrower was liable since the subsequent acts were reflex actions. Act of the plaintiff: if the plaintiff's own act is unreasonable ( McKew v Holland : a plaintiff with a weak leg went down steep steps and was injured; the chain was broken). A reasonable act in a dilemma, caused by the defendant's wrong, does not break the chain ( Haynes v Harwood , rescue cases). Natural events: Carslogie Steamship v Royal Norwegian Government (a later storm damage). The Oropesa (1943): a captain's decision to launch a lifeboat in a storm, in which the sailor drowned, did not break the chain (a reasonable decision in an emergency).

p: Remoteness of Damages · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: "But for" test: Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington Hospital Management Committee (1969). Material contribution to the damage: Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw (1956: silica dust). Material increase of risk: McGhee v National Coal Board ; Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services (2002) (mesothelioma: where multiple employers exposed the claimant to asbestos and the specific source could not be identified, each employer who materially increased the risk was liable, an exception to the but-for test). Wilsher v Essex AHA (1988) confined the exception. Loss of a chance: Hotson v East Berkshire AHA (not recoverable in general).

p: Remoteness of Damages · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Deceit/fraud: the defendant is liable for all direct consequences ( Doyle v Olby ), as an exception to foreseeability. Contract: Hadley v Baxendale , the rule on damages (Section 73, Indian Contract Act: damage which naturally arose in the usual course of things, or which the parties knew likely to result). Contrast between the tests in contract and tort is often asked. Strict liability: Cambridge Water and Transco require foreseeability of the type of damage also in nuisance and Rylands v Fletcher .

p: Remoteness of Damages · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Indian courts, in the absence of a unique doctrine, follow English principles , generally the Wagon Mound foreseeability test in negligence claims, and the direct consequence concept where the wrong is intentional. In claims involving public-law compensation or statutory no-fault compensation, remoteness is less relevant.

p: Remoteness of Damages · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Expect: Re Polemis vs Wagon Mound (directness vs foreseeability; which was overruled); facts (plank into ship's hold; oil and cotton waste); Hughes v Lord Advocate (kind of damage); Smith v Leech Brain (thin skull); Scott v Shepherd (squib) as a novus actus case; Bonnington and Fairchild for causation; contract remoteness ( Hadley v Baxendale ); Assertion–Reason on whether the thin skull rule is an exception to foreseeability.

p: Strict and Absolute Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: As a general rule, liability in tort depends on fault (intention or negligence). Strict liability is liability for damage even without fault , subject to certain exceptions. Absolute liability (an Indian innovation) is liability without any exception .

p: Strict and Absolute Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Facts: The defendants employed independent contractors to build a reservoir on their land. The contractors discovered old, unused mine shafts under the site that connected to the plaintiff's coal mine, but did not seal them. When the reservoir filled, water burst through the shafts and flooded the plaintiff's mine. The contractors were negligent but the defendants were not personally at fault. Held: The Court of Exchequer Chamber ( Blackburn J ) laid down the rule: the person who for his own purposes brings on his lands and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, must keep it at his peril, and, if he does not do so, is prima facie answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape. The House of Lords ( Lord Cairns ) affirmed with an added qualification that the use of land must be non-natural .

p: Strict and Absolute Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Dangerous thing: something likely to do mischief if it escapes (water, gas, electricity, fire, explosives, noxious fumes, chemicals, rusty wire, vibrations, etc.). ( Rylands : water; Miles v Forest Granite (explosives); Hale v Jennings (a chair-o-plane in a fair; Attorney-General v Corke (caravan dwellers)); Crowhurst v Amersham Burial Board (yew tree poisonous to cattle).) Escape: from a place where the defendant has occupation or control to a place outside his control. Read v Lyons (1947): the plaintiff, an inspector at a munitions factory, was injured by a shell explosion within the premises; no escape , no strict liability. Non-natural use of land: a special use bringing with it increased danger to others , not the ordinary use of land or such use as is proper for the general benefit of the community ( Rickards v Lothian , a water tap in the upper floor overflowed by a malicious act; ordinary domestic use). Industrial storage of chemicals ( Cambridge Water ) can be non-natural; a water supply in a building is natural; Transco v Stockport MBC (2003) held that a pipe supplying water to a block of flats was an ordinary use. Damage: to the plaintiff's property (damage to land and chattels). The House of Lords in Transco doubted claims for personal injuries; the usual rule is that the rule concerns property damage (Indian cases have accepted personal injuries).

p: Strict and Absolute Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Plaintiff's own default ( Ponting v Noakes : a horse that reached over the boundary and ate yew leaves). Act of God ( Nichols v Marsland ). Act of a stranger (an independent third party beyond the defendant's control: Box v Jubb , the overflow caused by a stranger; Rickards v Lothian ). Consent of the plaintiff / common benefit ( Carstairs v Taylor : water leaked from the upstairs rain-water box of a building shared by tenants). Statutory authority ( Green v Chelsea Waterworks : a main pipe laid under statutory duty burst). (Some authors also treat natural user as part of the definition and not as an exception.)

p: Strict and Absolute Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Cambridge Water Co v Eastern Counties Leather (1994): foreseeability of the kind of damage is necessary; the rule is an extension of nuisance. Transco v Stockport MBC (2003): the rule has not been abolished but is confined; the user must be extraordinary and unusual; personal injury not recoverable; a majority of the House left the matter of absorption into negligence undecided.

t: 6.6 Indian development: from *Rylands* to absolute liability
p: Strict and Absolute Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Application of Rylands in India: Indian courts applied the strict liability rule in many cases but found it inadequate for modern industrial hazards, because (i) the exceptions (Act of God, act of stranger) could allow powerful enterprises to avoid liability, and (ii) it covers only property damage and "escape". M.C. Mehta v Union of India (1987) (Oleum Gas Leak case, Shriram Foods and Fertilizers): after a leak of oleum gas from a Delhi factory caused the death of one person and injuries to many, a Constitution Bench ( Bhagwati CJ ) held that an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry which poses a potential threat to the health and safety of persons working in the factory and of those living around is strictly and absolutely liable to compensate for harm. The Court said it was not bound by the Rylands exceptions , because the law must evolve to meet changing social conditions (Article 32 powers). Key features of the rule of absolute liability: applies to hazardous or inherently dangerous activities; no exceptions (Act of God, stranger's act, plaintiff's default, consent are not available); compensation must be correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise (the "deep pocket" principle), so that it has a deterrent effect; the enterprise has a non-delegable duty to the community to ensure that no harm results, and must conduct the activity with the highest standards of safety ; no need to show escape from the premises: harm within or outside the premises is covered. Union Carbide Corporation v Union of India (Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster, 1989): the Supreme Court approved the settlement of US \$470 million ; Charan Lal Sahu v UOI (1990) upheld the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act 1985 (the State as parens patriae ); the 1991 review reaffirmed the settlement while directing that the insurance for victims be provided and that the criminal proceedings be revived. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v Union of India (1996) (Bichhri, Rajasthan: the sludge from chemical factories): applied absolute liability and the polluter pays principle ; the polluters were required to pay for remedial costs. Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v Union of India (1996): (tannery pollution): adopted the precautionary principle , the polluter pays principle and sustainable development as part of Indian environmental law, based on Articles 21, 47, 48A and 51A(g). Bhopal-linked statutory regimes: the Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 (compulsory insurance for owners handling hazardous substances; no-fault liability to pay relief for death, injury and property damage; Environmental Relief Fund); the National Green Tribunal Act 2010 (Section 17: the Tribunal can award relief and compensation on a no-fault basis for damage from hazardous substances; also polluter pays in NGT decisions such as the Ganga cases); the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 . Other illustrations: M.P. Electricity Board v Shail Kumari (2002): strict liability for the death by electrocution from a live wire fallen on the road; Kaushnuma Begum v New India Assurance (2001): strict liability principles in motor accidents; Section 140, MVA (no-fault liability).

p: Strict and Absolute Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Rylands v Fletcher : non-natural use , escape required, exceptions available, property damage primarily, not necessarily hazardous industry. M.C. Mehta : hazardous industry , no escape required (also applies within premises), no exceptions , compensation as per capacity , developed for India's conditions through Article 21 and 32.

t: 6.8 Other forms of strict or no-fault liability (for completeness)
p: Strict and Absolute Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Animals: the scienter rule (liability for harm by a dangerous animal ( ferae naturae ) or by an animal known to be dangerous); the Cattle Trespass Act 1871 (in India); in England, the Animals Act 1971. Employees' Compensation Act 1923 (injuries during employment, no-fault). Product liability under the Consumer Protection Act 2019 (Chapter VI). Vicarious liability (Topic 2 ). Fire: liability for the spread of fire arising from negligence (the Fires Prevention (Metropolis) Act 1774 protects against accidental fires).

p: Strict and Absolute Liability · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Expect: Rylands facts and ingredients; who decided what (Blackburn J vs Lord Cairns: "non-natural use"); Read v Lyons (escape); Cambridge Water (foreseeability); Transco ; M.C. Mehta (1987) and the features of absolute liability; Bhopal; the PLIA 1991 and NGT Act 2010, Section 17 ; Vellore Citizens ; "which defence is NOT available in absolute liability"; Assertion–Reason on strict and absolute liability.

t: 7.1 Background: the English rule and the Indian Constitution
p: Tortious Liability of the State · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: In old English law, "the King can do no wrong" and the Crown could not be sued in tort without its consent, although the servants were personally liable. In England the Crown Proceedings Act 1947 made the Crown liable like a private person. In India, the position stems from Article 300(1) of the Constitution : the Government of India or a State Government may sue or be sued in relation to its affairs in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces might have done if the Constitution had not been enacted, subject to any law enacted by Parliament or State legislatures. The earlier provisions: Section 65 of the Government of India Act 1858 , Section 32 of the GIA 1915 , Section 176 of the GIA 1935 .

t: 7.2 Sovereign vs non-sovereign functions (the pre-constitution cases)
p: Tortious Liability of the State · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Peninsular & Oriental Steam Navigation Co v Secretary of State for India (1861, Calcutta HC): the leading early case. A servant of the Government negligently drove a carriage from a government workshop, injuring the plaintiff's horse. Held: the Government was liable, because the act was in the course of a non-sovereign function (an undertaking that private persons might carry on); the immunity would apply only to acts done in the exercise of sovereign powers (e.g., declaring war, concluding treaties). Secretary of State v Hari Bhanji (1882, Madras HC): followed the P&O case; a distinction between sovereign and non-sovereign functions (dealing with the customs). Nobin Chunder Dey v Secretary of State (1875): the licensing of ganja trading was a sovereign act; no liability.

t: 7.3 After the Constitution: the Supreme Court cases
p: Tortious Liability of the State · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: State of Rajasthan v Vidhyawati (1962): a government driver negligently drove the jeep carrying a government officer, killing a pedestrian. Held: the State was vicariously liable , as the State is in the same position as any other employer; the maintenance of the vehicle was not an exercise of sovereign power. The Court rejected the idea that the immunity of the Crown in England applied in India, noting that the Constitution creates a democratic republic, not an absolute monarchy. Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v State of Uttar Pradesh (1965): the police seized gold from the plaintiff on suspicion of theft; the plaintiff was released, but the gold was misappropriated by the head constable, who fled to Pakistan. Held: the State was not liable because the act (seizure of property) was done in the exercise of statutory powers of the police , which were sovereign powers ; the P&O principle was applied. The Court expressed regret for the injustice and suggested that the legislature should intervene. This case has been extensively criticised and its scope has been narrowed. Saheli, a Women's Resources Centre v Commissioner of Police, Delhi (1990): death of a child due to police beating; the State was held liable to pay compensation ( ₹ 75,000 ); the Kasturi Lal principle was distinguished as the case involved violation of the right to life. N. Nagendra Rao & Co v State of Andhra Pradesh (1994): the Government seized fertiliser stock under the Essential Commodities Act, which deteriorated through the negligence of the officers. Held: the State was liable; Kasturi Lal was confined to the situation where the act is truly sovereign (exercise of powers of inalienable sovereign functions ); the statutory function does not mean sovereign function; the old distinction is unsustainable in a welfare State. Common Cause v Union of India (1999): the Court reaffirmed the principle that the State must be held accountable. State of Maharashtra v Kanchanmala Vijaysing Shirke (1995) ; M.S. Grewal v Deep Chand Sood (2001) (the drowning of school students on an excursion; the school and the State were held liable for the negligence of the supervisors).

p: Tortious Liability of the State · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The Supreme Court has evolved a remedy of compensation in public law for violation of the fundamental rights, enforceable under Articles 32 and 226 . This is distinct from private-law tort because it is not dependent on sovereign/non-sovereign distinction and does not need a trial of facts in a civil suit. Rudul Sah v State of Bihar (1983): the petitioner was kept in jail for 14 years after acquittal; the Supreme Court awarded ₹ 30,000 as interim compensation under Article 32, the first case of monetary relief in a habeas corpus petition. Bhim Singh v State of Jammu & Kashmir (1985): the illegal detention of an MLA to prevent him from attending the Assembly; compensation of ₹ 50,000 . Sebastian M. Hongray v Union of India (1984): the disappearance of two persons from Army custody (Manipur); exemplary costs of ₹ 1 lakh to each of the two wives. Nilabati Behera v State of Orissa (1993): the custodial death of a young man; the Court awarded ₹ 1.5 lakh and declared that the defence of sovereign immunity is not available in a claim under public law for the violation of fundamental rights; the compensation is a remedy under public law and may be adjusted against any amount awarded in a civil suit. D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal (1997): guidelines for arrest and detention (identification of police personnel, memo of arrest, medical examination, informing a relative, a register, etc.); custodial violence violates Articles 21 and 22. Chairman, Railway Board v Chandrima Das (2000): the rape of a Bangladeshi national in the Yatri Niwas by railway employees; the Union of India was liable to pay ₹ 10 lakh ; the Court held that fundamental rights under Article 21 are available to non-citizens also. People's Union for Democratic Rights v Union of India and other cases on police encounters and custodial deaths also apply this principle.

p: Tortious Liability of the State · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Section 79, CPC: suits by or against the Government are filed in the name of the Union of India or the State. Section 80, CPC: two months' prior notice is needed before the suit (the court may grant leave in urgent cases). Section 82, CPC: execution of decrees against the Government; Section 86, CPC: suits against foreign States and ambassadors require the consent of the Central Government. Article 361: personal immunity of the President and Governors for official acts, although the Government can be sued.

p: Tortious Liability of the State · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The First Law Commission (1956) (M.C. Setalvad) recommended abolishing the distinction between sovereign and non-sovereign functions and making the State liable like a private employer. The Government Liability Bill 1965 (and later proposals) lapsed. The Supreme Court has therefore largely developed the position through case law.

p: Tortious Liability of the State · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The State is vicariously liable for torts of its servants in non-sovereign functions ( Vidhyawati ). For sovereign functions (defence, administration of justice, legislative acts, acts of State), immunity may still apply in a narrow sense ( Kasturi Lal ), but the sovereign category is now very restricted . In public law , the State is liable to pay compensation for the violation of fundamental rights, irrespective of the sovereign immunity ( Rudul Sah , Nilabati Behera ). Public servants are personally liable for their wrongful acts, subject to statutory protections requiring sanction/notice (Section 197 CrPC, now BNSS Section 218; Section 80 CPC).

p: Tortious Liability of the State · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Expect: Article 300; P&O Steam Navigation Co (the earliest and most-cited); Vidhyawati vs Kasturi Lal (the contrasting results; the head constable who fled to Pakistan); Nagendra Rao ; Saheli ; Rudul Sah (first compensation in Article 32); Nilabati Behera ; D.K. Basu ; Chandrima Das ; Section 80 CPC; Assertion–Reason on public law compensation vs private law damages.

p: Consumer Protection Act · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The syllabus names the Consumer Protection Act 1986 (CPA 1986) . That Act was repealed and replaced by the Consumer Protection Act 2019 (CPA 2019) , which came into force on 20 July 2020 (Consumer Protection Rules 2020 followed on 24 July 2020). Many MCQs now test the 2019 Act directly or contrast the two. Learn both: first the 1986 framework, then the 2019 upgrades.

p: Consumer Protection Act · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The CPA 1986 was enacted for the better protection of the interests of consumers and the establishment of consumer councils and authorities for the settlement of consumer disputes. The remedy is in addition to , and not in derogation of, other remedies ( Section 3 of the 1986 Act; Section 100 of the 2019 Act ). It is social-welfare legislation and is interpreted liberally.

p: Consumer Protection Act · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Consumer (2(1)(d)): (i) a person who buys goods for a consideration (paid, promised, partly paid or under a deferred payment system), including a user of the goods with the approval of the buyer, but not a person who obtains goods for resale or any commercial purpose ; (ii) a person who hires or avails of any service for a consideration, including a beneficiary with the approval of the hirer, excluding services availed for a commercial purpose. Free services and services under a contract of personal service are excluded. Complainant (2(1)(b)): a consumer; a registered voluntary consumer association; the Central/State Government; one or more consumers having the same interest; or the legal heir/representative of a deceased consumer. Complaint (2(1)(c)): a written allegation of an unfair or restrictive trade practice, defective goods, deficiency in service, excess price charged, or hazardous goods offered for sale. Defect (2(1)(f)): any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard required to be maintained by law or claimed by the trader. Deficiency (2(1)(g)): any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance required by law or undertaken by contract in relation to a service. Service (2(1)(o)): service of any description made available to potential users, including banking, financing, insurance, transport, processing, supply of electrical or other energy, telecom, boarding or lodging, entertainment, amusement, or purveying of news or other information; not free services or contracts of personal service. Unfair trade practice (2(1)(r)): false representation, misleading advertisement, false claims about standard or quality, offering gifts or prizes not intended to be given, non-compliance with prescribed standards, hoarding, etc. Restrictive trade practice (2(1)(nnn)): a practice that tends to manipulate price or conditions of delivery or to affect the flow of supplies in an unjust manner (e.g., tie-in sale).

p: Consumer Protection Act · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Drawn from President Kennedy's 1962 Consumer Bill of Rights and the UN Guidelines for Consumer Protection (1985): Right to safety: protection against marketing of goods and services hazardous to life and property. Right to be informed: about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price. Right to choose: access to a variety of goods and services at competitive prices. Right to be heard: consumer interests receive due consideration at appropriate fora. Right to seek redressal: against unfair or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation. Right to consumer education. The 2019 Act defines "consumer rights" in Section 2(9) in similar terms (protection from hazardous goods and services, information, assured access at competitive prices, to be heard, to seek redressal, and consumer awareness).

p: Consumer Protection Act · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Three-tier quasi-judicial system: District Forum: headed by a person who is, or has been, or is qualified to be a District Judge, with two other members (one a woman). Pecuniary jurisdiction up to ₹ 20 lakh (after the 2002 amendment). State Commission: President is or has been a High Court Judge. Original jurisdiction above ₹ 20 lakh and up to ₹ 1 crore ; appeals from District Forums. National Commission: President is or has been a Supreme Court Judge. Original jurisdiction above ₹ 1 crore ; appellate and revisional jurisdiction over State Commissions. Appeal to the Supreme Court from the National Commission (Section 27A) within 30 days. Limitation: 2 years from the cause of action (Section 24A). Consumer Protection Councils (Central, State, District): advisory bodies promoting consumer rights. Reliefs (Section 14): removal of defects, replacement, refund of price, compensation for loss or injury, removal of deficiency, discontinuance of unfair trade practice, withdrawal of hazardous goods, punitive damages, costs. Procedure: summary; not bound by CPC technicalities, but natural justice applies.

t: 8.6 Consumer Protection Act 2019: key changes (highest-yield part)
p: Consumer Protection Act · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Wider "consumer" (Section 2(7)): covers buyers of goods or services through any mode , offline or online, including electronic means, teleshopping, direct selling and multi-level marketing . Free goods/services and purchases for resale or commercial purpose are excluded; "commercial purpose" does not include goods bought and used exclusively for earning a livelihood by self-employment . Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) (Sections 10–22): a regulator to promote, protect and enforce consumer rights as a class . Powers: inquiries and investigations (through an Investigation Wing headed by a Director General ), search and seizure, recall of goods , refunds , discontinuance of unfair practices, safety notices, class action , and penalties for false or misleading advertisements (up to ₹ 10 lakh on a manufacturer or endorser, with a ban on the endorser of up to one year ; for subsequent contraventions up to ₹ 50 lakh and a ban of up to three years ). Endorsers have a due diligence defence (Section 21). The CCPA does not adjudicate individual disputes. Product liability (Chapter VI, Sections 82–87): the product manufacturer , product service provider and product seller are liable for harm from defective products or deficient services. A manufacturer is liable for a manufacturing defect, design defect, deviation from manufacturing specifications, non-conformity with an express warranty, or failure to give adequate instructions or warnings. The seller's liability is in Section 86; Section 87 lists exceptions (e.g., misuse, alteration, claimant's knowledge of danger). Unfair contract (Section 2(46)): terms causing a significant change in the consumer's rights (excessive security deposit, disproportionate penalty, unilateral termination, etc.). The State and National Commissions can declare such terms null and void (Sections 49(2) and 59(2)). E-commerce and direct selling: e-commerce is defined (Section 2(16)); the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 and Direct Selling Rules 2021 impose disclosure and grievance-redressal duties. Mediation (Chapter V, Sections 74–81): consumer mediation cells attached to the Commissions; a mediated settlement is final and no appeal lies (Section 80). Easier filing: complaints can be filed electronically (e-Daakhil), hearings by video-conferencing ; the complaint may be filed where the complainant resides or personally works for gain (Section 34(2)(d)). Pecuniary jurisdiction is based on the value of the consideration paid (not the value of goods/services plus compensation claimed). The original 2019 Act provided District up to ₹ 1 crore and State up to ₹ 10 crore. Under the 2021 Jurisdiction Rules (from 30 December 2021): District Commission up to ₹ 50 lakh ; State Commission above ₹ 50 lakh up to ₹ 2 crore ; National Commission above ₹ 2 crore ( verify current limits ). Admissibility: the District Commission must decide admissibility within 21 days ; otherwise the complaint is deemed admitted. Appeals: District → State within 45 days (Section 41); State → National within 30 days (Section 51); National → Supreme Court within 30 days (Section 67). An appellant against a money award must deposit 50 percent of the amount. Limitation (Section 69): two years , with power to condone delay for sufficient cause. Composition: District Commission: President and at least two members; State Commission: President and at least four members; National Commission: President and at least four members. Penalties (Chapter VII): non-compliance with Commission orders (Section 72: imprisonment of one month up to three years, or fine of ₹ 25,000 to ₹ 1 lakh, or both); misleading advertisements (imprisonment up to 2 years and fine up to ₹ 10 lakh; repeat offence up to 5 years and ₹ 50 lakh); adulterated goods (Section 90: up to 1 year and ₹ 1 lakh if no injury; up to 7 years and ₹ 3 lakh for grievous hurt; for death, not less than 7 years up to life and fine not less than ₹ 10 lakh); spurious goods (Section 91: similar graded punishments).

p: Consumer Protection Act · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Misleading Advertisements, 2022 (CCPA). Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 (30 November 2023): 13 specified dark patterns such as false urgency, basket sneaking, confirm shaming, forced action, subscription trap, interface interference, bait and switch, drip pricing, disguised advertisement, nagging, trick question, SaaS billing and rogue malware. CCPA guidelines on misleading advertisements in the coaching sector and on greenwashing (2024) ( verify exact titles and dates ). National Consumer Helpline and the e-Daakhil portal.

p: Consumer Protection Act · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Lucknow Development Authority v M.K. Gupta (1994): statutory development authorities are covered; housing construction is "service"; compensation can be awarded for harassment. Indian Medical Association v V.P. Shantha (1995): doctors and hospitals charging fees are covered; free service to all patients in government hospitals and contracts of personal service are excluded; where some patients pay and others do not, all are covered. Laxmi Engineering Works v P.S.G. Industrial Institute (1995): meaning of commercial purpose ; dominant-intention test; machinery bought for self-employment is not commercial. Spring Meadows Hospital v Harjol Ahluwalia (1998): parents can be consumers for a child's treatment. Consumer Education and Research Centre v Union of India (1995): right to health of workers is part of Article 21. State of Karnataka v Vishwabharathi House Building Co-op Society (2003): constitutional validity of the Act upheld. Bangalore Development Authority v Syndicate Bank (2007): the Act and allotment of sites. Ireo Grace Realtech v Abhishek Khanna (2021) and Pioneer Urban Land v Govindan Raghavan (2019): one-sided builder–buyer clauses are unfair; buyers may claim refund with interest for inordinate delay. Bar of Indian Lawyers v D.K. Gandhi PS National Institute of Communicable Diseases (2024): the Supreme Court held that advocates' services are not "service" under the CPA; the profession is sui generis . The decision was later subject to further consideration, so verify the present status before the exam.

p: Consumer Protection Act · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Expect: who is a consumer (including exclusions); the six consumer rights ; the three-tier hierarchy and appeal periods ; CCPA's powers and the advertising penalty; pecuniary jurisdiction (basis: consideration paid; revised limits); product liability categories; mediation ; unfair contract ; e-commerce ; limitation of 2 years ; IMA v V.P.
