Shantha ; LDA v M.K. Gupta ; Laxmi Engineering ; Assertion–Reason on whether free services or commercial purposes are covered; "which is NOT a power of the CCPA."

p: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The Motor Vehicles Act 1988 (MVA) consolidates the law on motor vehicles: licensing, registration, traffic control, no-fault compensation (Chapter X), compulsory third-party insurance (Chapter XI) and Motor Accident Claims Tribunals (MACT) (Chapter XII). It was substantially amended by the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act 2019 (many provisions in force from 1 September 2019 ). The policy is that road-accident victims must receive speedy and certain compensation without the ordeal of proving negligence. Section numbers below follow the commonly cited text; because the 2019 amendment rearranged some provisions, verify section numbering against the current bare Act where an exam question turns on a number.

p: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Principle: compensation is payable on death or permanent disablement irrespective of any wrongful act, neglect or default of the owner or any other person. It is an exception to the fault principle, similar in spirit to strict liability . Section 140 (as it stood after the 1994 amendment): the owner is liable to pay ₹ 50,000 for death and ₹ 25,000 for permanent disablement; the claimant need not plead or prove wrongful act or negligence. (The original 1988 figures were ₹ 25,000 and ₹ 12,500.) Section 141: the right to claim under other laws is unaffected, but no-fault compensation paid is adjusted against the final award. Section 142: meaning of permanent disablement ; Section 143: application of the Chapter to claims under the Workmen's Compensation Act (now Employees' Compensation Act); Section 144: overriding effect . 2019 amendment (Section 164): no-fault compensation of ₹ 5 lakh for death and ₹ 2.5 lakh for grievous hurt ( verify the current section arrangement ). Section 163A (structured formula): compensation in death or permanent disablement cases according to the Second Schedule (based on age and income), where the claimant need not prove negligence ; applicable to persons with annual income up to ₹ 40,000. Deepal Girishbhai Soni v United India Insurance (2004): remedies under Section 163A and Section 166 are mutually exclusive ; the claimant must choose. Ningamma v United India Insurance (2009): the owner/borrower who is driving is not a third party for Section 163A. Section 161 (hit-and-run): compensation from the Solatium Fund . Earlier ₹ 25,000 (death) and ₹ 12,500 (grievous hurt); the 2019 amendment raised these to ₹ 2 lakh and ₹ 50,000 . Section 164B (2019): the Motor Vehicle Accident Fund for treatment and compensation of road-accident victims, with compulsory insurance for all road users.

p: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Section 146: necessity for insurance against third-party risks: no person shall use a motor vehicle in a public place unless a policy of insurance complying with the Chapter is in force (with limited exemptions for government vehicles). Section 147: requirements of policies and limits of liability. The policy must cover liability for death or bodily injury to any person (including owners of goods or their representatives carried in the vehicle) and for damage to third-party property . Liability for death and injury is unlimited ; property damage is subject to a prescribed limit. Section 149: duty of insurers to satisfy judgments and awards in respect of third-party risks, even if the insurer is entitled to avoid the policy, subject to the limited defences in Section 149(2) (breach of specified conditions such as use for hire or reward, or use by an unlicensed driver). The insurer then has the right to recover from the insured (the "pay and recover" principle). Section 150: rights of third parties against insurers on the insolvency of the insured. Key cases: Skandia Insurance Co v Kokilaben Chandravadan (1987): an insurer cannot escape its liability to the third party through policy exclusions; National Insurance Co v Swaran Singh (2004): the insurer must prove that the breach was fundamental and that the owner was aware of it (e.g., fake driving licence); otherwise it must pay the third party and may recover from the owner; Oriental Insurance v Meena Variyal (2007). Penalty for driving without insurance (Section 196): imprisonment up to three months , or fine up to ₹ 2,000 , or both (as amended in 2019).

p: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Section 165: the State Government may constitute Claims Tribunals to adjudicate claims for compensation arising from accidents (death, bodily injury, damage to third-party property). Section 166: application for compensation by (a) the injured person , (b) the owner of damaged property , (c) all or any legal representatives of the deceased , or (d) a duly authorised agent . It may be made to the Tribunal where the accident occurred, or where the claimant resides or carries on business, or where the defendant resides. A Section 166 claim is fault-based , so the claimant must prove negligence. 2019 amendment: the six-month limitation in Section 166(3) was omitted , so there is no limitation period; the Detailed Accident Report filed by the police may be treated as the claim application. Section 167: option to claim under the Workmen's/Employees' Compensation Act or the MVA, not both . Section 168: the Tribunal's award must be just compensation , and it specifies whether the insurer, owner or driver pays. Section 169: summary procedure , not bound by strict rules of evidence. Section 170: impleading the insurer . Section 171: interest . Section 172: compensatory costs for false or vexatious claims or defences. Section 173: appeal to the High Court within 90 days ; an insurer's appeal requires a deposit of ₹ 25,000 or 50 percent of the amount awarded, whichever is less. Section 174: recovery as arrears of land revenue. Section 175: bar on civil court jurisdiction over matters that the Tribunal can decide. Reporting duties: the police must prepare a Detailed Accident Report within a short time (48 hours for the interim report under the 2019 scheme) and forward it to the Tribunal.

t: 9.5 Determination of compensation: principles from cases
p: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Sarla Verma v Delhi Transport Corporation (2009): standard multipliers by age and deduction for personal expenses (one-third for 2–3 dependants; one-fourth for 4–6; one-fifth for more than 6; one-half for a bachelor). National Insurance Co v Pranay Sethi (2017) (Constitution Bench): upheld Sarla Verma ; future prospects must be added: for a person with a permanent job 50% (below 40 years), 30% (40–50), 15% (50–60); for self-employed or fixed-salary persons 40%, 25%, 10%; none above 60. Conventional heads: loss of estate ₹ 15,000 , funeral expenses ₹ 15,000 , loss of consortium ₹ 40,000 , increasing by 10% every three years . Magma General Insurance v Nanu Ram (2018): loss of consortium includes parental and filial consortium, not only spousal. R.D. Hattangadi v Pest Control (India) (1995): heads of compensation in personal injury (pecuniary and non-pecuniary: pain and suffering, loss of amenities, loss of expectation of life). Contributory negligence reduces compensation proportionately; in composite negligence the claimant may recover from any of the joint tortfeasors. The owner is vicariously liable for the driver's negligence in the course of employment ( Pushpabai Purshottam Udeshi v Ranjit Ginning , 1977); res ipsa loquitur is also invoked.

t: 9.6 The Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act 2019: key changes (trend)
p: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Higher penalties for traffic offences; where a juvenile commits an offence, the guardian or owner is deemed guilty and the vehicle registration may be cancelled. Good Samaritan protection (Section 134A): a person who voluntarily helps an accident victim is not liable to civil or criminal action. "Golden hour" (Section 2(12A)): the hour following a traumatic injury; cashless treatment during the golden hour (Section 162). A national cashless-treatment scheme has been framed in recent years ( verify the latest notified scheme ). Motor Vehicle Accident Fund (Section 164B); enhanced hit-and-run compensation ; removal of limitation for claims. Provisions on aggregators , recall of defective vehicles , digital licensing and road safety .

p: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Expect: the no-fault principle and amounts (old vs revised); Section 163A vs Section 166 ( Deepal Girishbhai Soni ); Section 149 (pay and recover; Swaran Singh ); MACT application, limitation (now omitted) ; appeal to the High Court in 90 days ; Section 175 (civil court bar); hit-and-run amounts; Good Samaritan and golden hour ; Motor Vehicle Accident Fund ; Sarla Verma and Pranay Sethi ; Assertion–Reason on mutually exclusive claims.

p: Competition Act, 2002 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: The Competition Act 2002 replaced the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act 1969 (MRTP Act) , which took a control-based approach suited to the licensing era. After the 1991 liberalisation and the Raghavan Committee Report (2000) , the law shifted to the promotion of competition . Duties of the CCI (Section 18): eliminate practices having an adverse effect on competition , promote and sustain competition , protect the interests of consumers , and ensure freedom of trade carried on by other participants in markets in India. The competition provisions (Sections 3 and 4) came into force on 20 May 2009 , and the combination provisions on 1 June 2011 . Brahm Dutt v Union of India (2005) upheld the Act's validity and the separation of advisory and adjudicatory functions, after which the 2007 amendment settled the present structure.

p: Competition Act, 2002 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Competition Commission of India (CCI) (Section 7): a quasi-judicial body with a Chairperson and not less than two and not more than six other members . The Director General (DG) (Section 16) assists in investigations. Appeals: CCI orders are appealable to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) (Section 53A; the Competition Appellate Tribunal (COMPAT) was merged into NCLAT by the Finance Act 2017 , from 26 May 2017), and then to the Supreme Court (Section 53T) within 60 days. Competition advocacy (Section 49): the Commission can give opinions and spread awareness. Extra-territorial reach (Section 32): the effects doctrine ; the Act applies to conduct outside India having an appreciable adverse effect on competition in India. Sectoral regulators (Sections 21 and 21A): mutual reference between the CCI and regulators like TRAI, SEBI and CERC. CCI v Bharti Airtel (2018): the Supreme Court held that TRAI has primary jurisdiction on certain telecom matters, and the CCI should await its determination. CCI v Steel Authority of India (2010): the Section 26(1) prima facie opinion is administrative , not adjudicatory, so no hearing is required at that stage.

p: Competition Act, 2002 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Section 3(1): no enterprise, association of enterprises, person or association of persons shall enter into any agreement in respect of production, supply, distribution, storage, acquisition or control of goods or provision of services which causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition (AAEC) within India . Section 3(2): any such agreement is void . Section 3(3) – Horizontal agreements (between enterprises at the same stage of the production chain) are presumed to have AAEC (a rebuttable presumption ) if they: (a) directly or indirectly determine purchase or sale prices ; (b) limit or control production, supply, markets, technical development, investment or services; (c) share markets by geography, type of goods or number of customers; or (d) amount to bid rigging or collusive bidding . A cartel (Section 2(c)) is an association of producers, sellers, distributors, traders or service providers who, by agreement among themselves, limit, control or attempt to control production, distribution, sale or price. The proviso excludes joint ventures that increase efficiency in production, supply, distribution or control. Section 3(4) – Vertical agreements (between enterprises at different stages of the chain) are judged by the rule of reason , so AAEC must be proved. Listed examples: tie-in arrangement , exclusive supply agreement , exclusive distribution agreement , refusal to deal , resale price maintenance (RPM) . The 2023 Amendment widened these provisions and added hub-and-spoke liability in Section 3(3): an enterprise not in the same line of business that participates in or facilitates a cartel can also be liable. Section 3(5) – Exceptions: (i) the right to restrain infringement of, or impose reasonable conditions to protect, intellectual property rights (copyright, patents, trademarks, geographical indications, designs, semiconductor layouts); (ii) the right to export, where the agreement relates exclusively to production, supply, distribution or control of goods for export . Factors for determining AAEC (Section 19(3)): creation of entry barriers; driving existing competitors out; foreclosure of competition; accrual of benefits to consumers; improvements in production or distribution; promotion of technical, scientific and economic development. Recent enforcement trend: the cement cartel order (2012; penalty about ₹ 6,307 crore), Maruti Suzuki (2021; ₹ 200 crore for resale price maintenance through its discount control policy), and cartel cases in beer, film and cable industries.

p: Competition Act, 2002 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Section 4(1): no enterprise or group shall abuse its dominant position . Dominance itself is not prohibited; abuse is. Dominant position (Explanation to Section 4): a position of strength in the relevant market in India that enables an enterprise to (i) operate independently of competitive forces , or (ii) affect its competitors, consumers or the relevant market in its favour. Relevant market (Section 2(r)): the relevant product market (Section 2(t): products regarded as interchangeable or substitutable by reason of characteristics, prices and intended use) and/or the relevant geographic market (Section 2(s): area where conditions of competition for supply or demand are distinctly homogeneous). Section 19(5)–(7) list the relevant factors. Factors for dominance (Section 19(4)): market share; size and resources of the enterprise; size and importance of competitors; economic power and commercial advantages; vertical integration; consumer dependence; monopoly or dominant position by statute; entry barriers; countervailing buying power; market structure and size; social obligations and costs. Abuse (Section 4(2)): (a) unfair or discriminatory conditions or prices (including predatory pricing ) in purchase or sale; (b) limiting or restricting production, services, or technical or scientific development ; (c) practices resulting in denial of market access ; (d) making contracts subject to supplementary obligations unconnected with the subject of the contract (tie-in or bundling); (e) using dominance in one relevant market to enter into, or protect, another relevant market (leveraging). Cases: Belaire Owners' Association v DLF (2011): CCI penalised DLF (₹ 630 crore) for unfair conditions in apartment buyer agreements; the finding of abuse was upheld on appeal ( verify procedural history ). CCI v Co-ordination Committee of Artists and Technicians of West Bengal Film and Television (2017): the Act applies to trade associations. Excel Crop Care v CCI (2017): penalty to be based on relevant turnover . Digital markets: the CCI's Google (Android and Play Store) orders of 2022 (penalties of about ₹ 1,337 crore and ₹ 936 crore respectively), later reviewed by the NCLAT and the Supreme Court, and the 2024 Meta/WhatsApp privacy-policy order (about ₹ 213 crore) ( verify the current status of these appeals ). Digital competition (trend): a draft Digital Competition Bill proposing ex ante regulation of systemically significant digital enterprises was released in 2024 (its status should be checked).

p: Competition Act, 2002 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Section 5: a combination is an acquisition of control, shares, voting rights or assets, an acquisition of control by a person already controlling a competing enterprise, or a merger or amalgamation , that crosses the asset or turnover thresholds specified in the Act (in India and worldwide, for the parties and for the group). The thresholds have been revised upwards by notification, and the de minimis (small target) exemption was updated in 2024 to ₹ 450 crore of assets or ₹ 1,250 crore of turnover in India ( verify current thresholds ). Deal value threshold (DVT): introduced by the 2023 Amendment , a transaction with a value above ₹ 2,000 crore where the target has substantial business operations in India must be notified even if the asset or turnover tests are not met (in force from 10 September 2024 ). Section 6(1): no combination shall cause or be likely to cause AAEC within the relevant market in India ; such a combination is void . Section 6(2): notice to the CCI before the combination takes effect. The earlier requirement to file within 30 days of the trigger event was first exempted in 2017 and then removed by the 2023 Act. A standstill (suspensory) obligation applies: the combination cannot take effect until the CCI approves or the time limit expires. Time limits (2023 Amendment): the CCI must form its prima facie opinion within 30 calendar days and decide within 150 days (earlier 210 days) from notice; otherwise the combination is deemed approved . Section 20: inquiry into combinations; Section 29: investigation procedure; Section 31: orders (approval, approval with modification, or disapproval). Section 43A: penalty for failure to notify (up to 1 percent of total turnover or assets, whichever is higher). Section 20(4) lists factors in assessing the effect of a combination (actual and potential competition, market share, entry barriers, failing-business defence, benefits, etc.). Green channel route (Combination Regulations): automatic approval for combinations with no horizontal, vertical or complementary overlaps.

p: Competition Act, 2002 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Section 27: after an inquiry the CCI may issue a cease and desist order, impose a penalty up to 10 percent of the average turnover (earlier, of the last three preceding financial years), direct modification of agreements, and so on. For a cartel , the penalty may be up to three times the profit for each year of continuance, or 10 percent of the turnover for each year, whichever is higher . Section 28 allows the division of an enterprise enjoying dominance. Compensation claims go to the NCLAT (Section 53N). Section 46 (lesser penalty / leniency): reduced penalty for cartel members making full, true and vital disclosure. The 2023 Amendment adds Leniency Plus : additional reduction where the applicant discloses a second cartel. Sections 48A and 48B (2023 Amendment): settlement and commitment mechanisms for abuse of dominance and vertical agreements ( cartels are excluded ). Global turnover: the 2023 Amendment allows penalties to be calculated on global turnover (not only relevant turnover, as under Excel Crop Care ). Time limit: information must be filed within three years of the cause of action (Section 19(6)). Other powers: interim orders (Section 33), search and seizure (DG), penalties for non-compliance (Sections 42, 43).

t: 10.7 The Competition (Amendment) Act 2023: summary (very high yield)
p: Competition Act, 2002 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Deal value threshold (₹ 2,000 crore) for notifiable combinations. Settlement and commitment procedure (Sections 48A and 48B). Global turnover -based penalties and a revised definition of "turnover". Hub-and-spoke cartels and wider scope of Section 3. Leniency Plus and revised lesser-penalty framework. Shorter time limits for combination review (30 days prima facie , 150 days overall). A wider definition of "control" ( material influence ) and of "agreement" to include concerted practices. Stronger DG investigation powers and penalties for non-cooperation. Appeals to the NCLAT with a reported pre-deposit requirement of 25 percent of the penalty ( verify ). The 2023 Amendment has been brought into force in phases, so verify the notified dates for each provision.

p: Competition Act, 2002 · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Expect: MRTP Act vs Competition Act ; CCI structure and appeal to the NCLAT and Supreme Court ; Section 3 (horizontal presumption vs vertical rule of reason); Section 4 (dominance, relevant market, abuse); Sections 5–6 (thresholds, DVT, time limits); Section 27 (penalty and cartel formula); leniency ; the 2023 Amendment ; Excel Crop Care , Belaire/DLF , SAIL , Brahm Dutt ; matching per se -style presumption vs rule of reason; Assertion–Reason on whether dominance itself is prohibited (it is not; abuse is).

x: Donoghue v Stevenson → neighbour principle; Caparo → three-stage test; Hedley Byrne → negligent misstatement; Bolam → professional standard; Byrne v Boadle → res ipsa loquitur . Basu → arrest guidelines. IMA v Shantha → doctors under the CPA; LDA v M.K. Gupta → housing authorities; Laxmi Engineering → commercial purpose. p: Rapid Revision Sheet · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: CPA limitation: 2 years. Appeals under CPA 2019: 45 days (District → State), 30 days (State → National), 30 days (National → Supreme Court); 50% pre-deposit. CPA 2019 pecuniary limits (2021 Rules): District up to ₹ 50 lakh; State above ₹ 50 lakh up to ₹ 2 crore; National above ₹ 2 crore ( verify ). CCPA advertising penalty: up to ₹ 10 lakh (first), up to ₹ 50 lakh (repeat); endorser ban 1 year / 3 years. MVA: no-fault ₹ 50,000 / 25,000 (older) and ₹ 5 lakh / 2.5 lakh (2019); hit-and-run ₹ 2 lakh / 50,000; High Court appeal in 90 days; claim limitation removed. Competition Act: DVT ₹ 2,000 crore; combination review 150 days; prima facie opinion 30 days; cartel penalty up to 3 times profit or 10% turnover, whichever is higher; appeals to the NCLAT. Limitation in tort: defamation, malicious prosecution and false imprisonment 1 year.

p: Rapid Revision Sheet · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Damnum sine injuria is not actionable; injuria sine damno is actionable. Volenti is a complete defence; contributory negligence is a partial defence. Motive is irrelevant in tort except in nuisance, conspiracy, defamation and malicious prosecution. Slander generally needs special damage (English rule) with four per se exceptions; Indian courts treat the distinction loosely. Statutory authority: permissive vs mandatory statutes. Rylands has exceptions; M.C. Mehta absolute liability has none. Public-law compensation (Articles 32/226) is not barred by sovereign immunity; private-law suits against the State follow Article 300 and Vidhyawati/Kasturi Lal . The CCPA protects consumers as a class; the Commissions decide individual complaints. Section 163A claims need no proof of negligence; Section 166 claims do. Dominance is not prohibited; abuse is. Horizontal agreements carry a presumption of AAEC; vertical agreements follow the rule of reason .

p: Rapid Revision Sheet · Law of Torts and Consumer Protection
x: Do fact-based questions first (case ↔ principle, section numbers); they are quick. For statement-type questions , test each statement independently; a single wrong detail (a period, an amount or an author) is often the trap. For recent-change questions (CPA 2019, MVA 2019, Competition Amendment 2023), prefer the latest law unless the question names the earlier Act. With no negative marking, attempt every question . In the final week, revise Topics 7 – 10 (statute-heavy and amendment-heavy) after the classic torts topics, and recheck every verify item against the official text.

t: 0.1 Exam pattern and where Communication fits
p: Exam Pattern and Question Trends · Communication
x: Overall UGC NET pattern (current, as followed through the 2026 cycles): The exam is a Computer-Based Test (CBT) with two papers taken in one continuous sitting of 3 hours (180 minutes) with no break between them. Paper 1 (General Teaching and Research Aptitude, common for all subjects): 50 MCQs, 100 marks , i.e. 2 marks per question. Paper 2 (your chosen subject): 100 MCQs, 200 marks. Total: 150 questions, 300 marks. There is no negative marking. Attempt every question. Paper 1 has 10 units with roughly 5 questions per unit . Communication is Unit 4 ; the others are Teaching Aptitude, Research Aptitude, Comprehension, Mathematical Reasoning, Logical Reasoning, Data Interpretation, ICT, People Development and Environment, and Higher Education System. Always re-check the latest NTA information bulletin before applying, because NTA can alter pattern details between cycles. Official syllabus of Unit 4 – Communication (the topic blocks you must cover): Communication: meaning, types and characteristics of communication Effective communication: verbal and non-verbal, inter-cultural and group communications, classroom communication Barriers to effective communication Mass media and society Everything below is organised to cover each of these blocks plus the theory background (models, theorists, laws, institutions) that MCQs commonly draw from.

t: 0.2 Question trends: how the unit is actually tested
p: Exam Pattern and Question Trends · Communication
x: Caution: the points below are patterns observed across past papers and coaching analyses, not official NTA statistics. Use them as a guide to priorities, and verify against the last 8 to 10 years of previous-year papers. Number of questions: usually about 5 per paper (sometimes 4 to 5). It is one of the more scoring units because it is theory-heavy and not calculation-heavy. Difficulty: generally easy to moderate. Paper 1 in the June 2026 cycle was reported by coaching analyses as easy to moderate overall. Highest-frequency areas (in rough order): Barriers to communication (types, examples, remedies) Classroom communication (teacher behaviour, feedback, interaction, Flanders) Verbal and non-verbal communication (kinesics, proxemics, paralanguage) Mass media and society (theories, media types, effects, Indian media institutions) Types and levels of communication (formal/informal, grapevine, directions) Models and elements of the communication process Inter-cultural and group communication (less frequent but recurring) Question formats you will see: Memory-based: "Who proposed X?", "Which is NOT an element of communication?", "Proxemics deals with...", "Grapevine is a type of..." Concept-based: identify the barrier or type from a short scenario; match a definition to a term. Analysis-based: statement I / statement II (true/false), assertion–reason, match-the-following (List I with List II), arrange in correct sequence, and "which of the following statements are correct" with combination options. Typical traps: options that mix up similar terms (hypodermic needle vs two-step flow; agenda setting vs cultivation; encoding vs decoding; semantic vs psychological barrier; downward vs horizontal communication), and "NOT / EXCEPT" questions. Study priority: master definitions + theorist names + one-line examples. For analysis questions, practise explaining why an option is wrong.

p: Meaning, Nature and Characteristics of Communication · Communication
x: The word communication comes from the Latin communis ("common") and communicare ("to share, to make common"). Communication is the process of sharing information, ideas, thoughts, feelings and meaning between two or more persons (or entities) so that a common understanding is created . The key idea is shared meaning : if the receiver does not understand what the sender intended, communication is incomplete even though a message was sent. A widely used working definition: communication is a two-way, dynamic process of exchanging messages through a medium so that the sender and receiver develop mutual understanding . In teaching, the aim is not only transmission of information but also change in knowledge, attitude and behaviour of the learner.

p: Meaning, Nature and Characteristics of Communication · Communication
x: Process, not an event: it is continuous and has no fixed beginning or end. Two-way (interactive): feedback completes the cycle. One-way communication (lecture, broadcast) is incomplete without feedback. Dynamic and transactional: both parties send and receive at the same time and change each other. Symbolic: words, gestures, images and sounds are symbols that stand for ideas; meaning lives in people, not in words. Irreversible: once a message is sent it cannot be taken back; you can only correct or clarify it. Unavoidable: "One cannot not communicate" (Watzlawick): even silence or absence sends a message. Purposeful / goal-oriented: it has an intention (inform, persuade, entertain, educate, instruct). Contextual: physical, social, cultural, psychological and temporal context shape meaning. Involves both content and relationship: the way something is said conveys the relationship between speakers. Can be intentional or unintentional, verbal or non-verbal, formal or informal.

p: Meaning, Nature and Characteristics of Communication · Communication
x: Informative: passing facts and knowledge. Educative / instructive: teaching and training. Persuasive / motivational: changing opinions and behaviour (advertising, propaganda, counselling). Expressive / emotive: sharing feelings. Integrative / social: building relationships and group unity. Control / regulatory: guiding conduct through rules and instructions. Entertainment (especially in mass communication).

t: 1.4 Principles of Effective Communication – the 7 Cs
p: Meaning, Nature and Characteristics of Communication · Communication
x: Clarity: clear, simple language and a single main idea. Conciseness: brief and to the point, without wasteful words. Correctness: accurate facts, grammar and tone. Completeness: all required information is provided. Courtesy: respectful, polite, positive tone. Consideration: a receiver-oriented approach ("you" attitude). Concreteness: specific facts and figures instead of vague statements. (Some books add Coherence and Credibility . If an MCQ gives the 7 Cs, the list above is the standard one.)

t: 1.5 In simple words: What communication really is
p: Meaning, Nature and Characteristics of Communication · Communication
x: Think of communication as passing a parcel and checking that it arrived undamaged . Sending is only half the job. If a teacher says "Photosynthesis is how plants make food using sunlight" and students can later explain it in their own words, communication happened. If students only heard sounds but understood nothing, then only transmission happened, not communication. Transmission is not the same as communication; shared understanding is what completes it. Why "two-way" matters: compare the blue ticks on a messaging app with an actual reply. Blue ticks only tell you the message was delivered . A reply tells you it was understood . That reply is feedback , and feedback is what makes communication a cycle instead of a one-way street.

t: 1.6 In simple words: Characteristics explained with everyday examples
p: Meaning, Nature and Characteristics of Communication · Communication
x: Process: it never "stops". A classroom conversation continues through looks, silence and later questions. Symbolic: the word "tree" is not a tree; it is a symbol agreed upon by speakers of a language. Different languages use different symbols for the same thing, which is why misunderstandings arise. Irreversible: once you say something harsh in anger, saying "sorry" does not erase it. You can only repair, not delete. Unavoidable: a student sitting with folded arms and a blank face is saying "I am bored or upset" without a single word. You cannot not communicate. Contextual: "Fine." can mean agreement, anger or sadness depending on tone, relationship and situation. Transactional: in a real conversation both people talk, listen and react at the same moment, and both change during the exchange. Purposeful: even small talk has a purpose (building friendship). Exam wording: "communication is goal-oriented".

t: 1.7 In simple words: Functions with examples
p: Meaning, Nature and Characteristics of Communication · Communication
x: Informative: the news bulletin or a notice board circular. Educative: a lecture, a tutorial video. Persuasive: an advertisement or an election speech. Expressive: telling a friend you are anxious about results. Integrative: a farewell party that strengthens team bonding. Control: college rules, traffic signs, exam instructions. Entertainment: films, songs, reels.

t: 1.8 In simple words: The 7 Cs with a before-and-after example
p: Meaning, Nature and Characteristics of Communication · Communication
x: Poor message: "Send the thing soon." (unclear, vague, incomplete, no courtesy) Better message: "Please submit your Unit 2 assignment on the college portal by 5 pm on Friday. Thank you." What changed: it is clear (what is wanted), concise (no extra words), concrete (a date and time), complete (where and when), correct (accurate), courteous (please and thank you) and considerate (written from the reader's point of view, so they know exactly what to do). Exam cue: "you attitude" means consideration ; "specific facts and figures" means concreteness ; "saying only what is needed" means conciseness .

t: Memory Capsule: Meaning, Nature and Characteristics of Communication
p: Meaning, Nature and Characteristics of Communication · Communication
x: Intrapersonal = within oneself; interpersonal = two people; mass = large, anonymous audience with delayed feedback.

p: Elements, Process and Models of Communication · Communication
x: Sender / source / communicator: originates the message. Encoding: converting ideas into symbols (words, signs, images). Message: the content, the idea or information being shared. Channel / medium: the route (speech, writing, phone, email, TV, internet). Receiver: the person who gets the message. Decoding: interpreting the symbols to extract meaning. Feedback: the receiver's response that tells the sender how the message was understood. Noise: anything that distorts or interferes with the message at any stage (physical, psychological, semantic, technical). Context / environment: the situation in which communication occurs. Sequence to remember: Sender → Encoding → Message → Channel → Decoding → Receiver → Feedback (noise can act at any point).

t: 2.2 Important Models and Theorists (High Memory Value)
p: Elements, Process and Models of Communication · Communication
x: Aristotle's model (c. 4th century BCE): the earliest, a linear model focused on public speaking. Elements: speaker, speech, occasion, audience, effect . Persuasion rests on ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion) and logos (logic). Lasswell's model (1948): " Who says what in which channel to whom with what effect ?" Linked to control analysis, content analysis, media analysis, audience analysis and effect analysis. A linear model for mass communication. Shannon and Weaver's model (1949): the mathematical / information theory model developed for telephone engineering. Components: information source, transmitter, signal, channel, noise source, receiver, destination. Linear and one-way, with the idea of noise . Weaver later added semantic noise . Originally lacked feedback. Schramm's models (1954): the idea of the field of experience (overlapping experiences needed for communication to occur) and the Osgood–Schramm circular model , in which each party is both encoder and decoder, with an interpreter role. It stresses circular, equal, interactive communication and feedback. Berlo's SMCR model (1960): Source, Message, Channel, Receiver . The source and receiver are influenced by communication skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system and culture. The message has content, elements, treatment, structure and code. Channels correspond to the five senses (seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, tasting). Newcomb's ABX model (1953): the sender (A) and receiver (B) are oriented toward an object (X) and seek symmetry / balance (a sociopsychological model). Westley and Maclean's model (1957): adds the gatekeeper / channel role (C) between source (A) and receiver (B), with objects of orientation (X) and feedback. Useful for mass communication. Gerbner's model (1956): a general model that includes perception and the selection of events. Dance's helical model (1967): communication as a helix , spiralling and evolving over time; it shows that communication is never a closed circle. Two-step flow model (Lazarsfeld, Berelson and Gaudet, 1944): see topic 9 . Classification quick-check: Aristotle, Lasswell, Shannon–Weaver, Berlo = linear . Osgood–Schramm, Westley–Maclean (with feedback) = interactive/circular . Dance = helical/transactional .

p: Elements, Process and Models of Communication · Communication
x: Developed by Joseph Luft and Harry Ingham (1955) . Four panes: Open (Arena) known to self and others; Blind spot unknown to self but known to others; Hidden (Façade) known to self but not to others; Unknown unknown to both. Self-disclosure and feedback enlarge the open area, which improves interpersonal communication.

t: 2.4 In simple words: Elements walked through one example
p: Elements, Process and Models of Communication · Communication
x: Priya wants to tell Ravi to bring his class notes tomorrow. Sender: Priya. Encoding: she turns her thought into words ("Please bring your notes tomorrow"). Message: the request itself. Channel: a phone call (it could be a text or a face-to-face chat). Noise: poor network signal makes parts of the sentence unclear (this is physical/technical noise ). Decoding: Ravi interprets the words. If Priya meant "class notes" but Ravi thinks of "currency notes", that mismatch is semantic noise . Receiver: Ravi. Feedback: Ravi replies "Which notes? Maths?" Now Priya knows how her message landed and can correct it. This is why encoding and decoding are described as the two "translation" steps: ideas to symbols, then symbols back to ideas. Errors can creep into either step. Types of noise (simple): physical (loud sound), technical (bad network), psychological (anger, worry), semantic (words with different meanings).

t: 2.5 In simple words: Models in plain language
p: Elements, Process and Models of Communication · Communication
x: Aristotle's model (speaker-centred persuasion). Imagine a speaker on a stage persuading a crowd. Three tools: ethos (the speaker's credibility, e.g., a doctor speaking about health), pathos (appeal to emotion, e.g., a moving story) and logos (appeal to logic, e.g., data and reasoning). Weakness: the audience is treated as passive and there is no feedback. Cue: "oldest", "public speaking", "ethos, pathos, logos". Lasswell's model (five questions). A reporter's checklist: Who? Says what? In which channel? To whom? With what effect? Useful to analyse a news broadcast or advertisement from five angles (communicator, message, medium, audience, effect). Weakness: ignores noise and feedback. Cue: "who says what...", "mass communication", "1948". Shannon and Weaver's model (the telephone line). Picture a phone call with crackling static on the line. The source sends a signal through a channel, noise interferes, and the receiver gets a slightly different signal. It was built by engineers for telephones, so it treats people like machines. Weaver described three levels of problems: technical (is the signal sent accurately?), semantic (does the message carry the intended meaning?) and effectiveness (does it change the receiver's behaviour as intended?). Weakness: linear, no feedback. Cue: "noise", "mathematical model", "1949". Osgood and Schramm's model (a ping-pong game). Both players hit and receive the ball. Each person is both sender and receiver, and each interprets before replying. There is no fixed start or end, which is why it is called circular . Cue: "circular", "encoder-decoder-interpreter", "equal participants". Berlo's SMCR model (a four-part checklist). S ource, M essage, C hannel, R eceiver. Berlo adds that both source and receiver are shaped by five factors: communication skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system and culture . A teacher with strong skills and the right attitude who knows the subject and understands the students' culture communicates better. Channels = the five senses. Cue: "SMCR", "five senses", "1960". Westley and Maclean's model (the editor in the middle). In mass communication, a news channel does not send everything. A gatekeeper (C) , like an editor, selects what reaches the audience. Cue: "gatekeeper", "mass media version". Newcomb's ABX model (two friends and a movie). A and B are friends, X is a film. If both like X, they are in harmony. If A loves it and B hates it, there is tension , and they will talk (communicate) to restore balance. Cue: "balance", "symmetry", "social-psychological". Dance's helical model (a growing spiral). Communication does not go round in the same circle. Each conversation builds on previous ones, so the circle widens into a helix as knowledge and experience grow, like a student whose understanding deepens each class. Cue: "helix", "spiral", "evolving". Linear vs circular vs transactional (very easy to confuse): Linear: one direction, sender to receiver (Aristotle, Lasswell, Shannon-Weaver, Berlo). Circular / interactive: messages go back and forth in turns (Osgood-Schramm). Transactional: both people send and receive at the same time and keep changing each other (a real conversation; Dance's helix is closest).

t: 2.6 In simple words: Johari Window made simple
p: Elements, Process and Models of Communication · Communication
x: Imagine a window with four panes: Open: things you and others both know (your name, your subject). Blind: things others notice about you but you do not (you say "you know" too often). Hidden: things you know but keep private (your fear of public speaking). Unknown: things nobody knows yet (a talent you have not discovered). When you share about yourself (self-disclosure) and receive feedback , the Open pane grows and the others shrink. Better communication means a bigger Open pane.

t: Memory Capsule: Elements, Process and Models of Communication
p: Elements, Process and Models of Communication · Communication
x: Aristotle: speaker, speech, audience, ethos–pathos–logos Lasswell: Who says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect Shannon–Weaver: noise and mathematical model Berlo: SMCR Osgood–Schramm: circular Dance: helix Newcomb: ABX symmetry

t: 3.1 Based on Level or Number of Participants
p: Types and Levels of Communication · Communication
x: Intrapersonal: communication within oneself (thinking, self-talk, reflection, decision-making). Interpersonal: between two persons or a small number, usually face to face (dyadic), with immediate feedback. Examples: conversation, interview, counselling, a teacher talking to a student. Group communication: among members of a small group with a common purpose (class, committee, team). Public communication: one speaker to a large live audience (lecture, speech, rally). Organizational communication: within and across an organization (formal and informal). Mass communication: from an organised source through a mass medium to a large, heterogeneous, anonymous and scattered audience, with delayed and indirect feedback.

p: Types and Levels of Communication · Communication
x: Verbal: uses words, oral or written. Non-verbal: uses body language, gestures, signs, silence, space, time, appearance. Visual: pictures, charts, maps, symbols.

p: Types and Levels of Communication · Communication
x: Formal communication follows the official hierarchy and channels, is documented, and includes: Downward: from superior to subordinate (orders, instructions, policies, circulars). Risk: distortion and delay. Upward: from subordinate to superior (reports, suggestions, grievances, feedback). Often limited by fear of authority. Horizontal / lateral: between people at the same level (coordination between departments). Diagonal / crosswise: between people at different levels and different departments. Informal communication is not bound by the official structure. Its main form is the grapevine . The term grapevine is traditionally linked to the American Civil War era, from the winding telegraph lines resembling grape vines. Keith Davis classified grapevine chains: single strand, gossip, probability and cluster . The cluster chain is the most common (one person tells a select few, who in turn tell a few others). Characteristics: fast, selective, spreads by word of mouth, often partly accurate, cannot be fully controlled but can be managed and used as feedback.

p: Types and Levels of Communication · Communication
x: Chain: information flows in a line through a hierarchy. Wheel (Star): one central person communicates with all others; fast and efficient for simple tasks but low member satisfaction. Y network: a mix of chain and wheel. Circle: each member communicates with two neighbours; moderate speed, higher satisfaction. All-channel (Comcon / Web): everyone communicates with everyone; best for complex problem-solving and high satisfaction, but slow to organise.

t: 3.5 In simple words: Levels with a college example
p: Types and Levels of Communication · Communication
x: Intrapersonal: you silently decide "I should revise Unit 4 tonight". Interpersonal: you discuss a doubt with your teacher. Group: a project team of five planning a presentation. Public: the principal addressing the entire college at an annual function. Organizational: university notices, official emails, and staff meetings. Mass: a newspaper or news channel reaching millions who are strangers to the source. Exam cue: immediate feedback and small numbers = interpersonal ; large, scattered, anonymous audience = mass ; talking to yourself = intrapersonal .

t: 3.6 In simple words: Direction of flow in an organization (with a college example)
p: Types and Levels of Communication · Communication
x: Downward: the principal issues a circular to all staff. Risk: messages get distorted as they pass through many levels. Upward: a lecturer submits a request or feedback to the HOD; students' feedback forms. Risk: fear of authority makes people hide bad news ( filtering ). Horizontal / lateral: two teachers from the same department coordinate the timetable. Purpose: coordination and teamwork. Diagonal / crosswise: a lecturer from the English department directly contacts an officer in the accounts section about a bill, skipping the usual chain of command. Purpose: speed and cross-department work.

t: 3.7 In simple words: Formal vs informal communication
p: Types and Levels of Communication · Communication
x: Formal: follows rules and the official chain, is documented, is slower, and is reliable (letters, circulars, meetings, reports). Informal: free of official rules, spontaneous, fast, builds relationships, but can carry rumours (canteen chat, WhatsApp groups of colleagues). Grapevine in plain words: the "canteen talk" about who might be promoted. It spreads quickly because people trust friends. Smart managers listen to it, because it reveals staff worries. Keith Davis's four grapevine chains (how the rumour moves): Single strand: A tells B, B tells C, C tells D, like a long chain of whispers. Very distorted by the end. Gossip: one person (A) tells everyone directly. Probability: A tells people at random, who tell others at random. Cluster: A tells a few selected people, and some of them tell a few others. This is the most common in real life, because people pass news only to those they trust.

t: 3.8 In simple words: Communication networks: easy picture
p: Types and Levels of Communication · Communication
x: Chain: orders passing down a ladder, person to person. Wheel (star): a class teacher at the centre; every student talks only to the teacher. Quick and efficient for simple tasks, but members may feel less satisfied. Y: a mixture, with one person at the junction. Circle: each person talks only to two neighbours; slow but friendly. All-channel: everyone talks to everyone, like a brainstorming session. Best for complex problems, but takes time. Exam cue: "central person" = wheel; "everyone with everyone" = all-channel; "each person with two neighbours" = circle.

t: 3.9 In simple words: Other useful classifications
p: Types and Levels of Communication · Communication
x: Synchronous vs asynchronous: a phone or video call is synchronous (real-time). An email or discussion forum post is asynchronous (reply later). One-way vs two-way: a TV broadcast is mostly one-way; a classroom discussion is two-way. Formal vs informal language: a research paper versus a chat with a friend. Private vs public: a counselling session versus a public lecture.

t: Memory Capsule: Types and Levels of Communication
p: Types and Levels of Communication · Communication
x: Keith Davis: grapevine types Downward = superior to subordinate; upward = subordinate to superior; horizontal = same level; diagonal = different level and different department. Grapevine is informal; its cluster chain is the most common. Intrapersonal = within oneself; interpersonal = two people; mass = large, anonymous audience with delayed feedback.

p: Verbal Communication and Listening · Communication
x: Uses spoken words: conversation, telephone, interviews, meetings, lectures, presentations. Advantages: immediate feedback, personal touch, flexible, faster, can use tone and expression, builds rapport. Limitations: no permanent record, chances of distortion, speaker may be impulsive, not suited to complex data, depends on memory.

p: Verbal Communication and Listening · Communication
x: Letters, emails, reports, memos, notices, manuals, circulars. Advantages: permanent record and legal evidence, careful drafting, wide reach, reference value, suitable for complex details. Limitations: delayed feedback, costly and time-consuming, needs literacy, lacks personal touch.

p: Verbal Communication and Listening · Communication
x: Hearing is a physiological act; listening is a psychological, active process of attending, interpreting and responding. Types of listening: appreciative (for enjoyment), empathic (for emotional support), comprehensive/informational (to learn), critical/evaluative (to judge arguments), discriminative (distinguishing sounds and cues). Active listening involves attention, eye contact, paraphrasing, clarifying, withholding judgment and giving feedback. Barriers to listening: distractions, prejudgment, daydreaming, emotional bias, speaker-listener speed gap.

p: Verbal Communication and Listening · Communication
x: Know your audience, structure the message (opening, body, closing), use simple and precise language, maintain appropriate pace and volume, use examples, invite and give feedback, and keep the tone respectful.

t: 4.5 In simple words: Choosing oral vs written
p: Verbal Communication and Listening · Communication
x: Use oral when it is urgent, emotional, needs immediate clarification, or involves a small group (e.g., resolving a student's misunderstanding). Use written when you need a record, legal proof, detailed data, or a message that must reach many people (e.g., an exam notification). Why written feels "permanent": an email can be saved and shown later as proof. That is why contracts, notices and reports are in writing.

t: 4.6 In simple words: Listening: why it is hard
p: Verbal Communication and Listening · Communication
x: People can think much faster than others can speak, so the mind gets spare time and wanders . This is the speed gap , and it is a major cause of poor listening. Good listeners use that spare time to summarise what they hear and predict the next point. Listening types with examples: Appreciative: enjoying music or a poem. Empathic: a friend is upset and you listen to understand their feelings, without rushing to give advice. Comprehensive / informational: listening to a lecture to learn and remember facts. Critical / evaluative: listening to a political speech and judging whether the claims are logical. Discriminative: noticing a change in someone's tone or telling similar sounds apart (the base of other types). Active listening steps: pay full attention, keep eye contact, do not interrupt, nod and use small encouragers, paraphrase ("So you mean..."), ask clarifying questions, and respond with feedback.

t: 4.7 In simple words: Written communication basics
p: Verbal Communication and Listening · Communication
x: Common forms are letters, emails, memos, notices, circulars, reports and minutes. A good written message has a clear purpose, logical order, simple sentences, correct grammar and a polite close . In emails, use a meaningful subject line, a greeting, a short body and a sign-off; avoid ALL CAPS (which reads as shouting) and think before pressing "send" (communication is irreversible).

p: Non-Verbal Communication · Communication
x: Kinesics (body language): facial expressions, gestures, posture, body movement (term associated with Ray Birdwhistell ). Ekman and Friesen classified gestures as emblems (direct verbal translation, e.g., thumbs-up), illustrators (accompany speech), affect displays (show emotion), regulators (control flow of conversation, e.g., nodding) and adaptors (self-touching to release tension). Oculesics: eye contact and gaze. Haptics: communication through touch (handshake, pat on the back); its acceptability varies by culture, gender and context. Proxemics: use of space and distance , coined by Edward T. Hall . Hall's four zones for North American norms: Intimate: up to about 18 inches (0 to 1.5 ft) Personal: about 1.5 to 4 ft Social: about 4 to 12 ft Public: beyond 12 ft Chronemics: use of time (punctuality, waiting, pace). Hall also described monochronic cultures (one thing at a time, strict schedules) and polychronic cultures (multitasking, flexible time). Paralanguage / Vocalics: how something is said: pitch, tone, volume, rate, pauses, stress, fillers. It is vocal but not verbal . Appearance and artifacts: dress, grooming, objects, colour, hairstyle. Olfactics: smell. Silence: can show agreement, disapproval, thoughtfulness, respect or anger. Environment / physical setting: seating arrangement, lighting, decor. Sign language and signals: traffic signs, sirens, flags, symbols (sometimes called sign communication or object language ).

p: Non-Verbal Communication · Communication
x: Mostly unconscious, culture-dependent, continuous, harder to control than words, ambiguous in isolation (read cues in clusters ), and highly influential for emotional meaning.

p: Non-Verbal Communication · Communication
x: Eye contact with students, positive posture, purposeful movement, appropriate gestures, pleasant tone, a smile, and a calm manner help build rapport and attention. Negative cues (frowning, turning your back, folded arms, monotone) reduce participation.

t: 5.4 In simple words: "Study of ..." cue list (one of the most asked patterns)
p: Non-Verbal Communication · Communication
x: Kinesics: study of body movement, gestures, posture, facial expression. Proxemics: study of space and distance between people. Haptics: study of touch. Chronemics: study of time use (being punctual, making someone wait). Oculesics: study of eye behaviour and gaze. Olfactics: study of smell. Paralanguage / vocalics: study of voice qualities apart from words (pitch, tone, volume, speed, pauses). Artifactics / appearance: study of dress, objects, and grooming. Semiotics: study of signs and symbols and how they create meaning.

t: 5.5 In simple words: Each one with an everyday example
p: Non-Verbal Communication · Communication
x: Kinesics: a teacher's smile and nod when a student answers shows approval; slumped shoulders show tiredness or low confidence. Oculesics: steady, friendly eye contact signals honesty and interest in many cultures. In some cultures, long direct eye contact with elders can seem disrespectful, so context matters. Haptics: a firm handshake in a job interview, a pat on a child's back. Appropriate touch depends on culture, gender, age and relationship. Proxemics: in a crowded lift you stand stiffly because strangers are inside your personal zone. A teacher who walks among desks reduces distance and builds rapport. Chronemics: arriving late to an interview says "I do not value this" even if you never say it. Making a student wait outside can signal status. Paralanguage: the sentence "I didn't say she stole the money" changes meaning depending on which word is stressed. Shouting, whispering and a trembling voice carry emotion beyond the words. Artifacts: a police uniform, a lab coat, or a graduation gown signals role and authority. Silence: a pause after a question gives students time to think; a long silence after a rude remark shows disapproval.

t: 5.6 In simple words: Functions of non-verbal cues in relation to words
p: Non-Verbal Communication · Communication
x: Repeating: saying "yes" and nodding. Contradicting: saying "I am fine" with a sad face (listeners believe the face). Substituting: waving instead of saying goodbye. Complementing: a warm smile with a warm greeting. Accenting: thumping the table to stress a point. Regulating: raising a hand or nodding to control who speaks next. Congruence: when words and body language match, the message feels honest and credible. When they clash, people trust the body language.

t: 5.7 In simple words: Quick note on Mehrabian
p: Non-Verbal Communication · Communication
x: Albert Mehrabian's "7-38-55" figures come from studies on how people judge a speaker's feelings or attitudes when the words, the tone and the face do not agree. They do not show that only 7% of all communication is verbal. If an MCQ states "93% of all communication is non-verbal" as a general fact, treat it with suspicion.

p: Non-Verbal Communication · Communication
x: Non-verbal communication conveys meaning without words . It often reinforces, contradicts, substitutes, complements, regulates or accents verbal messages. When verbal and non-verbal messages conflict, receivers tend to trust the non-verbal cues (especially for feelings and attitudes). Mehrabian's 7-38-55 rule: 7% words, 38% tone, 55% facial expression. This applies only when a person is communicating feelings or attitudes and the cues are inconsistent. It is not a general rule that 93% of all communication is non-verbal. Examiners sometimes test this nuance.

p: Non-Verbal Communication · Communication
x: Paralanguage is how you say it (tone, pitch); it is not verbal content, but it is vocal . Proxemics = space; chronemics = time; haptics = touch; kinesics = body movement; oculesics = eyes; olfactics = smell. Mehrabian's rule applies only to feelings and attitudes with inconsistent messages.

p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Meaning: communication between people from different cultural backgrounds (language, religion, values, customs, communication styles). It requires awareness of how culture shapes perception, meaning and behaviour.

p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Edward T. Hall – High-context vs low-context cultures: High-context (e.g., Japan, China, Arab countries; India has many high-context features): much of the meaning lies in the context, relationships and non-verbal cues; indirect, implicit communication. Low-context (e.g., USA, Germany, Scandinavia): meaning is carried in explicit words; direct, precise, detail-oriented. Geert Hofstede's cultural dimensions: power distance, individualism vs collectivism, masculinity vs femininity, uncertainty avoidance, long-term vs short-term orientation, and indulgence vs restraint. India is generally characterised by high power distance and collectivism. Ethnocentrism: judging other cultures by the standards of one's own, assuming one's own culture is superior. Stereotyping and prejudice: generalised, fixed beliefs or attitudes about a group. Cultural relativism: understanding behaviour within its own cultural context. Culture shock (Kalervo Oberg): stages commonly described as honeymoon, crisis/frustration, adjustment and acceptance/adaptation.

p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Language differences and translation problems, different meanings of gestures (e.g., the Indian head wobble, the thumbs-up, the OK sign), different time concepts, different attitudes to hierarchy, ethnocentrism, stereotypes, religion and food taboos, and differing norms of eye contact and personal space.

p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Develop cultural awareness and sensitivity, learn about other cultures, avoid assumptions, use simple language and avoid slang and idioms, be patient, seek feedback and clarification, listen actively and show respect.

p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Meaning: exchange of information among members of a group (generally 3 to about 20) who share a common goal, interact, and influence each other.

p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Primary groups (family, close friends; Charles Cooley) vs secondary groups (formal, goal-oriented, e.g., committees). Formal vs informal groups; in-group vs out-group. Group norms, roles, cohesion and status shape communication. Tuckman's stages of group development (1965; adjourning added 1977): Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, Adjourning. Benne and Sheats classified member roles as task roles, group-building/maintenance roles, and individual (self-centred) roles . Leadership styles (Kurt Lewin): autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire.

p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Groupthink (Irving Janis, 1972): the desire for harmony overrides critical thinking. Social loafing (Ringelmann effect): individuals put in less effort in a group. Group polarization: group discussion pushes opinions to extremes. Synergy: the group's combined output exceeds the sum of individual outputs.

t: 6.8 Group Communication Formats (Often Asked in Matching)
p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Group discussion (GD): free exchange among 8 to 12 participants on a topic, assessed on content, communication, leadership and teamwork. Panel discussion: a small panel of experts discusses a topic before an audience, led by a moderator. Symposium: several experts present formal papers or talks on different aspects of a topic, usually followed by audience questions. Seminar: participants present and discuss papers on a theme, usually in an academic setting. Workshop: hands-on, skill-oriented sessions. Conference: a large formal gathering for presenting and exchanging research or views. Brainstorming (Alex Osborn): rapid idea generation with no criticism in the idea-generation phase; quantity first. Buzz groups (Phillips 66): small groups of about six discussing for about six minutes. Debate: structured argument for and against a motion. Round table, forum, colloquium: variants of open discussion.

p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Listen actively, stay on topic, give everyone an opportunity, summarise points, respect differences, use polite assertiveness, manage conflict constructively and use feedback.

t: 6.10 In simple words: High-context vs low-context cultures
p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: High-context: the meaning is "between the lines". People rely on relationships, tone, and unspoken understanding. A polite "that might be difficult" often means "no". Examples often given: Japan, China, many Arab and South Asian cultures. Low-context: the meaning is in the words. "No" means no; contracts are detailed. Examples often given: USA, Germany, Scandinavia. Exam cue: "indirect, relationship-based, implicit" = high-context; "direct, explicit, detail in words" = low-context.

t: 6.11 In simple words: Hofstede's dimensions in plain words
p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Power distance: how comfortable a society is with unequal power. High power distance: students never question the teacher; titles are important. Low: first names, open challenge to bosses. Individualism vs collectivism: "I" versus "we". Individualist cultures stress personal goals; collectivist cultures stress family and group loyalty. Masculinity vs femininity: achievement, competition and success versus caring, quality of life and cooperation. Uncertainty avoidance: how uncomfortable people feel with ambiguity. High: many rules and detailed plans. Low: flexible and comfortable with risk. Long-term vs short-term orientation: future-focused thrift and perseverance versus respect for tradition and quick results. Indulgence vs restraint: freedom to enjoy life versus strict social norms controlling desires.

t: 6.12 In simple words: Three terms often mixed up
p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Stereotype is a belief ("all X are lazy"). Prejudice is a feeling or attitude (disliking X without evidence). Discrimination is an action (treating X unfairly). Ethnocentrism: treating your own culture as the standard and judging others by it. Cultural relativism is its opposite: judging a behaviour in its own cultural context.

t: 6.13 In simple words: Culture shock in four stages (simple)
p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Honeymoon: everything is new and exciting. Crisis / frustration: differences become irritating and homesickness appears. Adjustment: you learn local ways and feel more comfortable. Acceptance / adaptation: you function comfortably in the new culture.

t: 6.14 In simple words: Group communication simplified
p: Inter-Cultural and Group Communication · Communication
x: Group vs crowd: a group has a shared goal, interaction and roles (a project team). A crowd is a physical gathering without structure (people at a bus stop). Tuckman's stages as a project-team story: Forming: members meet, are polite and unsure of roles. Storming: disagreements and power struggles appear. Norming: rules and roles are accepted; cooperation grows. Performing: the team works smoothly and delivers results. Adjourning: the project ends and the team disbands. Group problems explained: Groupthink: everyone agrees quickly to avoid conflict, even when the plan is bad (nobody dares say "this will fail"). Social loafing: in a group assignment, one member puts in less effort because they think others will cover. Group polarization: after discussing among like-minded people, the group's view becomes more extreme than it was at the start. Synergy: the group achieves more together than the sum of individual efforts. Group formats: the distinguishing cue for each Group discussion: free exchange among participants, no formal speeches; often used in selection. Panel discussion: a few experts discuss in front of an audience with a moderator; informal conversation among panellists. Symposium: each expert gives a prepared formal presentation on one aspect of a theme. Seminar: participants present papers and discuss a theme, usually academic and led by a chairperson. Workshop: hands-on practical skill building. Conference: a large gathering with many sessions for research and policy exchange. Brainstorming: generate many ideas without criticism first, evaluate later. Debate: two sides argue for and against a motion. Panel vs symposium (common confusion): panel = conversation between experts; symposium = a series of formal talks by experts.

p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: Classroom communication is the purposeful, structured exchange of ideas and information between teacher and students (and among students) to achieve learning objectives. It is generally face to face, goal-directed, and involves verbal, non-verbal and visual elements.

p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: One-way (teacher to student): lecture; feedback is minimal. Two-way (teacher to student and back): question-answer, response, feedback. Three-way / multi-way (interaction among students and teacher): group work, discussion, peer teaching. Considered the most effective for active learning.

p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: Clear objectives and well-organised content, simple and audible language. Use of examples, analogies and learner-appropriate vocabulary. Effective questioning (clear, brief, graded, distributed fairly, with adequate wait time). Feedback: immediate, specific, constructive and encouraging. Use of teaching aids and ICT to support communication. Positive classroom climate, empathy, and acceptance of student ideas. Awareness of individual differences, language and cultural background of learners.

t: 7.4 Flanders' Interaction Analysis Categories (FIAC) – Memory Favourite
p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: Ned Flanders developed the system to observe and quantify verbal behaviour in the classroom . It has 10 categories , observed typically every 3 seconds : Teacher talk – indirect influence (1 to 4): 1 accepts feelings; 2 praises or encourages; 3 accepts or uses students' ideas; 4 asks questions. Teacher talk – direct influence (5 to 7): 5 lecturing; 6 giving directions; 7 criticising or justifying authority. Student talk (8 and 9): 8 student talk – response; 9 student talk – initiation. Silence or confusion (10). (Teacher talk = 7 categories; student talk = 2; silence = 1.) A classroom with more indirect influence is seen as more democratic and learner-friendly.

p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: A model showing a continuum from concrete (direct, purposeful experiences) at the base to abstract (visual and verbal symbols) at the top. The message: use varied, concrete, multi-sensory experiences for stronger understanding. (Popular percentages linked to the cone are not Dale's own research findings, so do not rely on them.)

p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: Language mismatch, poor audibility, a large class size, monotonous delivery, teacher-centred approach, lack of feedback, student anxiety or disinterest, prejudice, inadequate teaching aids, physical discomfort and noise, and distractions from mobile phones.

p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: Plan the lesson, use varied methods and media, encourage questions, vary pitch and pace, use positive reinforcement, arrange seating for interaction, use ICT meaningfully, maintain eye contact, and be sensitive to diversity.

t: 7.8 Communication in teaching and higher education
p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: Teaching is a communication process : teacher (sender) → content (message) → methods and media (channels) → learner (receiver) → feedback. Effective teacher communication is clear, learner-centric, interactive, supported by ICT , and aware of barriers. Verbal, non-verbal and visual modes combine in teaching aids (chalkboard, projector, videos, simulations). Online and blended learning rely on asynchronous and synchronous communication (discussion forums, video lectures), and need netiquette and digital literacy. Feedback should be timely, specific, constructive , and should focus on performance, not the person.

t: 7.9 In simple words: Flanders' system explained
p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: Imagine an observer sitting at the back with a stopwatch. Every 3 seconds he writes a number from 1 to 10 for what is happening. 1 Accepts feelings: "I can see this topic is worrying you." 2 Praises or encourages: "Very good", "Go on." 3 Accepts or uses students' ideas: "So, as Rahul suggested, we can try this method." 4 Asks questions: "Why do you think it happens?" 5 Lectures: giving facts, opinions or explanation. 6 Gives directions: "Open page 45." 7 Criticises or justifies authority: "Sit down, I am the teacher here." 8 Student talk, response: answering the teacher's question. 9 Student talk, initiation: asking their own question or sharing their own idea. 10 Silence or confusion: pauses, noise, or periods where communication cannot be understood. How to remember: 1 to 4 = indirect teacher influence (encourages freedom); 5 to 7 = direct influence (restricts freedom); 8 to 9 = student talk ; 10 = silence/confusion . Useful ratios (simple meaning): Teacher talk ratio: percentage of time the teacher talks. Student talk ratio: percentage of time students talk. I/D ratio (indirect/direct): more indirect than direct means a more democratic, student-friendly classroom. Flanders' rule of two-thirds: in a typical classroom, about two-thirds of the time someone is talking; about two-thirds of that is the teacher talking; and about two-thirds of the teacher's talk is direct influence. This highlights how teacher-dominated most classes are.

t: 7.10 In simple words: Questioning and wait time
p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: Low-order questions: recall facts ("What is the capital of India?"). High-order questions: analyse, evaluate, create ("Why might this policy fail?"). Wait time: pausing after a question (research by Mary Budd Rowe suggests around 3 seconds or more) leads to longer, better answers from more students. Good practice: ask the question first, pause, then choose who answers; give every student a chance; and respond with praise or probing rather than humiliation.

p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: Positive / encouraging: reinforces correct work. Corrective / constructive: shows what to improve and how. Immediate vs delayed: immediate feedback works best for new skills. Formative (during learning) vs summative (at the end).

t: 7.12 In simple words: Dale's Cone of Experience from base to top
p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: From most concrete to most abstract: Direct, purposeful experiences Contrived experiences (models, simulations) Dramatized experiences (role-play) Demonstrations Field trips Exhibits Educational television Motion pictures Recordings, radio and still pictures Visual symbols (charts, maps) Verbal symbols (spoken and written words) Idea: learners understand better when teaching moves from concrete experience toward abstract ideas and uses multiple senses. Exam cue: the base is direct purposeful experience ; the top is verbal symbols .

t: 7.13 In simple words: A good classroom communicator checklist
p: Classroom Communication and Teaching · Communication
x: Starts with a clear aim and connects to what students already know. Speaks audibly and not too fast, and varies pitch to avoid monotony. Uses simple examples and teaching aids. Watches students' faces to catch confusion early. Encourages questions and treats mistakes as part of learning. Uses inclusive language and respects different backgrounds. Ends by summarising and checking understanding.
